## Page 4648

as a close friend.” Thus he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that it was not fitting for him to take any created being as a close friend, and that, were this possible, Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, would have been the most deserving of it. Yet he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated that he loved particular people, as when he said to Muʿādh:

“By Allah, I truly love you.”

He said the same to the Ansār. Zayd ibn Hārithah was beloved to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as was Zayd’s son Usāmah, and there were other such examples.

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs asked him, “Whom do you love most?” He replied, “ʿĀʾishah.” He asked, “And among men?” He replied, “Her father.”

He said to his daughter Fātimah, may Allah be pleased with her, “Do you not love what I love?” She replied, “Yes.” He said, “Then love ʿĀʾishah.”

He also said concerning al-Hasan:

“O Allah, I love him, so love him and love whoever loves him.”

There are many similar examples. Thus he stated that he loved particular people, yet said:

“I renounce the close friendship of every close friend. Were I to take anyone on earth as a close friend, I would take Abū Bakr as a close friend.”

It is therefore clear that close friendship is more specific than love in general: it is love in its perfection, wholly permeating the lover, so that the beloved is loved for his own sake, not for anything else. For someone loved for the sake of another is secondary in love to that other. Such is the perfection of close friendship that it admits neither sharing nor rivalry, because it wholly permeates the lover. It thus embodies perfect devotion to Allah alone and perfect love. Close friendship therefore excludes rivalry and gives the other precedence, so that the beloved is loved for his own sake

---

## Page 4649

with a love in which no other rivals him. Such love is fitting only for Allah; no other may share in the love that is His due. He is loved for His own sake, and everything else rightly loved is loved only for His sake. Whatever is loved for the sake of anyone other than Him is falsely loved. Thus, this world is accursed, and everything in it is accursed, except what is for Allah Most High.

Since this is the nature of close friendship, it is clear that whoever denies that Allah is loved for His own sake denies close friendship with Him. Likewise, whoever denies His love for any of His servants denies that He takes a servant as a close friend, with the Lord loving him and the servant loving the Lord in the most perfect manner befitting a servant.

Similarly, they denied His speaking to Moses because they denied that any attribute or action could subsist in Him. Just as they deny that He possesses life, power or knowledge, or that He rises or comes, they likewise deny that He speaks or addresses anyone. This is the reality of their position:

“Those before them said the same. Their hearts are alike.”

But since Islam was manifest and the Quran was recited, and could not be denied by anyone professing Islam, they began to deviate concerning Allah’s names and distort words from their proper places. They interpreted the servants’ love for Him as merely their love of obeying Him or drawing near to Him. This is profound ignorance. For a person’s love of drawing near to the One he approaches follows from, and is an outgrowth of, his love for Him. Someone who does not love a thing cannot love drawing near to it, since drawing near is a means, and love of the means follows from love of the intended end. It is therefore impossible for the means to a beloved thing to be loved while the very thing sought through those means is not.

---

## Page 4650

The same applies to “worship and obedience.” If it is said of someone who is obeyed and worshipped that a person loves obeying and worshipping him, then this love follows from love for him. Otherwise, someone who does not love him does not love obeying and worshipping him. Whoever acts for another only to obtain recompense from him or to avert punishment is merely exchanging something with him or ransoming himself from him, not loving him. One cannot say that such a person loves him and explain this as love of obeying and worshipping him. For even if love of the intended end entails love of the means, or something other than love of the means, this would warrant using the two expressions “love of recompense” and “love of safety” to express love of the deed. Love of Allah, however, has no connection with merely loving recompense.

Do you not see that when someone hires a worker for payment, the worker cannot be said to love him merely on that account? Indeed, a man may hire someone who has no love for him whatsoever—even someone who hates him. Likewise, someone who ransoms himself through a deed to escape another’s punishment cannot be said to love him; rather, he hates him. Thus, Allah’s description of His believing servants as loving Him cannot mean merely that they love the deeds through which they attain certain created ends, without their Lord being loved at all.

Furthermore, the word “worship” encompasses love together with humble submission, as explained earlier. Hence, the heart’s love for human beings has different degrees. The first is “attachment”: the heart’s attachment to the beloved. Then comes “ardent longing”: the heart’s pouring itself out towards the beloved. Then comes “abiding love”: love that endures. Then comes “passionate love,” and the last of

---

## Page 4651

these degrees is “loving servitude,” which is devotion to the beloved. The mutayyam is the one worshipped, and Taym Allāh means “servant of Allah.” For the lover remains mindful of his beloved, enslaved and humbled before him. Moreover, turning to Him also implies love, as do similar expressions, as explained earlier.

Furthermore, even if their claim were true—that this usage is figurative because it involves omitted and implied words—a figurative expression may only be used with an indication clarifying the intended meaning. It is well known that neither Allah’s Book nor His Messenger’s Sunnah contains anything that rules out Allah Himself being loved and confines love to deeds alone, whether through an indication within the passage or separate from it. Nor does reason provide any such indication.

Moreover, one sign of figurative usage is that it may properly be negated without qualification. It would therefore have to be permissible to say without qualification that Allah neither loves nor is loved, just as their leader, al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, declared that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not truly speak to Moses. Yet it is well known that this is inadmissible by the consensus of the Muslims. Thus, consensus establishes that this usage is not figurative but literal.

Furthermore, Allah has distinguished between love for Him and love of deeds done for Him in His statement, Exalted is He:

“Dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause.”

Likewise, He has distinguished between love for Him and love for His Messenger in His statement, Exalted is He:

“Dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger.”

If loving Him meant nothing more than loving deeds, this would either be repetition or the conjunction of a specific instance with a general category. Both interpretations depart from the apparent meaning of the wording, which may not be set aside without evidence clarifying the intended meaning. And just as

---

## Page 4652

loving Him cannot be interpreted as merely loving His Messenger, so too it cannot be interpreted as merely loving deeds done for Him, even though loving Him necessarily entails loving His Messenger and loving deeds done for Him.

Furthermore, using love for something to mean merely loving to obey it, rather than loving the thing itself, is unknown in the language, whether literally or figuratively. Interpreting the wording in this way is therefore also sheer distortion.

In our discussions of major principles, we have established in several places that nothing other than Allah may rightly be loved and desired for its own sake, just as nothing other than Allah can exist independently. There is no Lord but Allah, and no god but Him: He is the One worthy of worship, who deserves to be loved and glorified for His own sake with perfect love and glorification.

Every child is born upon the natural disposition. For He, glorified is He, has created hearts with the innate recognition that, among all they love and desire, there is nothing in which they can find rest and their ultimate end except Allah alone. Whatever a beloved person loves—whether something eaten, worn, seen, heard, or touched—he finds within himself that his heart seeks something beyond it and loves something else, which it worships, turns to, and finds rest in; and he sees things resembling it among these categories.

For this reason, Allah Most High says in His Book:

“Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.”

In an authentic hadith, Iyād ibn Himār reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that Allah Most High said:

“I created My servants inclining to pure monotheism, but the devils led them astray, forbade them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them to associate with Me that for which I had sent down no authority.”

Likewise, in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to an intact offspring. Do you find any of them mutilated?”

Abū Hurayrah would then say: “Read

---

## Page 4653

if you wish: ‘The natural disposition upon which Allah created mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion.’”

Moreover, every attribute of perfection that hearts are innately disposed to love belongs to Allah in its fullest perfection. Whatever is lovable in others comes from Him, glorified and exalted is He. He therefore deserves to be loved truly and perfectly. Denying a servant’s love for his Lord is, in reality, denying that He is God and worthy of worship. Likewise, denying His love for His servant entails denying His will, which in turn entails denying that He is Lord and Creator. Thus, denying this love entails denying that He is the Lord of all worlds and the God of all worlds. This is the position of the proponents of negation and denial.

For this reason, the two religious communities before us have agreed, on the basis of the traditions and words of wisdom they possess from Moses and Jesus, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them both, that the greatest commandment is to love Allah with all your heart, mind, and resolve. This is the very essence of pure monotheism, the religion of Abraham, which is the foundation of the religious law of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran.

Denying this is a notion taken from the polytheists and the Sabians, the enemies of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend. Whoever agrees with them on this—whether a philosopher, a speculative theologian, a jurist, or a religious innovator—has taken it from them. This became manifest among the esotericist Qarmatians of the Ismā‘īlīs. For this reason, Allah’s intimate friend, the leader of the pure monotheists, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, said:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers? They are indeed enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds.”

He also said: “I do not love

---

## Page 4654

those that set.” Allah Most High also says:

“On the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit, except to one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

That is, a heart free from associating partners with Allah.

As for their statement, “There is no affinity between the created being and the Eternal One that would require the former to love Him and delight in beholding Him,” this statement is ambiguous. If by affinity they mean that there is no relationship of procreation between them, this is true. If they mean that there is no affinity between them like that between sexual partners, or between one who eats and what is eaten, or anything similar, this too is true. But if they mean that there is no affinity between them whereby one should be a loving worshipper and the other worshipped and loved, then this is precisely the point at issue. To invoke it as evidence is to beg the question, and rejecting the premise is sufficient.

It may then be said: on the contrary, no affinity calls for perfect love except that between the creature and the Creator, besides whom there is no god. He is God in heaven and God on earth, and to Him belong the highest attributes in the heavens and the earth. What these people say amounts, in reality, to denying that Allah is truly worshipped.

For this reason, certain groups of Sufis versed in speculative theology, who deny that Allah truly loves, have agreed on this point: they acknowledge that He is loved but deny that He loves. They adopted Sufism while retaining the doctrines of those speculative theologians, and thus took from the Sufis their teaching on love, although their treatment of it may involve confusion. The denial of love originated with the doctrine of the Mu‘tazilah and similar Jahmī groups. As for the Lord’s love for His servant, they deny it even more vehemently.

Those who deny it fall into two groups:

---

## Page 4655

One group interprets it as the very things He brings about that the servant loves, thus identifying His love with His act of creating. Another group identifies it with His will to bring those things about. We have discussed this at length in “Principles of the Divine Attributes and Decree,” and this is not the place for that discussion.

It is well known that the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community establish that Allah loves and is pleased with the obligatory and recommended acts He has commanded, even when they do not occur. They also establish that He may will the existence of entities and actions that He hates and is displeased with, such as sinful disobedience and disbelief. Allah Most High says:

“And Allah does not love corruption.”

And He Most High says:

“He does not approve of disbelief for His servants.”

Our purpose here, however, is simply to discuss the servants’ love for their God.

It has become clear that this is the foundation of the deeds of faith. No disagreement concerning this is known among the early generations of the Muslim community—the Companions and those who followed them in goodness. They would stir this love through the forms of worship Allah prescribed for awakening it, such as knowledge grounded in faith and listening to the Quran. He Most High says:

“And thus We have revealed to you a spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith.”

And so on to the end of the surah.

---

## Page 4656

Then, as time passed, some among the speculative theologians, including the Mu‘tazilah and others, came to deny this love. Some Sufis, meanwhile, sought to stir it through listening to various kinds of vocal performance, such as taghyīr, and to whistling and clapping. They listen to sayings and poems that arouse love in general, stirring whatever love each heart contains. Such material appeals to those who love idols, crosses, brethren, homelands, beardless youths, or women just as it appeals to those who love the Most Merciful. However, the spiritual masters who attended these gatherings stipulated a suitable place, suitable circumstances, and close companions. Sometimes they also stipulated the presence of a shaykh who would guard against Satan.

Others then took this further, falling into various sins and even flagrant wickedness. Indeed, some groups went as far as outright disbelief, inducing ecstatic states in themselves through poems containing disbelief and heresy—among the gravest forms of corruption. This produces spiritual states in them corresponding to its nature, just as the worship of devotees among the polytheists and the People of the Book produces states corresponding to its nature.

The position of the discerning spiritual masters is expressed in the words of al-Junayd—may Allah have mercy on him:

“Whoever deliberately seeks out such listening is put to trial by it; whoever happens upon it finds relief in it.”

This means that gathering for this newly introduced form of listening is neither prescribed nor enjoined, nor is it to be adopted as a religious practice or a means of drawing near to Allah. Acts of devotion and worship are learned only from the messengers—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them. Just as nothing is forbidden except what Allah has forbidden, so no religion is valid except what Allah has prescribed.

Allah Most High says:

“Or

---

## Page 4657

do they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?” For this reason, He Most High says:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.’”

Thus He made following His Messenger a requirement of their love for Allah, and made Allah’s love for them a consequence of their following His Messenger.

Ubayy ibn Ka‘b—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“Adhere to the right path and the Sunnah. Whenever a servant who follows the right path and the Sunnah remembers Allah and his skin shivers with fear of Allah, his sins fall away from him as dry leaves fall from a tree. Whenever a servant who follows the right path and the Sunnah remembers Allah in solitude and his eyes overflow with tears out of fear of Allah, the Fire will never touch him. Moderate effort upon the right path and the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort contrary to the right path and the Sunnah. So take care that your deeds, whether moderate or strenuous, conform to the way of the prophets and their Sunnah.”

This is discussed at length elsewhere. If this practice were enjoined and recommended, and served to set hearts right in their devotion to the One they worship and love, the scriptural proofs would have indicated it. It is well known that during the three most excellent generations, concerning which the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The best of generations is my generation, in which I was sent, then those who follow them, then those who follow them,”

none of the people of goodness and religious devotion—in the Hijaz, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Egypt, or Khurāsān—would gather for this newly introduced form of listening to reform their hearts. For this reason, the leading scholars, such as Imam Ahmad and others, disapproved of it. Al-Shāfi‘ī even counted it among the innovations of the heretics, saying:

“I left behind in Baghdad something introduced by the heretics, which they call taghbīr, by which they turn people away from the Quran.”

---

## Page 4658

As for what a person hears without intending to listen, neither prohibition nor blame attaches to it, by agreement of the imams. Thus, blame and praise attach to deliberate listening, not mere hearing. Someone who listens attentively to the Quran is rewarded for it, whereas someone who hears it without intention or deliberate choice is not rewarded for that, since deeds are judged by intentions.

Likewise, if someone unintentionally hears forms of entertainment that one is forbidden to listen to, this does not harm him. If he hears a line of poetry that accords with some aspect of his state, stirring something praiseworthy that lay dormant within him and rousing something beloved that had been still—or if he quotes such a line or does something similar—this is not prohibited. What is good and praiseworthy is his heart’s movement, which Allah and His Messenger love, towards love of Allah: a love that entails doing what Allah loves and refraining from what He hates.

An example is someone who passed by a house and heard a person saying:

“Every day you change your ways;
something else would better become you.”

He drew from this an allusion relevant to his own state, for such allusions fall within the realm of analogy, reflection, and illustrative comparisons. The question of “listening” is extensive and wide-ranging, and we have discussed it elsewhere.

The point here is that the goals sought by spiritual seekers can be attained through listening that accords with faith, the Quran, the Prophetic way, religion, and revealed law—the listening of the prophets, the learned, those who know Allah, and the believers.

Allah Most High says:

“Those are the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed His favour

---

## Page 4659

among the prophets, from the descendants of Adam”—up to His words:

“When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down prostrate and weeping.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall upon their faces in prostration”—up to His words: “and it increases them in humility.”

He Most High says:

“When they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized.”

He Most High says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

He Most High says:

“Allah has sent down the finest discourse: a Book consistent in its parts, repeating its teachings, at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver”—and the rest of the verse.

Just as He praises those who turn attentively to this listening, He condemns those who turn away from it, as in His words:

“Among people are those who purchase idle talk to lead others astray from Allah’s way without knowledge and to make a mockery of it”—up to His words: “When Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly, as though he had not heard them, as though there were deafness in his ears. So give him tidings of a painful punishment.”

He Most High says:

“Those who, when reminded of their Lord’s verses, do not respond to them as though deaf and blind.”

He Most High says:

“What, then, is the matter with them that they turn away from the reminder, like startled donkeys fleeing from a lion?”

He Most High says:

“Indeed, the worst of creatures in Allah’s sight are the deaf and mute who do not reason. Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear”—and the rest of the verse.

He Most High says:

“Those who disbelieve say, ‘Do not listen to this Quran, and make noise while it is recited, so that you may prevail.’”

He Most High says: “What, then, is the matter with them

---

## Page 4660

that they turn away from the reminder, like startled donkeys fleeing from a lion?” There are many such passages in the Quran.

This was the kind of listening practised by the early generations of this community and its leading shaykhs and imams: the Companions, the Successors, and the shaykhs who came after them, such as Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, Ma‘rūf al-Karkhī, Yūsuf ibn Asbāt, Hudhayfa al-Mar‘ashī, and others like them.

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, would say to Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī, “Abū Mūsā, remind us of our Lord.” He would then recite while they listened and wept.

When the Companions of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gathered, they would ask one of their number to recite the Quran while the others listened. It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed by Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī while he was reciting and began listening to his recitation. He said, “This man has been granted a melodious voice like those of the house of David.” He also said, “I passed by you last night while you were reciting, and I began listening to your recitation.” Abū Mūsā replied, “Had I known that you were listening, I would have made it especially beautiful for you”—meaning that he would have further beautified his recitation for him.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adorn the Quran with your voices.”

He also said:

“Allah listens more attentively to a man with a beautiful voice reciting the Quran than the owner of a singing girl listens to her.”

Here, adhan means listening, as in His words:

“And it listens to its Lord, as it must.”

That is, it listens.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah listens to nothing as He listens to a prophet with a beautiful voice reciting the Quran melodiously and aloud.”

He also said:

“He is not one of us who does not recite the Quran melodiously.”

---

## Page 4661

This kind of listening brings profound spiritual experiences, noble inward delights, increased knowledge, and great spiritual states that no discourse can encompass and no book contain, just as reflecting upon the Quran and understanding it brings an increase in knowledge and faith beyond description.

Something that deserves careful attention is that Allah, Glorified is He, says in His Book:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you.’”

Some of the early generations said that certain people in the Prophet’s time, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, claimed to love Allah, so Allah revealed this verse:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you’”—to the end of the verse.

He thus made clear that loving Him entails following the Messenger, and that following the Messenger brings about Allah’s love for His servant. This is a love by which Allah has tested those who claim to love Him, for claims and confusion abound in this matter.

Thus, it is related that when people discussed the subject of love in the presence of Dhū al-Nūn al-Misrī, he said, “Stop discussing this subject, lest people’s souls hear of it and lay claim to it.”

One of them said, “Whoever worships Allah out of love alone is a heretic; whoever worships Allah out of fear alone is a Harūrī; whoever worships Him out of hope alone is a Murji’ite; and whoever worships Him with love, fear, and hope is a believer who affirms Allah’s oneness.”

This is because love alone gives souls free rein, allowing them to indulge their desires unless restrained by reverent fear of Allah. It went so far that the Jews and Christians said:

“We are Allah’s children and His beloved.”

Among those who claim to love Allah, one finds violations of the revealed Law that are not found among those who fear Him. This is why He coupled love with reverent fear in His words:

---

## Page 4662

“This is what you were promised—for everyone who turns to Allah and keeps His commands,

who fears the Most Merciful without seeing Him and comes with a repentant heart.

Enter it in peace; this is the Day of Eternity.”

The scholars who wrote on the Sunnah used to include in their statements of belief the need to avoid those who frequently profess love for Allah and discourse upon it without reverent fear, because of the corruption into which some Sufi groups had fallen through this. The corruption in their beliefs and deeds led other groups to reject the Sufi path altogether. Those who went astray thus fell into two groups: one accepted both its truth and its falsehood, while the other rejected both its truth and its falsehood, as did various groups of speculative theologians and jurists. The correct approach is to affirm whatever accords with the Book and the Sunnah, whether in this path or elsewhere, and to reject whatever contradicts the Book and the Sunnah, whether in this path or elsewhere.

Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.’”

Following the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his revealed Law, inwardly and outwardly, brings about Allah’s love. Likewise, striving in His cause, allegiance to His allies, and enmity toward His enemies constitute the very essence of love for Him, as stated in the hadith:

“The firmest bonds of faith are love for Allah’s sake and hatred for Allah’s sake.”

---

## Page 4663

And in another hadith:

“Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

Many who claim to love Allah are further than others from following the Sunnah, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and striving in Allah’s cause. Yet they claim that their approach is more perfect in the path of love than any other, alleging that the path of love for Allah involves neither protective jealousy nor anger for Allah’s sake. This contradicts what the Book and the Sunnah teach. Hence the transmitted hadith:

“Allah Most High will say on the Day of Resurrection: ‘Where are those who love one another for the sake of My majesty? Today I shall shade them in My shade, on the day when there is no shade but Mine.’”

The words “Where are those who love one another for the sake of Allah’s majesty?” draw attention to the reverence and veneration for Allah in their hearts, alongside their mutual love for His sake. Through this, they observe His limits, unlike those who fail to observe His limits because of the weakness of faith in their hearts. These are the people described in the hadith:

“My love is assured to those who love one another for My sake; My love is assured to those who sit together for My sake; My love is assured to those who visit one another for My sake; and My love is assured to those who give generously to one another for My sake.”

There are many hadiths concerning those who love one another for Allah’s sake. In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Seven will be shaded by Allah in His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a young man who grew up worshipping Allah; a man whose heart remains attached to the mosque from the time he leaves it until he returns; two men who love one another for Allah’s sake, meeting and parting on that basis; a man who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends; a man who remembers Allah in solitude and whose eyes overflow with tears; and a man who was solicited by a woman

---

## Page 4664

of rank and beauty, but he said: ‘I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”

The foundation of love is knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted be He. Love has two foundations:

The first, known as the love of ordinary people, is love for His goodness to His servants. No one denies love founded on this basis, for hearts are naturally disposed to love those who treat them well and to hate those who treat them badly. Allah, glorified be He, is the true Bestower of blessings and goodness upon His servant. He graciously grants every blessing, even when it comes through an intermediary, for He makes the intermediaries available and brings about the causes. Yet if this love does not draw the heart to love Allah Himself, then the servant has, in reality, loved only himself. Likewise, whoever loves something because of its goodness to him has, in reality, loved only himself. This is not blameworthy; rather, it is praiseworthy. This is the love referred to in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Love Allah for the blessings with which He nourishes you; love me out of love for Allah; and love my family out of love for me.”

Someone whose love goes no further than this has recognized nothing in Allah that calls for loving Him except His goodness to him. This is as has been said: praise of Allah is of “two kinds”: “praise” that is gratitude, which is only for His blessings; and “praise” that is commendation, extolling Him, and love for Him, on account of what He deserves in Himself, glorified be He.

---

## Page 4665

So it is with love: its second foundation is loving Him for what He is worthy of. This is the love of someone who knows of Allah that which makes Him worthy of being loved. There is no aspect through which one knows Allah, as indicated by His names and attributes, in which He does not deserve perfect love. This extends even to everything He brings about, for every blessing from Him is grace, and every punishment from Him is justice. Thus, He deserves praise in every circumstance, in prosperity and adversity alike. This love is higher and more perfect: it is the love of the select.

These are the people who seek the delight of gazing upon His noble Face and find delight in remembering Him and speaking intimately to Him. This means more to them than water does to fish; were they cut off from it, they would experience unbearable pain. They are the foremost, as related in Sahīh Muslim from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed a mountain called Hamdān and said, ‘Proceed! This is Hamdān. The devoted have gone ahead.’ They asked, ‘Messenger of Allah, who are the devoted?’ He replied, ‘The men and women who remember Allah much.’”

In another narration, he said:

“Those wholly absorbed in remembering Allah: remembrance relieves them of their burdens, so they come to Allah on the Day of Resurrection lightly laden.”

Someone wholly absorbed in remembering Allah is captivated by it, delights in it, and is passionately attached to it, never flagging in it.

In the report narrated by Hārūn ibn ‘Antarah, from his father, from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said:

“Moses said, ‘My Lord, which of Your servants is most beloved to You?’ He replied, ‘The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me.’ He asked, ‘Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?’ He replied, ‘The one who seeks to add others’ knowledge to his own, hoping to find a word that guides him to

---

## Page 4666

guidance or turns him away from evil.’ He asked, ‘Which of Your servants is wisest?’ He replied, ‘The one who judges against himself as he judges against others, and rules in favour of others as he rules in his own favour.’”

This report thus mentions love, knowledge, and justice, which together encompass all goodness. Something that must be understood is that, in matters of loving Allah Most High, one must not entertain the notions associated with loving others, such as unfounded reproach, abandonment, estrangement without cause, and the like. Some groups fall into this error, even speaking of love for Him in the same terms they use for loving someone who spurns them and severs ties though they have done no wrong, or who keeps those seeking closeness at a distance. This is not permissible even if some authors have fallen into this error in their treatises, to the point that the substance of their words amounts to making a case against Allah. Rather, to Allah belongs the conclusive argument.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever remembers Me to himself, I remember him to Myself. Whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than it. Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by a cubit. Whoever draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by an armspan. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.’”

In some transmitted reports, Allah Most High says:

“Those who remember Me are those who sit in My company; those who thank Me are those who visit Me; those who obey Me are those whom I honour. As for those who disobey Me, I do not make them despair of My mercy. If they repent, I am the One who loves them”—for Allah loves those who repent—“and if they do not repent, I am their physician: I afflict them with hardships until I cleanse them of their faults.”

---

## Page 4667

Allah Most High has said:

“Whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer need fear neither injustice nor deprivation.”

They explained: Injustice means being made to bear another’s sins, while deprivation means having one’s own good deeds diminished.

Allah Most High has also said:

“We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.”

In an authentic hadith, Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another.

O My servants, all of you are astray except those whom I guide, so seek My guidance and I will guide you.

O My servants, all of you are hungry except those whom I feed, so ask Me for food and I will feed you.

O My servants, all of you are naked except those whom I clothe, so ask Me for clothing and I will clothe you.

O My servants, you sin by night and by day, and I forgive sins and do not mind doing so. Ask My forgiveness and I will forgive you.

O My servants, you can never harm Me, nor can you ever benefit Me.

O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, had hearts like that of the most pious man among you, that would add nothing to My dominion.

O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, had hearts like that of the most wicked man among you, that would diminish My dominion in no way.

O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, gathered on a single plain and asked of Me, and I gave each one what he asked for, that would diminish My dominion no more than a needle diminishes the sea when dipped into it.

O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you, then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.’”

Another example is what al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Shaddād ibn Aws, who said:

---

## Page 4668

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best supplication for forgiveness is for a servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but Allah. You created me, and I am Your servant. I abide by Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your blessings upon me, and I acknowledge my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ Whoever says this in the morning with firm conviction and dies that day will enter Paradise. Whoever says it in the evening with firm conviction and dies that night will enter Paradise.”

The servant is always between a blessing from Allah that calls for gratitude and a sin of his own that calls for seeking forgiveness. Both are constant duties for the servant, for he continually enjoys Allah’s blessings and bounties and continually needs to repent and seek forgiveness. This is why Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the foremost of Adam’s descendants and the leader of the God-fearing—would seek forgiveness in every circumstance.

In the authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O people, repent to your Lord, for I seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day.”

In Sahīh Muslim, he said:

“A veil comes over my heart, and I seek Allah’s forgiveness a hundred times a day.”

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said:

“In a single gathering, we would count the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying a hundred times: ‘My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepter of repentance, the All-Forgiving.’”

---

## Page 4669

For this reason, seeking forgiveness is prescribed at the conclusion of acts of worship. Allah Most High says:

“And those who seek forgiveness before dawn.”

Some said: “They spent the night in prayer, and when the time before dawn came, they were commanded to seek forgiveness.” An authentic hadith states:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, finished his prayer, he would seek forgiveness three times and say: ‘O Allah, You are Peace, and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Then, when you depart from ʿArafāt, remember Allah at the Sacred Monument,”

up to His words:

“And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

After His Prophet had conveyed the message, striven for Allah as He deserves, and fulfilled Allah’s commands to a degree attained by no one else, Allah commanded him, saying:

“When Allah’s help and victory come, and you see people entering Allah’s religion in crowds, then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

For this reason, religion rests upon affirming Allah’s oneness and seeking forgiveness, as Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then set forth in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware: ‘Worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good tidings. And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance; He will grant you good enjoyment’”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High says:

“So take a straight course towards Him and seek His forgiveness.”

And Allah Most High says:

“So know that there is no god but Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women.”

For this reason, it is related in a hadith:

“Satan says: ‘I destroyed people through sins, but they destroyed me by saying “There is no god but Allah” and seeking forgiveness.’”

Jonah said: “There is no god but You; glory be to You!

Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

Section: The Sickness of Hearts and Their Healing

Allah Most High said concerning the hypocrites:

“In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease.”

And He, Most High, said:

“So that He may make what Satan casts forth a trial for those in whose hearts is disease and those whose hearts are hardened.”

---

## Page 4672

and He said:

“If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is disease, and those who spread alarming rumours in Medina do not desist, We will surely stir you up against them; then they will remain your neighbours there only a little while.”

And He said:

“And so that those given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, ‘What does Allah intend by this as an example?’”

And He, Most High, said:

“There has come to you an admonition from your Lord, a healing for what is in the hearts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.”

And He said:

“We send down of the Quran that which is a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss.”

And He said:

“And heal the hearts of a believing people”

“And remove the rage from their hearts.”

“Illness of the body” is the opposite of its health and soundness. It is a disorder within the body that impairs its perception and natural functioning. Its perception may disappear, as in blindness and deafness, or it may perceive things other than as they really are: something sweet may taste bitter, or it may imagine things that have no external reality. As for the impairment of its natural functioning, its digestive capacity may weaken, or it may develop an aversion to the foods it needs and a liking for things that harm it. It experiences pain accordingly.

Despite this illness, however, the body has neither died nor perished. Rather, it retains, in general, some capacity to perceive voluntary movement. This gives rise to pain in the body, owing to a disorder of either quantity or quality. The first involves either a deficiency of substance, in which case nourishment is needed, or an excess of it

---

## Page 4673

in which case evacuation is needed. The second involves, for example, excessive heat or cold beyond the proper balance, and requires treatment.

Section

Likewise, “illness of the heart” is a kind of corruption that impairs its perception and its will. Its perception is impaired by the doubts that arise within it, until it no longer sees the truth, or sees it as other than it really is. Its will is impaired such that it hates beneficial truth and loves harmful falsehood. This is why illness is sometimes explained as doubt and uncertainty, as when Mujāhid and Qatādah explained His words:

“In their hearts is disease”

as meaning doubt. At other times, it is explained as the desire for illicit intercourse, as in the explanation of His words:

“Lest he in whose heart is disease should covet.”

For this reason, al-Kharā’itī composed The Book of the Ailments of Hearts—that is, their illness—by which he meant their affliction with lust.

A sick person is hurt by things that do not hurt a healthy person. Even slight heat, cold, exertion, and similar things harm him, because the weakness caused by his illness leaves him unable to withstand them. Illness generally weakens the sick person, diminishing his strength so that he cannot bear what can be borne by

---

## Page 4674

a strong person. Health is preserved by like conditions and lost through contrary ones, while illness is aggravated by conditions like those that caused it and dispelled by their opposite. If a sick person encounters something like the cause of his illness, his illness increases and his strength diminishes further, until he may even perish. If, however, he encounters what restores his strength and dispels his illness, the opposite occurs.

“Illness of the heart” is pain that arises in the heart, such as rage at an enemy who has overpowered you, for this causes the heart pain. Allah Most High says:

“and heal the hearts of a believing people”

“and remove the rage from their hearts.”

Their healing consists in the removal of the pain that has arisen in their hearts. Thus, one says, “So-and-so’s rage has been soothed.” Retaliatory execution likewise brings relief to the slain person’s next of kin, and there are other such examples. This is healing from distress, rage, and sorrow, all of which are pains that arise in the soul.

“Doubt and ignorance” likewise cause the heart pain. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for ignorance is simply to ask.”

Someone who doubts something and is uncertain about it feels pain in his heart until he attains knowledge and certainty. One may say to a scholar whose answer makes the truth clear, “He has healed me with his answer.”

Illness falls short of death: the heart dies through complete ignorance and becomes ill through a particular kind of ignorance. Thus, it experiences death, illness, life, and healing. Its life, death, illness, and healing are more consequential than those of the body. Hence, when a doubt or desire comes upon a diseased heart, it aggravates its illness; but if wisdom and admonition reach it, they are among

---

## Page 4675

the means of restoring its soundness and healing it.

Allah Most High says:

“so that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is disease”

This is because it gives rise to doubt in them. As for those whose hearts are hardened, their hardness is due to their dryness. The hearts of the former are weakened by illness, so what Satan casts becomes a trial for them; the hearts of the latter are hardened against faith, so it becomes a trial for them as well.

He also says:

“If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is disease, and those who spread alarming rumours in Medina do not desist”

And likewise:

“and so that those in whose hearts is disease may say”

Their hearts have not died as the hearts of the disbelievers and hypocrites have, nor are they healthy and sound like the sound hearts of the believers. Rather, they suffer from the illness of doubt and desires. Likewise, He says:

“lest he in whose heart is disease should be moved to desire”

This is the illness of lust. Someone with a sound heart would pay no attention to a woman even if she made advances to him. By contrast, a heart diseased with lust, because of its weakness, inclines towards such temptations as present themselves, to a degree corresponding to the severity of its illness. Thus, when women soften their speech, the man whose heart is diseased is moved to desire.

The Quran is a healing for what is in people's hearts. For those whose hearts suffer from the illnesses of doubts and desires, it contains clear proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood. It thereby dispels the illnesses of doubt that corrupt knowledge, understanding, and perception, enabling a person to see things as they truly are. It also contains wisdom and good admonition—through encouragement, warning, and instructive narratives—that restore the heart to soundness. The heart then desires what benefits it and turns away from what harms it. It thus comes to love right guidance and hate error, after having desired error and hated right guidance.

---

## Page 4676

Thus, the Quran removes the diseases that give rise to corrupt desires, until the heart becomes sound, its desires are set right, and it returns to the innate disposition upon which it was created, just as the body returns to its natural state. The heart draws from faith and the Quran the nourishment that makes it flourish and strengthens it, just as the body feeds on what promotes its growth and soundness. For the heart’s flourishing is like the body’s growth.

“Zakāh in its linguistic sense” means growth and increase in goodness. Something is said to flourish when it grows in goodness. The heart needs nurturing so that it grows and develops until it becomes complete and sound, just as the body needs to be nurtured with wholesome foods. Alongside this, whatever harms it must be kept away. The body grows only when it receives what benefits it and is protected from what harms it. Likewise, the heart can flourish, grow, and attain complete soundness only by receiving what benefits it and warding off what harms it. Crops, too, flourish only in this way.

Since “charity” extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, it causes the heart to flourish. This flourishing is something beyond its purification from sin. Allah Most High says:

“Take charity from their wealth to purify them and cause them to grow thereby.”

Likewise, abandoning indecencies causes the heart to flourish. So too does abandoning sins, for they are like harmful humours in the body and weeds among crops. When the body is purged of harmful humours—for example, by removing excess blood—its natural strength is freed of its burden and finds relief, allowing the body to grow. So too with the heart: when

---

## Page 4677

it repents of sins, it is purged of the admixture produced by combining righteous deeds with evil ones. When it repents of sins, its strength and will are freed for righteous deeds, and it finds relief from the corrupt influences that had arisen within it. The heart thus flourishes, growing and attaining completeness.

Allah Most High says:

“Were it not for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, not one of you would ever have become pure.”

And He Most High says:

And He Most High says:

Although the primary meaning of tazkiya is growth, blessing, and an increase in goodness, this is achieved only by removing evil. Thus, purification encompasses both meanings.

And He says:

“Woe to those who associate partners with Allah, who do not give zakāh.”

Here, zakāh refers to affirming Allah’s oneness and to faith, through which the heart flourishes. This entails rejecting within the heart the divinity of anything besides the True One and affirming His divinity within it. This is the true meaning of “There is no god but Allah,” and it is the foundation upon which hearts flourish.

Tazkiya means making something pure, either in itself or in how it is regarded and spoken of;

## Page 4678

just as one says, “I have rendered him upright,” meaning either that one has made him upright in himself or established his uprightness in people’s estimation. Allah Most High says:

That is, do not declare yourselves pure. This differs from His saying:

Zaynab’s name had been Barrah, but it was said that she was thereby claiming purity for herself, so the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, named her Zaynab.

This means that He makes a person pure and declares him to be so, just as someone who vouches for witnesses attests to their uprightness.

“Justice” means balance, and balance is the soundness of the heart, just as wrongdoing is its corruption. Thus, whenever a person sins, he wrongs himself. Wrongdoing is the opposite of justice: he has not treated himself justly, but has wronged himself. The heart’s soundness therefore lies in justice, and its corruption in wrongdoing. When a servant wrongs himself, he is both the wrongdoer and the one wronged. Likewise, when he acts justly, he is both the one who acts justly and the one treated justly. The deed proceeds from him, and its fruit, whether good or evil, returns to him.

Allah Most High says:

“Each soul will have the good it has earned and bear the evil it has earned.”

A deed affects the heart—benefiting it, harming it, or setting it right—before its effects appear outwardly. Setting the soul right is to do it justice, while corrupting it is to wrong it. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own benefit; and whoever does evil, it is to his own detriment.”

And He Most High says:

“If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against yourselves.”

One of the early generations said: “A good deed indeed produces light in the heart, strength in the body, radiance in the face, abundance in provision, and love in people’s hearts; an evil deed, by contrast, produces darkness in

To be “given up” means to be held in pledge, confined, and taken captive. Likewise, when the body recovers from illness, its temperament is said to have regained its balance; illness arises from a disturbance of that temperament. Similarly, the heart’s health and soundness lie in justice, while its illness arises from deviation, wrongdoing, and crookedness. Absolute justice in everything is unattainable, in both knowledge and practice; rather, one seeks the best, then the next best.

Hence one says, “This is better,” and the way of the early generations is called “the best way.”

Thus He likened them to someone who kindled a fire: whenever it gave light, Allah extinguished it. The word rabīʿ refers to rain that descends from the sky and causes vegetation to grow. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

The Arabs call the season in which the first rains fall rabīʿ, because that is when the rain falls that brings forth vegetation. Others use rabīʿ for the season following winter, since it is then that blossoms appear from which fruits develop, and leaves grow on trees.

Through the light within it, the living, illuminated heart hears, sees, and understands. The dead heart, however, neither hears nor sees. Allah Most High says:

## Page 4685

Some commentators, when discussing these verses and similar passages—such as His saying:

“When adversity touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, sitting, or standing. But when We remove his adversity, he goes on as though he had never called upon Us concerning the adversity that touched him”—

and other passages in which Allah mentions and condemns human failings, say: “This verse concerns the disbelievers; ‘man’ here means the disbeliever.” Those who hear this are then left thinking that none of this condemnation or warning applies to anyone who outwardly professes Islam. Rather, their thoughts turn to those Arabs who openly professed polytheism, or to those they know who openly profess disbelief, such as Jews, Christians, and polytheists among the Turks and Indians, and others like them. Thus, they derive no benefit from these verses, which Allah revealed to guide His servants.

The response is, first: those who outwardly profess Islam include both believers and hypocrites. Hypocrites are numerous in every age, and the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire.

Second: a person may have an element of hypocrisy and disbelief while also possessing faith, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in a hadith reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Whoever possesses four traits is a pure hypocrite, and whoever possesses one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted with something, he betrays that trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he acts wickedly.”

He thus stated that whoever possesses one of these traits has a trait of hypocrisy.

## Page 4686

It is also established in an authentic hadith that he said to Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Four practices in my community belong to the ways of pre-Islamic ignorance: boasting of ancestral distinction, disparaging people’s lineage, wailing over the dead, and seeking rain through the stars.”

Hearts are of “four kinds”: a bare heart with a lamp shining within it—that is the believer’s heart; a covered heart—that is the disbeliever’s heart; an overturned heart—that is the hypocrite’s heart; and a heart with two sources of nourishment, one nourishing it with faith and the other with hypocrisy. Such people have mixed righteous deeds with evil ones.

Once this is understood, it becomes clear that every servant benefits from what Allah has said concerning faith, praising the branches of faith and condemning the branches of disbelief. This is like what some people say concerning His words:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

They say: “The believer has already been guided to the straight path, so what

## Page 4687

benefit is there in seeking guidance?” Some answer that the intended meaning is, “Keep us steadfast upon guidance,” just as the Arabs say to someone asleep, “Sleep until I come to you.” Others say it means, “Bind our hearts to guidance,” with the object being bound left unexpressed. Still others say it means, “Increase me in guidance.”

They raise this question only because they have not properly understood the straight path to which the servant seeks guidance. What is meant is to do whatever Allah has commanded and refrain from whatever He has forbidden in all matters. Although a person may acknowledge in general terms that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and that the Quran is true, he remains unaware of most of what he needs to know about what benefits and harms him, and what Allah has commanded and forbidden in specific matters and their particulars. Even much of what he does know, he has not put into practice. Even supposing that every command and prohibition in the Quran and Sunnah had reached him, the Quran and Sunnah state only general, universal matters—it could not be otherwise—and do not specify what pertains individually to each servant. This is why a person is commanded to ask for guidance to the straight path in such matters.

Guidance to the straight path encompasses all of this: being taught in detail what the Messenger brought, being shown what falls under his universal commands, and being inspired to act upon what one knows. Merely knowing the truth does not make a person rightly guided unless he acts upon his knowledge. This is why Allah said to His Prophet after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah:

“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph, so that Allah may forgive you your past and future sins, perfect His favor upon you, and guide you

## Page 4688

to a straight path.” He also said concerning Moses and Aaron:

“We gave them both the clear Scripture, and guided them both to the straight path.”

Muslims have disagreed, as Allah has willed, over matters concerning reports, knowledge, belief, and practice, even though they all agree that Muhammad is truly Allah’s Messenger and that the Quran is true. Had each of them been guided to the straight path concerning their disputed matters, they would not have disagreed. Furthermore, most of those who know what Allah has commanded disobey Him and fail to follow His command. Had they been guided to the straight path in those actions, they would have done what they were commanded and refrained from what they were forbidden.

As for those of this community whom Allah has guided until they became His pious allies, one of the greatest means of attaining this was their supplicating to Allah with this prayer in every prayer, while recognizing their constant need of Allah and their utter dependence upon Him to guide them to the straight path. Through continually making this supplication and acknowledging their need, they became Allah’s pious allies.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī said, “No path brings a servant closer to his Lord than his need of Him.”

Whatever a person was guided in previously, he still needs guidance in it in the future. This is the true meaning of the interpretation:

“Keep us steadfast, and guide us to remain upon the path.”

The interpretation, “Increase us in guidance,” encompasses what has already been mentioned. Yet all of this is guidance from Him to the straight path in the future, for acting upon knowledge in the future has not yet occurred. A person will not be rightly guided until he acts upon that knowledge in the future. Moreover, knowledge may not be present in
