The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned this elsewhere, as in his statement (11/244): “They distinguish three ranks, saying: ‘The servant first witnesses obedience and disobedience, then obedience without disobedience, then neither obedience nor disobedience.’”

---

## Page 4798

As for Abraham and the family of Abraham—the sincere monotheists and prophets—they know that a distinction must be maintained between the Creator and creation, and between obedience and disobedience. They know that the more a servant advances in realization, the greater his love for Allah, his servitude and obedience to Him, and his turning away from worshipping, loving and obeying anyone other than Him.

These misguided polytheists equate Allah with His creation, whereas Allah’s intimate friend says:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping,
you and your forefathers?
They are enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds.”

They cling to ambiguous statements made by the spiritual masters, just as the Christians did. An example is the term “fanā” (annihilation). There are three kinds of fanā: one belonging to those who have attained perfection among the prophets and Allah’s friends; another belonging to those striving among Allah’s friends and the righteous; and another belonging to the hypocrites who deviate from the truth and liken Allah to His creation.

(As for the first), it is “ceasing to desire anything other than Allah,” such that a person loves none but Allah, worships none but Him, relies on none but Him, and seeks none but Him. This is the meaning that must be intended by the words of Shaykh Abū Yazīd when he said: “I desire to desire only what He wills.” That is, what He wills in the sense of loving and approving of it—what is intended by His prescriptive will. The servant’s perfection lies in desiring, loving and approving only what Allah wills, approves of and loves: what He has commanded, whether as an obligation or a recommendation. He loves only what Allah loves, such as the angels, the prophets and the righteous.

This is the meaning of their explanation of His words:

“Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

They said: “It is a heart free of anything other than Allah, or anything other than worship of Allah, or anything other than

---

## Page 4799

desiring Allah, or anything other than loving Allah.” The meaning is the same. Whether or not this is called annihilation, it is the beginning and end of Islam, the inward and outward reality of religion.

As for the second kind, it is “ceasing to perceive anything other than Allah.” This happens to many who follow the spiritual path. Their hearts are so intensely drawn to remembering, worshipping and loving Allah, yet too weak to perceive anything besides the One they worship or behold anything besides the One they seek, that nothing other than Allah enters their hearts. Indeed, they are not even aware of anything else. Thus, concerning His words:

“The heart of Moses’ mother became empty. She almost disclosed his identity, had We not strengthened her heart.”

They said: “Empty of everything except the thought of Moses.”

This often happens to someone overwhelmed by a concern—whether love, fear or hope—which turns his heart away from everything except what he loves, fears or seeks. When entirely absorbed in it, he is unaware of anything else. If this state intensifies in someone experiencing annihilation, he becomes so absorbed in the One he finds that he loses awareness of his own existence; in the One he beholds, of his own beholding; in the One he remembers, of his own remembrance; and in the One he knows, of his own knowledge. Eventually, that which once did not exist—the created beings other than Him, all subject to Him—vanishes, and He who has always existed—the Lord Most High—remains. What is meant is that these beings vanish from the servant’s awareness and remembrance, and that he ceases to perceive or behold them.

When this intensifies, the lover grows weak until his discernment becomes impaired. He may then imagine that he himself is his beloved, as in the story related of a man who threw himself into the sea, whereupon the one who loved him threw himself in after him. The first said: “I fell in, but what made you fall in after me?” He replied: “I became so absorbed in you that I lost awareness of myself, and thought that you were me.”

---

## Page 4800

And it is at “this point” that some people have gone astray, imagining that this is union, and that the lover becomes united with the beloved until there is no distinction between their very existences. This is an error, for nothing whatsoever can become united with the Creator. Indeed, nothing becomes united with anything else unless both are transformed and lose their original natures, their union producing a third thing that is neither the one nor the other—as when water and milk, or water and wine, are mixed together, and so forth. Rather, their objects of desire, love and aversion may be one and the same, and their willing and aversion may accord: one loves what the other loves, hates what the other hates, is pleased with what pleases the other, resents what the other resents, dislikes what the other dislikes, befriends those whom the other befriends, and opposes those whom the other opposes. All such annihilation involves some deficiency.

The greatest friends of Allah—such as Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers—did not experience this annihilation, let alone the Prophets, who rank above them. Something of this occurred only after the time of the Companions. The same applies to all experiences of this kind in which reason and discernment are lost because of states of faith that come upon the heart. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were too complete, strong and steadfast in their states of faith to lose their reason or experience fainting, swooning, intoxication, annihilation, bewilderment or madness. These phenomena first appeared among the devout worshippers of Basra belonging to the generation of the Successors. Some would faint upon hearing the Quran.

Some would even die, such as Abū Juhayr the Blind and Zurārah ibn Awfā, the judge of Basra. Likewise, some Sufi shaykhs later experienced annihilation and intoxication to such a degree that

---

## Page 4801

their discernment weakened, until they uttered things in that state which, upon regaining sobriety, they recognized as mistaken. Such things are related of Abū Yazīd, Abū al-Husayn al-Nūrī, Abū Bakr al-Shiblī and others like them. This was unlike Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, Ma‘rūf al-Karkhī and al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād—indeed, unlike al-Junayd and others whose reason and discernment remained with them throughout their spiritual states, so that they did not fall into such annihilation, intoxication or similar experiences.

Rather, those who attain perfection have hearts filled with nothing but love for Allah, seeking Him and worshipping Him. Yet their knowledge and discernment are sufficiently broad to perceive things as they truly are. Indeed, they perceive created beings as sustained by Allah’s command, governed by His will, responsive to Him and humbly obedient to Him. In them they find insight and a reminder. What they witness thus reinforces and nourishes the sincere devotion, unalloyed monotheism and worship of Allah alone, without partner, that reside in their hearts.

This is the “reality” to which the Quran calls, and which is upheld by those who have truly realized faith and those perfected in spiritual knowledge. Our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is their leader and the most perfect of them. Thus, when he was taken up to the heavens, witnessed the signs there, and received the revelation conveyed to him in various forms of intimate discourse, he was among his people the next morning with his state unchanged and no outward sign of that experience upon him. This contrasts with the signs of being overcome that would appear in Moses—may Allah bless them all and grant them peace.

---

## Page 4802

As for the third kind of what may be called annihilation, it consists in perceiving that nothing exists but Allah, and that the Creator and creation have one and the same existence, with no distinction between the Lord and the servant. This is the annihilation of those given to misguidance and heresy, who fall into indwelling and union.

When an upright spiritual master says, “I see none but Allah,” or “I look to none but Allah,” or something similar, he means: “I see no lord besides Him, no creator besides Him, no governor besides Him, and no deity besides Him. Nor do I look to anything else out of love for it, fear of it, or hope in it.” For the eye looks towards whatever occupies the heart. Whoever loves something, hopes in it, or fears it turns towards it. But when the heart has no love, hope, fear, hatred, or any other attachment to something, it does not deliberately turn towards it, look at it, or seek to see it. If one happens to see it, merely seeing it without any further involvement, it is like seeing a wall or anything else to which the heart has no attachment.

The righteous spiritual masters—may Allah be pleased with them—speak of aspects of pure monotheism and the realization of complete sincerity in all religious devotion, such that the servant neither turns towards nor looks to anything other than Allah out of love, fear, or hope. Rather, the heart is empty of created things, free of attachment to them, and looks upon them only by Allah’s light. Thus, through the True One he hears, through the True One he sees, through the True One he grasps, and through the True One he walks. Among created things, he loves what Allah loves and hates what Allah hates; he befriends those whom Allah befriends and is hostile to those opposed by

---

## Page 4803

Allah. He fears Allah in his dealings with them, but does not fear them in matters concerning Allah; he places his hope in Allah concerning them, but not in them concerning Allah. This is the sound heart: upright in faith, affirming Allah’s oneness, submitting to Him, believing in Him, knowing Him, realizing the truth, and affirming His oneness through the knowledge, spiritual realization, and monotheism of the prophets and messengers.

(As for the third kind)

It is annihilation in what exists: the realization, knowledge, and monotheism of Pharaoh’s people, such as the Qarmatians and their like. This kind, which the followers of the prophets adhere to, is “praiseworthy annihilation,” through which a person becomes one of those whom Allah has praised: His God-fearing allies, His successful party, and His victorious army.

By this statement, the spiritual masters and the righteous do not mean that the created things I see with my own eyes are the Lord of the earth and the heavens. Only someone steeped in utter misguidance and corruption would say this—whether corruption of reason or corruption of belief. His condition thus lies between madness and heresy.

All the spiritual masters who are followed as examples in religion agree with the consensus of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars: the Creator, glorified be He, is distinct and separate from created things. Nothing of His essence is within His creation, and nothing of His creation is within His essence. The Eternal must be distinguished from that which came into being, and the Creator from creation. Their statements on this are

---

## Page 4804

too numerous to mention here. They have discussed the diseases and misconceptions that afflict hearts, and how someone may behold the existence of created things and mistake it for the Creator of the earth and the heavens, because his heart lacks discernment and the ability to distinguish. He is like someone who sees the sun’s rays and imagines them to be the sun itself in the sky.

They also speak of “distinction and collectedness,” using striking expressions similar to those used in discussing annihilation. When a servant perceives the diversity and multiplicity of created things, his heart remains attached to them and scattered among them, attending to them and clinging to them through love, fear, or hope. When he moves to collectedness, his heart becomes wholly focused on affirming Allah’s oneness and worshipping Him alone, without partner. His heart turns to Allah after having turned to created beings: his love is now for his Lord, his fear is of his Lord, his hope rests in his Lord, and he seeks his Lord’s help. In this state, his heart may have no room to consider created beings so as to distinguish between the Creator and creation. He may thus be wholly focused on the Truth, turning away from creation in both attention and intention. This resembles the second kind of annihilation.

Beyond this, however, comes the “second distinction”: to perceive that created things are sustained by Allah and governed by His command, and to perceive their multiplicity as negated by the oneness of Allah, glorified and exalted be He; and that He, glorified be He, is the Lord, God, Creator, and Owner of all created things. Thus, while his heart is wholly focused on Allah—through sincere devotion to Him, love, fear, hope, seeking His help, placing his trust in Allah, and loyalty for His sake

---

## Page 4805

and enmity for His sake, and the like—he remains mindful of the distinction between the Creator and creation, distinguishing one from the other. He perceives the diversity and multiplicity of created things while also perceiving that Allah is the Lord, Sovereign, and Creator of everything, and that He is Allah: there is no god worthy of worship except Him. This is sound and upright perception. This is required in the heart’s knowledge, perception, remembrance, and recognition, as well as in its state, worship, purpose, will, love, loyalty, and obedience.

This is the realization of “the testimony that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah.” He denies in his heart the divinity of anything other than the Truth and affirms in his heart the divinity of the Truth. Thus, he denies the divinity of every created thing and affirms the divinity of the Lord of all worlds, the Lord of the earth and the heavens. This entails the heart’s complete devotion to Allah and its turning away from everything besides Him. He therefore distinguishes between the Creator and creation in his knowledge and purpose, his perception and will, and his recognition and love. He knows Allah Most High, remembers Him, and recognizes Him, while also knowing that He is distinct from His creation, separate from them, and uniquely One.

He loves Allah, venerates Him, worships Him, places his hope in Him, fears Him, maintains loyalty and enmity for His sake, seeks His help, and places his trust in Him. He refrains from worshipping any other, placing his trust in any other, seeking help from any other, fearing any other, placing his hope in any other, maintaining loyalty or enmity for the sake of any other, or obeying the commands of any other, and from directing to any other such acts as belong exclusively to the divinity of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

His acknowledgment of the divinity of Allah Most High alone, to the exclusion of all others, entails his acknowledgment of His lordship: that He is the Lord, Sovereign, Creator, and Disposer of everything. Only then does he truly affirm Allah’s oneness.

This is further clarified by the fact that the best remembrance is “There is no god worthy of worship except Allah,” as narrated by al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Abī

---

## Page 4806

al-Dunyā and others in a report traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“The best remembrance is ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘Praise be to Allah.’”

In al-Muwattaʾ and elsewhere, it is reported from Talhah ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best that I and the prophets before me have said is: ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

Those who claim that this is the remembrance of ordinary people, that the remembrance of the elite consists of the name alone, and that the remembrance of the elite of the elite consists of the pronoun are astray and mistaken.

Some of them cite His words as evidence for this:

“Say, ‘Allah,’ then leave them to amuse themselves in their vain discourse.”

This is among their most obvious errors, for the name is mentioned in a command to answer a question, namely His words:

“Say, ‘Who sent down the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for mankind?’”

Through to His words:

“Say, ‘Allah.’”

That is: Allah is the One who sent down the Book that Moses brought. The name is therefore the subject of a nominal sentence, whose predicate is indicated by the question. This is like other such expressions: you ask, “Who is his neighbour?” and someone answers, “Zayd.”

As for the name on its own, whether expressed as a noun or a pronoun, it is neither a complete utterance nor a meaningful sentence. It conveys neither faith nor disbelief, neither a command nor a prohibition. None of the early generations of the Muslim community mentioned this practice, nor did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribe it. In itself, it gives the heart neither beneficial knowledge nor a beneficial spiritual state. It merely provides a bare conception, without affirming or denying anything about it. So if it is not accompanied by something in the heart’s knowledge and state that is beneficial in itself,

---

## Page 4807

then it is of no benefit. The revealed Law prescribes only those forms of remembrance that are beneficial in themselves, not those whose benefit comes from something else. Some who have persevered in this form of remembrance have fallen into various forms of heresy and unionism, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

As for the statement attributed to one of the shaykhs, “I fear that I may die between the negation and the affirmation,” this is a state in which its possessor should not be followed, for the error involved is plain. If a servant were to die in that state, he would die only upon what he intended and meant, since deeds are judged by intentions. It is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed that the dying be prompted to say, “There is no god worthy of worship except Allah.” He also said:

“Whoever’s last words are ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah’ will enter Paradise.”

If what that shaykh mentioned were truly a danger, the Prophet would not have prompted the dying person with an utterance that might leave him dying in a blameworthy state before completing it. Rather, he would have prompted him with the remembrance that this shaykh preferred: the name alone.

Remembrance consisting of a pronoun alone is still further removed from the Sunnah, more deeply rooted in religious innovation, and more likely to lead to Satan’s misguidance. For when someone says, “Yā Hū, yā Hū” (“O He, O He”), or “Hū, Hū” (“He, He”), or the like, the pronoun refers only to what his heart conceives—and the heart may be rightly guided or may go astray. The author of al-Fusūs composed a book that he entitled Kitāb al-Hū (The Book of “He”). Some of them have claimed that His words,

“And none knows its interpretation except Allah,”

mean: none knows the interpretation of this name, namely “al-Hū” (“He”). Such a claim has been made, even though it is something that Muslims—indeed,

---

## Page 4808

all rational people—agree is among the most manifest falsehoods. Nevertheless, some of these people may believe it. I once said to someone who made such a claim: “If it were as you say, I would have written, ‘And none knows the interpretation of Hū,’ with ‘Hū’ written as a separate word.”

Some shaykhs frequently cite His words,

“Say, ‘Allah,’ then leave them,”

as evidence for saying “Allah” alone. They suppose that Allah commanded His Prophet to utter the name in isolation. This is an error by the agreement of the scholars, for His words, “Say, ‘Allah,’” mean: Allah is the One who sent down the Book that Moses brought.

This answers His words:

“Say, ‘Who sent down the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for people, which you make into sheets, displaying them while concealing much? You have been taught what neither you nor your forefathers knew.’ Say, ‘Allah.’”

That is, Allah is the One who sent down the Book that Moses brought. With this He refuted those who said, “Allah has revealed nothing to any human being.” He said, “Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?” Then He said, “Say, ‘Allah’”—He sent it down—then leave these deniers “to amuse themselves in their vain discourse.”

Further clarification of the foregoing is found in what Sībawayh and other leading grammarians stated: the Arabs use the verb “to say” to quote complete speech, not merely an utterance. What follows this verb as a quotation must be complete speech: a nominal or verbal sentence. This is why they pronounce the particle as inna when it follows the verb “to say.” An isolated noun is not quoted in this way.

Allah Most High does not command anyone to recite an isolated name, nor has He prescribed for Muslims a bare name on its own. A bare name does not convey faith

---

## Page 4809

by the agreement of the Muslims, nor is its utterance commanded in any act of worship or any form of address.

An analogy to someone who confines himself to an isolated name is the account of a Bedouin who passed a caller to prayer saying, “I bear witness that Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah…”—putting “Messenger” in the accusative. He asked: “What is this man saying? Here is the subject, but where is the predicate that completes the statement?”

The Quranic passages:

“Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself wholeheartedly to Him”;

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High”;

“He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself,”

“and remembers the name of his Lord and prays”;

“So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great”;

and similar passages do not imply uttering His name in isolation. Rather, the Sunan collections relate:

“When His words, ‘So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great,’ were revealed, he said, ‘Include this in your bowing.’ When His words, ‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,’ were revealed, he said, ‘Include this in your prostration.’”

He thus prescribed that they say when bowing, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great,” and when prostrating, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.” It is authentically reported that “he would say when bowing, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great,’ and when prostrating, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.’” This is what his words, “Include this in your bowing” and “your prostration,” mean, by the agreement of the Muslims.

Thus, glorifying the name of one’s Lord, the Most High, remembering the name of one’s Lord, and similar expressions mean doing so through complete, meaningful speech. As authentically reported, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best words after the Quran are four—and they are from the Quran—Glory be to

---

## Page 4810

Allah, praise be to Allah, none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest.”

It is also authentically reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy in the balance, and beloved to the Most Merciful: ‘Glory and praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah, the Most Great.’”

In the two Sahih collections, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Whoever says a hundred times in a day, ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs all dominion and all praise, and He has power over all things,’ Allah will decree for him protection from Satan that day until evening. No one will bring anything better than what he has brought except someone who says the same or more. Whoever says a hundred times in a day, ‘Glory and praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah, the Most Great,’ will have his sins erased, even if they are like the foam of the sea.”

In al-Muwatta’ and elsewhere, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The best words that I and the prophets before me have said are: ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs all dominion and all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

In Sunan Ibn Mājah and elsewhere, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The best remembrance is ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘Praise be to Allah.’”

There are many such hadiths concerning the various expressions of remembrance and supplication. Likewise, the words of Allah Most High in the Quran:

“Do not eat of that over which Allah’s name has not been mentioned,”

and His words:

“So eat of what they catch for you, and mention Allah’s name over it,”

refer simply to saying, “In the name of Allah.” This is a complete sentence: either a nominal sentence, according to the more evident

---

## Page 4811

of the grammarians’ two views—or a verbal sentence. The implied wording is either “My slaughtering is in the name of Allah” or “I slaughter in the name of Allah.” The same applies when someone reciting the Quran says, “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.” The implied wording is “My recitation is in the name of Allah” or “I recite in the name of Allah.” Some understand the implied wording in such cases to be “My beginning is in the name of Allah” or “I begin in the name of Allah.” The former interpretation is better, because the entire act is performed in the name of Allah, not merely its beginning. Thus, the otherwise implied wording is made explicit in His words:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created,”

and in His words:

“In the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage,”

and in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever slaughtered before the prayer must slaughter another animal in its place. Whoever has not yet slaughtered should slaughter in the name of Allah.”

Another example is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his stepson, ʿUmar ibn Abī Salamah, in an authentic hadith:

“Mention Allah’s name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest to you.”

What is meant is to say, “In the name of Allah,” not to mention the name alone. The same applies to his words to ʿAdī ibn Hātim in an authentic hadith:

“When you release your trained dog and mention Allah’s name, eat.”

Likewise, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a man enters his home and mentions Allah’s name upon entering, upon leaving, and when eating, Satan says, ‘You have neither a place to spend the night nor an evening meal.’”

There are many similar examples. Likewise, the remembrance of Allah Most High prescribed for Muslims in their prayers, their call to prayer, their pilgrimage, and their festivals consists only of complete sentences, such as the words of the caller to prayer:

“Allah is the Greatest. Allah

---

## Page 4812

is the Greatest. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah; I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

Likewise, the worshipper says:

“Allah is the Greatest. Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent. Glory be to my Lord, the Most High. Allah hears whoever praises Him. Our Lord, to You belongs all praise. All greetings belong to Allah.”

And the pilgrim reciting the talbiyah says:

“Here I am, O Allah, here I am.”

And there are other similar examples. Thus, all the remembrance that Allah has prescribed consists of complete statements, not an isolated name, whether stated explicitly or represented by a pronoun.

This is what is called a kalimah (utterance) in Arabic usage, as in the Prophet’s words:

“Two utterances are light on the tongue, heavy in the Balance, and beloved to the Most Merciful: ‘Glory and praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah, the Magnificent.’”

And his words:

“The finest utterance spoken by a poet is the saying of Labīd: ‘Indeed, everything apart from Allah is destined to perish.’”

This also includes the words of Allah Most High:

“Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths,”

and the rest of the verse; and His words:

“The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.”

In these and similar instances where the term kalimah is used in the Quran and Sunnah—and indeed throughout Arabic speech—it means a complete sentence. Likewise, they used harf (word) to refer to a noun, saying, “This is an unfamiliar harf,” meaning that the noun itself is an unfamiliar word.

Sībawayh divided speech into a noun, a verb, and “a harf that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb.” Each of these categories is called a harf, but what distinguishes the third is that it conveys a meaning while being neither a noun nor a verb. He also applied the term harf to the letters of the alphabet, which are names. The term harf encompasses these names and others, as in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever recites the Quran and recites it correctly will receive, for every letter,

---

## Page 4813

ten good deeds. I do not say that alif-lām-mīm is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter.”

[Al-Khalīl asked his companions to pronounce the letter zāy in Zayd. They replied, “Zāy.” He said, “You have given its name; the letter itself is ‘z’.”] (*)

The grammarians subsequently adopted the convention of calling what ordinary Arabic calls a harf a kalimah (word), and of reserving the term harf (particle) for something that conveys a meaning but is neither a noun nor a verb, such as prepositions and similar particles. As for the spoken letters of the alphabet, the term harf sometimes denotes the actual letter within an utterance and sometimes the name of that letter. When this convention became predominant, those accustomed to it began to imagine that this was also how these terms were used in ordinary Arabic. Some of them consider kalimah to have more than one meaning in Arabic, denoting, for example, both a noun and a sentence. Yet in unambiguous Arabic usage, kalimah is known only in the sense of a complete sentence.

The point here is that the prescribed remembrance of Allah, glorified is He, consists of remembering Him through “a complete sentence.” This is what is termed kalām (speech), an individual instance of which is called a kalimah. It is this that benefits hearts and brings reward and recompense, nearness to Allah, knowledge of Him, love for Him, fear of Him, and other lofty aims and noble objectives.

As for restricting oneself to “an isolated name,” whether stated explicitly or represented by a pronoun, this has no foundation, let alone being a form of remembrance particular to the spiritual elite and those who know Allah. Rather, it leads to various innovations and forms of misguidance, and opens the way to conceiving corrupt spiritual states of the kind found among those who deviate from the faith and those who profess divine union, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

## Page 4814

Religion is summed up in “two principles”: that we worship none but Allah, and that we worship Him only as He has prescribed, not through innovations. As the Most High says:

“Whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

This is the realization of the “two testimonies of faith”: the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. The first requires that we worship none but Him; the second affirms that Muhammad is His Messenger, who conveys His message. We must therefore believe what he tells us and obey his commands. He has explained how we are to worship Allah, forbidden us from introducing innovations into religion, and told us that they are misguidance.

The Most High says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah and does good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Just as we are commanded to fear none but Allah, to rely on none but Allah, to direct our hopes to none but Allah, to seek help from none but Allah, and to worship none but Allah, so too are we commanded to follow the Messenger, obey him, and take him as our example. What is lawful is what he has declared lawful; what is forbidden is what he has forbidden; and religion is what he has prescribed. The Most High says:

“If only they had been satisfied with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah we turn in hope.’”

Thus, He attributes giving to both Allah and the Messenger, as He says:

“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.”

But He makes reliance upon Allah alone, saying:

“And had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us.’”

He did not say, “and His Messenger.” Likewise, He says in (the other verse):

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

Similar to this is His saying:

“O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers who follow you.”

That is,

---

## Page 4815

Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers, as He says:

“Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?”

Then He says:

“Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger.”

Thus, He attributes giving to both Allah and the Messenger, mentioning His bounty first, because bounty is in Allah’s hand: He grants it to whomever He wills, and Allah possesses immense bounty. His bounty extends to His Messenger and to the believers. He also says:

“Indeed, to Allah we turn in hope.”

Thus, He makes Allah alone the object of hope, as in His words:

“So when you have finished, strive in worship, and to your Lord alone turn in hope.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ibn ‘Abbās: “When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah.”

The Quran teaches this in numerous places. Allah makes worship, reverent fear, and mindfulness of Him due to Him alone, while making obedience and love due to both Allah and His Messenger. Thus Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“Worship Allah, be mindful of Him, and obey me.”

And Allah says:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah, and is mindful of Him—it is they who will triumph.”

There are many similar passages. The messengers were commanded that worship should be devoted to Him alone, that hope and reliance should be directed to Him, and that they themselves should be obeyed.

But Satan led the Christians and those like them astray, so they associated partners with Allah and disobeyed the Messenger:

“They took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, as well as the Messiah, son of Mary.”

They began directing their hopes to them, relying upon them, and asking of them, despite disobeying their commands and departing from their way. Allah, however, guided the believers sincerely devoted to Him, the people of the straight path, who recognized the truth and followed it,

---

## Page 4816

and thus were neither among those who incurred wrath nor among those who went astray. They devoted their religion sincerely to Allah, submitted themselves to Him, turned repentantly to their Lord, loved Him, hoped in Him, feared Him, asked of Him, directed their longing to Him, entrusted their affairs to Him, and relied upon Him. They obeyed His messengers, supported them, revered them, loved them, gave them their allegiance, followed them, walked in their footsteps, and were guided by their beacons.

That is the religion of Islam with which Allah sent all His messengers, from the first to the last. It is the only religion Allah accepts from anyone, and it is the true essence of worshipping the Lord of all worlds.

We therefore ask Allah the Almighty to keep us steadfast upon it, perfect it for us, and cause us and all our fellow Muslims to die upon it. All praise belongs to Allah alone. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

## Page 4817

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked about the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The supplication of my brother Jonah, the Man of the Fish, is: ‘There is no deity except You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.’ No one in distress offers this supplication without Allah relieving his distress.”

What does this supplication mean? Why does it dispel distress? Are there inward conditions that must accompany its utterance? How must the heart’s conviction accord with its meaning for it to bring about relief from affliction?

What is the relevance of his saying, “Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers,” when affirming Allah’s oneness brings relief from affliction? Is his acknowledgment sufficient, or must there also be repentance and firm resolve for the future? What is the underlying reason that affliction is relieved and removed when one ceases to place hope in created beings and becomes detached from them? How can the heart turn away entirely from placing hope in created beings and being attached to them, and instead become attached to Allah Most High, place its hope in Him, and turn wholly to Him? What helps one achieve this?

He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. In the Quran, the terms du‘ā and da‘wah (invocation) encompass two meanings: invocation as worship

---

## Page 4818

and invocation as petition.

Allah Most High says:

“So do not invoke another deity alongside Allah, lest you be among those who are punished.”

He also says:

“Whoever invokes another deity alongside Allah, for which he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will never prosper.”

And He says:

“Do not invoke another deity alongside Allah. There is no deity except Him.”

And He says:

“When the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost crowded around him in throngs.”

And He says:

“They invoke none besides Him but female deities, and they invoke none but a rebellious Satan.”

Allah Most High also says:

“To Him alone belongs the true invocation. Those whom they invoke besides Him do not respond to them at all. They are like someone stretching out his hands towards water for it to reach his mouth, but it will never reach it.”

And He says:

“Those who do not invoke another deity alongside Allah, nor kill a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse.”

At the end of the surah, He says:

“Say, ‘My Lord would not care for you were it not for your invocation.’”

This has been interpreted as: “Were it not for your calling upon Him,” and also as: “Were it not for His calling you.” A verbal noun may be attributed either to its subject or to its object. Attributing it to its subject, however, is stronger, because it must necessarily have a subject. This is therefore the stronger of the two interpretations. That is, He would not care for you were it not that you call upon Him, worshipping Him and asking of Him.

“But you have denied, so the punishment will be inescapable.”

That is, an inescapable punishment for those who deny the truth. The word salāh (prayer) originally means invocation in Arabic. Prayer is called invocation because it encompasses the meaning of invocation: worship and petition.

## Page 4819

Allah Most High’s words,

“Call upon Me; I will answer you,”

have been interpreted in both senses. One interpretation is: “Worship Me and obey My command; I will answer you.” As Allah Most High says:

“He answers those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

That is, He responds to them. This usage is well established in Arabic: both istajābahu and istajāba lahu mean “he answered him.” As the poet said:

A caller cried, “O you who answer the call to generosity!”
Yet no one answered him then.

The other interpretation is: “Ask of Me; I will give to you.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is reported to have said:

“Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: ‘Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who asks of Me, that I may give to him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?’”

He first mentions calling upon Him, then asking and seeking forgiveness. The one who seeks forgiveness is asking, just as the one who asks is calling upon Him. However, mentioning the one who asks for harm to be averted after the one who asks for good, and mentioning both after the one who calls upon Him—a description encompassing them both and others besides—is an instance of mentioning the specific after the general.

Allah Most High says:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the invocation of the one who calls upon Me when he calls upon Me.”

Every petitioner has hope and fear, and thus worships the One he petitions; and everyone who worships Him

## Page 4820

likewise has hope and fear, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment. Thus every worshipper is a petitioner, and every petitioner is a worshipper.

Either term encompasses the other when used alone. When they are used together, however, “petitioner” means someone who seeks to obtain benefit and avert harm through expressions of request and petition, while “worshipper” means someone who seeks this by obeying the command, even without using expressions of petition.

The worshipper who seeks Allah’s Face and to look upon Him likewise has hope and fear, longing and dread: he longs to attain what he seeks and dreads missing it. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope.”

It is inconceivable that anyone who calls upon Allah—whether through worship or petition—should be without longing and dread, fear and hope. As for the reported statement of some spiritual masters that fear and hope belong to the spiritual stations of ordinary believers, their intention may be understood as follows: those brought near to Allah seek His Face, aiming to delight in looking upon Him, even if there is no created thing there from which they derive pleasure. These people hope to attain what they seek and fear being deprived of it. Thus they are not without fear and hope; rather, what they hope for and fear corresponds to what they seek.

As for anyone among them who says:

“I have not worshipped You out of longing for Your Paradise or fear of Your Fire,”

## Page 4821

he assumes that Paradise denotes a place where one enjoys created things, and that the Fire denotes a place where there is no torment other than pain inflicted by created things. This reflects their deficient understanding of what Paradise encompasses. Rather, everything Allah has prepared for His allies belongs to Paradise, including looking upon Him. Hence, the best of creation used to ask Allah for Paradise and seek His protection from the Fire. When he asked one of his Companions what he said in his prayer, the man replied:

“I ask Allah for Paradise and seek Allah’s protection from the Fire. But I am not adept at your murmured supplications or those of Mu‘ādh.” He replied, “That is what our supplications revolve around.”

A group of speculative theologians objected to anyone who uttered these words—meaning, “I ask You for the pleasure of looking upon Your Face”—because they supposed that no pleasure could be taken in looking upon Allah, and that bliss could only come through something created. These people misunderstood the meaning of Paradise, just as the others did. Yet the others sought what deserves to be sought, whereas these people denied it.

As for suffering pain in the Fire, this is inevitable. Whoever says, “Were He to cast me into the Fire, I would be content,” is expressing his resolve to remain content. Yet resolves may crumble when confronted with reality. Statements of this kind occur in the words of various people, such as Sumnūn, who said:

“I have no wish for anything but You;
so test me however You will.”

He was then afflicted with difficulty urinating and began going around to schoolchildren, saying, “Pray for your lying uncle.”

Allah Most High says:

“You certainly longed for death before you encountered it. Now you have seen it with your own eyes.”

---

## Page 4822

Some who have discussed the defects of spiritual stations have classified love, contentment, fear, and hope as stations belonging to ordinary people. They base this on witnessing divine decree, holding that whoever witnesses divine decree and the oneness of divine action—until that which once was not vanishes and He who has never ceased to exist remains—passes beyond these things. This claim is flawed both in reality and according to revealed law.

As for reality, it is inconceivable that a living being should lack sensation, love for what suits it, or aversion to what is disagreeable to it. Anyone who says that a living being is equally indifferent to everything decreed is one of two people: either he does not understand what he is saying and is simply ignorant, or he stubbornly denies what is evident.

Even supposing that someone experiences a state that deprives him of his reason—whether called istilām, effacement, annihilation, fainting, or weakness—this does not eliminate his capacity for sensation altogether. He still senses what suits him and what is disagreeable to him. Even if his awareness of some things disappears, his awareness of everything has not disappeared.

Thus, whoever claims that someone witnessing Allah’s oneness in lordship enters the station of undifferentiated awareness and annihilation, and consequently perceives no distinctions, is mistaken. Distinction is inevitable, for it is a necessary feature of human existence. But if he abandons the distinctions prescribed by revealed law, he remains subject to those dictated by his natural inclinations. He is then following his desires rather than obeying his Lord.

---

## Page 4823

This is why, when “this question” arose among al-Junayd and his companions, he spoke to them of the “second distinction”: distinguishing between what is commanded and what is forbidden, and between what Allah loves and what He hates, while witnessing the all-encompassing divine decree. Thus, one perceives distinctions within that all-encompassing decree.

Whoever does not distinguish between what is commanded and what is forbidden has departed from the religion of Islam. Those who speak of undifferentiated awareness do not abandon the distinctions prescribed by revealed law altogether. If they did, they would be among the worst disbelievers. Such are those who go so far as to place the messengers and others on an equal footing, then proceed to profess the oneness of existence, making no distinction between the Creator and creation. Not all these people, however, reach this heresy. Rather, they distinguish in some respects but not others, sometimes obeying Allah and His Messenger and sometimes disobeying Allah and His Messenger, like other sinners among those who face the qiblah. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that the terms “invocation” and “supplication” encompass both kinds. Allah Most High says:

“And their final invocation will be, ‘All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”

The hadith states:

“The best remembrance is ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘All praise is due to Allah.’”

It was narrated by Ibn Mājah and Ibn Abī al-Dunyā.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others:

“The supplication of my brother Jonah, the Man of the Fish, was: ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except You. Glory be to You! I have indeed been among the wrongdoers.’ No one in distress invokes Allah with it without Allah relieving his distress.”

He called it a “supplication” because it encompasses both kinds of supplication. The words “There is no deity worthy of worship except You” acknowledge Allah’s exclusive right to worship.

## Page 4824

And acknowledging Allah’s exclusive right to worship encompasses one of the two kinds of supplication, for the true deity is the One worthy of being invoked through worship and through petition. That is Allah; there is no deity worthy of worship except Him.

The words:

“I have indeed been among the wrongdoers”

are an admission of sin, which implicitly includes a request for forgiveness. A person seeking something may ask explicitly, or may express the request as a statement describing his own condition, the attributes of the One being asked, or both. An example is the statement of Noah, peace be upon him:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. Unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.”

This is not phrased as a request. Rather, it is a statement concerning Allah: unless He forgives him and has mercy upon him, he will be lost. Yet this statement implicitly includes a request for forgiveness. The words of Adam, peace be upon him, belong to the same category:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and unless You forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Another example is the statement of Moses, peace be upon him:

“My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me.”

This describes his condition: he is in need of whatever good Allah sends down to him. It implicitly includes a request that Allah send good down to him.

Al-Tirmidhī and others narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If reciting the Quran keeps someone from remembering Me and asking of Me, I will give him better than what I give those who ask.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated it and said, “It is a good hadith.” Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith also narrated it, with the wording:

“If remembering Me keeps someone from asking of Me, I will give him better than what I give those who ask.”

## Page 4825

And I believe al-Bayhaqī narrated it with this wording, tracing it back to the Prophet.

Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah was asked about the saying:

“The best supplication on the Day of ‘Arafah is: There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.”

He mentioned this hadith and recited the verses of Umayyah ibn Abī al-Salt praising Ibn Jud‘ān:

“Must I state my need, or has your modesty spared me?
For modesty is your nature.
When a man praises you,

He said: “Here is a created being addressing another created being. How much more so, then, with the Creator, exalted is He!”

“O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You complaints are brought, Your help is sought, You are called upon for relief, and upon You we rely.”

This is a statement that implicitly includes a request. Another example is the saying of Job, peace be upon him:

“Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”

He described himself and his Lord in terms that implicitly ask for His mercy through the removal of his affliction. It is a statement that implicitly includes a request.

This exemplifies good manners in asking and supplicating. Thus, when someone says to a person whom he holds in esteem and to whom he turns for help: “I am hungry; I am

---

## Page 4826

ill,” this shows good manners in asking. Although saying “Feed me,” “Treat me,” and similar expressions formulated as requests constitutes a firm request of the person addressed, the former discloses and describes one’s condition with humility and need, implicitly asking through that condition; the latter expresses wholehearted desire and a direct request in the form of a petition.

When this form—the form of requesting and petitioning—is addressed to someone whom the petitioner needs, or is used by someone able to compel the person addressed, or in similar circumstances, it is uttered as a command: either because of the petitioner’s need or because of the benefit it offers the person addressed. But when it comes from one who is needy in every respect and is directed to the One who is self-sufficient in every respect, it is purely a plea, expressed with humility, need, and disclosure of one’s condition.

Describing one’s need and dependence is a request conveyed through one’s condition. It is more eloquent in conveying knowledge and making matters clear, whereas an explicit request is clearer in expressing intent and desire. For this reason, most supplication belongs to the second category: the petitioner conceives of what he seeks and desires, then requests and asks for it. His words signify the request directly and as their primary intent, stating it explicitly, even if they do not describe the condition of either the petitioner or the One petitioned.

If the request also describes the condition of both, it is more complete than either type alone. It includes the statement and knowledge that call for the request and its answer, as well as the intention and petition that constitute the request itself. It thus encompasses the request, that which calls for it, and the answer.

---

## Page 4827

as in what the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said to Abū Bakr al-Siddīq (may Allah be pleased with him), when he asked, “Teach me a supplication to recite in my prayer.” He said:

“Say: ‘O Allah, I have greatly wronged myself, and none forgives sins but You. So grant me forgiveness from Yourself and have mercy on me. Indeed, You are the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.’”

Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim included it in their Sahīh collections. This supplication describes the servant’s own condition, which makes him need forgiveness. It also describes his Lord in a way that establishes that none but Him can grant what is sought. It explicitly states the servant’s request and identifies what calls for an answer: the Lord’s forgiveness and mercy. This and similar supplications are the most complete forms of petition.

Many supplications contain some of these elements, such as the words of Moses (peace be upon him):

“You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us. You are the best of those who forgive.”

This combines a request with a description of the Protector in terms that call for an answer.

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

These describe his own condition and express a request.

And his words:

“Indeed, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.”

These describe a condition that implicitly conveys a request. These, then, are different forms, each with its own distinctive quality. One question remains: why was describing and stating their condition, rather than making an explicit request, more fitting for the man of the whale and others like him?

---

## Page 4828

The answer is:

Because this is a situation calling for the acknowledgment that whatever evil has befallen me is due to my sin. Sin is the root of the evil, while the aim is to remove the harm; seeking forgiveness is a secondary aim. He therefore did not explicitly ask for the harm to be removed, conscious that he had done wrong and acted unjustly, and that he himself had brought the harm upon himself. It was thus fitting for him to acknowledge his wrongdoing, thereby addressing what would remove its cause. Nor did he explicitly ask for forgiveness, because this is a secondary aim for the distressed servant, whereas relief from distress, while it is present, is his primary aim. By its nature, the soul seeks the relief it needs from present harm before seeking, as a secondary aim, deliverance from harm it fears may occur in the future. The primary aim in this situation is forgiveness and seeking relief from harm. This therefore takes precedence in his intention and desire, and the most effective means of attaining it is to remove its cause. Thus, he expressed what would achieve his aim.

This becomes clear through a discussion of his words:

“Glory be to You.”

This expression entails magnifying the Lord and declaring Him free of imperfection. Here, the situation calls for declaring Him free of injustice and of punishing someone without sin. He is saying: “You are holy and far above wronging me or punishing me without sin. Rather, I am the wrongdoer who has wronged himself.”

Allah Most High says:

“We did not wrong them, but they used to wrong themselves.”

Allah Most High also says:

“We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.”

And He says:

“We did not wrong them, but it was they who were the wrongdoers.”

And Adam (peace be upon him) said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

---

## Page 4829

Likewise, in the authentic hadith recorded by Muslim, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said in the opening supplication of prayer:

“O Allah, You are the King; none is worthy of worship but You. You are my Lord, and I am Your servant. I have wronged myself and acknowledged my sin, so forgive me all my sins, for none forgives sins but You.”

And in Sahīh al-Bukhārī:

“The foremost supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; none is worthy of worship but You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I abide by Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your blessings upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ Whoever says this in the morning with firm conviction and dies that day will enter Paradise. Whoever says it in the evening with firm conviction and dies that night will enter Paradise.”

The servant must therefore acknowledge Allah’s justice and goodness. He does not wrong people in the least, nor does He punish anyone except for their sin, and He bestows goodness upon them. Every punishment from Him is justice, and every blessing from Him is grace.

Thus, the words:

“None is worthy of worship but You”

affirm that He alone possesses divinity. Divinity entails the perfection of His knowledge, power, mercy, and wisdom, and thus affirms His goodness towards His servants. For “God” means the One who is worshipped, and the One who is worshipped is the One who deserves to be worshipped. He deserves to be worshipped because His attributes necessarily entail that He be loved with the utmost love and submitted to with the utmost submission. Worship encompasses the utmost love together with the utmost humility.

## Page 4830

The words:

such negation constitutes praise only when it entails an affirmation. Mere negation contains no praise. Denying evil and imperfection in Him necessarily entails affirming His excellent attributes and His perfection. To Allah belong the most beautiful names. Likewise, the Quran’s statements denying evil and imperfection in Him generally entail affirming His excellent attributes and His perfection.

For example, the Most High says:

Denying that drowsiness or sleep overtakes Him entails the perfection of His life and His sustaining of all things. His words:

entail the perfection of His power, and similarly in other instances. Thus, glorification, which declares Him free from evil and denies any imperfection in Him, entails exalting Him.

The words:

“Glory be to You”

therefore declare Him free from injustice and affirm the greatness that necessarily precludes injustice on His part. Whoever acts unjustly does so only out of a need for injustice or out of ignorance. Allah, however, has no need of anything and knows all things. He is inherently self-sufficient, while everything besides Him stands in need of Him. This is perfect greatness.

This supplication also contains both the affirmation of Allah’s sole right to worship and His glorification. The words:

“None is worthy of worship but You”

affirm His sole right to worship, while the words:

“Glory be to You”

glorify Him. It is also recorded in an authentic collection, on the authority of

## Page 4831

the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), who said:

“The finest words after the Quran are four phrases, which are themselves from the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; none is worthy of worship but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

Praising Allah is coupled with glorifying Him and follows it, while declaring His greatness is coupled with affirming His sole right to worship and follows it. It is recorded in an authentic collection that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked, “Which words are best?” He replied:

“Those Allah has chosen for His angels: ‘Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Him.’”

Both authentic collections record that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy in the Balance, and beloved to the Most Merciful: ‘Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Him’ and ‘Glory be to Allah, the Magnificent.’”

The Quran says:

“So glorify your Lord with praise.”

And the angels said:

“We glorify You with praise.”

Of these two phrases, one couples glorification with praise, and the other with an affirmation of His greatness. As we have explained, glorification denies evil and imperfections in Him, which entails affirming His excellent attributes and perfection. Praise is offered only for excellent qualities.

Praise and reverence are paired together, just as majesty and honor are paired together: not everything revered is loved and praised, nor is everything loved praised and revered. We have already explained that worship entails perfect love, which includes the meaning of praise, and perfect humility, which includes the meaning of reverence. Worship thus includes loving Him and praising Him for His excellent attributes, as well as humbling oneself before Him on account of His greatness and grandeur. It therefore includes venerating and honoring Him. He—glorified be He—is worthy of reverence and honor, and deserves the utmost veneration and the utmost honor.

---

## Page 4832

Some people suppose that “majesty” refers to negative attributes and “honor” to affirmative attributes, as al-Rāzī and others have stated. The correct understanding is that both refer to affirmative attributes, and affirming perfection entails negating its opposites. What is mentioned, however, comprises two kinds of affirmative attributes: those for which He deserves to be loved and those for which He deserves to be revered. Thus, He says:

“Indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.”

And Solomon, peace be upon him, said:

“Indeed, my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous.”

Likewise, He says:

“His is the dominion, and His is the praise.”

Many who possess dominion and wealth are not praised but condemned, for praise entails speaking of the one praised in terms of his lovable, excellent qualities. It thus entails speaking of the beloved’s excellent qualities out of love for him. Conversely, many who receive some measure of praise and love suffer from incapacity, weakness, and lowliness incompatible with greatness, self-sufficiency, and dominion. The former is held in awe and feared, but not loved; the latter is loved and praised, but neither held in awe nor feared. Perfection lies in combining both qualities. As a report states:

“The believer has been granted sweetness and awe-inspiring dignity.”

And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was described as follows:

“Whoever saw him for the first time stood in awe of him, and whoever came to know him through close association loved him.”

Thus, glorification is paired with praise, and affirming Allah’s sole right to worship is paired with declaring His greatness, as in the words of the call to prayer.

Moreover, each of the two kinds includes the other when mentioned on its own. Glorifying and praising Allah entail reverence and affirming the qualities for which He is praised. This entails His divinity, for divinity entails His being loved; indeed, it entails that none but He deserves perfect love. Praise consists in describing the one praised by the attributes for which he deserves to be loved. Thus, divinity

---

## Page 4833

entails perfect praise. For this reason, “All praise is due to Allah” is the opening of an address, and every matter of importance that is not begun with praise of Allah is cut short. “Glory be to Allah” affirms His greatness, as explained earlier. Hence He says:

“So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Make it part of your bowing.”

This was reported by the compilers of the Sunan collections. He also said:

This was reported by Muslim. He thus assigned the extolling of Allah’s greatness more particularly to bowing than to prostration, and glorification entails extolling His greatness. Accordingly, the words “Glory and praise be to Allah” affirm His freedom from imperfection, His greatness, His divinity, and praise of Him.

As for the words “There is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest,” the declaration “There is no god but Allah” affirms all His praiseworthy qualities, for they are all included in affirming His divinity. The words “Allah is greatest” affirm His greatness, for supreme majesty includes greatness, but supreme majesty is more complete.

For this reason, the prescribed wording in prayer and the call to prayer is “Allah is greatest,” for this is more complete than saying “Allah is most magnificent.” As recorded in the Sahīh, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Supreme majesty is My cloak, and greatness is My lower garment. Whoever contests either of them with Me, I shall punish him.’”

He thus likened greatness to the lower garment and supreme majesty to the cloak, and it is well known that the cloak is more honorable. Since declaring Allah’s supreme greatness is more emphatic than extolling His greatness, the former is stated explicitly and includes the latter. In the words “Glory be to Allah,” His freedom from evil is stated explicitly, and this entails extolling His greatness. Thus, each of the two expressions

## Page 4834

encompasses the meanings of the other two when uttered separately; when combined, each expression conveys its distinctive meaning. This, however, is by necessary implication. Each name denotes its distinctive attribute and the Divine Essence together by denoting the whole, and either one of them by denoting a constituent part.

include the meanings of the four expressions that constitute the best speech after the Quran. These expressions encompass the meanings of Allah’s most beautiful names and His sublime attributes, and thus contain perfect praise.

## Page 4835

are an admission of sin and constitute a plea for forgiveness, for this admission implicitly includes a request for forgiveness.

affirm Allah’s oneness in worship. For nothing brings about good except Allah’s will: whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and what obstructs it
