## Page 4836

on the servant’s part is his sins. Whatever lies beyond the servant’s power is from Allah. Although the servants’ actions occur by Allah Most High’s decree, Allah has made doing what He commands and refraining from what He forbids a means to salvation and happiness. Thus, the testimony to Allah’s oneness opens the door to good, while seeking forgiveness for sins closes the door to evil.

For this reason, the servant should place his hope in Allah alone and should not fear that Allah will wrong him:

“Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves.”

Rather, he should fear that Allah will requite him for his sins. This is the meaning of the statement reported from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Let no servant hope in anyone but his Lord, nor fear anything but his sin.”

A hadith traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, relates:

“He visited a sick man and asked, ‘How are you feeling?’ The man replied, ‘I place my hope in Allah and fear my sins.’ He said, ‘Whenever these two come together in a servant’s heart in such a situation, Allah grants him what he hopes for and protects him from what he fears.’”

Hope should therefore be placed in Allah, not in any created being, nor in the servant’s own strength or deeds. Placing one’s hope in anything other than Allah is to associate partners with Him. Although Allah has established means to that end, no means operates independently: it needs something to assist it, and whatever opposes and obstructs it must be prevented. It can come into being and endure only by the will of Allah Most High.

---

## Page 4837

For this reason, it has been said:

“Placing one’s reliance on means violates Allah’s oneness by associating partners with Him; denying that means have a causal role betrays a deficiency in reason; and disregarding means altogether undermines the revealed Law.”

For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“So when you have finished, strive hard, and direct your longing to your Lord.”

He thus commands that longing be directed to Him alone. He also says:

“And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers.”

The heart places its trust only in what it hopes in. Whoever places his hope in his strength, deeds, knowledge, condition, friend, relatives, teacher, authority, or wealth, without looking to Allah, has some degree of reliance on that means. No one ever places his hope or trust in a created being without having his expectations disappointed, for he is associating partners with Allah:

“Whoever associates partners with Allah—it is as though he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind swept him into a distant place.”

Likewise, the one who associates partners with Allah fears created beings and places his hopes in them, and so terror takes hold of him. As Allah Most High says:

“We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve because they have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority.”

Those who are free of associating partners with Allah attain security, as Allah Most High says:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that “wrongdoing” here means associating partners with Allah. In the Sahih, Ibn Masʿūd reports:

“When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They said, ‘Which of us has not wronged himself?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘This refers only to associating partners with Allah. Have you not heard the righteous servant’s words: “Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong”?’”

---

## Page 4838

And Allah Most High says:

“Among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah. If only the wrongdoers could see—as they will when they see the punishment—that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is severe in punishment.”

“When those who were followed disown their followers, they will see the punishment, and all ties between them will be severed.”

“Those who followed will say, ‘If only we could return, we would disown them just as they have disowned us.’ Thus Allah will show them their deeds as a source of bitter regret, and they will never leave the Fire.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say: Call upon those you claim to be gods besides Him. They have no power to remove your affliction or divert it.”

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of drawing near to their Lord, striving to be closest to Him. They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is something to beware of.”

For this reason, Allah mentions the means, yet commands that they not be relied upon and that hope be placed in Allah alone. When He sent down the angels, Allah Most High said:

“Allah made it only as good news for you and to reassure your hearts thereby. Victory comes only from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

He also says:

“If Allah helps you, none can overcome you. But if He forsakes you, who can help you after Him? So in Allah let the believers put their trust.”

We have already explained that supplication is of two kinds: the supplication of worship and the supplication of petition. Both must be directed to Allah alone. Whoever sets up another god alongside Allah will be left condemned and forsaken. One who hopes is asking and seeking; he must therefore place his hope in Allah alone, nor ask

---

## Page 4839

anyone else. For this reason, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said in an authentic hadith:

“Whatever of this wealth comes to you without your asking for it or looking expectantly for it, take it. Whatever does not, do not set your heart on it.”

The one who looks expectantly does so in his heart, while the one who asks does so with his tongue. In the hadith recorded in the two authentic collections, Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī said:

“We fell into poverty, so I went to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) to ask him for help. I found him addressing the people, saying: ‘O people, by Allah, whatever good we have, we will never withhold from you. Whoever seeks independence from others, Allah will make him independent; whoever refrains from asking, Allah will enable him to refrain; and whoever strives to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. No one has been given a gift better or more abundant than patience.’”

“Seeking independence” means not placing one’s hope in anyone in one’s heart and looking expectantly to him. “Refraining from asking” means not asking anyone with one’s tongue.

Thus, when Ahmad ibn Hanbal was asked about trusting in Allah, he replied: “Ceasing to look expectantly to created beings”—meaning that you should not harbour in your heart the expectation that someone will bring you something. He was asked: “What is the evidence for that?” He replied: “The words of Allah’s intimate friend when Gabriel asked him, ‘Do you need anything?’ and he answered, ‘From you, no.’”

This and similar accounts make clear that, in seeking what benefits him and warding off what harms him, the servant must direct his heart to Allah alone. Hence the distressed man said:

“There is no god but You.”

Similar to this is the report in the two authentic collections from Ibn ‘Abbās that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would say at times of distress:

“There is no god but Allah, the Magnificent, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne.

---

## Page 4840

There is no god but Allah, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the Noble Throne.”

These words affirm true monotheism, the servant’s worship of his Lord, and his placing his hope in Him alone, without partner. They take the form of a statement but convey a supplication.

Although people say with their tongues, “There is no god but Allah,” the servant’s saying it sincerely from his heart is an altogether different reality. His obedience to Allah becomes complete in proportion to how fully he realizes monotheism.

Allah Most High says:

“Have you seen the one who has taken his own desire as his god? Would you then be his guardian? Or do you think that most of them listen or understand? They are only like cattle—indeed, they are even further astray.”

Whoever makes his own desires the object of his worship has taken his desire as his god; that is, he has made whatever he desires his object of worship. This is the condition of the polytheists: each worships whatever appeals to him. They set up rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah. Hence Allah’s intimate friend said:

“I do not love those that set.”

His people did not deny the Creator. Rather, each of them worshipped whatever appealed to him and he thought would benefit him, such as the sun, the moon, and the stars. Allah’s intimate friend explained that whatever sets disappears from its worshipper and is concealed from him by intervening barriers. It neither sees its worshipper, nor hears his words, nor knows his condition, nor benefits or harms him, whether through some means or without them. What grounds, then, are there for worshipping something that sets?

The more fully the servant realizes sincerity in saying, “There is no god but Allah,” the more his heart is freed of

---

## Page 4841

the worship of whatever he desires, and acts of disobedience and sins are averted from him. As Allah Most High says:

“Thus We turned evil and indecency away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

He explains that evil and indecency were turned away from him because he was one of Allah’s chosen servants. These are the ones of whom He says:

“Indeed, you have no authority over My servants.”

And Satan said:

“By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your chosen servants among them.”

It is established in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever says, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ sincerely from his heart, Allah will forbid the Fire to touch him.”

Sincerity removes the causes of entering the Fire. Thus, anyone who enters the Fire despite saying, “There is no god but Allah,” has not fully attained the sincerity in these words that would protect him from the Fire. Rather, his heart contained some element of associating partners with Allah, which led him to commit what caused him to enter the Fire. Associating partners with Allah is more imperceptible within this community than the creeping of ants.

For this reason, the servant is commanded to say in every prayer:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Satan commands the association of partners with Allah, and the soul obeys him in this. The soul continually turns toward something other than Allah, either fearing it or placing its hopes in it. Thus, the servant remains ever in need of purifying his monotheism of the taints of associating partners with Allah.

In the hadith narrated by Ibn Abī ‘Āsim and others, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Satan says: ‘I destroyed people through sins, but they destroyed me through “There is no god but Allah” and seeking forgiveness. When I saw that, I spread whims and desires among them, so they sin without seeking forgiveness, because they think they are doing good.’”

---

## Page 4842

Thus, whoever follows his desires without guidance from Allah shares in the condition of one who takes his own desire as his god. He thereby harbours an element of associating partners with Allah that prevents him from seeking forgiveness. As for whoever truly affirms Allah’s oneness and seeks His forgiveness, evil will certainly be removed from him. This is why Jonah said:

“There is no god but You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

This is also why Allah links monotheism with seeking forgiveness in several places, as in His words, Most High:

“So know that there is no god but Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women.”

And His words:

“Worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am a warner and bearer of good tidings to you from Him.”

“And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then repent to Him.”

And His words:

“And to ‘Ād We sent their brother Hūd. He said, ‘O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.’”

Further on, He says:

“And, O my people, seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then repent to Him.”

And His words:

“So be steadfast in your devotion to Him and seek His forgiveness.”

The supplication for concluding a gathering is:

“Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. I bear witness that there is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and repent to You.”

If it is a gathering of mercy, this serves as a seal upon it; if it is a gathering of idle talk, it serves as an expiation for it. It has also been narrated that this supplication is recited at the end of ablution, after saying:

“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. O Allah, make me among those who constantly repent, and make me among those who purify themselves.”

This remembrance includes monotheism and seeking forgiveness, for it begins with the two testimonies of faith

---

## Page 4843

which are the two foundations of the religion and encompass it in its entirety. Indeed, the whole religion is contained in the “two testimonies of faith,” for their meaning is that we worship none but Allah and obey His Messenger. The whole “religion” is contained in this: worshipping Allah by obeying Him and His Messenger. Everything obligatory or recommended falls within obedience to Allah and His Messenger.

It has been narrated that one says:

“Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. I bear witness that there is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and repent to You.”

This is the expiation for a gathering, and it has been prescribed both at the conclusion of a gathering and at the end of ablution. Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would conclude the prayer as described in the authentic hadith, which states that he would say at the end of his prayer:

“O Allah, forgive my past and future sins, what I have concealed and what I have made public, and what You know better than I. You are the One who brings forward and the One who puts back. There is no god but You.”

Here, he began with supplication and concluded with the affirmation of Allah’s oneness, because supplication is commanded at the end of the prayer. He concluded with the affirmation of Allah’s oneness so that he would end the prayer with the better of the two. Where this particular purpose is not intended, however, it is better to begin with the affirmation of Allah’s oneness.

Supplication consisting of praise and worship is, as a category, superior to supplication consisting of asking and requesting. Nevertheless, what is generally less excellent may take precedence over what is more excellent in a particular setting, owing to a specific reason or other considerations. Thus, prayer is superior to recitation, recitation is superior to remembrance consisting of praise, and remembrance is superior to supplication consisting of requests. Even so, the less excellent act has particular places and times

---

## Page 4844

and circumstances in which it is superior to the more excellent act. Yet religion, from beginning to end, outwardly and inwardly, consists in affirming Allah’s oneness and devoting all religion sincerely to Him. This is the true realization of the declaration, “There is no god but Allah.” Although Muslims share in acknowledging this declaration, they differ in the extent to which they truly realize it, to a degree we cannot measure. Indeed, many of them imagine that the obligatory affirmation of Allah’s oneness consists merely in acknowledging and believing that Allah is the Creator and Lord of everything. They do not distinguish between acknowledging Allah’s oneness in His lordship—which the Arab polytheists acknowledged—and affirming His exclusive right to worship, to which the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, called them. Nor do they combine affirming Allah’s oneness in word with doing so in deed.

The polytheists did not say that the universe was created by two creators, or that alongside Allah there was another lord who independently created anything without Him. Rather, they were as Allah described them:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’”

And He, the Exalted, said:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating partners with Him.”

And He, the Exalted, said:

“Say, ‘To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then take heed?’”

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Great Throne?’”

“They will say, ‘They belong to Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then fear Him?’”

“Say, ‘In whose hand is the dominion of all things, who protects while none can protect against Him, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘All belongs to Allah.’ Say, ‘How then are you deluded?’”

Yet despite acknowledging that Allah alone is the Creator, they would set up gods alongside Him

---

## Page 4845

—other gods whom they took as intercessors with Him. They would say, “We worship them only so that they may bring us nearer to Allah.” And they loved them as they loved Allah.

Associating partners with Allah in love, worship, supplication, and petition is distinct from associating partners with Him in belief and acknowledgment. As the Exalted said:

“Yet among people are those who take others as equals to Allah, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Whoever loves a created being as he loves the Creator has associated that being with Him: he has taken others as equals to Allah, loving them as he loves Allah, even though he acknowledges that Allah is his Creator. For this reason, Allah and His Messenger distinguished between someone who loves a created being for Allah’s sake and someone who loves a created being alongside Allah. For the former, Allah is the One he loves and worships, the ultimate object of his love and worship; he loves no other alongside Him. Yet because he knows that Allah loves His prophets and righteous servants, he loves them for His sake. Likewise, because he knows that Allah loves the fulfillment of His commands and the avoidance of His prohibitions, he loves these things. Thus, his love for what Allah loves follows from his love for Allah, branches out from it, and forms part of it.

This is unlike someone who loves another alongside Allah, making that being an equal to Allah: he places his hopes in him and fears him, or obeys him without knowing that obedience to him constitutes obedience to Allah. He takes him as an intercessor for himself without knowing that Allah permits that intercessor to intercede on his behalf. The Exalted said:

“They worship besides Allah that which neither harms nor benefits them, and they say, ‘These are our intercessors with Allah.’”

---

## Page 4846

And the Exalted said:

“They took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, as well as the Messiah, son of Mary, although they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no god but Him. Glory be to Him, far above what they associate with Him!”

‘Adī ibn Hātim said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “They did not worship them.” He replied, “They declared forbidden things lawful for them, and they obeyed them; they declared lawful things forbidden to them, and they obeyed them. That was their worship of them.”

The Exalted said:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

And the Exalted said:

“On the Day when the wrongdoer bites his hands, saying, ‘If only I had taken a path with the Messenger! Woe to me! If only I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend! He led me away from the Reminder after it had come to me.’ And Satan ever forsakes man.”

Obedience to the Messenger is obligatory, for whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah. What is lawful is what he has declared lawful; what is forbidden is what he has forbidden; and religion is what he has prescribed. As for anyone other than the Messenger—scholars, religious teachers, rulers, and kings—obedience to them is obligatory only when obeying them constitutes obedience to Allah. When Allah and His Messenger command obedience to them, obeying them falls within obedience to the Messenger. The Exalted said:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

He did not say, “And obey the Messenger and obey those in authority among you.” Rather, He made obedience to those in authority part of obedience to the Messenger, and obedience to the Messenger obedience to Allah. He repeated the verb “obey” with respect to the Messenger, but not with respect to those in authority, for whoever obeys the Messenger

---

## Page 4847

has obeyed Allah. When the Messenger commands something, no one is entitled to consider whether Allah has commanded it or not. Those in authority are different: they may command disobedience to Allah, so not everyone who obeys them is obeying Allah. Rather, what they command must be known not to constitute disobedience to Allah, and one must consider whether Allah has commanded it or not. This applies whether those in authority are scholars or rulers. It includes following scholars’ judgments, obeying the commanders of military detachments, and other such matters. In this way, religion is entirely for Allah. The Exalted said:

“And fight them until there is no more persecution and religion is entirely for Allah.”

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, a man fights to display bravery, another out of partisan zeal, and another to show off. Which of these is fighting in Allah’s cause?” he replied:

“Whoever fights so that Allah’s word is supreme is fighting in Allah’s cause.”

Many people love a caliph, a scholar, a religious teacher, or a ruler and make him a rival to Allah, even though they may say that they love him for Allah’s sake. Whoever regards obedience to anyone other than the Messenger as obligatory in everything he commands and forbids, even when it conflicts with the command of Allah and His Messenger, has made him a rival to Allah. He may even treat him as the Christians treat the Messiah: calling upon him, seeking his aid, allying himself with his allies, and showing enmity to his enemies, while insisting that he must be obeyed in everything he commands and forbids, and in whatever he declares lawful or forbidden. He thus puts him in the place of Allah and His Messenger. This is a form of associating partners with Allah, and those who practise it fall within the words of the Exalted:

“Yet among people are those who take others as rivals to Allah, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

---

## Page 4848

Thus, both monotheism and associating partners with Allah can involve the heart’s affirmations and its actions. This is why al-Junayd said:

“Monotheism is the heart’s affirmation, and reliance upon Allah is the heart’s action.”

By this he meant monotheism in the sense of assent: when he coupled it with reliance upon Allah, he made it the foundation of that reliance. When the term “monotheism” is used on its own, however, it encompasses both the heart’s affirmations and its actions. Reliance upon Allah is part of the perfection of monotheism.

The term “faith” is similar. When used on its own, it includes both inward and outward actions. Hence the statement, “Faith consists of speech and action,” meaning the affirmations of the heart, the speech of the tongue, and the actions of the heart and limbs. An example is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Faith has sixty-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

Another example is the saying of the Exalted:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

And His words:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

“Those who establish prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them.”

“It is they who are truly believers.”

And His words:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission.”

“Faith in its unrestricted sense” includes Islam, as reported in the two Sahīh collections, where the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“I command you to believe in Allah. Do you know what it means to believe in Allah? It is to testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah

---

## Page 4849

and to establish prayer, give zakat, and pay one-fifth of the spoils you acquire.” This is why some of the early generations said: “Every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer.”

When, however, the term “faith” is coupled with action or Islam, a distinction is made between them, as in the words of the Exalted:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds…”

This occurs frequently in the Quran. Another example is the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the authentic hadith in which Gabriel asked him about Islam, faith, and excellence in worship. He said:

“Islam is to testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House.”

He asked, “Then what is faith?”

He replied, “To believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death, and to believe in the divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

He asked, “Then what is excellence in worship?”

He replied, “To worship Allah as though you see Him; for even though you do not see Him, He sees you.”

In this text, he distinguished between Islam and faith because he mentioned the two terms together. In the earlier text, he included Islam within faith because he mentioned faith alone. The same applies to the term “action,” for the Islam mentioned here is a form of action. Outward action is the necessary consequence of the heart’s faith and is entailed by it. Thus, when faith is present in the heart, faith is necessarily expressed through the limbs. The heart’s faith must include both its assent and its submission. Otherwise, if someone’s heart assented that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, while he hated him, envied him, and was too arrogant to follow him, his heart would not have believed.

Although “faith” includes assent, it is not synonymous with it. Thus, one does not say

---

## Page 4850

of everyone who assents to something, “He has faith in it.” If someone said, “I accept as true that one is half of two, that the sky is above us and the earth beneath us,” or similar things that people observe and know, he would not be described as having faith in these things. Rather, this expression is used only in connection with someone reporting matters beyond direct observation, as Joseph’s brothers said:

“You will not believe us.”

They were reporting to him something he had not witnessed. They distinguish between believing someone and believing in something: the former expression applies to the person giving the report, and the latter to what is reported. Thus Joseph’s brothers said:

“You will not believe us.”

And the Exalted said:

“None believed Moses except some of his people’s offspring.”

The Exalted also said:

“Among them are those who offend the Prophet and say, ‘He listens to everyone.’ Say, ‘His listening is for your good: he believes in Allah and believes the believers.’”

He thus distinguished between his believing in Allah and his believing the believers, for the latter means that he accepts what the believers tell him as true, whereas his believing in Allah is a matter of acknowledging Him.

Another example is what the Exalted relates of Pharaoh and his chiefs:

“Shall we believe two human beings like ourselves?”

That is, shall we acknowledge them and accept what they say as true? Another example is His saying:

“Do you then hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the words of Allah and then knowingly distort them after understanding them?”

Another is the saying of the Exalted:

“So Lot believed him, and he said, ‘I am emigrating to my Lord.’”

Examples of the other meaning include the saying of the Exalted:

“They believe in the unseen.”

And His saying:

“The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’”

And His saying:

“Rather, righteousness is found in one who believes

---

## Page 4851

in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets.” That is, he acknowledges these things. There are many such examples in the Quran.

The point here is that the word īmān (faith) is used only in relation to certain kinds of reports. It is derived from amn (security), just as iqrār (acknowledgment) is derived from qarra (to become settled). Thus, the believer possesses security, just as the one who acknowledges possesses acknowledgment. This necessarily involves the heart acting in accordance with what it accepts as true. If someone knows that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, but this knowledge is not accompanied by love and reverence for him—rather, he hates and envies him and is too arrogant to follow him—then he does not believe in him; rather, he disbelieves in him.

The disbelief of Iblīs, Pharaoh, and those among the People of the Book who recognize him as they recognize their own sons, as well as others, falls into this category. Iblīs did not deny the truth of any report or reject any bearer of a report as untruthful; rather, he arrogantly refused to obey his Lord’s command.

Concerning Pharaoh and his people, Allah said:

“They denied them, though their souls were certain of them, out of injustice and arrogance.”

Moses said to him:

“You certainly know that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent these down as clear proofs.”

The Exalted also said:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their own sons.”

Thus, the heart’s mere knowledge of the truth does not benefit a person unless it is accompanied by the heart acting in accordance with that knowledge, such as loving the truth and following it. Indeed, the person most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection will be a scholar whom Allah did not cause to benefit from his knowledge. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to

---

## Page 4852

say:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that brings no benefit, a soul that is never satisfied, a supplication that goes unheard, and a heart that does not humble itself.”

The Jahmiyyah, however, supposed that knowledge and assent in the heart alone constitute faith, and that whenever revelation indicates that someone is not a believer, this indicates that his heart lacks knowledge. This is among the gravest forms of ignorance, judged by both revelation and reason. In reality, this view entails equating the believer with the disbeliever.

For this reason, Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other imams pronounced them disbelievers on this account. It is well known that a person may know the truth yet hate it because of some other interest. Not everyone who arrogantly refuses to accept the truth is ignorant of it. Faith, therefore, necessarily includes both the heart’s assent and its action. This is the meaning of the early generations’ statement: “Faith consists of speech and action.”

Furthermore, when the heart truly possesses assent and complete love that entails willing, outward actions necessarily follow. For when firm resolve is accompanied by full ability, what is willed will certainly occur. An action fails to occur only because either the ability or the will is incomplete; when both are complete, voluntary action must follow. Thus, if the heart fully acknowledges that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and loves him completely, it is impossible for a person not to utter the two testimonies of faith while being able to do so. But if he is unable because of muteness or the like, or because of fear or the like, then he lacks the ability to utter them.

---

## Page 4853

And although “Abū Tālib” knew that Muhammad was the Messenger of Allah and loved him, his love for him did not arise from love for Allah. Rather, he loved him because he was his nephew: his love was based on kinship. If he wished him to prevail, it was because of the honor and leadership this would bring him. Thus, what he fundamentally loved was leadership. For this reason, when the two testimonies of faith were presented to him as death approached, he saw that professing them would mean abandoning the religion he loved. His religion was dearer to him than his nephew, so he did not profess them.

Had he loved him because he was the Messenger of Allah, as did Abū Bakr, of whom Allah said:

“But the most righteous will be kept away from it—he who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay anyone for a favor, but only seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be pleased.”

—and as did the other believers in him, such as ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, and others, he would certainly have uttered the two testimonies of faith. His love was therefore love alongside Allah, not love for Allah’s sake. This is why Allah did not accept his support and assistance for the Messenger: he did not do it for Allah’s sake. Allah accepts only deeds done seeking His Face, unlike the one who acted seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High.

This confirms that “faith and monotheism” necessarily entail action of the heart, such as love. Religious devotion must therefore be sincerely dedicated to Allah alone. Religion cannot truly be religion without action, for religion includes obedience and worship.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed the two surahs of sincere devotion:

“Say, ‘O disbelievers,’”

and

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’”

One concerns affirming Allah’s oneness in speech and knowledge; the other concerns affirming His oneness in action

## Page 4854

and will. Concerning the former, He said:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One;
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor is born,
nor is there anyone comparable to Him.’”

He thus commanded him to declare this affirmation of His oneness. Concerning the latter, He said:

nor do you worship what I worship.

nor do you worship what I worship.
For you is your religion, and for me is mine.’”

He thus commanded him to declare that which entails disavowing the worship of anything other than Allah and devoting worship sincerely to Allah alone.

“Worship” is rooted in intention and will. When mentioned on its own, worship includes reliance upon Allah and similar acts. When mentioned alongside reliance upon Allah, however, reliance becomes a distinct category alongside worship, as we explained regarding the term “faith.” Allah Most High said:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

And Allah Most High said:

“O mankind, worship your Lord.”

These and similar statements encompass carrying out what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden; reliance upon Allah is included in this. Yet elsewhere He said:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

And He said:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

This occurs frequently in the Quran: a term’s scope varies, becoming broader or narrower depending on whether it appears on its own or alongside another term. Such is the case with the terms “right and wrong.” He said:

“You are the best nation brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said:

“The believing men and believing women are allies of one another: they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said:

“He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong.”

---

## Page 4855

Thus, “wrong” includes whatever Allah dislikes, just as “right” includes whatever Allah loves. Elsewhere, He said:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from immorality and wrongdoing.”

He thus mentioned wrongdoing alongside immorality; here, wrongdoing includes oppression. Elsewhere, He said:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice, good conduct, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.”

Here He mentioned immorality and oppression alongside wrongdoing. The terms “the poor and the needy” belong to the same category: when either occurs alone, it includes the other; when they occur together, a distinction arises between them. In the former case, however, one term is broader than the other, whereas here they stand in a relation of generality and specificity.

Loving Allah alone, relying upon Him alone, fearing Allah alone, and similar acts all fall within affirming the oneness of Allah Most High. Concerning love, Allah Most High said:

“Yet among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Say, ‘If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your relatives, wealth you have acquired, trade whose decline you fear, and homes you cherish are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command.’”

And Allah Most High said:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah, and is mindful of Him—it is they who will triumph.”

He thus made obedience due to Allah and His Messenger, while making fear and mindfulness due to Allah alone. Allah Most High also said:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us out of

---

## Page 4856

His bounty, and so will His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah alone we turn in hope.’” Allah Most High also said:

“So when you have finished, strive diligently.”

“And to your Lord alone turn your hopes.”

Thus, He made Allah alone the One to be regarded as sufficient and the One to whom hopes are directed. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

(The point) here is that saying, “There is no deity but You,” affirms that divinity belongs to Allah alone. This entails affirming Allah’s truthfulness in both word and deed. The polytheists acknowledged that Allah is the Lord of everything, yet they set up other gods alongside Him and did not acknowledge divinity as His alone.

Affirming that divinity belongs to Him alone requires that none but Him be worshipped and that supplication be addressed to none but Him, as in His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

A person may intend to ask Allah alone and rely upon Him, but in matters that Allah does not love—indeed, that He dislikes and forbids. Although such a person directs his requests and reliance exclusively to Allah, he is not sincere in worshipping and obeying Him. This is the condition of many people with corrupt spiritual orientations who experience unveilings and exercise powers contrary to the command of Allah and His Messenger: they are given assistance in these matters.

Many of them seek Allah’s help in these pursuits. Yet because these pursuits do not accord with the command of Allah and His Messenger, they receive a share of worldly gains, but their ultimate outcome is evil. Allah Most High said:

“When distress befalls you at sea, all those you invoke are forgotten except Him. But when He brings you safely to land, you turn away. Man is ever ungrateful.”

Allah Most High also said: “And when a person is touched by

---

## Page 4857

distress, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, sitting, or standing. But when We relieve his distress, he goes on as though he had never called upon Us to remove the distress that afflicted him.”

Another group may intend to obey Allah and His Messenger, yet fail to rely fully upon Him and seek His help. They are rewarded for their good intentions and obedience, but are left without aid in their pursuits because they have not truly sought Allah’s help and relied upon Him. Thus, a person of this kind is afflicted at times with weakness and anxiety, and at other times with self-admiration. If he fails to attain the good he seeks, it is because of his weakness, and he may become anxious. If he attains what he seeks, he looks to himself and his own strength, becoming self-admiring. He may also become impressed with his own condition and assume that he will attain his goal, only to be left without aid.

Allah Most High said:

“And on the day of Hunayn, when your great numbers pleased you, yet they availed you nothing; the earth, vast as it was, became straitened for you, and then you turned and fled.”

The passage continues to His words:

“Then, after that, Allah turns in mercy to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

People often combine showing off with self-admiration. Showing off is a form of associating created beings with Allah, while self-admiration is a form of associating oneself with Him. This is the condition of the arrogant person. The one who shows off does not truly fulfil His words:

“You alone we worship,”

while the self-admiring person does not truly fulfil His words:

“And You alone we ask for help.”

Whoever truly fulfils His words, “You alone we worship,” frees himself from showing off; and whoever truly fulfils His words, “And You alone we ask for help,” frees himself from self-admiration. The well-known hadith states:

“Three things bring ruin: avarice that is obeyed, desire that is followed, and a person’s admiration of himself.”

---

## Page 4858

And worse than either of these groups are those who neither worship Allah nor seek His help, but worship others and seek their help. These associate partners with Allah in both respects. Among them are those who associate devils with Allah, such as people who experience satanic states. They do what the devils love, including lying and wickedness; they call upon Him with supplications pleasing to the devils, and recite conjurations that the devils obey and that involve associating partners with Allah. They have been discussed at length elsewhere. Such people may perform extraordinary feats thought to be miraculous gifts granted to Allah’s righteous servants, when in fact they belong to the states experienced by sorcerers and soothsayers. It is therefore essential to distinguish between states rooted in faith and the Quran, states arising from the soul, and satanic states.

As for the fourth category, these are the people of monotheism who devote their religion sincerely to Allah: they worship none but Him and rely upon none but Him.

When a distressed person says,

“There is no god worthy of worship but You,”

he may be mindful of one of the two forms of monotheism but not the other. Those upon whom Allah has perfected His favour are mindful of both. A distressed person is intent upon warding off harm and securing benefit, so he may say,

“There is no god worthy of worship but Allah,”

with the awareness that none but You can remove harm, and none but You can bestow blessings. Such a person is mindful of Allah’s oneness in His lordship, and of singling Him out in supplication, petition, and reliance, while turning away from singling Him out in worship, which Allah loves, is pleased with, and commands

---

## Page 4859

—namely, worshipping none but Him, and worshipping Him only through obedience to Him and His Messenger. Whoever is mindful of this when he says,

“There is no god worthy of worship but You,”

is worshipping Allah and relying upon Him, and is complying with His words:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him”; 

“Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn”; 

“Remember the name of your Lord, and devote yourself entirely to Him”; 

“Lord of the east and the west; there is no god worthy of worship but Him, so take Him as the Disposer of your affairs.”

If what he seeks is forbidden, he incurs sin even if his need is met. If he seeks something permissible without intending to use it to help him obey and worship Allah, he incurs neither sin nor reward. But if he seeks something that will help him obey and worship Allah, intending to use it for that purpose, he earns reward.

This is one of the distinctions between the servant-messenger and his successors, on the one hand, and the prophet-king, on the other. Our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was given the choice of being a prophet-king or a servant-messenger, and he chose to be a servant-messenger.

The servant-messenger does only what he is commanded to do, so all his actions are worship of Allah. He is wholly a servant, carrying out the commands of the One who sent him. Thus, it is authentically reported from him in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that he said:

“By Allah, I give nothing to anyone, nor do I withhold anything from anyone. I am only a distributor, placing it where I am commanded.”

By saying, “I give nothing to anyone, nor do I withhold,” he did not mean that Allah alone determines this through His decree and governance of creation, for all created beings share this condition: no one gives or withholds except by Allah’s decree and predestination. Rather, he meant that Allah alone directs this through His religious law. That is, I give only to those whom I have been commanded

---

## Page 4860

to give to, and I withhold only from those from whom I have been commanded to withhold. Thus, I obey Allah in both giving and withholding. He therefore distributes charity, fayʾ revenues, and spoils of war just as he distributes inheritances among those entitled to them, because Allah has commanded him to make this distribution.

Hence, whenever wealth is attributed to Allah and His Messenger, what is meant is wealth that must be spent in obedience to Allah and His Messenger. It does not mean that it is the Messenger’s property, as some jurists have supposed. Nor does it mean that Allah owns it by virtue of His creation and decree, for all wealth is His in that sense.

This is illustrated by His words:

“Say, ‘The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger.’”

And His words:

“And know that whatever spoils you acquire, one-fifth belongs to Allah and the Messenger”—to the end of the verse.

And His words:

“As for whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you spurred neither horses nor camels to obtain it,”

through to His words:

“Whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah, the Messenger, and near relatives”—to the end of the verse.

Thus, concerning fayʾ, He mentioned the same recipients He mentioned concerning the fifth. Some jurists therefore supposed that attributing this wealth to the Messenger meant that he owned it just as people own their property.

Some of them then said that the spoils of Badr were the Messenger’s property. Others said that the fayʾ and four-fifths of it were the Messenger’s property. Others said that the Messenger was entitled only to one-fifth of the fifth. Some of the latter also said that he was likewise entitled to one-fifth of the fifth of the fayʾ.

These views appear in the writings of groups of scholars among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfa, and others. This is mistaken on several grounds:

---

## Page 4861

One is that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not own these funds as people own their property, nor did he dispose of them as kings dispose of their possessions. Both private owners and kings may spend their wealth on permissible things: the former for their personal purposes, and the latter in the interests of their kingdom. Such was the position of a prophet who was also a king, like David and Solomon. Allah Most High said:

“So give or withhold without account.”

That is: give to whomever you wish and withhold from whomever you wish; you will not be called to account. Our Prophet, however, was a servant and Messenger: he gave only to those whom he was commanded to give to, and withheld only from those from whom he was commanded to withhold. Thus, he spent wealth only in worship of Allah and obedience to Him.

(Another) is that a prophet’s property is not inherited, even if he is a king, for the prophets leave no inheritance. If even the kings among the prophets did not own wealth as people ordinarily own their property, how could the foremost of the Messengers, who was a servant and Messenger, have been an owner in that sense?

(Another) is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spent on himself and his dependants only what they needed, spending all the remaining wealth in obedience to Allah and retaining no surplus for himself. This is not how property owners act. Rather, all the wealth he administered was the wealth of Allah and His Messenger, meaning that Allah commanded His Messenger to spend it in obedience to Him. It is therefore obligatory to obey him in its distribution, just as it is obligatory to obey him in everything else he commands. For whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah, and in this he conveys Allah’s commands.

---

## Page 4862

The funds that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, distributed were of two kinds:

Some had designated beneficiaries and prescribed uses, as in the case of inheritances. Others required his judgment, deliberation, and assessment. For some of Allah’s commands are precisely defined by religious law, such as the five daily prayers and making seven circuits around the House. In other cases, the amount is left to the judgment of the person commanded, who increases or decreases it according to the benefit pleasing to Allah.

Some matters of this kind are agreed upon, while others are disputed. For example, the jurists disagree about the maintenance owed to wives: is it fixed by religious law, or is it determined by customary practice, so that its amount and nature vary according to people’s circumstances?

The majority of jurists hold the second view, which is correct, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Hind:

“Take what suffices for you and your child, according to what is reasonable.”

He also said in his well-known sermon:

“Women are entitled to their clothing and maintenance according to what is reasonable.”

Likewise, they also disagree about what is required for expiations: is it fixed by religious law or determined by customary practice?

Thus, the distribution of wealth ascribed to Allah and the Messengers was governed by the command of

---

## Page 4863

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, unlike wealth whose beneficiaries were specified, such as inheritances. Hence, in the year of Hunayn, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I am entitled to nothing of the spoils Allah has granted you except one-fifth, and that fifth is returned to you.”

That is, only the fifth was his to distribute according to his own judgment and discretion. Hence his words:

“And it is returned to you.”

This differs from the remaining four-fifths of the spoils, which belong to those who took part in the battle. Thus, commanders would distribute the spoils among those who had acquired them, while the fifth would be sent to the rightly guided caliphs who succeeded the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in leading his community, to be distributed at their command. As for the four-fifths, the caliphs were consulted only to ascertain the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, just as someone seeks a legal opinion, and just as they were consulted concerning prescribed punishments to determine what religious law required.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave those whose hearts were to be won over what he gave them from the spoils of Hunayn. It has been said that this came from the fifth, and it has also been said that it came from the spoils as a whole. According to the latter view, he did so because the believers willingly accepted it. Hence, he answered those of the Ansār who expressed resentment in a way that dispelled their resentment, and he intended to compensate them for it. Some hold that, before their distribution, the spoils do not yet belong to those who acquired them, and that the ruler may dispose of them according to his judgment, as discussed elsewhere.

The purpose here is to explain the condition of someone who is wholly Allah’s servant: he worships Him and seeks His help, acting for His sake and seeking His assistance, thereby putting His words into practice:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

This affirms Allah’s oneness in worship and His oneness in lordship. Although

---

## Page 4864

divinity encompasses lordship, and lordship necessarily implies divinity, the fact that either term includes the other when used alone does not prevent each from bearing its distinct meaning when used alongside the other. Thus Allah says:

“Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,
the Sovereign of mankind,
the God of mankind.”

And He says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

He thus brings together the two names: God and Lord. “God” is the One who is worshipped and deserves to be worshipped, while “Lord” is the One who nurtures His servant and directs his affairs. Hence worship is associated with His name Allah, and supplication with His name Lord. Worship is the ultimate purpose for which creation was created. Divinity is the ultimate end, whereas lordship encompasses creating creatures and bringing them into being, and thus encompasses the beginning of their existence.

When someone praying says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,”

he places the intended purpose, which is the ultimate end, before the means, which is the starting point. Worship is the end sought, and seeking help is the means to it: the former is the underlying purpose, and the latter is the cause. The distinction between a final cause and an efficient cause is well known. Hence the saying: “What comes first in thought comes last in action, and what comes first in aspiration comes last in attainment.” The final cause therefore comes first in conception and intention, but last in actual existence.

The believer intends from the outset to worship Allah, knowing that this can only be accomplished with His help. He therefore says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Since worship is associated with the name Allah, Exalted is He, the prescribed words of remembrance employ this name, such as the words of the call to prayer:

“Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest.”

Likewise, the two testimonies of faith:

---

## Page 4865

“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

Likewise, the tashahhud (testimony recited in prayer):

“All greetings of reverence belong to Allah.”

Likewise, the expressions of glorification, praise, affirmation of Allah’s oneness, and proclamation of His greatness:

“Glory be to Allah; all praise is for Allah; there is no god but Allah; Allah is the Greatest.”

As for supplication, it frequently employs the name Lord, as in the words of Adam and Eve:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

And the words of Noah:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You for that of which I have no knowledge.”

And the words of Moses:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

And the words of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend:

and the rest of the verse. And his words together with Ishmael:

“Our Lord, accept this from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

Likewise, the words of those who say:

“Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.”

There are many such examples.

It has been reported that Mālik said:

“I dislike a man saying in his supplication, ‘O my Master, O my Master! O Compassionate One, O Compassionate One!’ Rather, he should supplicate as the prophets did: ‘Our Lord, our Lord.’”

Al-Utbī transmitted this from him in al-Utbiyyah.

Allah Most High says concerning people of understanding:

“Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: ‘Our Lord, You have not created this in vain. Glory be to You! Protect us, then, from the punishment of the Fire,’”

and the verses that follow.

---

## Page 4866

Thus, when the intention to petition first comes into a servant’s heart, it is fitting for him to ask Allah by His name “Lord.” If he asks Him by His name “Allah,” which encompasses the name “Lord,” that too is good. But when the intention to worship first comes into his heart, the name “Allah” is more appropriate.

When beginning with praise, he mentions the name “Allah”; when intending to supplicate, he invokes the name “Lord.” Thus Jonah said:

“There is no god but You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

And Adam said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Jonah, peace be upon him, departed in anger. Allah Most High says:

“So be patient with your Lord’s judgment, and do not be like the man of the fish.”

And He Most High says:

“Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy.”

He had done something for which he deserved blame. It was therefore fitting for his condition that he begin by praising his Lord and acknowledging that there is no god but Him. He alone deserves to be worshipped, to the exclusion of all others; personal desires must therefore not be obeyed, for following them weakens the worship of Allah alone. It has been reported that Jonah, peace be upon him, regretted that the punishment had been lifted from his people after it had loomed over them. He feared that they would accuse him of lying, and so he became angry.

He acted in a way that called for the words Allah Most High has related, and for the declaration:

“There is no god but You.”

These words entail denying divinity to anything other than Allah, whether its attribution arises from personal desire, obedience to created beings, or anything else. Thus he said:

“Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

A servant says words such as these concerning what he supposes when it does not accord with reality, and what he desires when it is not good.

---

## Page 4867

As for Adam, peace be upon him, he first acknowledged his sin, saying:

“We have wronged ourselves.”

Adam had nothing within him that contested his desire to obey Allah’s command in a way that would rival Allah’s exclusive right to worship. Rather, he believed Satan to be truthful when he

“swore to them both, ‘I am indeed a sincere adviser to you.’”

“Thus he brought about their fall through deception.”

Satan deceived them both and presented himself as their sincere adviser. Having accepted his deception and apparent sincerity, their condition called for them to say:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

This was because of their negligence, not because of some desire or personal interest competing with Allah’s exclusive right to worship. They needed Him to nurture them as their Lord, perfecting their knowledge and intention so that they would not be deceived in such a way again. Thus they recognized their need for Allah, their Lord, whose place no one else could take in meeting their needs.

Jonah, the man of the fish, recognized that his departure in anger and his aversion to those people’s being saved had involved a failure to fulfil Allah’s exclusive right to worship. This involved a degree of opposition in action, arising from love for something else, which required him to devote his love and worship entirely to Allah and to say:

“There is no god but You.”

For when a servant says, “There is no god but You,” this eradicates his taking his own desire as a god. It has been reported:

“Beneath the vault of heaven, no object of worship is more grievous in Allah’s sight than desire that is followed.”

Thus Jonah, may Allah’s blessings be upon him, perfected his devotion to Allah as his only God and his rejection of desire taken as a god besides Him. When he fully realized the meaning of his words, “There is no god but You,” no desire remained in him—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—that competed with the True One’s exclusive right to worship. Rather, he devoted his worship sincerely to Allah, for he was among the finest of Allah’s sincere servants.

And (also), such a state may befall someone, leaving within him

---

## Page 4868

a measure of resentment towards the divine decree, opposition to Allah in His creation and commands, and troubling doubts about His wisdom and mercy. The servant therefore needs to rid himself of two things: corrupt opinions and corrupt desires. He must recognize that wisdom and justice lie in what Allah’s knowledge and wisdom dictate, not in what the servant’s own knowledge and wisdom dictate. His desires must follow what Allah has commanded, leaving him with no desire that opposes Allah’s command and judgment.

Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no discomfort over what you have judged and submit in full submission.”

It has been reported that the Prophet, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until his desires accord with what I have brought.”

Abū Hātim narrated it in his Sahīh. In the Sahīh, it is reported that Umar said to him, “O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, you are dearer to me than my own self.” He replied, “Now, O Umar!”

Also in the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, is reported to have said:

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his children, his parents, and all mankind.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your relatives, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose decline you fear, and the homes you delight in are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command.’”

Thus, if faith is not attained until the servant accepts Allah’s Messenger as judge, submits to him, and brings his desires into accord with what he brought, and until love for the Messenger and striving in Allah’s cause takes precedence over his love for himself, his wealth, and his family, then how much more must he accept Allah Most High as judge and submit to Him?

---

## Page 4869

So if someone believes that certain people deserve punishment, yet Allah has forgiven them and shown them mercy, and he resents this, his resentment stems either from a will that opposes Allah’s judgment or from an assumption that contradicts Allah’s knowledge. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise. Once you know that He is All-Knowing and All-Wise, no grounds remain for resenting what He has done. This applies to what He has commanded and to what He has left, which He has not commanded us to hate or resent.

As for things that exist which He has commanded us to hate—such as disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience—we must obey His command. This is unlike His acceptance of His servants’ repentance and His deliverance of them from punishment. These are among His deeds that He has not commanded us to hate; rather, they are things He loves, for He loves those who repent and those who purify themselves. To resent this is a form of following a will that rivals His divinity.

Anyone harbouring such a will must therefore make his worship sincerely devoted to Allah alone, saying:

“None has the right to be worshipped but You.”

We must love what He loves, be pleased with what pleases Him, enjoin what He commands, and forbid what He prohibits. Since He “loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves,” we must love them, rather than make gods of our own wishes that conflict with what He loves.

The discussion here rests upon a “principle”: by the consensus of the Muslim community, the prophets, may Allah’s blessings be upon them, are protected from error in what they report about Allah, glorified be He, and in conveying His messages. Hence, it is obligatory to believe in everything they were given, as

---

## Page 4870

He, the Exalted, said:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what Moses and Jesus were given, and what the prophets were given by their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.’”

“So if they believe as you believe, they are rightly guided. But if they turn away, they are only in opposition. Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

And He said:

“But righteousness is to believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture, and the prophets.”

And He said:

“The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ And they say, ‘We hear and obey. We seek Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.’”

Those who are not prophets, by contrast, are not protected from error as the prophets are, even if they are allies of Allah. Hence, whoever reviles any prophet is to be put to death, according to the consensus of the jurists, whereas whoever reviles anyone else is not to be put to death.

This protection from error established for the prophets is what ensures that the purpose of prophethood and messengership is fulfilled. A “prophet” is one who receives tidings from Allah, while a “messenger” is one whom Allah Most High has sent. Every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger. Their protection from error in what they convey from Allah is established; thus, by the consensus of the Muslims, no error is allowed to persist in it.

---

## Page 4871

But can something occur that Allah then rectifies, removing what Satan casts and making His verses firm? There are two views on this. What is transmitted from the early generations accords with the Quran on this matter.

Those among the later scholars who ruled this out challenged the reported addition to Sūrat al-Najm:

“These are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed to be hoped for.”

They said that this had not been established. Those who knew it to be established said that Satan had cast these words into the listeners’ ears, but the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had not uttered them. Yet the question still arises on this understanding as well.

They also interpreted His words:

“…except that, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation”

as referring to inner thoughts. Those who affirmed what was transmitted from the early generations, however, said that these reports were firmly established and could not be impugned, and that the Quran supported them in His words:

“We never sent a messenger or a prophet before you except that, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation. But Allah removes what Satan casts; then Allah makes His verses firm. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“So that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those whose hearts are diseased and those whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in profound opposition.”

“And so that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, believe in it, and have their hearts humbly submit to it. Indeed, Allah guides those who believe to a straight path.”

They said that the reports explaining this verse were well known and firmly established in the books of Quranic commentary and hadith, and that the Quran agreed with them. For Allah’s removal of what Satan casts and His making His verses firm serve precisely to remove what has intruded into His verses and to distinguish truth from falsehood, so that His verses are not confused

## Page 4872

with anything else. Making what Satan casts a trial for those whose hearts are diseased and those whose hearts are hardened can only occur if it is outwardly expressed and heard by people, not merely concealed within the soul. The trial arising from this form of abrogation is of the same kind as the trial arising from the other form of abrogation.

This form provides even stronger evidence of the Messenger’s truthfulness—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his freedom from personal desire than the other form. For if he is believed when he commands one thing and then commands its opposite, both being from Allah, then his own declaration that the latter is from Allah and is the abrogating revelation, whereas the material Allah removed and abrogated was not from Him, provides still stronger evidence of his commitment to truthfulness and his speaking the truth. This is like the statement of ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: “Had Muhammad concealed anything of revelation, he would have concealed this verse:

‘You concealed within yourself what Allah was going to reveal, and you feared people, whereas Allah was more deserving of your fear.’”

Thus, the Messenger’s explanation—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that Allah made His verses firm and removed what Satan had cast provides still stronger evidence of his scrupulous truthfulness and freedom from lying. This is the very purpose of his mission, for he is the truthful one whose truthfulness is attested—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For this reason, to declare him a liar is undoubtedly sheer disbelief.

As for protection from error in matters unrelated to conveying the message, scholars disagree over whether it is established by reason or by revelation. They also disagree over protection against major and minor sins, or against

---

## Page 4873

some of them; or whether protection consists only in not being allowed to persist in them, rather than in not committing them? Or is it obligatory to affirm such protection only in conveying the message? Must protection from disbelief and sins also be affirmed before the prophetic mission, or not? This question is discussed at length elsewhere.

The view held by the majority, which accords with the reports transmitted from the early generations, affirms that the prophets are protected from being allowed to persist in any sin whatsoever, and rejects the view that they may be allowed to persist in sins. When carefully examined, the arguments of those who affirm protection from sin establish only this position. Nor do the arguments of those who deny it establish any instance of a sin in which the prophets were allowed to persist.

Those who affirm protection from sin argue that following the prophets’ example is prescribed, and that this is permissible only if one allows that their actions may be sins. Yet it is well known that following their example is prescribed only in matters in which they were allowed to continue, not in matters which they were forbidden to do and from which they turned back. Likewise, obedience to their commands and prohibitions is obligatory only where these have not been abrogated. An abrogated command or prohibition may no longer be treated as prescribing or forbidding something, let alone as requiring compliance and obedience.

The same applies to their arguments that sins are incompatible with perfection, that they are more reprehensible when committed by someone who has received great blessings, that they cause people to turn away, and other such rational arguments. These apply only when someone persists in sin and does not turn back. Otherwise, through sincere repentance that He accepts, Allah raises the repentant person to a higher station than before, as stated by

such inclination is a general category encompassing “two types.” As Imam Ahmad said, “Inclination is of two kinds: passing thoughts and settled resolve.” It is established in an authentic report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

these matters have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that everything blameworthy in the account of Jonah was forgiven: Allah replaced it with good deeds and raised his rank. After emerging from the fish’s belly and repenting, he held a higher rank than before those events occurred. Allah Most High says:

“So be patient with your Lord’s decree, and do not be like the man of the fish when he called out, filled with anguish.”

“Had grace from his Lord not reached him, he would have been cast onto barren ground, condemned.”

“But his Lord chose him and made him one of the righteous.”

This contrasts with his state when the fish swallowed him, for Allah says:

“Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy.”

He thus states that Jonah was blameworthy at that time. A blameworthy person is someone who has done something deserving of blame. The blame therefore applied to that state, not to his state when he was cast onto barren ground, ailing. Thus, after saying:

“There is no deity except You; glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers,”

his state was more exalted than it had been before those events occurred. What counts is the perfection attained at the end, not what happened at the beginning; deeds are judged by their endings. Allah Most High created the human being and brought him forth from his mother’s womb knowing nothing, then taught him, taking him from deficiency to perfection. It is therefore not permissible to judge a person’s worth by what he did before attaining perfection; rather, he must be judged by his perfected state. In their final state, Jonah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the other prophets are in the most perfect of states.

## Page 4880

This is where those who preferred the angels over the prophets and the righteous went wrong: they compared the angels’ perfection with the righteous at their beginning, while they were still deficient. then, with that state taken into account, its superiority over the state of other created beings would have become apparent. Clearly, in these states he did not yet possess the qualities of perfection that would entitle him to the fullest praise and distinction, and to superiority over every kind and generation. Some people suppose that someone born into Islam who has never disbelieved is superior to someone who was a disbeliever and then embraced Islam. This is incorrect. Rather, what counts is the final outcome: whichever of them is more mindful of Allah in his final state is superior. Indeed, someone who has known evil and tasted it, then known good and tasted it

## Page 4881

may know and love good, and know and hate evil, more fully than someone who has not known and tasted both as he has. For this reason, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “The bonds of Islam are undone, one by one, only when people grow up within Islam without knowing pre-Islamic ignorance.”

It is just as ʿUmar said. Islam is perfected through enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and this is brought to completion through striving in Allah’s cause. Someone raised among what is right, knowing nothing else, may lack the knowledge of wrongdoing and its harm possessed by someone familiar with it. Nor will he strive against its practitioners as someone well acquainted with them would. Thus, a person familiar with evil and its causes, if his intentions are sound, takes precautions against it, restrains its practitioners, and strives against them in ways that others do not.

For this reason, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, surpassed those who came after them in faith and striving: their knowledge of good and evil, their love of good, and their hatred of evil were more complete. They knew the goodness of Islam, faith, and righteous deeds, and the ugliness of disbelief and sins. Likewise, someone who has tasted poverty, illness, and fear is more eager for prosperity, health, and security than someone who has not experienced them.

Hence the saying:

“A thing’s beauty is revealed by its opposite.”

## Page 4882

It is also said:

“Things become clear through their opposites.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say:

The praiseworthy, sound heart is one that desires good, not evil. Its perfection lies in knowing both good and evil. As for someone who does not recognize evil, this is a deficiency in him, not something deserving praise.

This does not mean that everyone who has tasted disbelief and sins necessarily knows them better and hates them more than someone who has never tasted them. This is not invariably the case: a physician may know more about diseases than the patients themselves. The Prophets—may blessings and peace be upon them—are physicians of faith. They know better than anyone else what sets hearts right and what corrupts them, even though a Prophet may not have tasted the evil that others have tasted.

Rather, the point is that some people, through tasting evil, gain a knowledge of it, an aversion to it, and a love of good when they taste it, which some others do not attain. An example is someone who was a polytheist, a Jew, or a Christian, and came to know the specious arguments, corrupt doctrines, darkness, and evil found in disbelief. Then Allah opened his heart to Islam and acquainted him with its virtues. Such a person may have a greater desire for Islam and a stronger hatred of disbelief than some who have not understood the reality of disbelief and Islam, but instead turn away from aspects of both, or merely follow others in praising the one and condemning the other.
