“Allah accepts the repentance only of those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterward. It is they whose repentance Allah accepts. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

Abū al-‘Āliyah said: “I asked the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, about this verse, and they told me: ‘Everyone who disobeys Allah is

---

## Page 4888

ignorant, and everyone who repents before death has repented soon afterward.’”

(The second response):

The distinction mentioned between one repentant person and another regarding Allah Most High’s love for those who repent has no basis. Rather, the Quran and the Sunnah indicate that Allah loves those who repent and rejoices at their repentance, whether or not they knew that what they had done was a sin.

Anyone who knew that what he had done was a sin and then repented must replace his blameworthy qualities with praiseworthy ones. If he hated the truth, he must come to love it; and if he loved falsehood, he must come to hate it. The repentant person’s knowledge of the truth, his love for it and adherence to it, and his hatred and avoidance of falsehood are all things that Allah Most High loves and is pleased with. Likewise, Allah’s love corresponds to the extent to which His servant does what He loves. The more a person does what Allah loves, the greater Allah’s love for him.

When he turns from what Allah dislikes to what He loves, intensely hating the falsehood he formerly followed and intensely loving the truth to which he has turned, Allah’s love and affection for him must therefore increase. Indeed, Allah replaces his evil deeds with good deeds: because he has replaced his blameworthy qualities with praiseworthy ones, Allah replaces his evil deeds with good deeds. For recompense is of the same nature as the deed.

Thus, if the repentant person does more of what Allah loves than someone else does, Allah’s love for him is greater. And if he does more of what Allah loves him to do than he did before repenting, then

---

## Page 4889

Allah’s affection for him after repentance is greater than His affection for him before repentance. How, then, can it be said, “Affection does not return”?

This also clarifies the answer to the misconception of those who say, “Allah sends as a prophet only someone who was protected from sin before prophethood,” as a group among the Rāfidah and others maintain. The same applies to those who say, “He sends as a prophet only someone who was a believer before prophethood.” These people mistakenly suppose that sins remain a deficiency even after a person repents of them. This is the source of their error. Whoever thinks that a person who has sinned remains deficient despite sincere repentance is gravely mistaken. None of the blame or punishment that befalls sinners befalls the repentant person. If he repents promptly, none of it befalls him; if he delays repentance, then, between his sins and his repentance, he may incur blame and punishment appropriate to his circumstances.

The prophets—Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them—did not delay repentance. Rather, they hastened and raced towards it. They neither delayed nor persisted in sin; indeed, they were protected from doing so. If any of them delayed repentance briefly, Allah expiated that through the trials He subjected him to, as He did with Jonah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is according to the well-known view that he was cast overboard after receiving prophethood. Those who hold that he was cast overboard before prophethood have no need of this explanation.

---

## Page 4890

A person who repents of disbelief and sins may be superior to someone who never fell into disbelief or sins. If he may be superior, then the superior person is more deserving of prophethood than someone who does not equal him in virtue. Allah has recounted the sins of Joseph’s brothers, yet they are the Asbāt (the Tribes) whom Allah Most High made prophets. Allah Most High also says:

“So Lot believed him, and he said, ‘I am emigrating to my Lord.’”

Lot thus believed Abraham, peace be upon him, and Allah Most High subsequently sent him to the people of Lot. Allah Most High says in the account of Shuʿayb:

“The arrogant chiefs among his people said, ‘We will certainly expel you, Shuʿayb, and those who believe with you from our town, unless you return to our religion.’ He said, ‘Even if we are unwilling? We would indeed be fabricating a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it. We cannot return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in His knowledge. In Allah we put our trust. Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of judges.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“Those who disbelieved said to their messengers, ‘We will certainly expel you from our land unless you return to our religion.’ Their Lord then revealed to them, ‘We will surely destroy the wrongdoers and settle you in the land after them. This is for whoever fears standing before Me and fears My warning.’”

Once it is understood that what counts is the perfection attained at the end, and that this perfection is attained only through repentance and seeking forgiveness, it follows that every servant must repent. Repentance is obligatory upon all, from the earliest generations to the latest. As Allah Most High says:

“So that Allah may punish the hypocritical men and women and the men and women who associate partners with Him, and turn in mercy to the believing men and women. Allah is ever All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

---

## Page 4891

Allah, glorified be He, has told us of the repentance of Adam, Noah, and those who came after them, down to the last of the messengers, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The last revelation he received—or among the last—was His saying, Most High:

“When Allah’s help comes and victory,
and you see people entering Allah’s religion in multitudes,
then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

In the two Sahīhs, ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would frequently say while bowing and prostrating: “Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me.” He was thereby putting the Quran into practice.

Before that, Allah had revealed to him:

“Allah has indeed turned in mercy to the Prophet, the Emigrants, and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of some of them had almost swerved. Then He turned to them in mercy. Indeed, He is Most Kind and Most Merciful to them.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O people, repent to your Lord. By Him in whose hand is my soul, I seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day.”

In Sahīh Muslim, al-Agharr al-Muzanī reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A veil comes over my heart, and I seek Allah’s forgiveness one hundred times a day.”

In the Sunan collections, Ibn ʿUmar said: We would count the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying one hundred times in a single gathering: “My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepter of repentance, the All-Forgiving.”

In the two Sahīhs, Abū Mūsā reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to

---

## Page 4892

say:

“O Allah, forgive my sins, my ignorance, my excesses in my affairs, and whatever You know better than I do. O Allah, forgive what I have done in jest and in earnest, unintentionally and deliberately—all of these are found in me. O Allah, forgive my past and future sins, what I have concealed and what I have made public, and whatever You know better than I do. You are the One who brings forward and the One who holds back, and You have power over all things.”

In the two Sahīhs, Abū Hurayrah relates that he said:

“O Messenger of Allah, what do you say during your silence between the opening declaration of Allah’s greatness and the recitation?”

He replied:

“I say: ‘O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of dirt. O Allah, wash away my sins with snow, hail, and cold water.’”

Sahīh Muslim and other works report that he would say something similar when he raised his head from bowing. In Sahīh Muslim, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in the opening supplication of prayer:

“O Allah, You are the King; there is no god but You. You are my Lord, and I am Your servant. I have wronged myself and done evil, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You. Guide me to the best character, for none guides to it but You. Turn bad character away from me, for none turns it away from me but You.”

Sahīh Muslim reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say while prostrating:

“O Allah, forgive all my sins, small and great, public and secret, first and last.”

---

## Page 4893

The Sunan also report from Alī that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was brought a mount to ride. He praised Allah and said:

“Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, for we could not have controlled it ourselves. And surely to our Lord we shall return.”

Then he proclaimed Allah’s greatness and praised Him, before saying:

“Glory be to You! I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.”

Then he laughed and said:

“The Lord marvels at His servant when he says, ‘Forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ He says, ‘My servant knows that none forgives sins but Me.’”

Allah Most High has said:

“Seek forgiveness for your sin, and for the believing men and women.”

And He has said:

“Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory, so that Allah may forgive your past and future sins.”

It is established in the two Sahīhs, in the hadith of intercession, that the Messiah will say:

“Go to Muhammad, a servant whose past and future sins Allah has forgiven.”

The Sahīh also reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would stand in prayer until his feet swelled. He was asked, “Do you do this when Allah has forgiven your past and future sins?” He replied:

“Should I not be a grateful servant?”

The texts of the Quran and Sunnah on this subject are numerous and mutually corroborating. There are also many reports concerning it from the Companions, the Successors, and the scholars of the Muslims. Those who dispute this, however, reinterpret these texts in the manner of the Jahmiyyah and the Bātiniyyah, as has been done by those who have written on this subject. Their interpretations make it clear to anyone who

---

## Page 4894

reflects on them that they are unsound and amount to distorting words from their proper places. One example is their interpretation of His words:

“ so that Allah may forgive your past and future sins.”

They claim that the past sin is Adam’s sin, while the future sin is that of Muhammad’s community. This interpretation is plainly false, as several considerations demonstrate:

(First)
Allah had already accepted Adam’s repentance before he descended to earth, long before the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, in which Allah revealed this surah. Allah Most High says:

“Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray.”

“Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.”

He also says:

“Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepter of repentance, the Most Merciful.”

It is also mentioned that he said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Second:
It may be said: According to your own position, Adam himself is among the cases at issue. Those who dispute this hold that he has no need for his sin to be forgiven, since he too is a prophet. Whoever maintains that the prophets committed no sin says this of Adam, Muhammad, and the other prophets alike.

The third consideration:
Allah does not attribute a sin to someone who has not committed it, for He is the One who says:

“No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.”

It is therefore impossible to attribute to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the sin of Adam, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or that of his community or anyone else. Allah Most High has said:

“He is responsible only for what he has been charged with, and you are responsible for what you have been charged with.”

Allah Most High also says:

“So fight in the cause of Allah; you are responsible only for yourself.”

Were this permissible, it would also be permissible

---

## Page 4895

to attribute to Muhammad the sins of all the prophets and to say that His words:

“so that Allah may forgive your past and future sins”

mean the sins of the prophets and their communities before you, since he will intercede for all creation on the Day of Resurrection. He is the master of the children of Adam, and he said:

“I am the master of the children of Adam, without boasting. Adam and all those beneath him will be under my banner on the Day of Resurrection. I am the spokesman of the prophets when they arrive, and their leader when they assemble.”

In that case, attributing his sin to Muhammad would not be unique to Adam. Rather, according to these people’s position, the sins of all people, earlier and later, would become his sins.

If someone says, “Allah has not forgiven the sins of all communities,” the reply is: “Nor has He forgiven the sins of everyone in his own community.”

The fourth consideration:
Allah has distinguished between his sin and the sins of the believers by saying:

“Seek forgiveness for your sin, and for the believing men and women.”

How, then, could the believers’ sins be his sins?

The fifth consideration:
It is established in an authentic report that when this verse was revealed, the Companions said, “O Messenger of Allah, this is for you, but what is there for us?” Allah then revealed:

“He is the One who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they might increase in faith along with their existing faith.”

This shows that the Messenger and the believers understood that His words:

“so that Allah may forgive your past and future sins”

applied specifically to him, not to his community.

The sixth consideration:
Allah has not forgiven the sins of everyone in his community. Rather, it has been established

---

## Page 4896

that some members of his community will be punished for their sins, either in this world or in the Hereafter. This is attested by mass-transmitted reports, foretold by the truthful and trusted Prophet, and agreed upon by the early generations of this community and its leading scholars. Instances witnessed in this world are more numerous than anyone but Allah can count. Allah Most High has said:

“It is not a matter of your wishes or the wishes of the People of the Book: whoever does evil will be recompensed for it.”

Seeking forgiveness and repenting may concern having neglected the better course. Someone who is brought to a better state than before may repent of his former state. Blame and threats of punishment, however, apply only to sin.

Section

As for the questioner’s words:

“Is merely acknowledging a sin, together with belief in Allah’s oneness, sufficient to ensure its forgiveness and relief from the distress arising from it, or is something else required?”

The answer is that what ensures forgiveness, together with belief in Allah’s oneness, is the repentance that has been commanded. Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him except through repentance, as He says in two places in the Quran:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills.”

Whatever falls short of associating partners with Allah is forgiven with repentance; without repentance, its forgiveness is subject to His will. As Allah Most High says:

“Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of

---

## Page 4897

Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.”

This concerns those who repent. That is why He states in general, unrestricted, and categorical terms that He forgives all sins. In the other verse, however, He says:

“But He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills.”

He thus specifies what falls short of associating partners with Him and makes its forgiveness subject to His will. Given, then, that associating partners with Allah is forgiven only through repentance, whereas Allah forgives lesser sins for those who repent and may forgive them without repentance for whomever He wills, acknowledging one’s sin together with belief in Allah’s oneness ensures forgiveness if that acknowledgment includes repentance. Once a sin is forgiven, its punishment is removed, for forgiveness means protection from the harm of sin.

Some people say, “Forgiveness means concealment.” They maintain that maghfirah (forgiveness) and al-Ghaffār (the Oft-Forgiving) are so called because they convey the meaning of concealment, and interpret Allah’s name al-Ghaffār as “the Concealer.” This, however, falls short of the full meaning of forgiveness. Forgiveness means protection from the harm of sin, such that one is not punished for it. Whoever has had his sin forgiven is not punished for it. Mere concealment, however, does not preclude inward punishment. Anyone who is punished for a sin, inwardly or outwardly, has not been forgiven for it. A sin is forgiven only when the person is spared the punishment that the sin deserves. If, despite being forgiven, he is subjected to a trial that serves to increase his reward, this does not contradict forgiveness.

---

## Page 4898

Likewise, if completing repentance requires a person to perform good deeds, then whatever repentance requires is part of its completion. A person may think that he has repented when he has not; he may merely have stopped committing the sin. Merely stopping is not the same as repenting. He may turn away from a sin because it does not occur to him, because something prevents him from committing it, or because his desire for it has ceased for a nonreligious reason. None of this is repentance. Rather, he must believe that it is a sin, hate committing it because Allah has forbidden it, and abandon it for Allah Most High—not out of hope for any created being’s favor or fear of any created being. Repentance is among the greatest good deeds.

All good deeds require sincerity to Allah and conformity to His command. Thus, commenting on His words,

“That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed,”

al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād said, “The most sincere and the most correct.” They asked, “Abū ‘Alī, what does ‘the most sincere and the most correct’ mean?”

He replied, “If a deed is sincere but not correct, it is not accepted; and if it is correct but not sincere, it is not accepted. It must be both sincere and correct. To be sincere means that it is done for Allah, and to be correct means that it accords with the Sunnah.”

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say in his supplication:

“O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them sincerely for Your Face alone, and give no one else any share in them.”

A detailed discussion of repentance belongs elsewhere. As for acknowledging one’s sin in humble submission to Allah without abandoning it, this amounts to merely seeking forgiveness without repentance. Such a person is like someone who asks

---

## Page 4899

Allah Most High to forgive his sin even though he has not repented of it. This is despair of Allah’s mercy, and his forgiveness cannot be assured, for he is merely offering a supplication.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“No one offers a supplication involving neither sin nor the severing of kinship ties without receiving one of three things: either Allah grants his request promptly, reserves an equivalent reward for him, or averts an equivalent evil from him.”

They said, “Messenger of Allah, then we shall supplicate abundantly!” He replied, “Allah has still more.”

Such a supplication may bring forgiveness. If it does not, it must bring either the averting of some other evil or the attainment of some other good. Thus, it is beneficial, as every supplication is beneficial.

As for the statement of some scholars, “Seeking forgiveness while persisting in sin is the repentance of liars,” this applies when the person seeks forgiveness as an act of repentance, or claims that his seeking forgiveness constitutes repentance and that he has thereby repented. There is no doubt that, while persisting in sin, he has not repented, for repentance and persistence in sin are opposites. Persistence in sin is incompatible with repentance, but not with seeking forgiveness without repentance.

As for the question, “Does acknowledging a particular sin necessarily avert the consequences of multiple sins, or must one call all one’s sins to mind?”—the answer rests on several principles:

---

## Page 4900

First: Repentance from one sin is valid even while a person persists in another, if the motive for repenting of one is stronger than the motive for repenting of the other, or the deterrent to one is stronger. This is the well-known position among both the early and later scholars.

A group of speculative theologians, such as Abū Hāshim, held that repentance from one evil deed is invalid while a person persists in another. They argued: “Unless repentance is motivated by fear of Allah, it is not valid repentance; yet fear of Allah restrains a person from all sins, not merely some of them.”

Al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and Ibn ‘Aqīl related this as a position reported from Ahmad, because al-Marwadhī reported that Ahmad was asked about someone who had repented of sexual immorality and said, “If I fell ill, I would not return to it,” but would not give up looking. Ahmad replied:

“What sort of repentance is this? Jarīr ibn ‘Abd Allāh said: ‘I asked the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, about an inadvertent glance, and he said: “Avert your gaze.”’”

The well-known position of Ahmad and the other imams, however, is that such repentance is valid. In this case, Ahmad meant only that this was not comprehensive repentance by which the person would be counted, without qualification, among the repentant. He did not mean that this person’s sin was equivalent to that of someone who persists in major sins. His statements transmitted through numerous independent reports, together with his firmly established pronouncements, contradict such an interpretation.

It is more appropriate to interpret an imam’s statements in a way that makes them mutually consistent than to interpret them as contradictory—especially when the alternative position is an innovation not known to have been held by any of the early scholars. Ahmad says:

---

## Page 4901

“Beware of speaking on a matter in which you have no imam to follow.” During the ordeal, he would say: “How can I say what has never been said before?” Ahmad’s adherence to the Sunnah and the transmitted reports, his eagerness to follow them, and his aversion to opposing them are established through numerous independent reports, known to scholars and ordinary people alike who are familiar with his life.

As for their assertion that fear of Allah necessarily restrains a person from all sins, the answer is that someone may recognize the wrongfulness of one sin but not another, and repent only of what he knows to be wrong. He may (also) know that both are wrong, yet his desires overpower him regarding one but not the other, so he repents of this one but not that one. This is like someone who fulfils some obligations but not others: what he fulfils is accepted from him.

The Mu‘tazilah, however, have a false principle in which they agree with the Khawārij in their judgment, although they differ from them in the designation they use. They say that those who commit major sins will remain in the Fire forever and will not leave it through intercession or anything else. In their view, it is impossible for Allah to punish a person and then reward that same person. Hence, they maintain that a major sin nullifies all good deeds.

The Companions and Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, however, hold that those who commit major sins will emerge

---

## Page 4902

from the Fire and will receive intercession, and that a single major sin does not nullify all good deeds. According to most of Ahl al-Sunnah, however, an equivalent amount of good deeds may be nullified. Nothing nullifies all good deeds except disbelief, just as nothing wipes out all evil deeds except repentance. Thus, if someone who commits a major sin performs good deeds seeking Allah’s pleasure, Allah rewards him for them, even though he deserves punishment for his major sin. The Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, distinguishes between a thief, a fornicator, and believers who fight one another, on the one hand, and disbelievers, on the other, in matters of “designations and rulings.” The Sunnah transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—through numerous independent chains, and the consensus of the Companions, establish this, as explained at length elsewhere.

Accordingly, people have differed over His words:

“Allah accepts only from the God-fearing.”

According to the Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah, no good deed is accepted except from someone who is God-fearing without qualification and has committed no major sin. According to the Murji’ah, Allah accepts only from those who avoid associating partners with Him; they thus include those who commit major sins within the designation “the God-fearing.”

According to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, a deed is accepted from someone who fears Allah in performing it, doing it sincerely for Allah and in accordance with His command. Whoever fears Him in a particular deed has it accepted from him, even if he disobeys Him in other matters. Whoever does not fear Him in that deed does not have it accepted from him, even if he obeys Him in other matters. Repenting of some sins but not others is like performing some of the enjoined good deeds

---

## Page 4903

while leaving others undone, provided that what is omitted is not a condition for the validity of what is performed—as faith is a condition for the validity of other deeds. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he ought, while being a believer—such people will have their striving appreciated.”

And He Most High says:

“Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer—such people will enter Paradise.”

And He says:

“Whoever among you turns away from his religion and dies a disbeliever—their deeds will come to nothing in this world and the Hereafter. They will be the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding there forever.”

(The second principle)

If someone has committed sins and repents of some but not others, his repentance entails forgiveness only for those of which he has repented. As for those of which he has not repented, he remains subject to the ruling applicable to someone who has not repented, not to someone who has. I know of no disagreement concerning this except in the case of a disbeliever who embraces Islam. His acceptance of Islam includes repentance from disbelief, so through Islam he is forgiven the disbelief of which he has repented. But is he also forgiven the sins he committed while a disbeliever and of which he has not repented after embracing Islam? There are two well-known views on this:

(The first)

He is forgiven everything, because of the unrestricted wording of the Prophet’s statement—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Islam wipes away whatever came before it.”

Narrated by Muslim. This is also supported by the words of Allah Most High:

“Tell those who disbelieve that if they desist, their past will be forgiven.”

(The second view)

His acceptance of Islam entitles him to forgiveness only for that of which he has repented;

---

## Page 4904

so if he embraces Islam while persisting in major sins short of disbelief, the ruling concerning him in this respect is the same as that concerning others who commit major sins. This view is supported by the foundational principles and scriptural texts. For it is reported in the two Sahīh collections that Hakīm ibn Hizām said to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“O Messenger of Allah, will we be held accountable for what we did in the days of ignorance?”

He replied:

“Whoever among you does well in Islam will not be held accountable for what he did in the days of ignorance. But whoever does wrong in Islam will be held accountable for both his earlier and later deeds.”

This text shows that accountability for deeds committed in the days of ignorance is lifted only from those who do well, not from those who do not. If someone does not do well, he is held accountable for both his earlier and later deeds; and whoever has not repented of those deeds has not done well.

The words of Allah Most High:

“Tell those who disbelieve that if they desist, their past will be forgiven.”

indicate that whoever desists from something is forgiven his past involvement in it. They do not indicate that whoever desists from one thing is forgiven his past involvement in something else.

For when someone says to another, “If you desist, I will forgive you what you have done before,” or words to that effect, this is understood, when stated without qualification, to mean: if you desist from this matter, you will be forgiven your past involvement in it. When you desist from something, you are forgiven your past involvement in it, just as a similar meaning is understood from the words, “If you repent.” It is not understood to mean that by desisting from one sin, you are forgiven the other sins you previously committed.

As for the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—“Islam wipes away what came before it,” and, in another narration, “effaces whatever came before it,” he said this when ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās embraced Islam and asked

---

## Page 4905

for his past sins to be forgiven. He said to him:

“O ‘Amr, do you not know that Islam wipes away what came before it, that repentance wipes away what came before it, and that migration wipes away what came before it?”

It is well known that repentance brings forgiveness only for what one repents of; it does not bring forgiveness for all sins.

The Third Principle

A person may call particular sins to mind and repent of them, or he may repent in general terms without calling his sins to mind. If, however, his intention is comprehensive repentance, it encompasses everything he regards as sinful. For comprehensive repentance includes a general resolve to do what is commanded and abandon what is forbidden, as well as general remorse for every forbidden act.

As for “remorse”—whether it is classified among beliefs, volitions, or the pains that afflict the soul because it has done something harmful to itself—when the heart becomes conscious that it has done something harmful to itself, it comes to recognize that what it did was evil. This belongs to the category of beliefs. It also feels an aversion to what it did, which belongs to the category of volitions, and experiences distress and grief over what it did. This belongs to the category of pains, such as sorrow and sadness, just as joy and happiness belong to the category of pleasures, not to that of beliefs or volitions.

As for those philosophers and their followers who say that pleasure is the perception of what is congenial

---

## Page 4906

insofar as it is congenial, and that pain is the perception of what is uncongenial insofar as it is uncongenial, they are mistaken. Pleasure and pain are two states that follow the perception of what is congenial and uncongenial.

For loving what is congenial to a person—such as food he craves—involves three states:

(First) Love itself, such as the desire for food.

Second: Experiencing the beloved object, such as eating the food.

Third: The pleasure resulting from that. Pleasure is distinct both from desire and from the desiring person’s tasting. Rather, it results from his tasting; it is not the tasting itself.

The same applies to “what is disliked,” such as being struck. Disliking it is one thing, its occurrence is another, and the pain resulting from it is a third.

Likewise, consider the bliss and joy experienced by those who know Allah and love Him. Their love for Allah is one thing; what occurs through remembering the Beloved is another; and the pleasure resulting from that is a third.

There is no doubt that love presupposes awareness of the beloved, just as desire presupposes awareness on the part of the one who desires. Yet the awareness required for pleasure differs from the awareness required for love. This latter kind is called perception, tasting, attainment, experience, communion, and other such expressions used to describe experiencing the beloved,

---

## Page 4907

whether inwardly or outwardly. This tasting, in turn, necessarily entails pleasure, which a living being experiences inwardly and outwardly. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said in an authentic hadith:

“He has tasted the flavour of faith who is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) as his Prophet.”

It is also reported from him in the two Sahih collections that he said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will experience through them the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person solely for Allah’s sake; and that he hates to return to disbelief after Allah has rescued him from it just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire.”

Thus, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) explained that tasting the flavour of faith belongs to those who are content with Allah as their Lord, Islam as their religion, and Muhammad as their Prophet. He also explained that the sweetness of faith is experienced by those whose love for Allah and His Messenger is stronger than their love for anything else, who love a person for Allah’s sake alone, and who hate the opposite of faith just as they hate to be thrown into the Fire.

This love of faith and hatred of disbelief necessarily entail the sweetness of faith, just as the contentment mentioned above necessarily entails tasting the flavour of faith. This is pleasure; it is neither the assent and knowledge present in the heart nor the love present in the heart. Rather, it is their result, their fruit, and their necessary consequence. These things are inseparably connected: pleasure cannot occur without love and tasting. For if someone loves something but has not tasted it

---

## Page 4908

at all, he experiences no pleasure, just like someone who craves food but has not tasted any of it. Likewise, if he tastes something he does not love, he experiences no pleasure, like someone who tastes what he does not want. When love for something and the tasting of it come together, pleasure follows. If, however, dislike of something is combined with experiencing that disliked thing, pain results. Thus, someone who hates a sin but does not commit it feels no remorse, while someone who does not hate it feels no remorse for committing it. But if he commits it and recognizes that it is something he hates and that harms him, he regrets having committed it.

In the Musnad, Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Remorse is repentance.”

Once this is clear, whoever repents comprehensively has offered a repentance that entails forgiveness of all sins, even if he does not bring the individual sins to mind—unless something counters this general scope and requires it to be restricted. For example, there may be a sin from which he would not repent if he brought it to mind, because of his strong desire for it or his belief that it is good rather than evil. Any sin from which he would not repent if he brought it to mind is not included in his repentance. But any sin from which he would repent if it came specifically to mind is included in comprehensive repentance.

As for “unqualified repentance”—meaning that a person repents in general terms without this entailing repentance from every sin—it neither necessarily includes every individual sin nor precludes its inclusion, just like an unqualified expression. Such repentance may, however, serve as a cause for the forgiveness of a particular sin, just as it may serve as a cause for the forgiveness of all sins, in contrast to

---

## Page 4909

comprehensive repentance, which entails forgiveness of all sins, since it encompasses them all.

Many people, when repenting, bring to mind only certain indecent acts or their preliminaries, or certain wrongs committed by word or deed. Yet their neglect of what Allah requires of them, inwardly and outwardly, among the branches and realities of faith may be more harmful to them than some of the indecent acts they have committed. For the realities of faith that Allah has commanded, through which a servant becomes a true believer, are more beneficial than abstaining from certain outward sins. One example is love for Allah and His Messenger, which is the greatest of positive good deeds. Indeed, it is established in the Sahīh:

“In the time of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), there was a man called Himār who used to drink wine. Whenever he was brought before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), he would administer the prescribed punishment of flogging. After this had happened repeatedly, the man was brought before him once more, and he ordered that he be flogged. A man cursed him, whereupon the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, ‘Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.’”

Thus, he forbade cursing him despite his persistent drinking, because he loved Allah and His Messenger—even though the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) cursed ten in connection with wine:

“He cursed wine, the one who presses it, the one for whom it is pressed, the one who drinks it, the one who serves it, the one who carries it, the one to whom it is carried, the one who sells it, the one who buys it, and the one who consumes its proceeds.”

However, a curse pronounced in general terms does not necessarily entail cursing a particular individual in whom there is something that prevents the curse from applying to him.

---

## Page 4910

The same applies to “general judgments of unbelief” and “general threats of punishment.” Thus, the general threats of punishment in the Quran and Sunnah apply only when the necessary conditions are met and no impediments are present. By agreement of the Muslims, they do not apply to someone who repents of the sin, nor to someone whose good deeds erase his evil deeds, nor to someone for whom intercession is accepted or who is forgiven.

For the punishment of sins—namely Hell—is averted through repentance, good deeds that erase sins, and afflictions that expiate them—though these are themselves punishments in this world—as well as through hardships experienced in the intermediate state after death and on the gathering grounds of the Day of Resurrection. It is also averted through the supplications of believers, such as their funeral prayer for a person, and through the intercession of an intercessor whose plea is accepted, as when the foremost of intercessors, “Muhammad”—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—intercedes for someone.

Accordingly, whatever sin a person repents of, its consequence is removed. Whatever he does not repent of remains subject to the ruling applicable to unrepented sins. If hardship befalls him because of sins and he repents of some of them, his hardship is alleviated in proportion to what he has repented of, but not in respect of what he has left unrepented. His case differs from that of someone who repents comprehensively.

People generally do not repent comprehensively, despite their need to do so. Repentance is obligatory upon every servant in every circumstance, for he continually becomes aware of duties he has neglected or prohibitions he has transgressed. He must therefore continually repent. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 4911

As for the questioner’s words:

“Why does relief come when hope in created beings is exhausted? How can one turn the heart away from attachment to them and attach it to Allah?”

The answer is:

This comes about through fully realizing Allah’s oneness: “oneness in lordship” and “oneness in worship.”

“Oneness in lordship” means that there is no creator but Allah, so nothing besides Him can independently bring anything about. Rather, whatever He wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. Anything besides Him, if considered a cause, necessarily has a cooperating factor that assists it and an opposing factor that impedes it. Thus, to ask anything besides Him to bring something about is to ask it for something it cannot accomplish independently or achieve on its own.

Even the voluntary actions asked of a servant cannot be performed without Allah’s assistance—for example, by making him perform them through the decisive will He creates within him and the complete ability He creates for him. When complete ability and decisive will are present, the act necessarily occurs.

Allah’s will alone necessarily brings about everything He wills. Whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. The will of anything besides Him, however, does not by itself bring anything about. Rather, what it wills can come about only through factors beyond its power. Unless the Lord assists it through those factors, it will not attain what it seeks. Its very will cannot arise except by the will of Allah Most High.

As the Most High said:

“For whoever among you wills to take the straight path.”

“But you do not will unless Allah, Lord of all worlds, wills.”

And He said:

---

## Page 4912

—exalted is He—:

“So whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.”

“But you do not will unless Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.”

And He said:

“So whoever wills may heed it.”

“But they will not heed it unless Allah wills. He is the One to be feared and the One who grants forgiveness.”

A person who places his hope in a created being seeks with his heart what he wants from that being, yet that being is powerless to provide it. Moreover, this is part of the association of partners with Allah that He does not forgive. Thus, among the manifestations of His perfect grace and kindness toward His believing servants is that He prevents them from attaining their aims through associating partners with Him, so that He may turn their hearts toward His oneness. Then, if the servant worships Him alone, he attains happiness in this world and the Hereafter.

But if he is among those described in His words:

“When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm, he carries on as though he had never called upon Us concerning the harm that afflicted him. Thus, what the transgressors used to do has been made appealing to them.”

And in His words:

“When harm befalls you at sea, those you invoke vanish from your thoughts, except Him. But when He delivers you safely to land, you turn away. Man is ever ungrateful.”

Then whatever realization of Allah’s oneness he had attained becomes evidence against him.

Likewise, Allah, glorified is He, established His case against the polytheists who acknowledge that He is the Creator of everything, yet associate partners with Him rather than worship Him alone, without partner. The Most High said:

“Say, ‘To whom belong the earth and everyone upon it, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then take heed?’”

---

## Page 4913

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then fear Him?’”

“Say, ‘In whose hand is the dominion of all things, who grants protection while none can protect against Him, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘How then are you deluded?’”

And the Most High said:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ How then are they turned away?”

This is mentioned in several places in the Quran. Among the manifestations of Allah’s perfect favor toward His believing servants is that He afflicts them with hardship, suffering, and circumstances that compel them to worship Him alone. They then call upon Him with sincere devotion, place their hope in Him alone, and attach their hearts to Him rather than anyone else. Through this, they attain such reliance upon Him, such turning to Him, such sweetness of faith and experience of its savor, and such freedom from associating partners with Him, that these are a greater blessing for them than relief from illness, fear, or drought, or the attainment of ease and relief from hardship in their livelihood. Those are bodily pleasures and worldly blessings, of which a disbeliever may receive more than a believer.

But what is attained by those who worship Allah alone with sincere devotion is too great for words to express its true nature or for the mind to encompass its details. Every believer has a share of this in proportion to his faith. Thus, one of the early Muslims said:

“O son of Adam, you have indeed been blessed through a need that has led you to knock often at your Master’s door.”

One of the spiritual teachers said:

“At times I have a need that I ask Allah to fulfill. As I call upon Him, He opens to me such delight in knowing Him and such sweetness in speaking intimately to Him that I do not wish Him to hasten the fulfillment of my need, for fear that my soul might turn away

---

## Page 4914

from this; for the soul seeks only its own satisfaction, and once its desire is fulfilled, it turns away.”

Some reports from the Israelites contain the words: “O son of Adam, affliction brings you and Me together, while well-being brings you and your own self together.”

This theme occurs frequently. It is a reality that the believer tastes and perceives through his inner sense. Every believer has experienced enough of it to recognize what we have described, for it belongs to the realm of taste and perception, known only to those who have tasted and perceived it.

Although the word “taste” may be thought originally to refer exclusively to tasting with the tongue, its use in the Quran and Sunnah shows that its scope is broader: it is used for sensing both what is agreeable and what is disagreeable. Similarly, in customary usage, the word “perception” encompasses whatever is perceived through the five senses, and indeed inwardly as well. In its linguistic origin, however, it means “seeing,” as in His words:

“Do you perceive any one of them?”

(The point at issue) is the word “taste.” The Most High said:

“So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear.”

He thus described fear and hunger as things tasted, and associated the garment with them to indicate that it clothed the hungry and fearful person, enveloping and surrounding him just as a garment surrounds its wearer;

---

## Page 4915

unlike someone whose pain does not encompass all his senses but is confined to particular parts of his body. The Most High said:

“So taste the painful punishment.”

The Most High also said:

“Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble!”

And He said:

“Taste the touch of Hellfire.”

And He said:

“They will not taste death therein.”

The Most High also said:

“There they will taste neither coolness nor drink, except scalding water and foul discharge.”

And He said:

“We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“He has tasted the sweetness of faith who is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet.”

Thus, the word “taste” is frequently used for perceiving both what is agreeable and what is disagreeable. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“There are three qualities which, if present in a person, enable him to experience the sweetness of faith.”

This hadith has already been mentioned. A believer’s experience of the sweetness of faith in his heart, and his tasting of faith, are known to those who have had this experience. Those who taste it do so in varying degrees.

Thus, what the people of faith experience when they devote their hearts exclusively to Allah and turn to Him rather than anything besides Him—as pure monotheists, sincerely devoting their religion to Him, loving nothing except for His sake, relying on none but Him, forming allegiances only for His sake, bearing enmity only for His sake, asking none but Him, hoping in none but Him, and fearing none but Him; worshipping Him and seeking His help for His sake, so that they are with the True One without distraction by creation, and with creation without being driven by personal desire; their desire for anything besides Him having faded away through their desire for Him, their love of anything besides Him through their love of Him, and their fear of

---

## Page 4916

anything besides Him through their fear of Him, their hope in anything besides Him through their hope in Him, and their calling upon anything besides Him through their calling upon Him—is something known through direct experience and inward feeling only to those who have a share in it. And every believer has a share in it.

This is the very essence of Islam, with which Allah sent the messengers and revealed the Scriptures. It is the central axis around which the Quran revolves. And Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

---

## Page 4917

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section: “Fanā” (Passing Away)

The term fanā, as it occurs in Sufi writings, is explained in three ways.

(The first): The heart’s ceasing to direct its desire, reliance, worship, and related acts toward anything besides the Lord. This is true and sound; it is pure monotheism and sincerity. In “reality,” it is the heart’s worship, reliance, seeking help, adoration, repentant return, and turning toward Allah alone, without partner, together with the knowledge and spiritual states that follow from this. No one is exempt from this.

This is the “sound heart” of which Allah says:

“Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

It means the heart’s freedom from corrupt beliefs, corrupt desires, and all that follows from them.

---

## Page 4918

This “passing away” does not conflict with “subsistence”; rather, the two coexist. The servant’s desire for anything besides Allah passes away, even while he remains aware of Allah and of other things. This is expressed by the declaration, “There is no god worthy of worship but Allah.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“There is no god worthy of worship but Allah, and we worship none but Him. His are all blessings and bounty, and to Him belongs all good praise.”

This, in broad terms, is the beginning and end of religion.

(The second): The heart’s losing awareness of everything besides the Lord. The former concerns the passing away of desire for anything else; this concerns the passing away of awareness of anything else. The former means ceasing to worship or rely upon another; this means ceasing to be conscious of another or to attend to it.

This kind of passing away involves a deficiency. For perceiving realities as they truly are—that is, perceiving the Lord as governing His servants and commanding His revealed laws—is more complete than perceiving His existence, one of His attributes, or one of His names, and thereby losing awareness of everything else. The Companions’ perception was therefore too complete for a general awareness of Allah to diminish their detailed awareness of Him. Nevertheless, much of this occurred among many later members of this community.

Likewise, when certain realities became manifest to them, they experienced death, fainting, cries, and agitation. This was because their hearts were too weak to perceive realities as they truly are, and to perceive distinction within unity and multiplicity within oneness. They even disagreed over whether this was possible. Many of them believe that no other state is possible, having found that remembering creation or the divine command distracts them from the Creator who issues the command. And when they are challenged with the example of the Prophet

---

## Page 4919

, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs, they claim an exception, evade the question, or become perplexed. This is because they have judged all people by their own experience.

Thus, some of them say that when the Real manifests Himself, it is impossible to hear His speech. It is related that when Ibn Arabī was told that Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn al-Suhrawardī considered both experiences possible together, he said: “We are speaking to him about perceiving the Essence, while he is telling us about perceiving the attributes.”

Shihāb al-Dīn was correct, for his belief concerning the distinction between the Lord and the servant was sound. Ibn Arabī merely based his view on his premise, which constitutes disbelief, that the Real is the existence flowing into contingent beings. It is evident that perceiving this involves no speech addressed to the perceiver; such speech occurs only at the station of the intellect (1).

In this state of passing away, a person may say, “I am the Real,” “Glory be to me,” or “There is nothing within this robe but Allah.” This happens when absorption in the One he perceives makes him lose awareness of his own perception; absorption in the One whose existence he apprehends, of his own existence; absorption in the One he remembers, of his own remembrance; and absorption in the One he knows, of his own knowing.

They relate, for example, that a man was so absorbed in his love for another that, when his beloved fell into the sea, he threw himself in after him. The beloved asked, “What made you throw yourself in after me?” He replied, “I was so lost in you that I forgot myself and thought that you were me.”

In such a state, an intoxication occurs that abolishes discernment, even in the presence of

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) This word is unclear in the author’s handwriting owing to damage to the original manuscript.

---

## Page 4920

the sweetness of faith, just as happens with the intoxication of wine or of one infatuated with physical beauty.

Likewise, passing away may result from a state of fear or hope, just as it may result from a state of love. The heart then loses awareness of certain realities, and the person says or does things resembling the behaviour of the intoxicated. Such are the ecstatic excesses of certain shaykhs—for example, one of them saying, “I shall pitch my tent over Hell,” and similar statements and actions contrary to the revealed Law.

The person responsible may be free of sin. If he is not, this category resembles the case of those who protect the enemy, or someone who assists an unbeliever or an oppressor through a spiritual state and claims to be overpowered by it. The ruling concerning such people is that, if someone loses his reason through a cause that is not forbidden, he incurs no blame for the forbidden statements or actions that proceed from him. This differs from the case in which his loss of reason and the state that overwhelms him arise from something forbidden.

This is as we have said concerning the “sane madmen” and those bewildered by ecstasy, for whom this has become a permanent condition, whereas it overtakes these others only at certain times. Some scholars have made the same distinction concerning someone whose loss of reason causes him to neglect an obligation: if he loses his reason through a cause that is not forbidden—such as fainting through illness, or being forcibly made to drink something that deprives him of his reason—he incurs no sin. But if he loses it through drinking wine or through similar forbidden states, he sins by neglecting the obligation. The same applies to committing a forbidden act.

Although they incur no blame, it is not permissible to follow their example or to construe their words and deeds as sound. Rather, in the sphere of the spiritual elite, they are like the heedless and the insane with respect to religious obligations

---

## Page 4921

of outward observance; and one scholar said of them: “These are people whom Allah granted intellects and spiritual states. He then took away their intellects while leaving their spiritual states, and lifted the obligations He had imposed because of what He had taken away.”

For this reason, those who know Allah agree that the state of abiding is superior to this: it is witnessing realities through Allah’s enabling one to witness them. As Allah Most High said, according to what His Messenger related from Him:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely grant him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks.”

In another version:

“Through Me he speaks, and through Me he understands.”

Thus, when he hears through Allah and sees through Him, he hears things as they really are and witnesses the truth as it really is. Most of what you find concerning passing away in the writings of sound Sufis, such as Shaykh al-Islām and those before him, is of this kind. Nevertheless, some of them may err in certain judgments concerning it, as I have discussed elsewhere.

In sum, this passing away is valid and occurs among those of a Jesus-like disposition within the Muhammadan community. It resembles the fainting and cries that appeared among the Successors. Yet many of these people consequently fall into a kind of error, because passing away from witnessing realities ultimately amounts to an absence of knowledge and awareness. This is an attribute of deficiency, not perfection. It is praiseworthy only in respect of

---

## Page 4922

not desiring anything other than Him; for remembering a created being may lead one to desire it and become infatuated with it. Thus, worshippers of a “Jesus-like disposition” generally lack awareness of anything other than Him, desire for it, and infatuation with it, and are described as sound-hearted. Scholars of a “Moses-like disposition,” by contrast, generally possess knowledge of other things, desire them, and become infatuated with them, and are described as knowledgeable. Yet the former are characterized by ignorance and justice, while the latter are characterized by injustice (1). Both descriptions are accurate.

As for knowing the True One and creation while desiring Allah alone, without any partner, this characterizes those of a Muhammadan disposition who have attained perfection in knowledge and will. The soundness of heart that deserves praise is soundness . . . (2), for ignorance is not, in itself, a praiseworthy quality. It may, however, be praised because it keeps a person safe from evils. For most souls, upon learning of an evil they desire, follow it, become frightened of it, or are seduced by it.

Third: Passing away from the existence of anything other than Him. This means that a person regards Allah as existence itself and holds that nothing else exists, whether through Him or through anything else. This doctrine and spiritual state belong to the heretical proponents of union among later figures, such as al-Balyānī, al-Tilimsānī, al-Qūnūnī, and others like them. They hold that the ultimate truth is that He is identical with existing things and is the very reality of all beings, and that

## Page 4923

nothing other than Him exists—not in the sense that things subsist through Him and owe their existence to Him, as expressed in the Prophet’s saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

And as has been said concerning His words:

## Page 4924

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

“Commands and prohibitions,” which some scholars call “obligation under the Sharia,” are conditional upon the capacity to know and to act. Thus, the obligations of the Sharia do not apply to those incapable of understanding, such as the insane and young children. Nor do particular obligations apply to those incapable of fulfilling them, as with the blind, the lame, and the sick in the case of jihad. Likewise, purification with water, praying while standing, fasting, and other such duties are not obligatory for those unable to perform them.

This holds whether imposing obligations beyond a person’s capacity is considered permissible or not, for there is no disagreement that imposing an obligation upon someone who has absolutely no capacity to perform the act does not occur in

---

## Page 4925

the Sharia. Indeed, the Sharia may exempt those whose faculties of understanding and action are not yet fully developed, both to ease their burden and to establish a clear criterion for legal responsibility, even when imposing obligations upon them would be possible. Thus, the pen is lifted from a child until he reaches puberty, even though he possesses understanding and discernment. This is because his understanding is not yet complete, and because reason develops gradually in people, who differ in this respect. Since the underlying consideration is difficult to ascertain and varies widely, puberty was made the defining criterion.

Likewise, according to the majority of scholars, Hajj is obligatory only upon someone who possesses provisions and a mount, even if walking is possible, because of the hardship involved. Similarly, a traveller is not obliged to fast, even if able to do so, as a concession to ease his burden. Obligations are also waived because of an illness when performing them is feared to worsen the illness and delay recovery, even though their performance remains possible.

These, however, are matters in which revealed laws differ. In one revealed law, Allah may make obligatory something difficult and prohibit something that is difficult to forgo—as with the burdens and shackles imposed upon the Children of Israel—while granting relief in another revealed law. Thus the believers said:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

He Most High also said:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you.”

And He said:

“He has imposed no hardship upon you in religion.”

And He said:

“Allah intends to lighten your burden.”

---

## Page 4926

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his Companions concerning the incident involving the Bedouin:

“You were sent only to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”

He said to Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā:

“Make things easy, and do not make them difficult.”

He also said:

“This religion is easy, and no one overburdens himself in practicing it without being overwhelmed by it.”

He said:

“Do not impose hardship upon yourselves, lest Allah impose hardship upon you. Some people imposed hardship upon themselves, so Allah imposed hardship upon them. Those who remain of them are there in hermitages and monasteries: ‘Monasticism which they invented—we did not prescribe it for them.’”

He said:

“There is no monasticism in Islam.”

He also said:

“But I fast and refrain from fasting; I pray at night and sleep; I marry women and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

He said:

“Allah loves that His concessions be accepted, just as He hates that He be disobeyed.”

It is also reported that he said:

“I was sent with the upright, accommodating faith.”

As for whether a person desires what he is commanded to do or dislikes it, revealed laws take no account of this; nor, indeed, do the commands of any rational person. Rather, a person is commanded to oppose his own whims. “Desire” is what distinguishes the people of Paradise from the people of Hell, as Allah Most High said:

“Whoever desires this fleeting life, We hasten for him therein whatever We will, for whomever We please. Then We assign Hell to him, where he will burn, condemned and banished. But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is they whose striving will be appreciated.”

Allah Most High also said:

“That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who desire neither supremacy on earth nor corruption.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We shall repay them in full

---

## Page 4927

for their deeds therein,” and so on. Allah Most High also said:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

There are many similar passages. These principles are well established in the Quran, the Sunnah, and the words of scholars and those with spiritual insight. The purpose here is not to establish them.

Rather, the purpose is to address another matter: if religious accountability is conditional upon the ability to acquire knowledge, which rests upon reason, and upon the ability to act, then we say:

Either of these capacities may be lost through prohibited causes or through causes that are not prohibited. If someone deprives himself of his reason by drinking wine, taking henbane, or the like, this does not absolve him of sin for the obligations he neglects and the prohibited acts he commits, if intoxication leads to that conduct. This differs from losing his reason through a cause that is not prohibited, such as fainting from illness or fear, or becoming intoxicated through drinking that is not prohibited—for example, being compelled to swallow wine. Such a person incurs no sin.

As for his being required to make up the prayers according to Ahmad, and according to those who say that he must make up the prayers of one day and night, this is analogous to the obligation to make up prayers for someone who sleeps through them or forgets them, neither of whom incurs any sin. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is no negligence in sleep; negligence is only while awake.”

He also said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must pray it when he remembers it, for that is its appointed time. There is no expiation for it other than that.”

---

## Page 4928

The same applies to “a person’s capacity to act”: if, after Hajj becomes obligatory for him, he is negligent and squanders his wealth, Hajj remains an obligation upon him. Likewise, regarding permission to do what is prohibited, Allah Most High said:

“But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limits, incurs no sin.”

Necessity arising from a prohibited act does not make prohibited things permissible, unlike necessity arising from a cause that is not prohibited. Scholars have differed over whether someone whose journey is itself sinful may avail himself of the concessions granted to travellers. The position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that he may not.

As for the states experienced by devoted worshippers, those with spiritual insight, ascetics, and others like them, these may deprive a person of his reason and awareness, leaving him like someone who is insane, distraught, intoxicated, or asleep. They may also deprive him of his capacity to act, leaving him helpless, or like someone compelled to act, whose words and deeds occur without his will or choice. Losing reason and capacity may render him unable to fulfil obligations and may cause him to commit prohibited acts.

Concerning such people, we say: if this loss results from a cause that is not prohibited, they incur no sin for the obligations they neglect or the prohibited acts they commit. Nor, however, is it permissible to follow them in any of their words or deeds that fall outside the Sharia. We do not blame them for that; rather, they may be praised for what accords with the Sharia in their

---

## Page 4929

words and deeds, and they are absolved of blame wherever the Lawgiver has excused them. Exactly the same is said of a scholar who errs in exercising independent judgment. Indeed, such a scholar belongs to this category, since he is absolved of blame because he was unable to attain the requisite knowledge. If, however, their loss of reason or capacity results from a prohibited cause, they deserve blame and punishment for the obligations they neglect and the prohibited acts they commit.

An example of the “first” case is someone who listens to the Quran in the prescribed manner, whereupon a spiritual emotion that he cherishes, or fear or hope, surges within him. Unable to bear it, he dies, falls unconscious, cries out loudly, or becomes violently agitated. If this results in his missing an obligatory prayer or committing an aggression against someone, he is excused for that. In this state, he is like those distraught people described as the wise among the insane, who have lost their reason despite being righteous and possessing spiritual insight. This may be due to the intensity of the inward experience that comes upon them, their hearts’ inability to bear it, an imbalance in their bodily temperaments and the potency of a bodily humour, or an affliction caused by the jinn.

Their condition is as described in the report that has reached us from Imam Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī. When asked about them, he said:

[These are people whom Allah endowed with reason and spiritual states. He then took away their reason while leaving their spiritual states intact, and relieved them of the obligations He had imposed because of what He had taken away.] (*)

Thus, this category and the preceding one were found among the Successors and those who

## Page 4930

came after them, especially among the devout worshippers of Basra. Some of them died upon hearing the Quran, such as Zurāra ibn Awfā, Abū Juhayr the blind, and others. As for the Companions, their spiritual state was too perfect for any of them to become insane or fall unconscious.

Among these people are also those so overwhelmed by remembrance of Allah, affirmation of His oneness, and love for Him that, absorbed in the One they remember, witness, love and worship, they lose awareness of everything else. Something similar happens to a lover who becomes oblivious to everything but his beloved. In this state, one of them may say, “I am the Truth,” “Glory be to me,” or “There is nothing in this robe but Allah.” Others are so overwhelmed by hope and mercy that they say, “I shall spread my prayer rug over Hell.” Whoever says this while deprived of his reason, so that he resembles someone drunk or distraught, incurs no sin, provided that the cause of his condition was not prohibited by Islamic law.

An example of the “second” case is what may happen to many who attend listening sessions when they hear whistling and clapping. Someone may recite poetry containing things contrary to Islamic law, using vocal sounds that also contravene it. If a listener is predisposed to such reactions, this may cause mental confusion and loss of reason, to the point that some kill others, either outwardly or inwardly through their wills and hearts. It also leads to neglect of the obligations of Islamic law and aggression against believers in their religious and worldly affairs, to an extent known to Allah.

---

## Page 4931

Likewise, one of them may engage in forms of worship contrary to Islamic law, in both belief and practice. These acts of worship and practices produce powerful, overwhelming states in him, causing him to neglect obligations and commit prohibited acts against people’s lives and property more grievous than those committed by a tyrannical king intoxicated with wine.

When someone addresses him while he is sober and in possession of his reason, he says: “I was overpowered. A spiritual impulse came upon me and did this to me, and the spiritual impulse rules.” Such is the condition of many who protect the enemy, and of many among those who experience spiritual states who assist unbelievers and oppressors and commit aggression against Muslims and believers. Such a person says that he was overpowered in this, that a spiritual impulse came upon him and compelled it, and that he was instructed to perform that act.

He should be told:

“As for your loss of reason, to the point that you no longer understand Allah’s commands and prohibitions, and your loss of control, to the point that you are compelled to perform those acts—even if you are truthful about this, it results from your own initial negligence and transgression, which brought you into the condition of the insane and the intoxicated. You are therefore like someone who drinks wine and becomes intoxicated, or someone who exposes himself to passionate love until he falls in love and it wreaks havoc upon him. There is no difference between intoxication through sounds, beautiful forms, and drink: one is intoxication of the body, another intoxication of the soul, and another intoxication of the spirit. If its cause is prohibited, the intoxicated person is not excused in Islam.

---

## Page 4932

This is why these states occur only in those who have something of Christianity in them, which inclines them towards intoxication, as Christians seek it through drink, sounds, and beautiful forms. This is why such people dwell in the realm of misguidance.

As for your claim that you were addressed in this way and commanded to act, which of the two kinds of words was involved: words expressing religious commands, or words expressing the universal decree?

The former include His words:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct,”

“It is He who sent among the unlettered,”

and “We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs.”

The latter include His words:

“We commanded its affluent inhabitants,”

“We sent against you servants of Ours,”

and “that We have sent the devils.”

If you claim that it was of the “former” kind, your claim is false, for it contradicts the Quran and the Sunnah. If you acknowledge that it was of the “latter” kind, that is correct. But this is the condition of unbelievers and hypocrites, such as Iblīs, Pharaoh, Nimrod, and all others who obeyed the commands of universal decree and followed the decreed will, while turning away from the commands of revealed law and failing to abide by His will concerning religion.

Reflect upon this principle, for it is immensely important and beneficial: it exposes the nature of states that contravene Islamic law. Those who experience them are divided into those who are excused and those who bear sin, just as the states themselves are divided into

---

## Page 4933

those recorded against the person experiencing them and those forgiven. They are comparable to the states experienced by people other than worshippers and ascetics: sanity and sobriety, fainting, intoxication and insanity, compulsion and free choice. The states of kings and rulers, guides and scholars, and shaykhs and the spiritual poor all fall under this noble principle, and Islamic law judges them by distinguishing between them.

If to this is added the fact that disclosures of knowledge or effects brought about under divine decree by those experiencing such states do not necessarily entail friendship with Allah—not even righteousness, nor indeed faith, since such things may occur in an unbeliever, a hypocrite, an evildoer or a sinner—and that the friends of Allah, who shall have no fear nor grieve, are only those who believe and are mindful of Him, then a distinction is drawn between friendship with Allah and these states, just as a distinction is drawn between the prophetic caliphate and kingship in general, and between the knowledge that is the prophets’ legacy and discourse in general.

These two categories overlap without coinciding. A man may be a friend of Allah who experiences a state involving extraordinary effects and disclosure, or he may be a friend of Allah without possessing that state in its fullness. Conversely, he may possess something of these states without being a friend of Allah. Likewise, a man may be a prophet’s successor who commands obedience, or a prophet’s successor who is weak and oppressed; or he may be a tyrant who commands obedience yet has no connection whatsoever with prophethood. A man may also be a scholar who does not engage in discourse contrary to the words of the prophets, or a scholar whose discourse consists of the words of the prophets.
