## Page 4934

Section

Know that most innovations relating to knowledge and worship, in these matters and others, arose within the Muslim community only towards the end of the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold when he said:

“Those of you who live after me will see much disagreement. So adhere to my Sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs who come after me.”

It is well known that when “those in authority,” who govern people’s lives and property, remain upright, people generally remain upright. Thus, as al-Bukhārī relates in his Sahīh, when the woman from the Ahmas tribe asked Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, “How long will we continue in this good state?” he replied, “As long as your leaders remain upright in governing you.”

A transmitted report states:

“There are two groups who, when they are righteous, bring righteousness to the people: scholars and rulers.”

These are the bearers of scripture and the wielders of iron, as indicated by His words, “We have certainly sent…” and the remainder of the verse. They are also “those vested with authority” in His words:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those vested with authority among you.”

---

## Page 4935

Likewise, corruption arises through them, as stated in a hadith attributed to the Prophet and in reports from several Companions:

“What I fear most for you is a scholar’s lapse, a hypocrite’s disputing by means of the Quran, and leaders who lead people astray.”

The leaders who lead people astray are the rulers, while the scholar and the disputant belong to the ranks of scholars. However, (the first) holds sound beliefs but makes mistakes: this is the scholar, as happens among the leading jurists of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah. And (the second) is like the philosophers and speculative theologians who dispute using specious arguments drawn from the Quran, although in reality they have cast off Allah’s signs. They invoke it only to rebut their opponent, not to seek its guidance or rely upon it. This is why he said:

“A hypocrite’s disputing by means of the Quran.”

For the Sunnah and scholarly consensus refute his specious argument.

The religion established in the heart—faith, both as knowledge and as an inward state—is the “root,” while outward deeds are the “branches,” and they constitute the perfection of faith. Religion is thus first built upon its foundations and brought to completion through its branches. Accordingly, in Mecca Allah revealed its foundations: monotheism; parables, which are rational analogies; narratives; promises of reward; and warnings of punishment. Then, in Medina—once the religion had gained strength—He revealed its outward branches: Friday prayer, congregational prayer, the call to prayer, the announcement that prayer is about to begin, jihad, fasting, the prohibition of wine, unlawful sexual intercourse and gambling, and its other obligations and prohibitions.

---

## Page 4936

Its roots thus nourish and strengthen its branches, while its branches perfect and preserve its roots. Whenever an outward deficiency occurs in it, it begins in its branches. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The first thing you will lose from your religion is trustworthiness, and the last thing you will lose from your religion is prayer.”

It is also reported that he said:

“The first thing to be taken away is trustworthy governance.”

“Governance” is the work of rulers and those in authority, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and, when you judge between people, to judge with justice.”

As for prayer, it is the first obligation prescribed and is among the foundations of religion and faith, coupled with the two testimonies of faith. It therefore disappears only at the end, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Islam began as something strange and will return to being strange as it began, so glad tidings to the strangers.”

He thus stated that its return would resemble its beginning. When the rule of the Rightly Guided Caliphs ended and gave way to kingship, deficiency appeared among the rulers; it was therefore inevitable that it would also appear among people of knowledge and religious devotion. Thus, toward the end of ‘Alī’s caliphate, the two innovations—those of the Khawārij and the Rāfidah—arose, for they concern leadership, the caliphate, and the practices and rulings of Islamic law that follow from them.

Mu‘āwiyah’s rule was a merciful kingship. When Mu‘āwiyah—may Allah have mercy on him—passed away and Yazīd’s rule began, there occurred during it the turmoil surrounding the killing of al-Husayn in Iraq and the turmoil involving the people of al-Harrah in Medina. They also laid siege to Mecca when ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr rose up.

---

## Page 4937

Then Yazīd died, and the Muslim community became divided: Ibn al-Zubayr held the Hijāz, the house of al-Hakam held Syria, and al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ‘Ubayd and others rose up in Iraq. It was during this period, towards the end of the era of the Companions, while men such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abbās, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, and others were still alive, that the innovations of the Qadariyyah and the Murji’ah arose. The surviving Companions, such as Ibn ‘Abbās, Ibn ‘Umar, Jābir, Wāthilah ibn al-Asqa‘, and others—may Allah be pleased with them—refuted these innovations, alongside their own and others’ refutations of the innovations of the Khawārij and the Rāfidah.

At that time, the Qadariyyah’s discussions chiefly concerned people’s deeds, just as the Murji’ah’s did. Their discussions thus concerned obedience and disobedience, the believer and the sinner, and similar questions of “religious designations and rulings” and “the promise of reward and the threat of punishment.”

They did not discuss their Lord or His attributes until towards the end of the era of the younger Successors, in the closing years of the Umayyad state, when most of the third generation—the successors of the Successors—began to pass away—for the three generations are reckoned according to the majority of the people of each generation, who belong to its middle period. Most of the Companions had passed away by the end of the caliphate of the four caliphs, so that only a few of those who had fought at Badr remained. Most of the Successors, who followed them in righteousness, had passed away towards the end of the era of the younger Companions, during the rule of Ibn al-Zubayr and ‘Abd al-Malik. Most of the successors of the Successors had passed away towards the end of the Umayyad state and the beginning of the Abbasid state—and there came to be

## Page 4942

And among the people of Kufa were both truthful narrators and liars. Among the people of Syria there were not many liars, nor were there great leading authorities in Quranic recitation and hadith.

The same applies to the leading jurists: Mālik was the scholar of Medina; al-Thawrī, Abū Hanīfa and others were from Kufa; Ibn Jurayj and others were from Mecca; Hammād ibn Salama and Hammād ibn Zayd were from Basra; and al-Awzā'ī and his contemporaries were in Syria. It has been said that Mālik modelled his Muwatta' on the book of Hammād ibn Salama; it has also been said that Ibn Jurayj’s book preceded that.

Then came al-Shāfi'ī. Although he had Meccan origins, he studied jurisprudence according to the approach of the scholars of hadith, without confining himself to his own city. Likewise, although Imam Ahmad’s forebears were from Basra, he studied jurisprudence according to the approach of the scholars of hadith, without confining himself to the scholars of Basra or any other group. The same applies to 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm, Muhammad ibn Ismā'īl al-Bukhārī and other scholars from Khurasan.

Likewise, the leading ascetics and devoted worshippers came from these centres, as Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī mentioned in Safwat al-Safwa (The Choicest of the Choice).

Thus, knowledge and devotion sanctioned by the religion are derived from the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As for what has come down from those after them, it should not be made

---

## Page 4943

a foundation, even if its proponent is excused—indeed, rewarded—for exercising independent judgment or following an authority.

Whoever bases scholarly discussion of fundamentals and subsidiary matters on the Quran, the Sunnah and the reports transmitted from the early predecessors has followed the prophetic path. Likewise, whoever bases aspiration, worship, action and listening—in relation to the fundamentals and particulars of practice, encompassing states of the heart and bodily actions—on faith, the Sunnah and the guidance followed by Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions, has followed the prophetic path. This is the way of the leading scholars of guidance.

Thus, when Imam Ahmad discusses the foundations of the Sunnah, you find him saying: “They consist in holding fast to the way followed by the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” He compiled works of Quranic commentary based on what was transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions and the Successors. He also recorded hadiths and reports transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions and the Successors. These are what he relies upon in the fundamentals and subsidiary matters of his scholarship. He even said in his letter to al-Mutawakkil, the caliph of his time:

“I do not like to speak about any of these matters except on the basis of what is in Allah’s Book or in a report from Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or from the Companions or the Successors. As for anything beyond that, discussing it is not praiseworthy.”

## Page 4944

The same applies to “asceticism,” “heart-softening exhortations,” and “spiritual states.” In his Book of Asceticism, he relied on reports transmitted from the prophets—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—from Adam to Muhammad, and then on the way of the Companions and the Successors, without mentioning those who came after them. Likewise, he instructed the student of knowledge to record what was transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then from the Companions, then from the Successors. In another version, he said: “Then, regarding the Successors, you have a choice.”

He also made statements concerning “speculative theology,” “juristic opinion,” “Sufi books,” and “Sufi listening practices,” which this is not the place to discuss. A precise treatment requires elaboration and an explanation of how his statements apply in some circumstances but not others. This rests on the principle we have already stated: good deeds may be accompanied by sins, whether forgiven or unforgiven. A spiritual wayfarer may find it impossible or difficult to follow the purely prescribed path without some newly introduced practice, because there is no one who upholds the prescribed path in knowledge and practice.

If pure light is unavailable, and the only light to be found is not pure, while a person would otherwise remain in darkness, one should not disparage or forbid a light mingled with darkness unless a light free of darkness is available. Otherwise, how many who turn away from this leave the light altogether when someone else turns away from it because of the darkness he has seen in people’s ways!

## Page 4945

I have set out this “principle” only so that the early generations’ and scholars’ condemnation of a thing may be understood in its proper context, and so that it may be recognized that departure from the full realization of succession to prophethood, as prescribed by the revealed law, sometimes results from negligence in omitting good in knowledge and action, and sometimes from transgression in committing evil in knowledge and action. Either may occur because a person is overwhelmed, or despite having the ability to act otherwise. The “former” may result from inability and limited capacity, or occur despite having the ability and opportunity. The “latter” may occur under conditions of need and necessity, or despite having sufficient means and ample alternatives.

Both the person unable to attain the full measure of good and the person compelled by necessity to commit some evil are excused, for Allah says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And He says:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity”—in al-Baqarah and al-Talāq (1).

And He says:

“But those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity—those are the people of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

And He, glorified be He, says:

“He has placed no hardship upon you in religion.”

And He says:

“Allah does not intend to place you in hardship.”

And He says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And He says:

“But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, incurs no sin.”

And He says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake.”

## Page 4946

And this is a great principle: to recognize what is good in itself, in knowledge and action, whether obligatory or recommended; and to recognize what is evil in itself, in knowledge, speech, and action, whether prohibited or not—if what is not prohibited may be called evil. Religion consists in securing good and benefit, and preventing evil and harm.

These two aspects often coexist in a single act or a single person. Blame, prohibition, and punishment may be directed at the evil contained in either, but the good within it must not be overlooked. Likewise, praise, commands, and reward may be directed at the good contained in either, but the evil within it must not be overlooked. A man may be praised for refraining from certain evils involving religious innovation and wickedness, yet he may lack the good deeds, in accordance with the Sunnah and righteousness, for which another is praised. This is the way of weighing things fairly and giving each its due. Whoever follows it upholds the justice for which Allah sent down the Book and the Balance.

## Page 4949

The name “Sufis” is derived from sūf (wool), since wool was the usual clothing of ascetics. It has also been said to derive from Sūfah ibn Murr ibn Udd ibn Tābikhah, an Arab tribe whose members used to reside around the Sacred House.

As for those who derive it from suffah (the shaded platform), the objection has been raised that the proper form would be Suffiyyah. Likewise, those who derive it from safāʾ (purity) are told that the proper form would be Safāʾiyyah. If the word ended instead in an unhamzated long ā, the form would be Safawiyyah; if derived from safwah (the elect), it would be Safwiyyah. Those who derive it from saff, meaning the foremost rank before Allah, are told that the proper form would be Saffiyyah. There is no doubt that these would be the required forms of attribution and affiliation if due regard were given to the rules of Arabic.

The correct explanation, however, is that these derivations were proposed on the basis of greater and intermediate derivation, rather than minor derivation. This resembles Abū Ja‘far’s statement that al-‘āmmah (the common people) is a name derived from ‘amā (blindness). Such derivations take account either of shared letters without regard to their order—which is intermediate derivation—or of letters belonging to the same kind without being identical—which is greater derivation. An example of intermediate derivation is the Kufan grammarians’ assertion that ism (name) derives from simah (mark). The same applies when “Sufi” is said to derive from safāʾ (purity). If, however, it is said to derive from suffah or saff, this falls under greater derivation.

A number of the leading scholars, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, used this designation.

---

## Page 4950

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī and others also used this designation. As for al-Shāfi‘ī, what is reported from him is criticism of the Sufis, and likewise from Mālik—as far as I recall. Ahmad used this designation when addressing Abū Hamzah al-Khurāsānī, Yūsuf ibn al-Husayn al-Rāzī, and Badr ibn Abī Badr al-Maghāzilī. Their path was criticized by a number of scholars and devout worshippers among the followers of Ahmad, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Abū Hanīfah, as well as by hadith scholars and other devout worshippers, while others praised it.

The sound assessment is that, like other paths, it contains both praiseworthy and blameworthy elements. Its blameworthy elements may or may not result from independent scholarly judgment. In this respect, they are comparable to jurists in their use of legal opinion, for many groups of scholars and devout worshippers have criticized legal opinion. The principle I set out earlier encompasses all of this. Among those who bear this designation are countless allies of Allah, His chosen ones, and the finest of His servants, just as among those who employ legal opinion are people of knowledge and faith whose number none but Allah can count. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

This makes it clear to you that, although innovation in religion is in principle blameworthy—as the Book and the Sunnah indicate, whether such innovations involve words or deeds—and I have written elsewhere that it is imperative to uphold the general scope of the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Every innovation is misguidance,” that one must act upon its general scope, and that whoever begins dividing innovations into good and bad and makes that

---

## Page 4951

a pretext for denying that something’s being an innovation is grounds for prohibiting it has erred. This is what some of those engaged in jurisprudence, speculative theology, Sufism, and devotional worship do: when forbidden from engaging in “innovated acts of worship” and “discourse concerning innovated forms of religious observance,” they claim that no innovation is blameworthy unless it has been prohibited. The hadith would then amount to saying: “Everything that has been prohibited,” or “Everything that has been forbidden,” or “Everything that contradicts a prophetic text is misguidance.” This is too obvious to need explanation. Rather, everything in religion that has not been prescribed is misguidance.

As for anything called an “innovation” whose goodness is established by the evidence of revelation, one of “two things” must follow. Either it is said that it is not an innovation in religion, even though it may be called an innovation in the linguistic sense—as ‘Umar said, “What an excellent innovation this is!”—or it is said that this is a general statement from which this particular case has been excepted on the strength of outweighing counterevidence. It then retains its general application to everything else, like other general statements in the Book and Sunnah. I have explained this in Iqtidā’ al-Sirāt al-Mustaqīm (Following the Straight Path), Qā‘idat al-Sunnah wa-l-Bid‘ah (A Treatise on Sunnah and Innovation), and elsewhere.

“The point here” is simply that when a person commits something whose blameworthiness is established—whether an innovation or another act prohibited in the Book and Sunnah or contrary to them—he may do so under circumstances in which he is excused, either

---

## Page 4952

because of an excusable exercise of independent judgment or reliance on another’s judgment, or because of a lack of ability, as I have explained elsewhere. I have also explained this under the principle of “declaring someone an unbeliever or a sinful transgressor,” which rests on the principle governing threats of punishment.

The texts containing “threats of punishment” in the Book and Sunnah, and the statements of the leading scholars declaring people unbelievers or sinful transgressors and the like, do not entail that their consequences apply to a particular individual unless the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments are absent. There is no distinction in this respect between fundamentals and subsidiary matters.

This concerns punishment in the Hereafter. One who deserves the threatened chastisement, curse, and wrath of Allah in the Hereafter will either remain in the Fire eternally or not. The corresponding designations of disbelief and sinful transgression fall under this “rule,” whether they arise from an innovation in belief or worship, or from sinful conduct in worldly life—that is, sinful transgression through deeds.

The same also applies to rulings in this world. Fighting unbelievers must be preceded by calling them to Islam, since punishment applies only to those whom the message has reached. Likewise, punishment of sinful transgressors is not warranted until the proof has been established against them.

---

## Page 4953

There is an important principle here that deserves careful attention: for sins that harm others in their religion and worldly affairs, the punishment we impose in this world is more severe. As for sins through which a person harms himself, his punishment in the Hereafter may be more severe, even though we do not punish him in this world.

Harming a person in his religion and worldly affairs constitutes wrongdoing against others. Anyone who wrongs another necessarily deserves punishment in this world, to prevent people from wronging one another. Such wrongdoing is of two kinds:

First: withholding the rights due to others, which is neglect.

Second: doing what harms another, which is aggression. Thus, neglect of people’s rights . . . (1)

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A lacuna in the original manuscript.

---

## Page 4954

For this reason, one who promotes religious innovations is subjected to punishments not imposed on one who remains silent; one who openly commits wrongdoing is subjected to punishments not imposed on one who conceals it; and we refrain from punishing the religious hypocrite, even though he will be in the lowest depth of the Fire.

This is because, in principle, punishment is administered by Allah Most High: He recompenses people for their deeds in the Hereafter, and He may also recompense them in this world. As for us, we punish people only to the extent needed to secure the performance of obligations and the abandonment of prohibited acts, as far as we are able. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. If they do so, they safeguard their lives and property from me, except where a rightful claim warrants otherwise, and their reckoning rests with Allah.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and religion is wholly devoted to Allah.”

And He said:

“Persecution is worse than killing.”

For this reason, if unbelievers, those who wage war, or other transgressors repent before they are apprehended, the punishment pertaining to Allah’s right is waived. Thus, if an unbeliever at war with the Muslims embraces Islam before being captured, he thereby safeguards his life, family, and property. The same applies to highway robbers, those who commit unlawful sexual intercourse, thieves, and those who drink intoxicants, if they repent before being apprehended, because repentance achieves the intended purpose.

But if they repent after being apprehended, the punishment is not entirely waived, because that would lead to the prescribed penalties being rendered ineffective and to the spread of corruption, and because such repentance cannot be relied upon. For this reason, if an unbeliever at war with the Muslims embraces Islam during battle, his acceptance of Islam is valid, because he embraced Islam before being captured

---

## Page 4955

unlike one who embraces Islam after being taken captive: although his life is protected, his enslavement is not precluded.

It follows from this “principle” that some disbelievers and hypocrites may be left unpunished, even though their punishment in the Hereafter will be more severe, provided their harm does not extend to others. Examples include those who pay the jizyah willingly while humbled, and those who outwardly profess Islam and observe its laws despite their hypocrisy. These two groups have withheld their harm from Muslims in both religious and worldly affairs, and they will be punished in the Hereafter for the disbelief and hypocrisy they have committed.

As for anyone who openly engages in harmful conduct, his harm must be prevented, even through punishment—even if he is a Muslim who is flagrantly sinful or disobedient, or an upright person who errs in exercising independent judgment; indeed, even if he is righteous or a scholar. This applies equally to those who can be apprehended and those who resist apprehension.

As an example concerning those who can be apprehended, people who openly commit unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking intoxicants, false testimony, highway robbery, and similar acts are punished only because these acts violate lives, property, and sexual inviolability. This is so even though the sinful Muslim’s condition in the Hereafter is better than that of disbelievers under covenant and hypocrites, for the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish that a sinful Muslim is better than a disbeliever or hypocrite.

Likewise, anyone who promotes a religious innovation that harms people in their religion is punished, even though he may in fact be excused for it on account of his independent judgment or his following another’s opinion.

---

## Page 4956

Likewise, it is permissible to fight “rebels”: those who rise against the ruler or others on the basis of a defensible interpretation, even though they remain upright, we uphold their judicial rulings, and we recognize as valid their collection of jizyah, land tax, and other revenues. There is no disagreement that the Companions retained their upright standing; their defensible interpretation precluded judging them to be flagrantly sinful.

As for fighting them, its purpose is to make them fulfil the obligations they have neglected and desist from the prohibited acts they have committed, even though they act on an interpretation. Likewise, we enforce the prescribed punishment upon someone who drinks a fermented beverage whose permissibility is disputed, even if those who do so are righteous people.

Consider, then, how people are punished in this world for neglecting an obligation or committing an act clearly forbidden in religious or worldly affairs, even though they may be excused for it. This is done to avert the worldly harm caused by their actions. Similarly, the prescribed punishment is enforced upon someone who repents after his case has been brought before the ruler, even if his repentance is entirely sincere. Likewise, an army will march against this House, and while they are on a stretch of open ground, the earth will swallow them up. Among them will be people compelled to accompany them, but they will be resurrected according to their intentions. Likewise, the armies of the disbelievers are fought even though their ranks include people compelled to join them, as at Badr, when al-ʿAbbās and others were among them.

The same applies if the disbelievers use Muslims as shields and their harm cannot be repelled except by fighting them. Thus, punishments prescribed by religious law and those divinely decreed may, in this world, extend to people who do not deserve them in the Hereafter. For such people, they count among the calamities that befall them. As has been said concerning some of them: “The killer is striving in Allah’s cause, and the one killed is a martyr.”

Accordingly, the instruction given by the later adherents of the Sunnah—that an advocate of religious innovation

---

## Page 4957

is to be shunned—his testimony is not to be sought, no narrations are to be transmitted from him, no legal opinions are to be sought from him, and prayer is not to be performed behind him—may fall into this category. Shunning him is a disciplinary measure and a punishment intended to deter people from that sin, whether it is a religious innovation or something else, even if he has in fact repented or is excused.

For shunning serves one of two purposes: either avoiding the sins that must be shunned and those who commit them, or punishing the offender and making an example of him. As for shunning him by refraining from . . . (1) elsewhere.

This category includes Imām Ahmad’s shunning of those who yielded during the inquisition before being put in fetters, those who repented after yielding, and those who committed some religious innovation, even though they included leading figures in hadith, jurisprudence, Sufism, and worship. His shunning them, together with the Muslims who joined him, does not preclude recognizing their merit. Similarly, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered the Muslims to shun the three who had been left behind, this did not negate their earlier merits.

Indeed, it has been said that two of them participated in Badr, and Allah said to the people of Badr:

“Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.”

One of the three was Kaʿb ibn Mālik, the Prophet’s poet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and one of those present at al-ʿAqabah.

This, then, is “a fundamental principle”: a worldly punishment prescribed by religious law, ranging from shunning to execution, does not preclude the person punished from being upright or righteous. This accords with the distinction I have explained between worldly punishment—whether prescribed by religious law or divinely decreed—and punishment in the Hereafter. Allah, glorified is He, knows best.
