## Page 4958

Section

Related to this subject is the saying: “So-and-so’s state is to be accepted without objection,” or “His state is not to be accepted without objection.” Disputes over this frequently arise concerning things done by certain shaykhs, spiritual mendicants, and Sufis that are said to contravene the Sharia.

Someone who considers these things reprehensible, and regards forbidding wrongdoing as part of religion, condemns those acts and censures both the man concerned and anyone who thinks well of him. He hates him, denounces him, and punishes him. By contrast, someone who sees the man’s righteousness and devotion—his asceticism, spiritual states, scrupulous piety, and knowledge—does not condemn those acts. Rather, he considers them permissible or good, or turns away from the matter.

Either of these two may go to extremes. The first may be carried by his condemnation to the point of declaring people unbelievers or grave sinners in matters open to scholarly judgment, following the apparent meaning of evidence from the Sharia. The second may be carried by his acceptance to the point of approving things contrary to the religion of Islam—things indisputably known to contradict what the Messenger brought—claiming to follow something resembling the account of Moses and al-Khidr.

The first tendency is common among those whose approach resembles that of Moses, and those among them who have strayed into Judaism. The second is common among those whose approach resembles that of Jesus, and those among them who have strayed into Christianity.

---

## Page 4959

And the (first) tendency often occurs among people of knowledge, but coupled with hardness of heart and the pursuit of personal desires. The (second) often occurs among people of compassion, but coupled with misguidance and ignorance. As for the “community of the middle way,” they possess both knowledge and mercy, as Allah has described Himself in the words:

“Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge.”

And He, Most High, says:

“My mercy encompasses all things.”

And He says:

“Your only God is Allah, other than whom there is no deity. He encompasses all things in knowledge.”

Likewise, He described the servant whom Moses met, saying:

“We had granted him mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our own presence.”

The just approach in “this matter,” in both word and deed, is to recognize that accepting someone’s state without objection has two meanings:

The first is to absolve him of blame, so that he is neither censured nor held sinful . . . (1).

The second is to judge what he has done to be correct, so that he deserves praise and reward. Thus, the “first” means the absence of censure and punishment, while the “second” means the presence of praise and reward. The “first” means the absence of Allah’s displeasure and punishment, while the “second” means the presence of His pleasure and reward. For this reason,

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A lacuna in the original.

---

## Page 4960

you will often find those who object affirming displeasure, censure, and punishment, while those who approve affirm pleasure, praise, and reward. Both may be mistaken, with the correct view lying in “a third, intermediate position”: that there is neither praise nor censure, neither reward nor punishment.

The explanation is this: when something a person says or does is known to contradict the Quran and Sunnah, constituting a false statement or a forbidden act, he may nevertheless be excused in two circumstances: (the first) is his inability to obtain the relevant knowledge; (the second) is his inability to follow the truth prescribed by the revealed law.

An example of (the first) is when the person experiencing the state is bewildered and insane, and is no longer held accountable. If it is said of him, “His state should be accepted without objection,” meaning that he is neither censured nor punished—not that he is judged correct in it—then this is sound, just as it is said of other insane people. But if what is meant is that the statement itself is correct, then this is mistaken.

The same applies when his state results from an exercise of independent judgment, as in matters disputed among people of knowledge and religion. If it is said, “His state should be accepted without objection,” just as one says, “He is allowed to maintain his independent judgment,” meaning that he is neither censured nor punished, then this is sound.

---

## Page 4961

But if this is said to mean that it is correct or sound, evidence must be provided to establish its correctness. A statement or action proceeding from anyone other than the Messenger is not, in itself, proof that the speaker or doer is correct. If that exercise of independent judgment is known to be mistaken, accepting his state means exempting him from censure, not declaring him correct.

Likewise, accepting his state and allowing him to continue may mean letting his judicial ruling stand without overturning it, allowing his legal opinion to stand without objection, or permitting those entitled to rely on his authority and follow him to do so. Those lacking the requisite knowledge may rely on and follow scholars and religious teachers whom it is permissible to follow, in matters they have not recognized as mistaken. Some of this, however, falls within the second category: that which is not known to contravene the revealed law.

In such cases, his state is accepted when he is known to be excused, or known to be sincere in his path and the matter may be an exercise of independent judgment on his part. These, then, are “three circumstances” in which his state is accepted because he is unable to obtain the relevant knowledge and the truth is hidden from him in a way that excuses him.

An example of (the second)—his inability to comply—is when he experiences states that compel him to tear his clothes, slap his face, utter objectionable cries, or shake violently. If it is known that the cause of this was not forbidden and that he is overcome by it, his state is accepted. If there is doubt whether he is overcome or merely pretending, but he is known to be truthful, it is said, “His state should be accepted without objection,”

---

## Page 4962

but if he is known to be lying, he is reproved. If there is doubt about him, both acceptance and censure are withheld until his situation becomes clear, just as with someone who gives testimony or is accused of theft. If his truthfulness and uprightness become evident, the testimony is accepted and it is handed over to them. If his lying and dishonesty become evident, the testimony is rejected and he is punished for theft. If the matter remains uncertain, judgment is withheld, for the believer pauses and seeks clarity. This is what al-Hasan al-Basrī said.

The same applies when someone neglects obligatory duties, presenting himself as overcome and unable to perform them—for example, when he neglects prayer, presenting himself as being like someone unconscious or asleep who is unable to perform it. This may happen to some who collapse under an overwhelming experience of fear of Allah, love of Him, or something similar, losing their discernment and becoming unable to pray. The obligatory duties he neglects are thus comparable to the forbidden acts he commits. Accepting his state, in the sense of refraining from blame, may mean judging him to be excused, or it may mean refraining from judging him blameworthy.

This concerns words and deeds known beyond doubt to contravene the revealed law, such as the ecstatic outbursts reported from certain shaykhs. One example is Ibn Hūd’s statement:

“When the Day of Resurrection comes, I will pitch my tent over Hell.”

Another is al-Shiblī’s practice of shaving his beard and tearing his clothes, until they admitted him to the hospital twice. There is also the statement attributed to one of them:

“If you have a need, come to my grave and seek help through it.”

Other examples include one person’s abandoning Friday prayer behind a righteous imam because he had supplicated for the ruler of his time and called him just; another’s abandoning prayer behind an imam because of what had been disclosed to him of that imam’s inner thoughts; and what is related about the rational madmen, of whom it was said:

“Allah gave them intellects and spiritual states, then took away their intellects and left

---

## Page 4963

their spiritual states, and lifted the obligations He had imposed because of what He had taken away.”

In sum, these matters must be accorded their due under the Quran and Sunnah. Whatever the Quran and Sunnah convey—whether statements, commands, or prohibitions—must be followed. No consideration is to be given to anyone who opposes it, whoever he may be, nor may anyone be followed in contradicting it, whoever he may be. This accords with what the Quran, Sunnah, and consensus of the Muslim community establish concerning following and obeying the Messenger.

At the same time, the person responsible for such conduct must be excused wherever the revealed law excuses him: if he has lost his reason or discernment; if he has erred in exercising independent judgment, whether in word or deed; or if he is so overcome in committing that act or neglecting that duty that, through no sin of his own, he cannot prevent the objectionable act he commits, or, through no sin of his own, he cannot perform that obligation.

The general principle governing this matter must be safeguarded: whatever contradicts the Quran and Sunnah must neither be followed nor made into a religious law or a path to follow. Rather, there is no path to Allah and no religious law except what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. As for those individuals who have contravened some of this in the circumstances described above, they are excused, and are neither blamed nor punished.

For the words and deeds of anyone may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Every imam has said or done things in which he is not to be followed, even though he is not blamed for them.

As for words and deeds that are not known with certainty to contradict the Quran and Sunnah, but rather

---

## Page 4964

fall within areas of independent judgment over which people of knowledge and faith have differed, such matters may be definitively settled for someone to whom Allah has made the truth clear. Yet he cannot bind others to what has become clear to him but not to them. Thus, in one respect, such a matter belongs to the first category, and in another to the second. These matters may also remain open to independent judgment in his own view. In such cases, those exercising independent judgment, together with those who follow them, are allowed their respective approaches as a general concession, without being censured for them, just as an individual concession is granted in the first category.

As for someone whose state is not to be accepted as an excuse, this includes one who is known to be of sound mind but feigns derangement to escape blame—as do many who affiliate themselves with Shaykh Ahmad ibn al-Rifāʿī and the “Yūnusiyya” regarding the forbidden acts they commit and the obligations they neglect. It also includes one who is known to affect ecstasy and feign intoxication in that state so that others will think well of him and excuse the objectionable acts he commits; or one who is known to have recognized the truth but follows his own desires; or one who is known to regard deviation from the requirements of Muhammad’s revealed law as permissible, who may utter statements contrary to it, and who holds that some men can dispense with the Messenger, oppose him, or simply go along with the divine decree in opposition to religion.

Thus, some misguided liars relate that the people of the Suffa fought against the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, alongside the disbelievers when his Companions were defeated, saying: “We are with Allah; whoever prevails, we are with him.” They also relate that, on the morning following the Night Journey, the intimate discourse that had taken place between him and his Lord was heard from him,

---

## Page 4965

and that he gave himself over to ecstasy in heaven until his cloak fell from him; and that he deposited the secret communicated to him in a patch of earth where reeds grew, so that the flute came to bear the meaning of that secret. Or they hold that anyone after Muhammad may depart from his revealed law, just as al-Khidr was permitted to depart from Moses’ command. Moses, however, had not been sent to al-Khidr, whereas Muhammad was sent to all humankind.

These people, and others like them who violate the revealed law and turn away when the truth becomes clear to them, must be opposed in accordance with what the revealed law prescribes: by physical intervention, by speech, and in the heart. Likewise, anyone who follows those previously mentioned whose contrary statements and actions were excusable must be censured, for the excuse that applied to them does not apply to him. He therefore has no grounds for following them in this.

When it is unclear to which of the two categories someone belongs, judgment concerning him should be withheld, for it is better for a ruler to err in pardoning than to err in punishing. However, there should be no hesitation in rejecting whatever contradicts the Book and Sunnah, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever performs an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected.”

It is therefore impermissible to depart, on doubtful grounds, from what the general and unqualified wording of the Book and Sunnah requires. Nor is it permissible to condemn or punish on doubtful grounds, or to declare something true or false, right or wrong, on such grounds.

May Allah guide us to the straight path—the path of those whom He has blessed among the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous—not those who have incurred His anger, nor those who have gone astray.

---

## Page 4966

There remains here a “question” that often causes confusion: someone whose circumstances are unknown may outwardly do something contrary to the revealed law, yet possibly have an excuse recognized by that law. Examples include a state of ecstasy in which he transgresses the revealed law, when it is unclear whether his state is genuine or feigned; or taking property apparently without its owner’s permission, when he may know that the owner willingly consents.

If it is said that such a person should be censured, he may in fact have an excuse. But if it is said that he should not be censured, this entails allowing people whose circumstances are unknown to persist in apparent violations of the revealed law. In such cases, one must first address the person gently, saying: “Outwardly, this is wrong. As for the inward reality, Allah has entrusted you with responsibility for yourself. So explain your circumstances to us, or refrain from displaying this where doing so would cause confusion and temptation.” In doing so, you should follow a course that neither condones wrongdoing nor blames the innocent.

The governing principle is that someone habitually known for truthfulness and trustworthiness should be left unchallenged unless his words or actions are known to be false or unlawful. Someone known for lying or dishonesty should not be left unchallenged when the facts are unclear. As for someone whose character is unknown, judgment concerning him should be withheld.

---

## Page 4967

The shaykh, imam, learned scholar and great authority, Shaykh al-Islām, an heir to the noble early generations, the godly scholar into whose heart the light of the Quran had been cast, Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah al-Harrānī—may Allah sanctify his soul, illuminate his grave, and grant him an abode in the spacious Gardens of Paradise—also said:

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, seek His help, ask His forgiveness, and seek His guidance. We seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. We bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, with no partner, and we bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and Allah suffices as a witness.

He conveyed the message, fulfilled the trust, sincerely counselled the community, dispelled its distress, strove in Allah’s cause as he ought, and worshipped Allah with sincere devotion until death came to him from his Lord. May Allah bestow His blessings and abundant peace upon him until the Day of Judgment.

---

## Page 4968

Section: “Acts of Worship” and “The Distinction between Their Prescribed and Innovated Forms”

Much confusion has arisen in this area, just as it has concerning what is lawful and unlawful. Some people have deemed lawful certain things Allah has forbidden, while others have forbidden certain things Allah Most High has made lawful. Likewise, some have introduced acts of worship that Allah has not prescribed but has, rather, prohibited.

The “foundation of religion” is that what is lawful is what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful; what is unlawful is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden; and religion consists of what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. No one may depart from the straight path with which Allah sent His Messenger.

Allah Most High says:

“And this is My path, perfectly straight, so follow it. Do not follow other paths, for they will lead you away from His path. This is what He has commanded you, so that you may be mindful of Him.”

In the hadith of ‘Abdullāh ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—it is reported: “The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—drew a line, then drew other lines to his right and left. He then said: ‘This is Allah’s path, and these are other paths. On each of these paths is a devil calling

---

## Page 4969

to it.’ He then recited: ‘And this is My path, perfectly straight, so follow it. Do not follow other paths, for they will lead you away from His path.’”

In Sūrat al-An‘ām, Sūrat al-A‘rāf, and elsewhere, Allah Most High mentions the grounds on which He condemned the polytheists: they prohibited what Allah Most High had not prohibited, such as the bahīrah and sā’ibah; deemed lawful what Allah had forbidden, such as killing their children; and instituted a religion that Allah had not authorized. Allah Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have ordained for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

This included forbidden things that they made into acts of worship, such as associating partners with Allah and committing indecencies, including circumambulating the House naked, and other such practices. The discussion of “the lawful and the unlawful” belongs elsewhere. Our concern here is “acts of worship,” so we say:

Among the acts of worship by which people seek nearness to Allah Most High are those that Allah and His Messenger love and approve of. These are either obligatory or recommended, as reported in the Sahīh from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He:

“My servant draws near to Me through nothing like the performance of what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks

---

## Page 4970

, so through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he strikes, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I have never hesitated over anything I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike distressing him, yet he must undergo it.”

It is well known that some prayers are obligatory—namely, the five daily prayers—while others are voluntary, such as the night prayer. Likewise, some fasting is obligatory, namely fasting the month of Ramadan, while some is voluntary, such as fasting three days each month. Similarly, travelling to the Sacred Mosque is obligatory, while travelling to the other two mosques—the Mosque of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the mosque in Jerusalem—is recommended.

Likewise, some charity is obligatory and some is recommended, the latter being what is given from one’s surplus, as Allah Most High says:

“They ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever is beyond your needs.’”

An authentic hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O son of Adam, spending your surplus is better for you, while withholding it is worse for you. You are not to blame for retaining what suffices for your needs. The upper hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with those you support.”

The distinction between what is obligatory and what is recommended belongs elsewhere. Our concern here is the distinction between what is prescribed, whether obligatory or recommended, and what is not prescribed. What is prescribed is that by which one draws near to Allah Most High, and it is Allah’s path

---

## Page 4971

, and it is righteousness, obedience, good deeds, goodness, and right conduct. It is the path of spiritual wayfarers and the way of seekers and worshippers. It is followed by everyone whom Allah wills to guide and who takes the path of asceticism and worship, and what is called poverty, Sufism, and the like.

Undoubtedly, this includes the prescribed prayers, both obligatory and recommended. It includes the prescribed night prayer, reciting the Quran in the prescribed manner, and the prescribed remembrances and supplications. Some of these are assigned particular times, such as the beginning and end of the day; others are connected with particular occasions, such as the prayer upon entering a mosque, the prostration of recitation, the eclipse prayer, and the prayer for guidance in making a choice, together with the prescribed remembrances and supplications transmitted for these occasions. This encompasses many things, whose various forms would take a long time to describe.

It likewise includes prescribed fasting, such as fasting half the time, a third, two thirds, or a tenth—the last being fasting three days each month. It includes prescribed travel, such as travelling to Mecca and to the other two mosques. It includes jihad in its various forms; most Prophetic hadiths concern prayer and jihad. It also includes reciting the Quran in the prescribed manner.

The foundations of “religious acts of worship” are prayer, fasting, and recitation, as mentioned in the hadith of Abdullāh ibn Amr ibn al-Ās in the two Sahīh collections. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to him and said:

“Have I not been told that you said, ‘I will certainly fast

---

## Page 4972

by day, stand in prayer by night, and recite the Quran in three days’?”

He replied, “Yes.” He said, “Do not do that, for if you do, your eyes will become sunken and you will grow exhausted.” He then instructed him to fast three days each month. He replied, “I can manage more than that.” Eventually, he instructed him to fast on alternate days. He said, “I can manage more than that.” He replied, “There is nothing better than that.” He also said:

“The best fasting is the fasting of David, peace be upon him: he would fast one day and not fast the next, and he would not flee when he met the enemy. The best night prayer is that of David: he would sleep half the night, pray for a third of it, and sleep for a sixth.”

He instructed him to recite the Quran in seven days.

Since these were the familiar forms of worship, he said in the hadith concerning the Khawārij recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“Any one of you would consider his prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not go beyond their throats. They pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry.”

He thus mentioned their strenuous devotion to prayer, fasting, and recitation, and that they go to such extremes in these that the Companions would consider their own worship insignificant beside theirs.

These people went to excess in worship without understanding, which ultimately led them into religious innovation. He therefore said:

“They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you find them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

For they had deemed it lawful to shed the blood of Muslims and declared those who disagreed with them to be disbelievers. Hadiths have been transmitted concerning them

---

## Page 4973

that are authentic. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah Most High have mercy on him, said, “The hadith concerning them has been authentically transmitted through ten routes.” Muslim included these in his Sahīh, and al-Bukhārī included some of them.

These three kinds of worship are prescribed; the question that remains, however, concerns the prescribed extent of each. It was on this subject that the Book of Moderation in Worship was written. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and others said:

“Moderation in following the Sunnah is better than strenuous devotion to innovation.”

The question concerning fasting continuously, fasting throughout the year except for the two Eid days and the days of Tashrīq, and spending the entire night in prayer is whether this is recommended—as a group of jurists, Sufis, and devout worshippers have held—or disliked, as the Sunnah indicates, even if permissible. Yet fasting on alternate days is better, and praying for a third of the night is better. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The purpose here is to discuss kinds of worship that are not prescribed and that arose among later generations, such as retreats in seclusion, which resemble the prescribed retreat in the mosque. The prescribed retreat in mosques, as practised by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions, is indeed one of the prescribed acts of worship. As for retreats in seclusion, some cite his devotional worship in the Cave of Hirā’ before revelation as evidence for them, but this is a mistake;

---

## Page 4974

for whatever he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did before prophethood, we are commanded to follow him in it if he prescribed it after prophethood; otherwise, we are not. From the time Allah Most High made him a prophet, he never again ascended to the Cave of Hirā’, nor did his Rightly Guided Caliphs. He, may Allah’s blessings be upon him, lived in Mecca for a little over ten years before the Hijrah. He entered Mecca for the make-up ‘umrah, stayed there for nearly twenty nights in the year of the Conquest, and came there for the Farewell Pilgrimage, staying for four nights. Although the Cave of Hirā’ was nearby, he did not visit it.

People used to visit this cave during the pre-Islamic period of ignorance. It is said that ‘Abd al-Muttalib instituted this practice among them, because they did not have the prescribed acts of worship that he, may Allah’s blessings be upon him, brought after prophethood, such as prayer and devotional retreat in mosques. These dispense with the need to visit Hirā’, unlike their situation before revelation began. For he did not read; rather:

“The angel, peace be upon him, said to him, ‘Read.’ He, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, said, ‘I replied, “I cannot read.”’”

Nor did they know this prayer. Thus, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed it, some polytheists, such as Abū Jahl, forbade him from doing so. Allah Most High said:

“Have you seen the one who forbids
A servant when he prays?
Have you seen if he is upon guidance
Or enjoins righteousness?
Have you seen if he denies and turns away?
Does he not know that Allah sees?
No! If he does not desist, We will surely drag him by the forelock—
A lying, sinful forelock.
Then let him call his associates;
We will call the angels of Hell.
No! Do not obey him, but prostrate and draw near.”

And “a group” make the retreat in seclusion forty days long and attach great importance to this forty-day observance.

---

## Page 4975

and they argue in its support that Allah Most High appointed thirty nights for Moses, peace be upon him, and completed them with ten more. It is also reported that Moses, peace be upon him, fasted throughout them, and that the Messiah likewise fasted forty days for Allah Most High and was spoken to afterward. They therefore say that after this period one is spoken to and receives visitations, just as they say that revelation descended after the retreat in the Cave of Hirā’.

This too is mistaken, for this practice is not part of the religious law of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, it was prescribed for Moses, peace be upon him, just as the Sabbath was prescribed for him, whereas Muslims do not observe the Sabbath. Likewise, certain things were forbidden under his law that were not forbidden under the law of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Thus, the former argument appeals to an abrogated law, while the latter appeals to a practice preceding prophethood.

Experience has shown that those who engage in these innovated acts of worship are visited by devils and receive demonic visitations and communications. Some are carried through the air by their devils. I know a number of these people who sought visitations of the kind received by the prophets, but devils descended upon them because they had departed from the law of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which they had been commanded to follow.

Allah Most High said:

“Then We set you upon a prescribed way in matters of religion, so follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.

“They will be of no help to you whatsoever against Allah. The wrongdoers are allies of one another, while Allah is the Protector of the righteous.”

Many of them prescribe neither a particular place nor a particular duration for seclusion, but simply instruct a person to withdraw into seclusion.

---

## Page 4976

Then, some practitioners of seclusion came to adhere to prescribed forms of worship: prayer, fasting, Quran recitation and remembrance of Allah. Most, however, depart into forms that have not been prescribed. One example is the method of Abū Hāmid and his followers. They instruct the person in seclusion to do nothing beyond what is obligatory: no recitation, no study of prophetic hadith, nor anything else. Instead, they may instruct him to engage in remembrance, and may then repeat what Abū Hāmid says:

“The remembrance of ordinary people is: ‘There is no god but Allah.’ The remembrance of the elite is: ‘Allah, Allah.’ The remembrance of the elite of the elite is: ‘He’ ‘He.’”

Invoking the name alone, whether explicitly or through a pronoun, is an innovation in religion and an error in speech and language. A bare name does not constitute a statement and expresses neither faith nor disbelief.

It is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best words after the Quran are four, and they are themselves found in the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

Another hadith states:

“The best remembrance is: ‘There is no god but Allah.’”

He also said:

“The best thing that I and the prophets before me have said is: ‘There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs all sovereignty, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

There are many authentic hadiths concerning the virtues of these words. As for invoking the name alone, this is an innovation that has not been prescribed. It is not intelligible speech, nor does it contain any expression of faith. For this reason, some later proponents of this practice have come to explain that it is not

---

## Page 4977

their aim to remember Allah Most High, but rather to concentrate the heart on a particular thing until the soul becomes receptive to whatever comes upon it. Such a person would instruct his disciple to repeat this name several times. Once his heart was fully focused, he would induce a satanic state in him, and Satan would take hold of him. He would imagine that he had entered the highest assembly and had been granted what neither Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was granted on the night of the Ascension, nor Moses, peace be upon him, on the day he was at Mount Sinai. This and similar things have happened to some people in our own time.

More extreme still are those who say, “Our only aim is to concentrate the soul by any means whatsoever,” going so far as to say, “There is no difference between saying, ‘O Ever-Living One,’ and saying, ‘O young donkey.’” One of them said this to me, and I rebuked him for it. Their purpose is to concentrate the soul until Satan descends upon it.

Some of them say, “If there is an intention, one who intends, and that which is intended, make them all one.” Thus, from the very outset, he leads the disciple into the doctrine of the unity of existence.

As for Abū Hāmid and others like him who advocated this method, they did not think it would lead to disbelief—though it should be understood that religious innovations are precursors to disbelief. They nevertheless instructed the disciple to empty his heart of everything. They might even tell him to sit in a dark place, cover his head, and say, “Allah, Allah.” They believe that by emptying his heart he becomes receptive, so that the knowledge they seek descends upon his heart. Indeed,

---

## Page 4978

they may even say that he receives something of the same kind as the prophets receive. Some of them claim to have received more than the prophets received. Abū Hāmid frequently praises this method in al-Ihyā and elsewhere, just as he praises asceticism to excess. This reflects the lingering influence of philosophy upon him. For philosophers such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him claim that all knowledge received in the hearts of prophets and others comes solely from the active intellect.

For this reason, they say that prophethood can be acquired: when a person frees himself from distractions, his heart—according to them—becomes pure, and something of the same kind as flowed into the hearts of the prophets flows into his heart. They hold that Moses son of ‘Imrān, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was spoken to from the heaven of his own intellect; he did not hear speech from outside himself. They therefore say that they receive the same as Moses received, or something even greater.

Abū Hāmid says that he heard the address just as Moses, peace be upon him, heard it, even though he himself was not its intended recipient. All this stems from their deficient faith in the messengers, and from their believing in some of what the messengers brought while disbelieving in other parts. What they have said is false on several grounds:

First: What they call the “active intellect” is false and has no reality, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Second: What Allah places in hearts sometimes comes through the mediation of angels

---

## Page 4979

when it is true, and at other times through the mediation of devils when it is false. Angels and devils are living, speaking beings, as abundant evidence conveyed by the prophets establishes, and as those versed in spiritual realities who have encountered them directly also claim. Yet these philosophers maintain that angels and devils are merely attributes of the human soul. This is grave misguidance.

Third: Angels came to the prophets with revelation from their Lord. Among them were those to whom Allah Most High spoke, drawing them near and calling to them, as He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him. What they received was not merely an emanation, as these people claim.

Fourth: If a person empties his heart of every thought, how can he know that what enters it is true? This could only be known through reason or revelation, and neither provides evidence for that.

Fifth: What is known through revelation and reason is that when a person empties his heart of everything, devils dwell within it and then descend upon him, just as they used to descend upon soothsayers. What prevents Satan from entering a human being’s heart is the remembrance of Allah within it, with which He sent His messengers. When the heart is devoid of that remembrance, Satan takes charge of it. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We assign to him a devil to be his companion. The devils surely turn them away from the path, while they think they are rightly guided.”

And Satan said, as Allah relates:

“He said, ‘By Your might, I will surely lead them all astray, except Your servants among them

---

## Page 4980

who are chosen.’” Allah Most High also says:

“You have no authority over My servants, except those of the misguided who follow you.”

Those who are chosen are those who worship Him alone, associating nothing with Him. Allah is worshipped only in the manner He has commanded through His messengers; whoever does otherwise falls under the control of devils. This is an area in which many spiritual wayfarers have fallen into grave error: they have confused spiritual states bestowed by the Most Merciful with satanic states. They have experienced things like those experienced by soothsayers and sorcerers, imagining them to be miracles granted to Allah’s pious friends. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Sixth: Even if this method were sound, it could apply only to someone to whom no messenger had come. But when a messenger has come to someone and he has been commanded to follow a particular path, whoever opposes that messenger goes astray. The last of the messengers, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded his community to perform prescribed acts of worship, including prayer, remembrance, supplication, and recitation. He never commanded them to empty their hearts of every thought and wait for whatever might descend upon them.

Even supposing this method had been followed by some prophets, it would have been abrogated by the law brought by Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. How, then, could it be valid when it is a method of pagan ignorance that leads to the intended goal only by chance, when Allah Most High casts into the heart of

---

## Page 4981

a servant an inspiration that benefits him? This may happen to anyone; it is not a necessary consequence of this path. Rather, the emptying and clearing of the heart taught by the Messenger means emptying it of what Allah does not love and filling it with what He loves. One empties it of worship of anything other than Allah and fills it with worship of Allah. Likewise, one empties it of love for anything other than Allah and fills it with love for Allah; removes from it fear of anything other than Allah and instils in it fear of Allah Most High; and removes reliance upon anything other than Allah and establishes reliance upon Allah within it.

This is Islam, which encompasses faith—a faith that the Quran nourishes and strengthens, rather than contradicts and negates. As Jundub and Ibn ʿUmar said:

“We learned faith, then learned the Quran, and so increased in faith.”

As for confining oneself to prescribed remembrance alone, such as saying, “There is no god worthy of worship but Allah,” a person may sometimes benefit from this. Yet this remembrance alone, to the exclusion of everything else, is not the path to Allah Most High. Rather, the best bodily act of worship is prayer, followed by recitation of the Quran, then remembrance, then supplication. An otherwise lesser act, performed at its prescribed time, is better than a superior act. Thus, glorifying Allah while bowing and prostrating is better than reciting the Quran, and supplication at the end of prayer is likewise better than recitation.

Moreover, a person may find doors opened to him through a lesser deed that are not opened to him through a superior one. One deed may also be made easy for him while another is not, so the former is better for him because he is unable to perform the superior deed. This is like a hungry person who finds inferior bread readily available while better bread is difficult to obtain

---

## Page 4982

for him; he benefits from this inferior bread, and satisfying his hunger and nourishing himself with it is then better for him.

Seventh:

Abū Hāmid likens this to the work of Chinese and Byzantine artisans in decorating a wall: one group polished their wall until it reflected what the other group had polished. This analogy is unsound, because the person who emptied his heart had no other heart through which his own could acquire adornment, as one wall acquires it from the other. Rather, he says that knowledge is inscribed in the celestial soul, which he calls “the Preserved Tablet,” following Ibn Sīnā.

We have explained elsewhere that “the Preserved Tablet” mentioned by Allah and His Messenger is not the celestial soul. Ibn Sīnā and his followers took terms found in the revealed Law and assigned them referents different from those intended by the one who brought that Law. They then began using these terms, leading the uninformed to suppose that they intended the same meanings as the one who brought the Law. Thus, they took the kernel of philosophy and clothed it in the husk of the revealed Law. Examples include the terms “mulk” (dominion), “malakūt” (sovereignty), “jabarūt” (might), “the Preserved Tablet,” “angel,” “devil,” “coming into existence,” “beginninglessness,” and others.

---

## Page 4983

We have discussed some of this in our refutation of the “advocates of union,” when discussing the statements of Ibn Sabʿīn and Ibn ʿArabī, and the principles of these heretical philosophers found in the writings of Abū Hāmid and others like him. These philosophers distort the words of Allah and His Messenger, taking them out of their proper contexts, as did the esotericist Qarmatians.

(The point) here is that, if knowledge descended upon hearts from the celestial soul, as these people claim, there would be no difference in this respect between someone who reflects, someone who reasons from evidence, and someone who empties his heart. Thus, likening this to the decorative work of the Chinese and Byzantine artisans is an invalid analogy.

Some who undertake these retreats have specific formulas of remembrance and a fixed diet, and experience known descents. Ibn ʿArabī al-Tāʾī and those who followed his path, such as al-Tilimsānī, have discussed these at length. They are satanic descents. I am familiar with them and have examined the matter in various ways, but this is not the place to elaborate on them. The purpose is merely to draw attention to this kind of thing.

Among the things they prescribe are hunger, sleeplessness, and silence, together with seclusion, without any limits set by the revealed Law. Rather, they prescribe unrestricted sleeplessness, unrestricted hunger, and unrestricted silence, together with seclusion, as Ibn ʿArabī and others have mentioned. These practices produce satanic states in them.

Abū Tālib has mentioned some of this, but he adheres more firmly to the Quran and Sunnah than these people do. Nevertheless, he cites many weak—indeed, fabricated—hadiths

---

## Page 4984

such as the reports concerning the sevenfold recitations (al-musabbaʿāt), which he narrated from al-Khidr, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. These are pure falsehood, even though they contain nothing but Quran recitation. He also sometimes mentions innovated acts of worship, such as the excessive praise of hunger offered by him, Abū Hāmid, and others. They describe weighing bread against moist wood, so that the amount eaten decreases as the wood dries. They also cite accounts of prayers for the various days and nights, all of them false and fabricated. Alongside this, they may therefore mention some corrupt imaginings. This is not the place to discuss that at length.

The purpose here is simply to draw attention to a category of innovated worship: “innovated retreats,” whether their duration is fixed or not. They involve innovated acts of worship: either practices whose general kind is prescribed but for which no fixed measure has been laid down, or practices whose very kind is not prescribed. As for lawful retreat, withdrawal, and solitude, these are whatever has been commanded as obligatory or recommended.

(The former) includes withdrawing from forbidden matters and avoiding them, as Allah Most High says:

“When you see those who speak offensively about Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in some other discourse.”

This also includes His words concerning His intimate friend:

“When he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, We granted him Isaac and Jacob, and made each of them a prophet.”

And His words concerning the people of

---

## Page 4985

the Cave:

“Now that you have withdrawn from them and from what they worship other than Allah, take refuge in the cave.”

Those men were not in a place where Friday or congregational prayers were held, nor was there anyone who enjoined adherence to a prophet’s revealed law. That is why they took refuge in the cave. Moses also said:

“If you do not believe in me, then leave me alone.”

As for withdrawing from people when it comes to superfluous permissible pursuits and things of no benefit, by renouncing such things, this is recommended. Tāwūs said: “What an excellent hermitage a man’s home is, where he restrains his gaze and hearing!”

If someone wishes to attain proficiency in knowledge or practice and therefore seeks solitude somewhere while continuing to attend Friday and congregational prayers, this is right. Thus, it is related in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked, “Who is the best of people?” He replied:

“A man who holds the reins of his horse in Allah’s cause: whenever he hears a cry of alarm, he rushes towards it, seeking death wherever it is likely to be found; and a man who lives apart in a mountain valley, establishes prayer, gives zakat, and leaves people alone except to do good.”

His words, “establishes prayer and gives zakat,” indicate that this man possesses wealth on which he pays zakat, and that he lives among people, giving the call to prayer among them, with prayer established in their midst. For the Prophet, may Allah’s blessings be upon him, said:

“There are no three people in a village or in the desert among whom prayer is not established in congregation but that Satan has gained mastery over them.”

He also said:

“Keep to the congregation, for the wolf devours only the sheep that strays away.”

---

## Page 4986

Section

Those who undertake these “retreats” may seek out places where neither the call to prayer nor the announcement of its commencement is made, and where there is no mosque in which the five daily prayers are offered. These may be abandoned mosques or places other than mosques, such as caves and caverns in the mountains, graveyards—especially the grave of someone held in high regard—or places said to contain a trace of a prophet or a righteous man. Consequently, they undergo satanic experiences in these places which they imagine to be miraculous gifts bestowed by the Most Merciful.

Some of them see the occupant of a grave coming to them, although he has been dead for many years, and saying, “I am so-and-so.” He may even say, “When we are placed in the grave, we come out,” as happened to al-Tūnisī with Nu‘mān al-Salāmī.

Devils frequently assume human form, both in waking life and in dreams. They may approach someone who does not recognize them and say, “I am Shaykh so-and-so,” or “I am the scholar so-and-so.” Sometimes they say, “I am Abū Bakr,” or “I am ‘Umar.” A devil may even appear while someone is awake rather than dreaming and say, “I am the Messiah,” “I am Moses,” or “I am Muhammad.” I know of various occurrences of this kind.

---

## Page 4987

And there are those who believe that the prophets appear in their own forms to people who are awake. There are also shaykhs known for asceticism, learning, scrupulousness and religious devotion who believe such things. Some of them imagine that when they visit a prophet’s grave, the prophet emerges from it in his own form and speaks to them.

Some have seen the figure of a shaykh in the area around the top of the Kaaba and said that it was Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah. Others imagine that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, has come out of his burial chamber and spoken to them. They count this among their own miraculous gifts. Some believe that if they ask the person buried in a grave a question, he answers them.

Some used to relate that whenever Ibn Mandah found a hadith difficult to understand, he would go to the Prophet’s burial chamber, enter it and ask the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, about it, and he would answer him.

Another man from the Maghreb had a similar experience and counted it among his miraculous gifts. Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr therefore said to someone who believed this:

“Alas for you! Do you consider this man superior to the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers? Did any of them question the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, after his death and receive an answer? The Companions disagreed over various matters; why, then, did they not ask the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and receive his answer? Here was his own daughter Fātimah disputing over his inheritance; why did she not ask him and receive his answer?”

---

## Page 4988

Section

We have been commanded to believe in what the prophets—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them all—were given, and to follow them and their guidance. Allah Most High says:

“Say: We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and what Moses and Jesus were given, and what the prophets were given by their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance.”

Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, is the Seal of the Prophets; there is no prophet after him. His law has abrogated those parts of earlier prophets’ laws that it supersedes. Thus, no path to Allah remains except through following Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Whatever acts of worship he commanded, whether as obligations or recommendations, are prescribed in religion. The same applies to whatever he encouraged and whose reward and merit he mentioned.

It is not permissible to declare something recommended or prescribed in religion without evidence from revelation, nor is it permissible to establish a religious ruling on the basis of a weak hadith. However, if an act has been established as recommended through evidence from revelation, and reports describing its merits are transmitted through weak chains, those reports may be narrated provided they are not known to be false. This is because the amounts of reward are unknown. Thus, if a hadith concerning the amount of reward is transmitted and is not known to be false, it is not permissible to reject it as false

---

## Page 4989

, and this is what Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others permitted, along with narrating hadiths concerning the merits of deeds.

But that they would establish, on the basis of a weak hadith, that an act is recommended and prescribed in religion—Allah forbid! Likewise, when they knew that a hadith was false, they did not consider it permissible to narrate it without explaining that it was false, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said in an authentic hadith:

“Whoever narrates a hadith from me, believing it to be false, is one of the liars.”

Whatever the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did as an act of worship is worship in which following his example is prescribed. If he singled out a particular time or place for an act of worship, then singling it out for that worship is Sunnah. Examples include his singling out the last ten nights for spiritual retreat and the Station of Abraham for prayer. Following his example means doing what he did, in the manner he did it, because he did it. This is only achieved by intending the same purpose that he intended. Thus, if he travelled for Hajj, ʿumrah, or jihad, and we travel for the same purpose, we are following him. The same applies when he struck someone to carry out a prescribed punishment. This is unlike someone who travelled as he did but had a different purpose, or struck as he did but had a different purpose: such a person is not following him.

If, however, he did something incidentally—such as stopping at a place during a journey, pouring water left in his waterskin at the base of a tree, or his mount walking along one side of the road, and similar things—is it recommended to deliberately follow his example in that? Ibn ʿUmar liked to

---

## Page 4990

do such things. The Rightly Guided Caliphs and the majority of the Companions, however, did not regard this as recommended, because it does not constitute following his example. Following his example necessarily involves intention: if he did not intend that particular action, but it occurred merely by chance, then deliberately doing it does not constitute following his example.

Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, maintained that even if the Prophet had not intended it, the act itself was good, however it occurred, and so he liked to do the same—either because this increased his love for him or because of the blessing of resembling him. This includes giving dates as zakāt al-fitr when dates are not one’s staple food. Ahmad agreed with Ibn Umar on such matters and permitted actions like those Ibn Umar performed. Likewise, following Ibn Umar, Ahmad permitted rubbing one’s hand over the place where the Prophet sat on the pulpit.

Two positions are reported from Ahmad concerning rubbing one’s hand over the pulpit. The better-known position is that it is disliked, as the majority hold. Mālik and other scholars disliked these practices even though Ibn Umar performed them, since the leading Companions, such as Abū Bakr, Umar, Uthmān and others, did not do so.

It is established through an authentic chain of transmission that Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was travelling when he saw people frequenting a place to pray there. He asked, “What is this?”

They replied, “A place where the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed.”

He said, “Do you wish to turn the sites associated with your prophets into places of worship? This is precisely what destroyed those before you. Whoever happens to be there when prayer is due should pray there; otherwise, let him continue on his way.”

---

## Page 4991

Likewise, scholars hold two views concerning the permissible acts he performed without any particular intent: is imitating him in these acts merely permissible, or is it recommended? Both views are found in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere, as has been explained in detail in its proper place. Neither Ibn Umar nor any other Companion would deliberately seek out the places where he stayed or spent the night, such as his wives’ houses or his encampments during military expeditions. The discussion concerned only resembling him in the outward form of an action, even when he had not intended it as an act of worship. As for the places themselves, the Companions agreed that none should be venerated except those venerated by the Lawgiver.

Section

As for those who practise “innovated acts of worship,” Satan makes these acts seem attractive to them and makes them dislike the ways prescribed by Islamic law. Eventually, he makes them averse to religious knowledge, the Quran and hadith, so that they dislike hearing the Quran and hadith or having them mentioned. He may even make them averse to books themselves, so that they dislike any book and anyone carrying one, even if it is a copy of the Quran or a collection of hadith.

Thus, al-Nasrābādhī related that they used to say, “He abandons the knowledge of patched cloaks and takes up the knowledge of written pages!” He said, “I used to hide my writing tablets from them, but when I grew older, they needed my knowledge.”

Likewise, al-Sarī al-Saqatī related that one of them came to see him, but when he saw an inkwell and a pen beside him, he left without sitting down with him. This is why Sahl ibn Abd

---

## Page 4992

Allah al-Tustarī said:

“O Sufis, do not abandon black ink on white paper, for no one has abandoned black ink on white paper without falling into heresy.”

Al-Junayd said:

“This knowledge of ours is founded upon the Book and the Sunnah. Whoever has not read the Quran and written down hadith is not to be followed in this matter.”

Many of these people recoil from anyone who mentions Islamic law or the Quran, carries a book, or writes. This is because they have sensed that such material contains things that contradict their way. Their devils therefore drive them away from it, just as a Jew or a Christian keeps his son from hearing what Muslims say, lest his beliefs about his religion change, and just as Noah’s people would put their fingers in their ears and cover themselves with their garments so that they would neither hear his words nor see him.

Allah Most High said of the polytheists:

“Those who disbelieve say, ‘Do not listen to this Quran, but make noise during its recitation, so that you may prevail.’”

He Most High also said:

“Why, then, do they turn away from the reminder, like startled wild donkeys fleeing from a lion?”

They are among those most eager for innovated listening practices—listening to musical instruments—and among those least inclined toward the listening prescribed by Islamic law: listening to the verses of Allah Most High.

One thing that made their way seem attractive to them was finding many of those occupied with religious knowledge and books turning away from worshipping Allah Most High and following His path, whether through preoccupation with worldly affairs, involvement in sins, or ignorance and denial of what those devoted to Allah and His worship attain. The presence of such people thus helped to alienate them, and a kind of mutual hatred developed between the two groups, resembling

---

## Page 4993

in some respects, that between the adherents of the two faiths: one group says, “The other has no sound foundation,” and the other says, “They have no sound foundation.”

They may think that through their path they attain something greater than what can be attained through books. Some imagine that they can learn the Quran without being taught. They relate that someone attained this, but this is false. He may, however, have heard Allah’s verses and then, after purifying his soul, remembered and recited them. Spiritual discipline refines the soul, enabling a person to recall things he had forgotten.

Some of them say—or it is related that one of them said:

“They took their knowledge from one dead man transmitting from another, whereas we took our knowledge from the Ever-Living, who never dies.”

This does occur. Yet some of them imagine that whatever is imparted to them, whether words addressed to them or a thought arising within them, comes directly from Allah Most High, without an intermediary, when it may come from Satan. They have no criterion by which to distinguish what comes from the Most Merciful from what comes from Satan. The unfailing criterion is the Quran and the Sunnah: whatever accords with the Book and the Sunnah is true, and whatever contradicts them is erroneous.

Allah Most High has said:

“Whoever turns away from the reminder of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil to be his companion. These devils turn them away from the path, while they think they are rightly guided. Then, when he comes to Us, he says, ‘If only there were between you and me the distance between east and west! What an evil companion!’”

The reminder of the Most Merciful is what He revealed to His Messenger. Allah Most High said:

“This is a blessed reminder which We have sent down.”

He Most High also said:

“It is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds.”

And He Most High said:

---

## Page 4994

“When guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer. But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection. He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’ He will say, ‘Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; likewise, today you will be forgotten.’”

He Most High also said:

“Indeed, this Quran guides to what is most upright and gives glad tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward, and that for those who do not believe in the Hereafter We have prepared a painful punishment.”

He Most High also said:

“And thus We have revealed to you a revelation by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We have made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path—the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. Surely, to Allah all matters return.”

He Most High also said:

“A Book We have sent down to you so that you may bring people out of darkness into light, by their Lord’s permission, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.”

He Most High also said:

“So those who believe in him, honour him, support him, and follow the light sent down with him—it is they who will prosper.”

Then, because these people imagined that this came to them from Allah without an intermediary, they came to regard themselves as above following the Messenger. One of them says:

“So-and-so receives his gift through Muhammad, whereas I receive mine from Allah without an intermediary.”

He also says:

“So-and-so takes his knowledge from the Book, whereas this shaykh takes his from Allah,” and similar things.

Saying, “He takes from Allah,” or “Allah has given me,” is ambiguous. If

---

## Page 4995

he means giving and receiving in the general sense, “pertaining to existence and creation”—that is, “This has come to me through Allah’s will and power”—then this is true. Yet everyone shares in this, and the person who acquires his knowledge from the Book has also received it from Allah in this sense. The disbelievers, both polytheists and People of the Book, are likewise in this position.

But if he means that what has come to him is something Allah loves and is pleased with, which brings one closer to Him, and that the words conveyed to him are the speech of Allah Most High, then there are two approaches:

The first is to ask him: How do you know that this comes from Allah alone, rather than from Satan, his suggestions, and his whisperings? For the devils inspire their allies and descend upon them, as Allah Most High has told us in the Quran. This occurs frequently among the devout worshippers of the polytheists and the People of the Book, among soothsayers, sorcerers, and their like, and among the people of religious innovation, according to the nature of their innovations.

These states may be satanic, or they may come from the Most Merciful. There must therefore be a criterion by which to distinguish the allies of the Most Merciful from the allies of Satan. That criterion is none other than the Criterion with which Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For He is:

“the One who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he might be a warner to the worlds.”

It is through this that Allah has distinguished truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, right conduct from waywardness, the path to Paradise from the path to Hell, and the way of the allies of the Most Merciful from the way of the allies of Satan. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 4996

The point here is that they should be told: “Since states of this kind are shared by those who follow truth and those who follow falsehood, there must be evidence showing that what you have experienced is the truth.”

The second approach is to say: “Rather, this comes from Satan, because it contradicts what Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to convey.”

This is determined by examining what the person has experienced, its cause, and its ultimate outcome. If its cause is an act of worship not prescribed by Allah—for example, if he is told, “Prostrate before this idol so that you may obtain what you desire,” or “Seek the intercession of the one depicted in this image so that you may obtain what you seek,” or “Call upon this created being and seek his aid”—this includes invoking the heavenly bodies, as described in books on invoking them, or calling upon a created being as one calls upon the Creator, whether that being is an angel, a prophet, or a shaykh. If he calls upon that being as he calls upon the Creator, glory be to Him, whether through worship or through supplication, he has made that being a partner to Allah. Whatever he obtains through this means has therefore been obtained through associating partners with Allah, just as happened to the polytheists.

The devils would sometimes appear to them, and might speak to them from within an idol, inform them of certain unseen matters, or fulfil some of their needs. They would give them this slight benefit in exchange for what they had purchased from them: their affirmation of Allah’s oneness and their faith, the loss of which brought about their ruin. This is like sorcery. Allah Most High says:

“But the two would teach no one without first saying, ‘We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.’ Yet they learned from the two that by which they caused division

---

## Page 4997

between a man and his wife. Yet they harm no one through it except by Allah’s permission. They learn what harms them and does not benefit them. They certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. Wretched indeed is that for which they sold themselves, if only they knew.”

Such an experience may also be caused by listening to musical instruments. This is like what is related from ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said:

“Beware of wine, for it is the mother of all evils. A man propositioned a woman, and she said, ‘I will not agree until you prostrate before this idol.’ He replied, ‘I will not associate partners with Allah.’ She said, ‘Then will you kill this boy?’ He replied, ‘I will not take a life that Allah has forbidden.’ She said, ‘Then will you drink this cup?’ He replied, ‘This is less serious.’ But when he drank the wine, he killed the boy, prostrated before the idol, and committed fornication with the woman.”

Musical instruments are the wine of souls: they affect souls more powerfully than potent wine does. When people become intoxicated by sounds, associating partners with Allah takes hold of them, and they incline toward sexual immorality and injustice. Thus they associate partners with Allah, take lives that Allah has forbidden them to take, and commit fornication. These three things are common among those who listen to musical instruments—to whistling and clapping. As for associating partners with Allah, it predominates among them: they love their shaykh or someone else as they love Allah, and become ecstatic in their love for him.

---

## Page 4998

As for “sexual immorality,” singing is an incantation that invites fornication and is among the greatest causes of sexual immorality. A man, a boy, or a woman may be exceptionally chaste and dignified until attending such a gathering. Then their restraint dissolves, sexual immorality becomes easy for them, and they incline toward it, whether as the active or passive partner, or both—just as happens among wine-drinkers, and even more so.

As for “killing,” they frequently kill one another during listening sessions. They say, “He killed him through his spiritual state,” and count this as evidence of his power. In fact, devils accompany them and attend their gatherings; whoever has the stronger devils kills the other. They are like people who drink wine with supporters around them: once they drink, they become belligerent, and whoever has the stronger supporters kills the other. Such things have happened to many of them. Some kill a person, a horse, or something else through their spiritual state. Then someone seeking vengeance appeals to his shaykh for help, and the shaykh kills that person along with a group accompanying him—perhaps ten, fewer, or more. Such incidents have happened to more than one person.

The ignorant used to consider this a form of (miraculous gifts). But when it became clear that these were satanic states, and that these people had devils helping them in sin and aggression, those whom Allah Most High granted insight recognized the truth, and these people’s deception and fraud were exposed.

Early in my life, I attended a gathering with a group of people devoted to “asceticism, worship, and spiritual aspiration.” They were among the best people of this class. We spent the night at a place, and they wanted to

---

## Page 4999

hold a listening session and have me attend with them. I declined, so they set aside a separate place for me, where I sat. When they began listening and experienced ecstasy and spiritual states, the senior shaykh began calling out to me in his ecstasy, saying, “So-and-so! A great share has come your way. Come and take your share!”

I said to myself—and later told them when we gathered—“You are under no obligation to give me this share. Any share that does not come through the way of Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I will not partake of at all.” Some among them who possessed knowledge and understanding came to realize that devils had been present with them, and that someone among them was drunk on wine.

What I meant was that this share, this gift, this bestowal, and this spiritual state arose from a cause not sanctioned by the revealed law. It was neither an act of obedience to Allah and His Messenger nor something the Messenger had prescribed. It is like someone saying, “Come and drink wine with us, and we will give you this money,” or, “Venerate this idol, and we will appoint you to this office,” and the like.

Its cause may also be a vow made to someone other than Allah, glorified and exalted is He: for example, making a vow to an idol, a church, a grave, a star, a shaykh, or the like—vows that involve associating partners with Allah. If someone associates partners with Allah through such a vow, Satan may fulfill some of his needs, as discussed earlier concerning sorcery.

This is unlike making a vow to Allah Most High. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that Ibn ‘Umar reported: “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade making vows and said, ‘It does not bring

---

## Page 5000

any good; it merely extracts something from the miser.’” A similar report from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appears in the two Sahīh collections. One version reads:

“For a vow brings the son of Adam to what has been decreed.”

The vow prohibited here is one that must nevertheless be fulfilled: making it is prohibited, but once a person has made it, he must fulfill it. Thus, in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited making vows because doing so brings no benefit beyond binding oneself to what one has undertaken, which one may then be unwilling to fulfill and thus remain sinful.

It would be better for a person to perform those acts of worship without making a vow. People intend through vows to obtain what they seek, but the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that vows bring no good. A vow is therefore not a means of obtaining what they seek. For example, someone making a vow might say, “If Allah enables me to memorize the Quran, I pledge to Allah that I will fast three days,” or, “If Allah cures me of this illness, repels this enemy, or settles this debt for me, I will do such-and-such.” He has thereby made the act of worship he has undertaken an exchange for what he seeks.

Yet Allah, glorified is He, does not fulfill that need merely because of the vowed act of worship. Rather, He grants His servant what he seeks to test whether he will be grateful or ungrateful. Gratitude to Him consists in doing what He has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden. As for that vowed act of worship, it does not suffice as gratitude for that blessing. Nor does Allah bestow that blessing so that His servant will perform that vowed act of worship, which was recommended but has become

---

## Page 5001

obligatory; for He, glorified is He, did not make that act of worship obligatory in the first place. Rather, He is pleased with His servant fulfilling the obligatory duties and avoiding what is forbidden. Yet the person making this vow may have neglected many of Allah’s rights, then offered that vow in return for that blessing. That blessing is too great for Allah to bestow it merely in exchange for such a paltry offering.

If, however, the offering is great and the servant is obedient to Allah, then he is too dear to Allah for Him to make him resort to such a great offering. A vow is therefore not a means of obtaining what one seeks, unlike supplication, which is among the greatest means. Likewise, Allah Most High has made charity and other acts of worship means of obtaining good and warding off evil when the servant performs them on his own initiative.

As for what he does by way of a vow, it neither brings him benefit nor wards off harm. Rather, he was miserly, but once he made the vow, fulfilling it became binding upon him. Thus, through vows Allah Most High extracts something from the miser: he gives because of the vow what he would not have given without it. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 5002

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“What are the deeds of the people of Paradise, and what are the deeds of the people of Hell?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

“The deeds of the people of Paradise” are faith and piety, while the deeds of the people of Hell are disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience.

The deeds of the people of Paradise include believing in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day; believing in the divine decree, both its good and its evil; bearing the two testimonies—that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; establishing prayer; paying zakat; fasting Ramadan; and performing pilgrimage to the Sacred House. They also include worshipping Allah as though you see Him, for although you do not see Him, He sees you.

Among “the deeds of the people of Paradise” are speaking truthfully, fulfilling trusts, keeping covenants, being dutiful to parents, maintaining ties of kinship, and showing kindness to neighbours, orphans, the needy, and those in one’s possession, whether human slaves or animals.

---

## Page 5003

Among “the deeds of the people of Paradise” are sincere devotion to Allah, reliance upon Him, love for Him and His Messenger, fear of Allah, hope for His mercy, turning back to Him, patience with His judgment, and gratitude for His blessings.

Among “the deeds of the people of Paradise” are reciting the Quran, remembering Allah, supplicating to Him, asking of Him, and turning eagerly to Him.

Among “the deeds of the people of Paradise” are enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and striving in Allah’s cause against the disbelievers and hypocrites.

Among “the deeds of the people of Paradise” are maintaining ties with those who sever them with you, giving to those who withhold from you, and pardoning those who wrong you. For Allah has prepared Paradise for the God-fearing: those who spend in prosperity and adversity, restrain their anger, and pardon others. And Allah loves those who do good.

Among “the deeds of the people of Paradise” are acting justly in all matters and towards all creation, even disbelievers, and other deeds of this kind.

As for “the deeds of the people of Hell,” these include associating partners with Allah, rejecting the messengers, disbelief, envy, lying, betrayal, injustice, shameful deeds, treachery, severing ties of kinship, shrinking from jihad out of cowardice, miserliness, being inwardly different from what one outwardly displays, and despairing of

---

## Page 5004

relief from Allah, feeling secure against Allah’s devising, being distraught when calamities strike, boasting and becoming arrogant when blessed, neglecting Allah’s obligations, transgressing His limits, violating what He has made inviolable, fearing created beings rather than the Creator, placing hope in created beings rather than the Creator, relying upon created beings rather than the Creator, acting to be seen and praised by others, opposing the Quran and Sunnah, obeying created beings in disobedience to the Creator, partisan zeal in support of falsehood, mocking Allah’s signs, denying the truth, and concealing knowledge or testimony that must be disclosed.

Among “the deeds of the people of Hell” are sorcery, mistreating one’s parents, unlawfully killing a soul whose life Allah has made inviolable, consuming an orphan’s wealth, consuming usury, fleeing the battlefield, and accusing chaste, unsuspecting believing women of unchastity.

It is not possible to detail “these two categories” exhaustively. However, all “the deeds of the people of Paradise” fall under obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and all “the deeds of the people of Hell” fall under disobedience to Allah and His Messenger:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.”

“And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, abiding therein forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

And Allah knows best.
