As for giving preference merely through personal choice—so that, when the evidence appears evenly balanced, a person favors one position solely through his own will and choice—this is not the position of any of the imams of Islam. It is only the position of a group of speculative theologians. Some jurists, however, have held this view regarding a layperson seeking a legal ruling, saying that he may choose between muftis whose rulings differ.

Likewise, some who follow the spiritual path, when two courses appear equal to them under religious law, give preference solely on the basis of their own spiritual feeling and will. Yet none of the leading authorities in religious learning and asceticism endorses giving preference solely through a will that rests on no inward or outward basis in knowledge. The leading jurists and Sufis do not hold this view. Whoever permits a jurist exercising independent legal judgment, or a follower, to give preference merely through personal choice and will is like someone who prescribes for the spiritual wayfarer giving preference merely through his own will and spiritual feeling.

It may, however, be said: when a heart filled with piety gives preference according to its will, that preference is sanctioned by religious law. Under this assumption, it does not fall into the category just discussed. Thus, if someone whose heart is dominated by the desire for what Allah loves and aversion to what Allah dislikes does not know, concerning a particular matter,

---

## Page 5053

whether it is beloved to Allah or disliked by Him, and finds that his heart loves or dislikes it, this gives him grounds for preferring one course over the other. This is like receiving information from someone who is more often truthful than untruthful: when no other grounds for preference are available, giving preference on the basis of that person’s report rests on evidence recognized by religious law.

In sum, whenever something provides grounds for believing that one of two courses is more beloved to Allah and His Messenger, preferring it rests on evidence recognized by religious law. Those who categorically deny that inspiration can provide guidance are mistaken, just as those who unconditionally regard it as a means of guidance sanctioned by religious law are mistaken. However, if the spiritual wayfarer diligently examines the outward evidence of religious law and finds nothing that favors either course, then receives an inspiration favoring one of the two actions, while his intention is sound and his heart is filled with piety, such inspiration constitutes evidence for him. It may be stronger than many of the weak analogical arguments, weak hadiths, weak indications drawn from the apparent meanings of texts, and weak applications of the presumption of continuity invoked by many who discuss legal doctrine, juristic disagreement, and legal theory.

Al-Tirmidhī relates from Abū Saʿīd that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beware the believer’s discernment, for he sees by the light of Allah.” Then he recited the words of the Most High: “Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb said: “Draw close to those who obey Allah and listen to what they say, for matters become clear to them

---

## Page 5054

as they truly are.”

It is authentically reported that Allah Most High says:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks.”

Furthermore, Allah—glorified and exalted is He—created His servants with an innate inclination to pure faith: love of what is right and hatred of what is wrong. So long as this innate disposition has not been altered, hearts are naturally inclined to the truth. If this disposition is strengthened by true faith and illuminated by the light of the Quran, yet the implications of the outward scriptural evidence remain unclear, and a person finds his heart favoring one of two courses, this is among the strongest indications for someone in his position. That is because Allah has taught the Quran and faith. Allah Most High says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger”—to the end of the verse.

Then He says:

“And thus We have revealed to you a spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We have made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.”

Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: “We learned faith, then we learned the Quran and thereby increased in faith.”

The two Sahīh collections relate from Hudhayfah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah sent down trust into the very roots of men’s hearts; then they learned from the Quran and learned from the Sunnah.”

Al-Tirmidhī and others also transmit the hadith of al-Nawwās from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

---

## Page 5055

who said:

“Allah sets forth a parable: a straight path, with two walls along its sides. In the walls are open doors, and over the doors hang lowered curtains. A caller calls at the entrance to the path, and another caller calls from above it. The straight path is Islam, the curtains are the limits set by Allah, and the open doors are the things Allah has forbidden. Whenever a servant wishes to open one of those doors, the caller calls out to him—or words to that effect—‘O servant of Allah, do not open it, for if you open it, you will enter it.’ The caller at the entrance to the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller above the path is Allah’s admonisher in the heart of every believer.”

He thus made clear that within the heart of every believer there is an admonisher. Admonition consists of commanding and forbidding through encouragement and warning. These commands and prohibitions that arise in the believer’s heart accord with the commands and prohibitions of the Quran; thus, each strengthens the other.

As Allah Most High says:

“Light upon light.”

Some of the early Muslims said concerning this verse: “It refers to the believer who speaks with wisdom even though he has heard no transmitted report concerning it. Then, when he hears such a report, it becomes light upon light.” The light of faith in his heart accords with the light of the Quran, just as the rational balance accords with the revealed Book. For Allah sent down the Book and the balance so that people might uphold justice. A servant may be granted one of the two without being granted the other.

Thus, the two Sahīh collections relate from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The believer who recites the Quran is like a citron: its taste is pleasant and its fragrance is pleasant. And the likeness of

---

## Page 5056

the believer who does not recite the Quran is like a date: its taste is pleasant, but it has no fragrance. The hypocrite who recites the Quran is like sweet basil: its fragrance is pleasant, but its taste is bitter. The hypocrite who does not recite the Quran is like a colocynth: it has no fragrance, and its taste is bitter.”

Inspiration in the heart may take the form of speech, knowledge, supposition, or belief; at other times, it may take the form of action, love, will, or pursuit. It may occur to a person that a particular view is stronger, clearer, and more correct, or his heart may incline towards one of two alternatives rather than the other.

The two Sahīh collections relate that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Among the nations before you were people who received inspiration. If there is anyone like that in my nation, it is Umar.”

A muhaddath is someone who is inspired and addressed. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith of Wābisa:

“Righteousness is that with which the soul feels reassured and the heart is at ease. Sin is that which troubles you inwardly, even if people give you verdicts again and again.”

This is related in the Sunan collections.

Sahīh Muslim relates from al-Nawwās that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Righteousness is good character. Sin is that which troubles you inwardly and which you would dislike people discovering.”

Ibn Mas‘ūd said: “Sin is what pricks hearts.”

(Moreover, if matters pertaining to the created world may be disclosed to a believing servant, whether with certainty or as a matter of probability, then religious matters may all the more readily be disclosed to him, since his need for their disclosure is greater. In most cases, however, this disclosure must be based on evidence, and it may be

---

## Page 5057

based on evidence that dawns in the believer’s heart but that he cannot express. This is one interpretation of “istihsān” (juristic preference). Those who have criticized this, such as Abū Hāmid and Abū Muhammad, have said: “Whatever one cannot express is mere fancy.” That is not so, for not everyone can clearly express the meanings present in his heart, and many people explain them only imperfectly.

Many who experience spiritual disclosure have it cast into their hearts that a particular food is unlawful, or that a particular man is a disbeliever or an evildoer, without any apparent evidence. Conversely, love for someone may be cast into a person’s heart, together with the conviction that he is a friend of Allah, or that certain wealth is lawful. The purpose here is not to establish that this alone constitutes evidence for rulings of Islamic law. Rather, something of this kind may give the seeker of truth grounds for preferring one conclusion when the apparent scriptural evidence seems equally balanced to him. Giving preference on this basis is certainly better than treating two contradictory alternatives as equal, for treating them as equal is certainly false.

As we have said, acting on a probable judgment arising from the apparent meaning of a text or from analogy is better than acting on its contrary when one must act on one or the other.

The correct position, held by the early generations and the majority of scholars, is that there must be evidence from Islamic law for every case. The evidence therefore cannot, in reality, be equally balanced. It may, however, appear equally balanced to the person examining it because the grounds for preferring one conclusion are not apparent to him. As for those who say that there is, in reality, no single determinate truth, but that every jurist exercising independent judgment knows the underlying truth of the matter, and that neither has any advantage over the other in knowledge or practice—such people

---

## Page 5058

may—or at least some of them may—allow that the evidence is equally balanced and hold that the obligation is fulfilled by choosing either opinion. They say that, in reality, there is no evidence underpinning a probable judgment; rather, one opinion is preferred merely because of inclination and desire, just as an angry disposition favours vengeance and a forbearing disposition favours pardon.

This view is mistaken. There must, in reality, be a determinate truth that the person reasoning from evidence sometimes reaches and sometimes misses. This is like the Kaaba for someone uncertain of the direction of prayer. If his independent judgment leads him to a particular direction, he discharges his obligation by praying towards it, just as a jurist acts according to an opinion reached through independent judgment. Both are obedient to Allah. Each is correct in the sense that he is obedient to Allah and receives a reward for that; this does not mean, however, that he has correctly identified the determinate truth. That truth can only be one, and whoever reaches it receives two rewards.

This concerns discerning the categories for which evidence exists in Islamic law, although it may be hidden from the servant. For the Lawgiver has explained (the general rulings).

As for (judgments concerning particular cases), termed “tanqīh al-manāt” (refining the basis of a ruling)—such as whether a particular person is upright or an evildoer, a believer or a hypocrite, a friend of Allah or His enemy; whether a particular person is an enemy of the Muslims who deserves to be killed; whether a particular property belongs to an orphan or a poor person deserving kindness; or whether particular wealth is threatened by an oppressor’s injustice, such that, if the oppressor loses interest in it, its rightful owners will benefit from it—these

---

## Page 5059

matters need not be established through the general, universal evidence of Islamic law; rather, they are known through specific evidence that points to them. One means of this is “inspiration”: Allah may inspire some of His servants with knowledge of the circumstances of a particular property or person, even when there is no outward evidence accessible to others.

The story of Moses and al-Khidr falls into this category. It contains no violation of Allah’s Law, for no one—neither a prophet nor a friend of Allah—may ever violate His Law. Rather, it involves knowledge of a particular case in which a hidden circumstance makes what al-Khidr did obligatory under the Law. This is like someone who enters a house and takes the property inside, knowing that its owner has given him permission, while others do not know this. Likewise, someone might find a stray animal and take it without announcing that he has found it, knowing that it was brought as a gift for him; and there are other similar examples. Such things are common among those who receive genuine inspiration.

(The second type) is the opposite: they follow their desires rather than Allah’s command. They do and command only what their desires incline them to love, and they refrain from and forbid only what their desires incline them to hate. These are the worst of creation.

Allah Most High says:

“Have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god? Will you then be a guardian over him?”

Al-Hasan said: “This is the hypocrite: whatever he desires, he pursues.”

And Allah Most High says:

---

## Page 5060

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?”

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “Do not be one who follows the truth when it agrees with his desires and opposes it when it goes against them. For then you will receive no reward for the truth you follow, yet you will be punished for opposing it.”

It is just as he said—may Allah be pleased with him—for in both cases, the person intends only to follow his own desires; he does not act for Allah’s sake. Do you not see that Abū Tālib supported the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and defended him more than others did? Yet he did so because of their kinship, not for the sake of Allah Most High. Allah therefore neither accepted this from him nor rewarded him for it. Abū Bakr al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him—supported him with his person and wealth for Allah’s sake. Allah therefore said of him:

“But the most righteous will be kept far from it—he who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay anyone for a favour, but only to seek the Face of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be well pleased.”

(The third type): One who sometimes wills what Allah loves and sometimes wills what Allah hates. Most Muslims fall into this category: sometimes they obey Allah and desire what He loves, and sometimes they disobey Him and desire what their own inclinations lead them to, even though He dislikes it.

And (the fourth type): To have neither intention, intending neither to act for Allah’s sake nor to follow one’s own desire. This happens to many people in certain matters, and it also happens to many

---

## Page 5061

ascetics and devout worshippers in many matters.

A person cannot, however, be entirely devoid of will, for he is naturally disposed to desire what he cannot do without and to dislike what harms and hurts him. An ascetic, devout worshipper who is a Muslim must desire some things that Allah loves, such as fulfilling religious obligations and avoiding what is forbidden. Indeed, the same applies to believers in general: each must desire some things that Allah loves. Otherwise, someone who neither loves Allah nor loves anything for His sake, and thus loves no act of obedience—neither the two testimonies of faith nor anything else—and has no desire for any of it, cannot be a believer. Every believer must therefore desire at least some of what Allah loves. As for a servant desiring what appeals to his own inclinations but Allah does not love, this necessarily occurs in everyone who disobeys Allah: he has willed the sin, which Allah neither loves nor approves.

Being devoid of both kinds of will—the praiseworthy and the blameworthy—occurs in two forms:

(The first): When the servant turns away from worshipping and obeying Allah Most High, even though he knows about it. He may know that he is commanded to do many things, yet neither desire to do them nor dislike others doing them. When Muslims and disbelievers fight, he desires neither the victory of the former, which Allah loves, nor the victory of the latter, which Allah hates.

And (the second form): This occurs among many ascetics and devout worshippers who comply with what

---

## Page 5062

they know Allah has commanded, and avoid what they know Allah has forbidden. As for other matters, they do not know whether these are commanded or forbidden, so they neither desire nor dislike them because of their lack of knowledge. They may accept them on the grounds that they have been created and decreed, and may even assist in bringing them about. They regard this as being in accord with Allah, believing that, once free of their own desires, they are commanded to be content with everything that occurs—indeed, even to assist in bringing it about.

This is a point at which error arises. We must love whatever Allah and His Messenger love, and hate whatever Allah and His Messenger hate. As for what Allah and His Messenger neither love nor hate—such as actions for which there is no accountability, including those of a sleeping or insane person—if Allah neither loves and approves of these actions nor dislikes and condemns them, then the believer likewise should neither love and approve of them nor dislike them. Their being decreed and created by Allah is not peculiar to them; rather, it is something shared by all created things. Allah Most High created what He created as He willed in His wisdom, and He has made everything He created excellent.

Contentment with the divine decree is of “three kinds”:

(The first) is contentment with acts of obedience. This is itself an act of obedience that is commanded.

(The second): Contentment with afflictions. This is commanded, whether as something recommended or as an obligation.

---

## Page 5063

And (the third) is disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience: one is not commanded to be content with these, but rather to hate and disapprove of them, for Allah neither loves nor approves of them. As He Most High says:

“When they plot by night to say what He does not approve of.”

And He says:

“Allah does not love corruption.”

And He says:

“He does not approve of disbelief for His servants.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah does not love the disbelievers.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.”

Although He created it for a wise purpose, nothing precludes His creating what He does not love because it leads to a wise end that He loves, just as He created the devils. We are therefore content with Allah in His creating whatever He wills, and He is praised for that. As for the blameworthy act itself and the person who performs it, we neither approve of nor praise either.

There is a difference between what is loved for its own sake and what is willed because it leads to something loved, even though it is hated in another respect. The same thing may be willed in one respect and disliked in another. Consider a sick person who takes unpleasant medicine: he hates and dislikes the medicine, yet he wishes to take it because it leads to what he loves, not because the medicine itself is loved.

In the authentic hadith, Allah Most High says:

“I have never hesitated over anything I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet he must undergo it.”

Thus, since He, glorified be He, dislikes causing distress to His believing servant, who

---

## Page 5064

dislikes death, this entails His disliking putting him to death, even though He wills to do so because of His wisdom in it, glorified and exalted is He. Thus, things that Allah Most High hates and forbids are neither to be loved nor approved of. Rather, we are content with what Allah is pleased with in creating them, because of His wisdom in doing so. Likewise, actions that He neither loves nor hates should neither be loved nor approved of, just as they should not be hated. The contentment established by the revealed texts is to be content with Allah as one’s Lord, Islam as one’s religion, and Muhammad as one’s Prophet.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet has a right upon Allah that He make him content.”

As for divine decree, one is content with Allah, for He deserves praise in every circumstance. One is also content with the wisdom that pleases Him, for the sake of which He created what He created, even though we hate those created things that He hates. Where there is no revealed command, or the revealed command is unclear, compliance, contentment, and love do not apply as they do in relation to a revealed command, even if the matter is divinely decreed.

This is a point on which many of the elite among the “spiritual wayfarers” and their shaykhs err, let alone their ordinary followers. They differ in this according to their knowledge of the revealed commands and their obedience to them. Some have greater knowledge of the revealed commands than others and are more obedient to them. Such a person

---

## Page 5065

is in a better state than someone who falls short of him in knowledge of the revealed commands and obedience to them. Others distance themselves from the revealed commands and let themselves drift until they cast off Islam entirely, remaining guided by their desires and divine decree. Some of these die as disbelievers, while Allah enables others to repent; some die as evildoers, while Allah enables others to repent.

These people consider the reality of divine decree while turning away from the revealed commands. Yet they must still follow commands and prohibitions other than those of revelation, whether originating from themselves or from someone other than Allah and His Messenger. For passively going along with divine decree in every respect is inherently impossible, since, as explained earlier, the servant is naturally disposed to love some things and hate others.

As for the saying:

“The servant is to be with Allah as a corpse is with the one who washes it,”

this is neither correct nor permissible as an unqualified statement about any Muslim. It may be said only in certain circumstances, and even then only because Allah’s command is unclear to him. Otherwise, once he knows what Allah has commanded and loves, he must love what Allah loves and hate what He hates.

---

## Page 5066

Section

Just as the path of knowledge produces knowledge through sound examination of evidence and means—as in reflecting upon the Quran and hadith—so the path of action produces action through soundness of will and means. Hence, they call someone who follows this path an “aspirant,” just as those following the former path call him a “seeker.” “Examination” is a general category encompassing what is true and false, praiseworthy and blameworthy; the same applies to “will.”

The path of knowledge necessarily requires the knowledge conveyed by the Prophets through revelation: what you know must be the religious truths conveyed by the Prophets, and your knowledge of them must accord with what the Messengers have reported. Otherwise, no knowledge you acquire, nor any belief you hold concerning what the Messengers have reported, will benefit you. Rather, you must believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, and the Last Day.

Likewise, with regard to “will,” one must identify “the One sought,” who is Allah, and “the path to Him,” which is what the Messengers commanded. You must therefore worship Allah, and your worship of Him must follow what He prescribed through His Messengers. For in matters of knowledge, one must believe the Messenger in what he reported, and in matters of action, one must obey him in what he commanded.

---

## Page 5067

This is why “faith” consists of speech and action in conformity with the Sunnah. Knowledge of the truth is that which accords with Allah’s knowledge, and righteous will is that which accords with Allah’s love and good pleasure—that is, His prescriptive judgment. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise. Matters conveyed in reports must accord with Allah’s knowledge and what He has reported, while matters of practice must accord with what Allah loves and commands. The latter concerns His judgment, and the former His knowledge.

As for someone who reduces His judgment to predestination alone, as the author of “Manāzil al-Sā’irīn” (The Stations of the Wayfarers) did, and holds that the gnostic’s witnessing of this judgment prevents him from regarding a good deed as good or an evil deed as evil—this involves grave error, as we have pointed out elsewhere.

Thus, it does not benefit the aspiring seeker to worship just any object of worship, nor to worship Allah through just any form of worship. Rather, this is the way of those who associate partners with Allah and introduce religious innovations: they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion that Allah has not authorized. Such are the Christians and those religious innovators who resemble them, who worship other than Allah without His command. By contrast, the followers of Islam and the Sunnah worship Allah alone and worship Him as He has prescribed. They do not worship Him through innovations, except when one of them does so in error.

Those who follow the path of aspiration may err at times concerning what they seek, and at other times concerning the path to it. At times, they deify other than Allah by fearing them, placing hope in them, venerating and loving them, petitioning them, and directing their longing towards them. This is the very essence of associating partners with Allah, which is forbidden. For the essence of

---

## Page 5068

monotheism is that none but Allah be worshipped. “Worship” encompasses perfect love and veneration, and perfect hope, fear, reverence, and honour.

“Fanā” (effacement) within this monotheism is the fanā of the messengers and their followers. It means that, through worshipping Him, you cease worshipping anyone else; through obeying Him, you cease obeying anyone else; through asking Him, you cease asking anyone else; through fearing Him, you cease fearing anyone else; through hoping in Him, you cease hoping in anyone else; and through loving Him and loving for His sake, you cease loving anything else and loving for its sake.

As for those who err concerning the path, they may seek Allah, yet fail to follow the revealed command in seeking Him. Sometimes one of them worships Him through what he supposes pleases Him, though it does not. At other times, they contemplate predestination because it is what He wills, and experience fanā in those decrees in which they have no personal interest. Absolute fanā in predestination, however, is impossible. One of these people experiences fanā while following his own spiritual taste and ecstasy contrary to the revealed command, or while contemplating predestination. Many of their foremost figures are afflicted with this.

“Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir” and others like him were among the leading shaykhs of their time who most strongly urged adherence to the revealed law, its commands and prohibitions, and giving it precedence over spiritual taste and predestination. They were also among the shaykhs who most strongly urged the abandonment of personal desires and self-will. For error in the will as such arises only from this source. Thus he instructs the wayfarer

---

## Page 5069

to have no will whatsoever arising from his own desires, but rather to will what the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, wills: to follow His revealed will if it becomes clear to him; otherwise, to go along with His decreed will. Thus he follows either the Lord’s command or His creation, and to Him, glorified be He, belong creation and command.

This is a “sound path in accordance with the revealed law.” The only concern for one who follows it is that he might abandon something prescribed by Allah’s revealed will without knowing that it is prescribed, or give precedence to His decreed will over His revealed will. For if he does not know that something is prescribed, he may abandon it or desire its opposite, thus neglecting a command or committing a prohibition without knowing it.

For one who follows the “path of the will,” there is a concern about deficient knowledge, deficient practice accompanying that knowledge, and falling into error. Likewise, for one who follows the path of knowledge, there is a concern about deficient practice and deficient knowledge accompanying that practice. Yet Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity in either respect. The Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

If the wayfarer gains understanding and learns the commands and prohibitions to the best of his ability, and his knowledge and will accord with that, then this is the extent of his capacity. Likewise, if the seeker fulfils what he has been commanded to do, refrains from what he has been forbidden, and his knowledge accords with his practice, then this is the extent of his capacity.

---

## Page 5070

Section

Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

“Become detached from created beings through Allah’s judgment, from your desires through His command, and from your own will through His action. Only then will you be fit to become a vessel for the knowledge of Allah.”

I say: His judgment encompasses both His creation and His command. That is, become detached from worshipping created beings and relying upon them by worshipping Allah and relying upon Him. Do not obey them in disobedience to Allah Most High, nor attach yourself to them to obtain a benefit or avert harm.

As for detachment from desire through His command, and from one’s own will through His action, this means that a person’s actions should conform to the revealed command rather than his desires, and that his will concerning what Allah creates should follow Allah’s action rather than his own wishes. A person’s will sometimes concerns his own actions and sometimes concerns created things. In the first case, it “is governed by the command,” while in the second, “he is to have no will of his own.”

This must, however, be qualified: he should have no will that he has not been commanded to have. Otherwise, if he is commanded to will one thing rather than another among the matters subject to divine decree, he should will what he has been commanded to will, whether or not it accords with what has been decreed. This is a point on which some wayfarers may err.

---

## Page 5071

And what generally happens with the sincere among them is that they have not understood what the revealed law requires them to will in that particular matter. Having no will driven by personal desire, they relinquish any will for something other than what has been decreed.

The Shaykh said:

“The sign of your detachment from Allah’s creation is that you sever your dependence upon them, cease frequenting them, and abandon hope of obtaining what they possess.”

It is as he said. When the heart neither places its hopes in them nor fears them, a person will not frequent them to seek anything from them. This resembles going to them as one is commanded, to enjoin upon them what Allah has commanded and forbid them what Allah has forbidden—as the messengers and their followers go to those to whom they convey Allah’s messages. Reliance upon Allah is sound only when accompanied by fulfilling what the servant has been commanded to do, so that he both worships Allah and relies upon Him. Otherwise, if someone relies upon Him but does not do what He has commanded, the command he has neglected may be more important for him than the reliance he has practiced, or equally important, or less important. Likewise, someone who carries out a command but neither relies upon Him nor seeks His help has not fulfilled his obligation. Indeed, the reliance and seeking of help that he has neglected may be more important for him than the command he has carried out, or equally important, or less important.

The Shaykh said:

“The sign of your detachment from yourself and your desires is that you give up striving for gain and depending upon means to secure benefit and ward off harm. You make no movement within yourself by your own power, nor rely upon yourself for your own sake. You neither come to your own aid nor defend yourself, but entrust all of that

---

## Page 5072

to the One who managed it at the outset, so that He may manage it in the end, just as it was entrusted to Him when you were hidden in the womb and when you were a nursing infant in your cradle.”

I say:

This is because the soul desires to obtain what it loves and what benefits it, and to ward off what it hates and what harms it. When, through obedience to the command, a person becomes detached from those concerns, he does what Allah loves and abandons what Allah hates. He thus substitutes doing what Allah loves for pursuing what he himself loves, and abandoning what Allah hates for avoiding what he himself hates. Yet the soul still needs to secure benefit and ward off harm, so in this he relies upon Allah.

The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—mentioned reliance upon Allah here, rather than obedience, because the soul must secure benefit and ward off harm. Unless it relies upon Allah in this and trusts Him, it cannot set those concerns aside and comply with the command unconditionally. Rather, it will inevitably disobey the command in seeking benefit and warding off harm. Thus, worship of Allah and obedience to His command cannot be sound without reliance upon Him, just as reliance upon Him cannot be sound without worshipping and obeying Him.

Allah Most High says:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

And He says:

“Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him,”

“and provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him.”

And He says:

“Remember the name of your Lord, and devote yourself wholeheartedly to Him.”

“Lord of the East and the West—there is no deity except Him, so take Him as your Trustee.”

And (the point) is that unconditional compliance with the command cannot be sound without

---

## Page 5073

reliance upon Allah and seeking His help. Whoever trusts Allah to bring him what benefits him and ward off what harms him can abandon his own desires and obey His command. Otherwise, his soul will not allow him to relinquish something for which he says he needs another’s help.

The Shaykh—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“The sign that your will has been effaced through Allah’s action is that you no longer desire anything at all. You have no aim, nor does any need or aspiration occupy you, for you desire no will alongside Allah’s will. Rather, His action unfolds within you, so that you yourself become the will and act of Allah Most High: your limbs still, your heart tranquil, your breast expanded, your face radiant, your inner being flourishing, and the Creator making you independent of created things. The hand of power turns you about, the voice of beginningless eternity calls you, and the Lord of dominion teaches you. He clothes you in light from Him and in robes, and raises you to the stations of those predecessors who possessed the original knowledge. Thus you remain forever broken in spirit.

“No desire or will remains within you. You are like a broken vessel that retains neither liquid nor dregs. Your human traits fade away, and your inner being admits no resident other than Allah’s will. Then the bringing of things into being and departures from the customary order are attributed to you. Outwardly, reason and judgment perceive these as proceeding from you, though in the light of knowledge they are truly the action of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. You then enter the company of the brokenhearted, whose human wills have been broken and whose natural desires have been removed, while divine volitions and desires attributed to them have become firmly established in them. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

‘Made beloved to me, from

---

## Page 5074

your world: women and perfume; and the delight of my eyes has been placed in prayer.’ Thus this was attributed to him after it had left him and passed away from him, confirming what I indicated and explained earlier. Allah Most High said: ‘I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake.’”

He continued his discourse, which also includes: “My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship”—and the remainder of the hadith.

I say: This station is the ultimate one to which Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir—may Allah be pleased with him—points. Its reality is that a person does not desire anything to come about unless he is commanded to desire it. His statement, “The sign that your will has been effaced through Allah’s action is that you no longer desire anything at all,” means that you do not desire anything you have not been commanded to desire. As for what Allah and His Messenger command you to desire, desiring it is either obligatory or recommended, while abandoning that desire is either disobedience or a deficiency.

This point confuses many spiritual wayfarers. They suppose that the perfect path requires the servant to have no will whatsoever, and that Abū Yazīd’s statement, “I desire not to desire”—when asked, “What do you desire?”—is deficient and self-contradictory, since he has indeed expressed a desire. They interpret the words of shaykhs who are praised for relinquishing their will as meaning that all will should be relinquished without exception. In this, they misunderstand the upright shaykhs. If, however, any shaykh does command the abandonment of all will without exception, then whoever says this is mistaken, for that is neither possible nor commanded.

---

## Page 5075

for every living being must have a will; it is impossible for a living being to have no will. As for the desire that Allah and His Messenger love and enjoin, whether as an obligation or a recommendation: if it is obligatory, only a disbeliever, a defiantly disobedient person, or a sinner abandons it; if it is recommended, whoever abandons it has forsaken what is better for him. Allah Most High has described the prophets and those of utmost truthfulness as possessing this “desire.” He Most High said:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

He Most High said:

“He owes no one a favor to be repaid, but seeks only the Face of his Lord, the Most High.”

He Most High said:

“We feed you only for the sake of Allah. We desire neither reward nor thanks from you.”

He Most High said:

“But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Hereafter, then Allah has prepared a tremendous reward for those of you who do good.”

He Most High said:

“Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—such people will have their striving appreciated.”

He Most High said:

“So worship Allah, devoting your religion sincerely to Him. Indeed, sincere devotion belongs to Allah alone.”

He Most High said:

“Say: It is Allah I worship, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.”

He Most High said:

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him.”

He Most High said:

“I did not create jinn and humankind except to worship Me.”

There can be no worship without desiring Allah and what He has commanded. He Most High said:

“Indeed, whoever submits his face to Allah while doing good…”

That is, he directs his intention sincerely to Allah. He Most High said:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him.”

And devoting one’s religion sincerely to Him

---

## Page 5076

means seeking Him alone in worship. He Most High said:

“He loves them, and they love Him.”

He Most High said:

“But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

He Most High said:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

Everyone who loves also desires. Allah’s intimate friend, peace be upon him, said:

“I do not love those that set.”

Then he said:

“Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth.”

There are many such passages in the Quran: Allah commands people to desire Him and what He commands, and forbids them to desire anything besides Him or what He has forbidden. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Actions are judged only by intentions, and each person will have only what he intended. Whoever emigrates to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger. Whoever emigrates for worldly gain or to marry a woman, his emigration is to whatever he emigrated for.”

Thus, there are “two kinds of desire”: desire that Allah loves and is pleased with, and desire that Allah neither loves nor is pleased with—the latter being either something He has forbidden or something He has neither commanded nor forbidden.

With regard to desire, people fall into “three categories.” Some desire whatever gratifies their whims; these are slaves to themselves and to Satan. Others claim that they have entirely relinquished desire and no longer desire anything except what the Lord decrees, and that this station is the most perfect of all stations. They claim that whoever occupies this station has attained reality—namely, the reality of the divine decree governing creation—and that he

---

## Page 5077

has witnessed Allah’s sustaining and governing of all things. They regard absorption in witnessing Allah’s oneness in lordship as the ultimate goal. They may call this unitive awareness, absorption, istilām, or similar names. Many shaykhs have stumbled at this point.

It was concerning “this station” that disagreement arose between al-Junayd ibn Muhammad and a group of his Sufi companions. They agreed upon witnessing Allah’s oneness in lordship—that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything—which is witnessing the divine decree. They called this “the station of unitive awareness,” because through it a person moves beyond the first differentiation: the natural differentiation that consists in desiring one thing and disliking another, and seeing this person act and that person refrain.

Before witnessing this oneness, a person sees created beings as acting, and his heart becomes scattered as he observes their various actions. He also follows his whims in what he desires. When he seeks Allah, that desire takes him beyond the desires of whim and natural inclination. Then he witnesses that Allah is the Creator of everything, and through witnessing this unitive awareness he moves beyond that differentiation.

Once they had agreed upon this, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad explained to them “the second differentiation,” which follows this unitive awareness: differentiation according to the revealed law. Do you not see that you desire what you have been commanded to do, and do not desire what you have been forbidden? You witness that Allah alone deserves worship, and that worshipping Him consists in obeying His messengers. Thus, you distinguish between what is commanded and what is forbidden, and between His allies and His enemies, and you witness that Allah alone is to be worshipped. They disputed this “differentiation” with him.

---

## Page 5078

Some of them rejected it, while others did not understand it. Still others claimed that the one speaking of it had not attained it. You will find that many shaykhs reach no further than that unitive awareness—“Allah’s oneness in lordship”—and absorption in it. This appears in the words of the author of Manāzil al-Sā’irīn (The Stations of the Wayfarers), despite his eminent standing and the certainty that he observed the recognized commands and prohibitions. Yet they may claim that this is for the sake of the common people.

(Some of them contradict themselves.) And (some say: Adhering to the command serves the welfare of the common people), whom they may describe as hospital patients. And (some call this the station of talbīs [concealment]). And (some say: True realization means witnessing unitive awareness in your heart while expressing differentiation with your tongue). Thus, in his heart he witnesses what is commanded and what is forbidden as equal, even as he distinguishes between them.

And (some regard this as the reality that is the ultimate goal of the spiritual journey of

---

## Page 5079

those who know Allah, and the highest station of His utterly truthful friends). And (some think that adherence to the divine will expressed in commands and prohibitions belongs to the spiritual journey and its beginnings, whereas at its culmination nothing remains but the will expressed in the divine decree. In reality, this amounts to claiming that worship and obedience are no longer required. For worship of Allah and obedience to Him and His Messenger consist in complying with the commands of the revealed Law, not in going along with whatever is decreed, even if it is disbelief, wickedness, or disobedience. This is how many spiritual wayfarers have become helpers and protectors of the disbelievers and the wicked: they perceived the divine decree as being on their side, but disregarded the commands and prohibitions of the revealed Law.

Some of these people say:

“Whoever witnesses the divine decree is no longer subject to blame.”

They say that al-Khidr ceased to be subject to blame only because he witnessed the divine decree. Someone devoted to witnessing the divine decree may be granted dominion through extraordinary means—disclosure of hidden things and power over events—and imagine this to be perfection in friendship with Allah. Yet these “extraordinary feats” may have arisen only through satanic means and personal desires.

Perfection in friendship with Allah consists only in using extraordinary feats to uphold the commands and prohibitions of the revealed Law, with both being attained through doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden. If these feats arise through means not sanctioned by the revealed Law, they are blameworthy. If they arise through means sanctioned by the revealed Law but are used to attain something forbidden, they are blameworthy. If they are used to attain something permissible

---

## Page 5080

without being used to aid obedience, they belong to the righteous, not to those brought near to Allah. But if they arise through means sanctioned by the revealed Law and are used to help fulfil its commands, these are the extraordinary feats of the foremost, those brought near to Allah.

“Extraordinary feats” must therefore be examined in terms of their causes and purposes: how they arose and what they led to—just as wealth is examined in terms of how it was acquired and how it was spent. Whoever uses them—I mean extraordinary feats—to serve his natural desires is blameworthy. As for someone devoid of both natural desire and a will that accords with the revealed Law, the most he can hope for is to be pardoned because he did not know what the revealed Law required him to will. But if he knew this and turned away from it, he is blameworthy and deserves punishment unless he is pardoned.

He is praised insofar as his will is not governed by his desires; nevertheless, it must also conform to the command of Allah Most High and His Messenger. It is not enough for it to follow neither one nor the other. Moreover, he cannot be entirely devoid of will: he must will something. If he does not will what Allah and His Messenger love, he wills what Allah and His Messenger do not love. Yet if he strives against himself to abandon what he desires, he continues to will what he supposes he has been commanded to do, and thus goes astray. This resembles the condition of those Christians who have gone astray.

Allah Most High has said:

“Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your wrath

---

## Page 5081

nor those who have gone astray.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Jews have incurred Allah’s wrath, and the Christians have gone astray.”

The Jews direct their will toward corrupt, forbidden ends, as Allah has stated of them: they disobeyed and habitually transgressed. They know the truth but do not act upon it: they possess knowledge but do not put it into practice. In directing their will toward blameworthy and forbidden ends, they follow their desires rather than exercising the praiseworthy will they have been commanded to exercise—namely, willing what Allah and His Messenger love.

The Christians have purpose, worship and asceticism, but they are astray, acting without knowledge. They do not know the kind of willing that Allah and His Messenger love. Rather, the utmost aim of any one of them is to divest himself of all will. Thus, he no longer wills what Allah and His Messenger have commanded, just as he does not will much of what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden. Such people have lost their way to the goal they seek, for that goal can only be attained through obedience to Allah and His Messenger. This is why they are accursed—that is, far removed from the mercy attained through obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The “sinful scholar” resembles the Jews, while the “ignorant worshipper” resembles the Christians. Among people of knowledge are some who have something of the former in them, and among people devoted to worship are some who have something of the latter.

---

## Page 5082

On this matter, the children of Adam have differed and diverged so greatly that only Allah encompasses the full extent of their differences. Among them is one whom no creature surpasses in honor before Allah, and who is the best of creation. Among them, too, are those who are the worst of creation. The highest state in this regard is that of the two close friends of Allah: Abraham and Muhammad—may Allah bless them both and grant them peace.

Muhammad is the master of the children of Adam, the best of all generations, first and last, the Seal of the Prophets, their leader when they assemble, and their spokesman when they come as a delegation. He is the one who was taken up above all the prophets—Abraham, Moses, and the others.

The best of the prophets after him is Abraham, as established in the Sahīh in a report from Anas, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Abraham is the best of creation.”

It is also established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of Jābir, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his Friday sermon:

“The best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

Likewise, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd used to address people with these words on Thursdays, as al-Bukhārī related in his Sahīh.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never struck a servant of his, a woman, an animal, or anything at all, except when fighting in Allah’s cause. He never avenged any wrong done to him personally, unless Allah’s sacred limits were violated. When Allah’s sacred limits were violated, nothing could withstand his anger until he had exacted retribution for Allah’s sake.”

---

## Page 5083

Anas said:

“I served the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for ten years. He never once uttered a word of irritation to me. He never said about anything I had done, ‘Why did you do that?’ or about anything I had not done, ‘Why did you not do that?’ If a member of his household rebuked me for something, he would say, ‘Leave him alone. Had something been decreed, it would have happened.’”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the best of creation and the master of the children of Adam. His is the rank of nearness to Allah in every station. His state was neither to will nothing nor to will everything that occurred, just as he did not follow his own desires. Rather, he was free of both these extremes. Allah Most High said:

“Nor does he speak from desire.”
“It is nothing but revelation sent down.”

Allah Most High also said:

“And when Allah’s servant stood up to call upon Him.”

And He said:

“And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant.”

And He said:

“Glory be to Him who took His servant by night.”

What is meant by ‘His servant’ is one who worships Him and obeys His command. Otherwise, all created beings are servants in the sense that they are subjected to Him, created by Him, and governed by Him.

Allah said to His Prophet:

“And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.”

Al-Hasan al-Basrī said, “Allah has appointed no end to the believer’s deeds short of death.”

Allah Most High also said to him:

“And indeed, you are of sublime character.”

Ibn ʿAbbās and those who agreed with him, such as Ibn ʿUyaynah and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, explained this as following a sublime religion. ‘Religion’ means doing what one has been commanded to do.

ʿĀʾishah said:

“His character was the Quran.”

This was narrated by Muslim. She also related that he would neither punish nor exact retribution for his own sake, but he would punish for Allah’s sake

---

## Page 5084

and exact retribution for Allah’s sake. Anas likewise reported that he would forgo his personal claims. As for Allah’s prescribed limits, he said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, if Fātimah, the daughter of Muhammad, were to steal, I would cut off her hand.”

This was narrated in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim. This is perfection of will: he willed the faith and righteous deeds that Allah loves and is pleased with, and commanded them; he hated the disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience that Allah hates, and forbade them. Thus Allah Most High described him, saying:

“My mercy encompasses all things. I shall ordain it for those who are mindful of Me, give zakah, and believe in Our signs.”

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find described in the Torah and the Gospel they possess. He commands them to do what is right and forbids them from doing what is wrong; he makes good things lawful for them and forbids them impure things; and he relieves them of their burdens and the shackles that bound them. So those who believe in him, honour him, support him, and follow the light sent down with him—it is they who will prosper.”

As for his own personal claims, he would neither punish nor exact retribution. Rather, he would uphold his Lord’s right and forgo his own claims. In matters concerning his own claims, he would look to divine decree, saying:

“Had something been decreed, it would have happened.”

But where Allah’s right was concerned, he would uphold the command, doing what Allah had commanded and striving in Allah’s cause to the fullest extent possible. He first strove against them with his tongue, through the Quran revealed to him, as Allah Most High said:

“Had We willed, We could have sent a warner to every town.”

“So do not obey the disbelievers, but strive mightily against them with it.”

Then, when

---

## Page 5085

he migrated to Medina and was given permission to fight, he fought them with his own hands.

This accords with the report narrated in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim from Abū Hurayrah, and also known through the narration of Umar ibn al-Khattāb, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), concerning the debate between Adam and Moses. When Moses blamed Adam for having caused himself and his descendants to be expelled from Paradise through the sin he had committed, Adam answered that this had been decreed for him long before he was created. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument.”

This was because Moses’ reproach of Adam did not concern Allah’s right, but rather the calamity that had befallen him and other human beings because of that deed. Adam therefore explained to him that this was something decreed and bound to happen. When calamities befall Allah’s servants, they are commanded to be patient, for that is what benefits them. Blaming those who caused these calamities brings them no benefit.

Likewise, when they miss out on things that would benefit them, they are commanded to consider the divine decree; regret and sorrow bring no benefit. Whatever the divine decree has brought about—whether the loss of some benefit or the occurrence of some harm—they should view it in light of that decree. As for whatever results from their own deeds, they should strive to repent of their sins and mend their ways in the future. This benefits them and is within their power, with Allah’s help.

---

## Page 5086

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both. Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give in to helplessness. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘Had I done such-and-such, this and that would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah decreed, and He has done whatever He willed,’ for ‘if only’ opens the way for Satan’s work.”

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded the servant to strive for what benefits him and to seek Allah’s help, and forbade him to give in to helplessness. What benefits the servant most is obedience to Allah and His Messenger, which constitutes worship of Allah Most High. These two principles embody the meaning of His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He forbade helplessness, meaning wastefulness, negligence, and sluggishness. As he said in another hadith:

“The prudent person is one who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death. The helpless person is one who lets his soul follow its desires and entertains wishful hopes concerning Allah.”

Narrated by al-Tirmidhī.

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd:

“Two men brought their dispute before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and he ruled against one of them. The man against whom he ruled said, ‘Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’ The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, ‘Allah blames helplessness. Rather, you must act prudently. Then, if something overcomes you, say: Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

Prudence is thus the opposite of helplessness. Another hadith states:

“Everything is by divine decree, even helplessness and prudence.”

Narrated by Muslim. By helplessness, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) does not mean that which is the opposite of

---

## Page 5087

ability; for someone who has no ability whatsoever is neither blamed nor commanded to do what he is wholly unable to do. Then, having commanded him to strive and seek Allah’s help, and forbidden him to give in to helplessness, he instructed him, when something overwhelms him, to consider the divine decree and say, “Allah decreed, and He has done whatever He willed,” rather than succumb to regret, anguish, and sorrow, saying, “Had I done such-and-such, this and that would have happened.” For “if only” opens the way for Satan’s work.

Someone expressed this meaning as follows: “Matters are of two kinds: those about which something can be done, and those about which nothing can be done. One should not give in to helplessness regarding the former, nor to distress regarding the latter.” This is what the leading scholars of religion teach, as Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir and others have mentioned. One must do what is commanded, refrain from what is forbidden, and meet what is decreed with acceptance and patience.

Allah Most High relates that Joseph said:

“I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever is mindful of Allah and patient—Allah never lets the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

“Mindfulness of Allah” encompasses doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden. “Patience” encompasses patiently bearing what is decreed.

Allah Most High also says:

“O you who believe, do not take as confidants those outside your ranks; they spare no effort to bring you ruin”—up to His words—“But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all.”

He, glorified be He, thus made it clear that, with mindfulness of Allah and patience, no harm comes to

---

## Page 5088

the believers from the plotting of their hypocritical enemies.

Allah Most High also says:

“Yes indeed! If you are patient and mindful of Allah, and they come upon you at once, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels bearing marks of distinction.”

He thus made it clear that, with patience and mindfulness of Allah, He reinforces them with angels and grants them victory over the enemies who fight them.

Allah Most High also says:

“You will surely be tested in your possessions and yourselves, and you will surely hear much abuse from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah. But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, that is indeed a matter requiring firm resolve.”

He informed them that their enemies among the polytheists and the People of the Scripture would inevitably harm them with their tongues. He also informed them that being patient and mindful of Allah is a matter requiring firm resolve. Patience and mindfulness of Allah therefore ward off the evil of enemies who openly display their hostility—whether they inflict harm with their tongues or their hands—as well as the evil of enemies who conceal their hostility, namely the hypocrites. This conduct, which was the character and way of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the most perfect course.

As for someone who sometimes desires what Allah loves and sometimes what He does not love, or someone who desires neither, both fall short of the character of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, even if neither incurs any sin. An example is someone who seeks the gratification of desire, anger, and retaliation within the bounds of what is permissible, as was characteristic of some prophets and righteous people. Although this is permissible and entails no sin, the character of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is more perfect.

---

## Page 5089

The same applies to someone who does not desire lawful pleasures, even when they can help him perform a recommended deed, and does not wish to become angry, exact retribution, or engage in jihad when pardon is permissible, even when taking retribution for Allah’s sake would be more pleasing to Him. This, too, was characteristic of some prophets and righteous people. Although this is permissible and entails no sin, the character of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is more perfect.

If this conduct or that described previously forms part of the law prescribed for a prophet, then no prophet is to be faulted for what Allah has prescribed for him. Yet Allah has favored some prophets over others and some messengers over others. The law with which Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the best of all revealed laws, for Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the best of the prophets and messengers, and his community is the best community ever raised for mankind.

Commenting on the words of Allah Most High,

“You are the best community ever raised for mankind,”

Abū Hurayrah said: “You are the best people for other people: you bring them in fetters and chains until you bring them into Paradise.”

They expend their wealth and their lives in jihad for people’s benefit, making them the most beneficial of all communities to creation. All creatures are dependent on Allah, and those most beloved to Allah are those most beneficial to His dependents.

As for those who are not prophets, some follow this as their prescribed law because they follow that prophet. But for someone who follows the law and way of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, if what he has neglected is obligatory for him and what he has done is forbidden to him, then he deserves blame and punishment—unless he is acting on a mistaken interpretation, for Allah has excused this community for

---

## Page 5090

mistakes and forgetfulness. Allah may also pardon the sin of any one of them for various reasons.

One cause of this deviation is that some people’s personal inclinations are dominated by “the ascetic path,” so they renounce what desire and anger prompt them to do. This is also practiced by some devotees among the polytheists and the People of the Book, such as monks and others like them. They regard jihad as a failing because it involves killing people, taking their offspring captive, and seizing property. They also hold that Allah did not entrust the building of the Temple in Jerusalem to David because blood had been shed at his hands.

Some of them consider the slaughter of any animal impermissible, as is the position of the Brahmins. Others do not consider it forbidden, but personally seek nearness to Allah by refraining from slaughtering animals, eating their meat, and marrying women. Someone praising such a man says: “So-and-so has neither married nor slaughtered an animal.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rebuked such people, as reported in the two Sahīh collections from Anas:

“A group of the Prophet’s Companions asked the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about what he did in private. One of them said, ‘I will not marry women.’ Another said, ‘I will not eat meat.’ Another said, ‘I will not sleep on a bed.’ When word of this reached the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he praised and extolled Allah, then said: ‘What is the matter with people who say such-and-such? But I pray and sleep

---

## Page 5091

and I fast and break my fast, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.’”

Allah Most High has said:

“O you who believe, do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you.”

This was revealed concerning ‘Uthmān ibn Maz‘ūn and a group with him who had resolved upon celibacy and a form of monasticism. In the two Sahīh collections, Sa‘d reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, refused to allow ‘Uthmān ibn Maz‘ūn to embrace celibacy. Had he permitted him, we would have castrated ourselves.”

The beneficial, prescribed form of “renunciation” that Allah and His Messenger love is to renounce whatever brings no benefit in the Hereafter. As for what benefits one in the Hereafter, and what helps one attain that benefit, renouncing it amounts to renouncing a form of worship and obedience to Allah. Renunciation is sought only because it means renouncing what is harmful or what brings no benefit. Renouncing what is beneficial, however, is ignorance and misguidance, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not falter.”

What benefits a servant is worshipping and obeying Allah and obeying His Messenger. Whatever diverts him from that is harmful, not beneficial. Moreover, what benefits him most is for all his deeds to be acts of worship and obedience to Allah. If he fulfils his obligatory duties and does something permissible that does not help him obey Allah, then he has done both what benefits him and what neither benefits nor harms him.

Likewise, the prescribed form of “scrupulousness” is to refrain from what may have adverse consequences, namely

---

## Page 5092

what is known to be forbidden and what one doubts is forbidden, provided that refraining from it does not cause greater harm than doing it—for instance, by leading to a definite forbidden act. Someone may, for example, scrupulously refrain from taking something doubtful despite needing it, yet take something clearly forbidden instead; or neglect an obligation when neglecting it causes greater harm than fulfilling it despite the doubt involved. An example is someone who is required to repay debts owed by himself or his father, but has no means of repayment except wealth about which there is some doubt. He scrupulously avoids it, leaving his own debts or his father’s debts undischarged.

“Scrupulousness” also includes taking the precaution of doing something whose obligatory status is uncertain, but subject to the same qualification. Complete “scrupulousness” requires a person’s concern to encompass the better of two goods and the worse of two evils, and requires him to recognize that the Sharia is founded upon securing and perfecting benefits, and eliminating and reducing harms. Otherwise, someone who does not weigh the benefits and harms recognized by the Sharia in both acting and refraining may neglect obligations and commit forbidden acts, believing this to be scrupulousness.

Such is the person who refrains from jihad under unjust rulers and regards this as scrupulousness; who abandons Friday prayer and congregational prayer behind imams guilty of religious innovation or wickedness and regards this as scrupulousness; or who refuses to accept a truthful person’s testimony or learn from a scholar because the person concerned adheres to a subtle religious innovation, regarding his refusal to hear and accept this truth—which he is obliged to hear—as scrupulousness.

---

## Page 5093

The same applies to “renunciation and desire.” Anyone who fails to consider what Allah and His Messenger love and dislike in these matters may neglect obligations and commit forbidden acts. For example, someone may forgo the food or fatty foods he needs until his reason becomes impaired or he becomes too weak to fulfil his duties towards Allah Most High or His servants. Or he may abandon enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and jihad in Allah’s cause because these involve harming some people and exacting retribution from them, until the disbelievers and the wicked gain ascendancy over the righteous and virtuous. He fails to consider the greater benefit of such action.

Allah Most High has said:

“They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say, ‘Fighting in it is a grave offence, but barring people from Allah’s path, disbelieving in Him, barring access to the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it are graver in Allah’s sight. And strife is graver than killing.’”

He, glorified and exalted be He, is saying that although taking lives entails evil, the strife caused by disbelief and the ascendancy of its adherents is greater. Thus, the greater of two evils is averted by accepting the lesser.

Likewise, someone who refrains from slaughtering animals, or considers slaughtering an animal an injustice to it, is ignorant. For this animal must inevitably die; if it is killed for the benefit of human beings

---

## Page 5094

and to meet their needs, it is better than its dying a death from which no one benefits. Human beings are more perfect than animals, and their welfare cannot be fully secured without using animals for food, riding, and similar purposes. Allah has, however, forbidden inflicting needless suffering upon animals, such as restraining them as live targets or slaughtering them anywhere other than the throat or the base of the neck when slaughtering them there is possible. In the killing and slaughter He has permitted, Allah has required kindness to the extent possible.

Thus, Sahīh Muslim records from Shaddād ibn Aws that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has prescribed excellence in all things. When you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal suffering.”

In contrast to those who have renounced “desires,” even those desires which Allah and His Messenger love, there are “two groups.”

One group desires disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience—things which Allah and His Messenger dislike, along with the desire for them.

Another group desires what Allah and His Messenger have commanded, but out of personal inclination, not to worship Allah Most High. These people perform outward acts of obedience while their intentions are corrupt. Thus, the two Sahīh collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked:

“O Messenger of Allah, a man fights to display his courage, another fights out of partisan zeal, and another fights to show off. Which of these is fighting in Allah’s cause?”

He replied:

“Whoever fights so that Allah’s word is supreme

---

## Page 5095

is fighting in Allah’s cause.”

Allah Most High says:

“The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but it is He who deceives them. When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off before people and remembering Allah only a little.”

These people have corrupt, blameworthy desires. Besides neglecting what is obligatory, they commit what is forbidden. They resemble the Jews, just as the others resemble the Christians.

Allah Most High says:

“Humiliation has been laid upon them wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from people. They have incurred Allah’s anger, and destitution has been laid upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in Allah’s signs and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and transgressed.”

Allah Most High also says:

“I shall turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on earth without right. Even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. If they see the path of right guidance, they will not take it as their path; but if they see the path of error, they will take it as their path.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Relate to them the account of the man to whom We gave Our signs, but who cast them off. Satan then overtook him, and he became one of those who went astray.”

“And had We willed, We would have raised him through them,” up to His words:

“and followed his own desire. His likeness is that of a dog: if you chase it away, it pants; and if you leave it alone, it pants. That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So recount these accounts, that they may reflect.”

These people follow their desires in wilful error despite knowing the truth, while the others follow their desires in misguidance and ignorance of the truth.

As Allah Most High says:

“Do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before, led many astray, and strayed from the straight path.”

---

## Page 5096

Both groups neglect the righteous intentions and deeds that Allah and His Messenger have commanded, and embrace the corrupt intentions and deeds that Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

Section

When Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir, his teacher Hammād al-Dabbās, and other upright shaykhs—may Allah be pleased with them—instructed that the seeker should desire nothing whatsoever, and should have no will alongside the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but rather let Allah’s action take effect in him, becoming himself the object of the True One’s will, they meant this only concerning matters in which the servant does not know what Allah and His Messenger have commanded. As for what he knows Allah has commanded, he must will it and act upon it. They explicitly stated this in several places.

Others, however, mistakenly regard conformity to Allah’s will governing creation as perfection, calling it “annihilation in affirming Allah’s oneness in lordship.” They hold that once the spiritual journey reaches this point, the seeker observes the divine commands only for someone else’s sake, or that he no longer needs to observe them. These are corrupt doctrines and paths, which have been discussed elsewhere.

As for those who remain upright on the path, such as the majority of the early shaykhs—including al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, and Ma‘rūf

---

## Page 5097

al-Karkhī, al-Sarī al-Saqatī, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, and others among the early shaykhs, as well as Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir, Shaykh Hammād, Shaykh Abū al-Bayān, and others among the later shaykhs—they do not permit the seeker, even if he flies through the air or walks on water, to depart from the commands and prohibitions of the revealed Law. Rather, he must do what is commanded and refrain from what is forbidden until he dies. This is the truth established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations.

Statements to this effect abound in their writings. For example, Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir says in his book Futūh al-ghayb (Revelations of the Unseen):

“Leave your self behind, stand apart from it, and relinquish your dominion. Surrender everything to Allah—Blessed and Exalted is He—and be His gatekeeper at the door of your heart. Obey His command—Blessed and Exalted is He—by admitting whomever He commands you to admit, and heed His prohibition by barring whomever He commands you to bar. Do not let whims enter your heart after they have departed from it. Whims are expelled from the heart by opposing them and refusing to follow them in any circumstances; they are admitted into the heart by following them and yielding to them. Will nothing other than what He—Blessed and Exalted is He—wills. Any other course on your part is a departure from this: it is the valley of fools, wherein lie your death and destruction, your loss of His regard—Blessed and Exalted is He—and your being veiled from Him. Always observe His commands, always heed His prohibitions, and always surrender to Him whatever He decrees. Do not associate anything of His creation with Him, for your will, your whims, and your desires are His creation. So do not will, follow whims, or desire, lest this become an association of partners with Him.

Allah Most High says:

‘So whoever

---

## Page 5098

hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.’
