Associating partners with Allah is not merely worshipping idols; it also includes following your whims and choosing, alongside your Lord, anything other than Him, whether this world and what it contains or the Hereafter and what it contains. Everything besides Him—Blessed and Exalted is He—is other than Him. If you rely on anything other than Him, you have associated it with Him. So beware, and do not rely on anything else; be fearful, and do not feel secure; examine yourself, and do not become heedless and thus complacent. Attribute no spiritual state or station to yourself, and lay claim to none of these.”

Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir also said:

“There are only Allah and your self, and you are the one being addressed. The self opposes Allah and is His enemy, while all things are subject to Allah. If you side with the Truth in opposing the self and treating it as an enemy, you become His advocate against your own self.”

He went on to say:

“Worship consists in opposing your self and your whims. Allah Most High says:

‘Do not follow your desires, lest they lead you astray from the path of Allah.’”

He went on to say:

“There is the well-known account of Abū Yazīd al-Bistāmī—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—who saw the Lord of Might in a dream and asked Him, ‘What is the way to You?’ He replied, ‘Leave your self behind and come.’ Abū Yazīd said, ‘So I cast off my self as a snake sheds its skin.’ Once it is established that all good lies, as a general rule, in opposing the self in every circumstance, then if

---

## Page 5099

you are in a state of piety, oppose your self by freeing yourself from attachment to created beings—their bodily forms and likenesses, their favors—and from reliance upon them, trust in them, fear of them, hopes placed in them, and desire for the fleeting worldly goods they possess. Do not hope for their gifts, whether as presents, zakah, charity, expiation, or the fulfillment of vows. Cease looking to them in any way or through any means. Truly detach yourself from created beings, and regard them as a door that is closed and opened, or a tree that bears fruit at one time and is barren at another. All this occurs through the action of One who acts and the governance of One who governs: Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He.

When this understanding becomes firmly established in you, you will truly affirm His oneness—Blessed and Exalted is He. Yet do not forget that people acquire their deeds, lest you fall into the doctrine of the Jabriyyah. Believe that they cannot accomplish their actions independently of Allah—Blessed and Exalted is He—lest you worship them and forget Allah Most High. Do not regard their actions as independent of Allah, lest you fall into disbelief and become a Qadarī.

Rather, say: ‘These actions belong to Allah in their creation and to His servants in their acquisition.’ This is what the transmitted reports affirm, clarifying the basis for recompense, whether reward or punishment. Obey Allah’s command in your dealings with them, and obtain your allotted share from them according to His command, without overstepping it. His ruling remains in force, governing both you and them; do not make yourself the judge. Your being among them is a matter of divine decree, and divine decree is darkness. Enter that darkness with a lamp, namely ‘the ruling’: the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Do not depart from either of them.

If a thought occurs to you or you experience an inspiration, weigh both against the Book and the Sunnah. If you find that they prohibit it—for example, if you are inspired to commit unlawful sexual intercourse, engage in usury, or associate with

---

## Page 5100

people of disobedience and wickedness, or commit other sins—then repel it, abandon it, neither accept it nor act upon it, and be certain that it comes from the accursed Satan. If you find that they permit it, as with permissible desires for food, drink, clothing, and marriage, reject it too and do not accept it. Know that it is prompted by the self and its desires, which you have been commanded to oppose and treat as an enemy.”

I say:

By abandoning what is permissible, he means when it has not been commanded, as he has explained elsewhere. When a person does something permissible in obedience to a command, this is among Allah’s greatest blessings upon him, and it is obligatory for him. I have already explained that he calls people to the path of the foremost, those brought near to Allah; he does not stop at the path of the righteous, the people of the right.

He said:

“If you find neither its prohibition nor its permissibility in the Book and the Sunnah, but it is something whose purpose you do not understand—for example, you are told, ‘Go to such-and-such a place and meet so-and-so, a righteous man,’ although you have no need to go there or to meet that righteous man, since Allah Most High has rendered you independent of him through the blessings of knowledge and understanding He has bestowed upon you—then pause and do not rush into it.

Would you then say, ‘Could this inspiration come from anyone but the True One?’ and act upon it? Rather, wait for the good in this matter and for the True One to act, through the recurrence of that inspiration and a command to proceed, or through a sign appearing to those who know Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He—a sign brought about by the discerning among Allah’s friends and the divinely supported among the abdāl. You should not rush into it because you do not know its consequences or how the matter will turn out, and it may be that

---

## Page 5101

it entails trial, ruin, a stratagem from Allah, and a test. So wait patiently until it is He, Mighty and Majestic, who brings about the action in you. Once the action is entirely His and you are carried there, should a trial confront you, you will be sustained and protected through it. For Allah Most High does not punish you for His action; punishments only come your way because of your own involvement in the matter.”

I say:

He—may Allah be pleased with him—has thus instructed that whatever is prohibited by the revealed law must be abandoned without exception. Whatever is known to be permissible in itself is also to be left aside, because it is done at the behest of desire rather than by the Lawgiver’s command.

As for something whose particular permissibility is unknown—whether it is harmless or entails harm—such as travelling to a particular place or person, or going to a particular place or person: this kind of action is not prohibited in general, yet neither is every instance of it permissible. Rather, a person is forbidden to go somewhere where his religion will suffer harm. He therefore instructed him to refrain from going until it becomes apparent, or inwardly clear to him, that doing so is beneficial. For if it has not become clear to him that going is obligatory or recommended, he should not do it; and if he fears harm, he should refrain. If he is compelled to go, however, no blame attaches to him, and he is not held accountable for the action, unlike when he does it by his own choice or desire. When it becomes clear to him that its benefit outweighs its harm, doing so is good.

Evidence from the Sunnah establishes that whoever is subjected to a trial without seeking it is granted help, whereas there is cause to fear for someone who exposes himself to a trial. An example is the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Samurah:

“Do not ask for authority, for if you are given it upon asking, you will be left to shoulder it on your own; but if you are given it

---

## Page 5102

without asking, you will be granted help in discharging it.” Another example is his saying:

“Do not wish to meet the enemy, and ask Allah for well-being. But when you meet them, stand firm.”

The Sunan collections contain the following report:

“Whoever asks to be appointed a judge and enlists intercessors to secure the appointment will be left to shoulder it on his own. But whoever neither asks for the appointment nor seeks help to obtain it, Allah will send down an angel to guide him aright.”

Another version says: “and if he is compelled to accept it.”

The two Sahīh collections report that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning the plague:

“If you hear of it in a land, do not enter it; and if it breaks out in a land while you are there, do not leave to flee from it.”

It is also reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “forbade making vows.” Another example is his saying:

“Leave me be as long as you refrain [from questioning], for those before you were destroyed only because of their excessive questioning and their disagreements with their prophets. When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Section

Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir said:

“If you are in the state of spiritual realization, which is the state of friendship with Allah, oppose your desires and follow the command as a whole. Following the command is of two kinds:

(The first): Take from this world the sustenance that is the soul’s due, forgo personal gratification, fulfil your obligations, and devote yourself to abandoning sins, both outward and inward.

---

## Page 5103

And the second kind is that which follows an inward command: the command of the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, by which He commands and forbids His servant. This command applies only to permissible matters concerning which the revealed Law gives no ruling—meaning that they are neither prohibited nor obligatorily commanded. Rather, they are left open, with the servant free to exercise his choice; hence they are called permissible. The servant therefore initiates nothing in such matters of his own accord, but awaits the command. When commanded, he complies. Thus, all his movements and moments of stillness come to be through Allah Most High: where the revealed Law provides a ruling, he follows it; where it provides none, he follows the inward command. He then becomes one who has attained spiritual realization, one of the people of spiritual reality. Where there is no inward command, there is simply action in a state of surrender.

If you are in the state of the reality of the Truth—which is the state of true realization and self-effacement, the state of the abdāl, whose hearts are broken for the sake of the Truth, who affirm His oneness and know Him, masters of knowledge and action, leaders and princes, generous guardians serving the Truth, deputies of the Most Merciful, His eminent ones, His foremost ones and His beloved ones, peace be upon them—then following the command in this state means opposing your own self, disclaiming all power and strength, and having no will or aspiration whatsoever concerning anything in this world or the Hereafter. Be a servant of the King, not of the kingdom; a servant of the command, not of desire. Be like an infant with its wet nurse, a corpse with the person washing it, or an unconscious patient with the physician—in matters other than those governed by commands and prohibitions.”

He also said:

“Follow the revealed Law in everything that befalls you, if you are in

---

## Page 5104

the state of piety, which is the first step. Follow the command in the state of sainthood while desire is still present, and do not go beyond it; this is the second step. Be content with Allah’s action, conform to it, and efface yourself in the states of badaliyya, ‘ayniyya, and siddīqiyya (supreme truthfulness), which mark the final attainment.

Turn away from the filthy path; abandon its course. Restrain your self and your desire, and hold your tongue from complaint. When you do so, if what befalls you is good, the Lord will increase you in contentment, delight, and joy. If it is evil, He will keep you obedient to Him through it, remove blame from you, and keep you in it until it passes, granting you relief when its appointed term expires—just as night ends and gives way to daylight, and winter’s cold gives way to summer. You have this example before you, so take heed of it.

There are, moreover, sins, offenses, crimes, and defilement through all kinds of disobedience and wrongdoing. Only someone purified of the filth of sins and lapses is fit to sit in the presence of the Most Generous. Only someone pure, free of pretension and turmoil, can face His severity—just as only someone cleansed of filth, foul odors, and dirt is fit to sit in the company of kings. Afflictions therefore expiate sins. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘A day’s fever expiates a year’s sins.’”

I say:

Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir—may Allah be pleased with him—has thus explained that adherence to the commands and prohibitions is indispensable at every station. He mentioned three states, which he designated as the state of the person of piety, the state of spiritual reality, and the state of the truth of the Truth. He explained his meaning: in every state, the servant must will to do what he has been commanded

---

## Page 5105

by the revealed Law, and to refrain from what the revealed Law forbids. When the servant is instructed to relinquish his own will, this concerns matters that are neither commanded nor forbidden. This is correct: such a matter has not been commanded, so that he should will its occurrence, nor has it been forbidden, so that he should will its nonoccurrence. In such matters, he therefore relinquishes the will for either alternative.

It has been explained that the person of spiritual reality must always adhere to the command: the outward command of the revealed Law, if he knows it, or the inward command. It has also been explained that the inward command applies only to matters that are neither obligatory nor forbidden in the revealed Law. In such matters, one awaits a particular command, so that one acts on its authority.

If you ask, “What, then, distinguishes this person from the person of piety who precedes him, and from the person of the Truth who follows him?”

The answer is:

As for those who follow him, whom he called the “abdāl,” they act only at the command of the Truth, and only through Him. They do not witness their own agency in the acts of obedience they perform; rather, they witness that it is He who brings about, through them, their obedience to His command.

For this reason, he said:

“Following the command in this state means opposing your own self by disclaiming any power or strength of your own.”

These people thus witness Allah’s oneness in lordship together with His oneness in worship, and they witness

---

## Page 5106

that Allah is the One who created the righteous and good deeds they perform. They therefore see themselves as deserving no praise and as having conferred no favor upon anyone. They recognize that Allah creates the deeds of His servants, so they do not regard anyone as having wronged them, nor do they see themselves as having any claim upon anyone, for they have witnessed that Allah creates everything, including His servants’ deeds and all else. They know that His servants have no claim upon Allah in their own right or by virtue of themselves; rather, He is the One who has prescribed mercy for Himself. They witness that He deserves to be worshipped without anything being associated with Him, and that He deserves to be feared as He ought to be feared. To fear Him as He ought to be feared is to obey Him without disobeying Him, to remember Him without forgetting Him, and to thank Him without being ungrateful to Him. Thus, they see whatever righteous deeds they perform as the fruit of His bounty, grace, and generosity; all praise belongs to Him for that.

They also witness that there is no power or strength except through Allah. As for the harm that others inflict upon them, He created it, and it proceeds from His justice. As for the rights owed to them that people have failed to fulfil, He is the One who did not bring their fulfilment into being. To Him belongs all praise in every circumstance, for what He has done and what He has not done. Their hearts are therefore humbled and broken, because they witness His perfect existence and their own sheer nonexistence. No one is more profoundly humbled than one who sees nothing in himself but nonexistence, who sees nothing as belonging to him and nothing as coming about through him.

The person of spiritual reality, whose rank is below this, shares with him in devoting his religion sincerely to Allah and in doing only what he has been commanded, acting for Allah alone. Yet he falls short of him in witnessing and perceiving Allah’s oneness in lordship, and in witnessing that there is no power or strength except through Allah

---

## Page 5107

and that nothing truly belongs to him. Rather, the Lord is the Creator and Doer of everything that takes place within him, and perfect witnessing of this leaves no room for self-admiration, arrogance, or anything of that kind. Both men fulfil the command and obey Allah, but this one witnesses that Allah is the One who made him a Muslim and enabled him to pray, and that he himself has not, in reality, brought anything into being. The other, although he believes and affirms this, acknowledging that Allah creates His servants’ deeds, may not witness it in a way that makes him regard himself as though he were nonexistent.

There is also a second respect in which they differ:

The first has desires and aspirations concerning certain matters, yet gives them up. He thus distinguishes among his aims between what is commanded, what is forbidden, and what is neither commanded nor forbidden. Consequently, he has no aim left at all except what the Lord wills: either something He commands, which the man carries out through Allah’s help, or something He brings about within him, which Allah effects through him. This is why he likened him to an infant with its wet nurse in matters outside the sphere of commands and prohibitions.

As for (the first), who occupies the station of general piety, he has desires for forbidden things, turns his attention toward created beings, and remains conscious of himself. He therefore needs to strive for piety by restraining himself from forbidden things and from gratifying his desires without a command. He needs to distinguish between what he should do and what he should not do: this is piety. The person of spiritual reality, however, has nothing left to do except what he is commanded. He therefore does only what he has been commanded in the revealed Law; even among permissible things, he does only what he has been commanded to do.

---

## Page 5108

As for (the third), his witnessing has become complete: he acts only for Allah and through Allah. He does only what Allah has commanded, doing it for Allah’s sake, and witnesses that Allah is the One who has, in reality, brought it about. He has no desire or resolve to act for his own sake or for anyone other than Allah, nor does he act through his own power or through anything other than Allah Most High. The (three) share the same path in that each does only what constitutes obedience, but they differ in the completeness of their knowledge and witnessing, and in the purity of their intention and will. And Allah knows best.

If it is said:

Everything the shaykh says revolves around following the command whenever it can be discerned, inwardly or outwardly. Where there is no command, either inwardly or outwardly, the person submits to what the Lord brings about, exercising no choice of his own in either case. Rather, if he knows the command, he follows it; if he does not, he follows the divine decree. Thus, he conforms to the Lord’s command if he knows it; otherwise, he conforms to what He creates, for to Him—glory be to Him—belong creation and command.

This entails that some events are subject to neither command nor prohibition, so that Allah has no ruling concerning them, neither recommending nor discouraging them. Both he and Shaykh Hammād al-Dabbās have explicitly stated this, and that the spiritual wayfarer reaches matters concerning which there is no ruling in the revealed Law commanding or forbidding anything; rather, the servant abides by the divine decree. This is the point at which, according to them, the wayfarer is in accord with the pure “reality of divine decree,” since there is no reality of the revealed Law here.

---

## Page 5109

And this is a point on which those learned in the revealed Law dispute with them. They say:

An “act,” viewed in relation to the revealed Law, is either preferable to perform rather than omit—as with obligatory and recommended acts—or preferable to omit rather than perform—as with forbidden and disliked acts—or equally permissible to perform or omit. This last category is the permissible. This classification is in general terms.

A “particular act” described as permissible may, however, yield greater benefit for the servant because he uses it to help him obey Allah and undertakes it with a good intention. In this respect, it too becomes pleasing to Allah and preferable to perform. Alternatively, it may cause the servant to miss something better for him, as when a permissible act distracts him from a recommended one. In that case, omitting it is better for him.

For the wayfarer who draws near to Allah through voluntary acts after fulfilling the obligatory ones, performing and omitting a particular permissible act are not equal. If he does not use it to help him obey Allah, then leaving it and performing an act of obedience instead is better for him. Performing and omitting it are equal in value only when, upon omitting it, he occupies himself with another, equivalent permissible act.

It may then be said that there is no difference between the two. This applies to the righteous, the people of the right, who draw near to Allah through obligatory duties—fulfilling what is required and refraining from what is forbidden—while also engaging in permissible activities. For them, performing and omitting a particular permissible act may be equal if, upon omitting it, they occupy themselves with another permissible act. And there is no way for the soul to refrain from an action if

---

## Page 5110

it does not occupy itself with another act opposed to the first, for it cannot be devoid of all movement and stillness. On this basis, al-Ka'bī denied the existence of “the permissible” in the revealed Law: every permissible act occupies a person to the exclusion of a forbidden act; refraining from the forbidden is obligatory, and one cannot refrain from it without engaging in its opposite. This permissible act is its opposite. A command to do something entails a prohibition of its opposite, while a prohibition entails a command to do its opposite if it has only one opposite; otherwise, it entails a command to do one of its opposites. Thus, whichever opposite a person engages in becomes obligatory, as an obligation allowing a choice among alternatives.

This objection of al-Ka'bī perplexed many theoretical scholars. Some, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī, admitted that they could not answer it. Others, such as Abū al-Ma'ālī, lent it support on the premise that prohibiting something entails commanding its opposite. Still others said: This applies when its opposites are limited in number. When they are not limited in number, prohibiting it does not entail commanding any one of them. This resembles the distinction between an unrestricted obligation and an obligation allowing a choice among alternatives. In the latter case, it is said that the command requires one of the three alternatives; in the former, that it requires the element common to them. Our grandfather, Abū al-Barakāt, inclined toward this view.

They also challenged al-Ka'bī with the case of someone who avoids one forbidden act by committing another. He might, however, reply: A person must abandon all forbidden acts in favour of something that is not forbidden—whether permissible, recommended, or obligatory.

---

## Page 5111

And “the precise resolution of the matter” is this: our statements that a command to do something prohibits its opposite and its opposites, and that prohibiting something commands its opposite or one of its opposites, are of the same kind as our statements that commanding something also commands whatever it necessarily requires; that whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory; and that prohibiting something also prohibits whatever is indispensable to avoiding it.

For the existence of what is commanded entails the existence of whatever it necessarily requires and the absence of its opposites. Indeed, the existence of anything likewise entails its existence, the absence of its opposites, and the absence of a prohibition against it. Moreover, the nonexistence of anything entails the nonexistence of whatever necessarily entails it. If it can cease to exist only through an opposite that He creates—as with states of being—then its absence necessarily entails the existence of one of its opposites. This is true in itself. These necessary consequences, however, arise from the requirements of existence, even when commanding them is not intended. There is an established distinction between what is deliberately commanded and what necessarily accompanies its existence.

(The first) is what one is blamed and punished for omitting, unlike (the second). Someone commanded to perform Hajj or attend the Friday prayer who is far away must travel from that distant place, whereas someone nearby travels only from a nearby place. Traversing those distances is therefore a necessary requirement of what is commanded. Nevertheless, if these two duties—the Friday prayer and Hajj—are neglected, the punishment of the person farther away is not greater than that of the person nearby. Indeed, the reverse would be more fitting, even though the reward of the person farther away is greater. If these necessary requirements were themselves intended by the command, a person would be punished for omitting them, which would mean that the person farther away incurred a greater punishment. This is categorically false.

Likewise, when someone does what is commanded, he must refrain from its opposites, but

---

## Page 5112

refraining from these opposites is a necessary consequence of doing what is commanded, not an intended object of the command. Thus, if someone omits what is commanded, he is punished for that omission, not for the opposite acts with which he occupied himself. Likewise, the intent of the one who prohibits something is that it not occur, not that any of its opposites be done. If someone refrains from it while engaging in an opposite act, this is a necessary consequence of refraining.

Accordingly, if someone refrains from one forbidden act by committing another, he is punished for the latter. It is not said that he has fulfilled an obligation by refraining from the former, because what is intended is that the former not occur. Thus, the permissible act with which he occupies himself instead of a forbidden act is not the object of a deliberate command, either to perform it or to undertake it in obedience. Rather, he has been forbidden to commit the unlawful act, and refraining from what is forbidden necessarily involves engaging in one of its opposites. This therefore occurs as a necessary consequence of refraining from what is forbidden; it is not an obligation as defined in our statements:

“An obligation is that for whose omission a person is blamed and punished,”

or:

“That whose omission is a cause for blame and punishment.”

Thus, our statements:

“Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory,”

or:

“One must use what is not itself obligatory as a means to fulfill an obligation,”

entail requiring the necessary means. There remains an established distinction between the “first” and the “second” kind of obligation. Whoever omits the first is blamed and punished. The second, however, is obligatory in the sense that it must occur—that is, the obligation cannot be fulfilled without it. It is commanded as a means, and a person is rewarded for it, but punishment is not for omitting it.

---

## Page 5113

Another instance of this is when carrion cannot be distinguished from lawfully slaughtered meat. Only one of the two is forbidden in the sense that eating it incurs punishment. Thus, if someone eats both, he is punished for eating one dead animal, not two. Avoiding the other is obligatory as a means.

Accordingly, the statement, “Both are forbidden,” is correct in this respect. The statement, “Only one of them is forbidden in itself,” is also correct in its corresponding respect. This parallels the statement, “One must use what is not itself obligatory as a means to fulfill an obligation.” The objection of Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī and Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī to those who say this, and to those who say that only one of the two is forbidden, does not accord with the jurists’ approach. Ultimately, it amounts to a “verbal dispute.” For the obligation and prohibition attaching to one do not attach to the other; rather, those attaching to the other are of a different kind.

Thus, even if a man could not distinguish his slave woman from an unrelated woman at night and had intercourse, believing intercourse with one to be lawful and with the other forbidden, his child by his slave woman would be legally recognized as his, unlike a child by the other woman. Suppose that he could not distinguish his slave woman from an unrelated woman, married one of them and was, hypothetically, subjected to the prescribed punishment, then married the other: he would not be liable to two prescribed punishments. In fact, no prescribed punishment applies in this case, since the woman he married might be the unrelated woman.

This also resolves “al-Kaʿbī’s objection.” Refraining from the forbidden act is itself intended, whereas engaging in one of its opposites is a means. Thus, if it is said that a permissible act is obligatory in the sense that means are obligatory—that is, it may serve as a means to perform an obligation or refrain from a forbidden act—this is true.

---

## Page 5114

Intention must also be considered here. If a person intends to occupy himself with something permissible in order to avoid what is forbidden—for example, looking at his wife and having intercourse with her in order to refrain from looking at an unrelated woman and having intercourse with her, or eating lawful food to keep himself from unlawful food—he is rewarded for both this intention and the act. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained this when he said:

“In having intercourse, each of you has an opportunity for charity.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, can one of us satisfy his desire and receive a reward for it?” He replied, “Consider: if he satisfied it unlawfully, would he not incur sin? Why, then, do you count the unlawful against yourselves but not count the lawful in your favor?”

Another example is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Allah loves His concessions to be taken, just as He hates to be disobeyed.”

This was narrated by Ahmad and by Ibn Khuzayma in his Sahīh.

It may be said that a permissible act becomes obligatory in this respect: if it is the only means, it becomes specifically obligatory; otherwise, it becomes one of several obligatory alternatives—but this is with that intention. When a person is oblivious to this, however, it is not obligatory at all except insofar as a means of refraining from the forbidden is obligatory. Refraining from what is forbidden does not require intention; the same therefore applies to the means by which one refrains from it. Thus, there is no objection to saying that an act is permissible in itself, yet may become obligatory as one of several alternatives because it serves as a means. The dispute in this matter is therefore one of wording and perspective. Otherwise, whoever understands the sound meanings does not dispute them.

The point here is that the righteous and those on the right may occupy themselves with a permissible act

---

## Page 5115

rather than another, so that, for them, doing or not doing either permissible act is equivalent. As for those who are foremost and brought near to Allah, they engage in permissible acts only when these become acts of obedience through their good intentions and their use of them as aids to obeying Allah. Their permissible acts thus become acts of obedience. Accordingly, their actions are either those that are better performed, which the revealed Law therefore recommends, or those that are better left undone, which it is preferable for them to refrain from, even though doing them entails no sin. The revealed Law has explained the rulings governing all actions. This, then, is one “objection.”

A “second objection” is that, supposing some actions are neither commanded nor forbidden—as is the case for the righteous—such an action is neither praised nor blamed, neither loved nor hated. All that is considered is whether the divine decree brings it about or not. Indeed, they receive no praise for doing it, nor do they receive praise for refraining from it. Thus, it cannot be counted to their credit that, in this action, they are like a corpse before the one washing it, when the action proceeds from their own choice and will. For that is precisely what is under discussion.

As for actions other than “voluntary actions”—namely, what is done to a person, such as being carried when he cannot resist—these fall outside the scope of moral responsibility. Nevertheless, in such circumstances, the servant is commanded to love what is done if it is good, to hate it if it is evil, and to feel neither love nor hatred for it if it is neither good nor evil. Thus, whoever regards a person, in the voluntary actions for which the divine decree employs him, as being like a corpse before

---

## Page 5116

the one washing it has thereby exempted him from commands and prohibitions concerning voluntary actions. This is false.

A “third objection” is that this position effectively abolishes commands and prohibitions for the servant in these circumstances, even though his actions are voluntary. Granted that he has no personal desire, not everything in which he has no personal desire is thereby exempt from commands and prohibitions. Rather, he must love what Allah and His Messenger love and hate what Allah and His Messenger hate.

The reply is: These objections are valid. The decisive explanation is that the spiritual wayfarer may be unaware of what is commanded and prohibited, such that he does not know whether a particular action is commanded or prohibited by the revealed Law. His personal inclination thus remains, so that he has no personal inclination in the matter; he then submits it to the divine decree—which is the Lord’s action—because he does not know what the Lord approves, commands, and loves concerning that action.

This happens to many leading worshippers and scholars. They may encounter actions and statements whose ruling under Allah’s revealed Law they do not know, either because the evidence appears contradictory to them or because it is entirely unknown to them. They are therefore excused because the revealed ruling is unknown to them. A ruling of the revealed Law becomes binding upon the servant only when he is able to

---

## Page 5117

learn it. As for what has not reached him and he has been unable to learn, he is not held accountable for it. He is only required to fear Allah as much as he can. This is an error in knowledge, not an error in action. He is like a scholar who errs in exercising independent judgment: he is rewarded for his intention and effort, and his error is pardoned.

If it is objected:

If that is so, then the servant must refrain in such circumstances, when it has not become clear to him whether that action is commanded or prohibited, and he does not wish to do anything that merits neither praise nor blame. He must refrain, rather than surrender to the divine decree and become a passive instrument for whatever actions he is made to perform. The only exception is when someone else performs an action: he neither praises nor censures it, neither approves nor disapproves of it, if its ruling has not become clear to him.

But for him, in his own voluntary actions, to surrender to whatever the divine decree employs him in—like a child with its wet nurse or a dead person with the one washing him—is something neither Allah nor His Messenger has commanded. Rather, it is forbidden, even if the person doing it is pardoned. It is enough for him to be pardoned on account of his exercise of judgment and good intention. But that he should be praised for this, and that this should be regarded as the highest of spiritual stations—that is not so. Being free of his own desires does not justify his surrendering to everything done to him.

It may then be said: Even so, these matters fall into two categories:

---

## Page 5118

The first is when something is done to him against his will, as when a person is carried away and cannot resist, or a woman is forcibly laid down and subjected to intercourse. There is no sin upon the person subjected to this, by scholarly consensus. Alternatively, a person may be subjected to legally recognized coercion until he performs the act. Such deeds are also pardoned according to the majority of scholars. This is the sounder of the two reports from Ahmad, because Allah Most High says:

“If anyone compels them, then after they have been compelled, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

But if he has not been subjected to legally recognized coercion, he is not commanded to surrender indiscriminately to an action without knowing whether it is good or evil. Whether or not something extraordinary occurs at his hands, he is commanded to do only what is good in the sight of Allah and His Messenger.

It may be replied:

This objection is valid. The reality is that when those following the spiritual path reach this station, their intentions, their surrender and submission to their Lord, and their asking Him to choose what is best for them are commendable. If, in their affairs, they undertake [something] (1) whose ruling under Islamic law they do not know, they hope that it will be good, because they have been unable to ascertain its ruling. A person does not know in every circumstance what is best for his religion or what is most pleasing to Allah and His Messenger. Their situation thus remains that of someone seeking Allah’s guidance concerning a matter whose outcome he does not know, saying:

“O Allah, I seek Your choice through Your knowledge, and I seek ability through Your power, and I ask You of Your immense bounty. For You have power, and I have none; You know, and I do not; and You are the Knower of all that is unseen. O Allah, if You know that this matter is good for me in my religion

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) The text in square brackets is absent from the printed edition, and I could not find it in Siyānat Majmū‘ al-Fatāwā min al-Saqt wa-l-Tashīf (Safeguarding Majmū‘ al-Fatāwā against Omissions and Scribal Errors).
> Usāma ibn al-Zahrā’ — book coordinator for al-Mawsū‘a al-Shāmila.

---

## Page 5119

and my livelihood and the outcome of my affairs, then decree it for me, make it easy for me, and bless it for me. And if You know that this matter is bad for me in my religion, my livelihood, and the outcome of my affairs, then turn it away from me and turn me away from it. Decree good for me wherever it may be, then make me content with it.”

When he seeks Allah’s guidance, whatever Allah opens his heart to and makes easy for him is what Allah has chosen for him. For he has no evidence from Islamic law indicating that this particular act is commanded in these circumstances. The evidences of Islamic law prescribe in unrestricted, general terms, rather than specifying every individual act by every individual person, as that would be impossible. A particular act may nevertheless fall within the scope of some general pronouncement of the Lawgiver, when the specific instances come under a general, universal command. But not everyone can bring this to mind or recall the various kinds of the Lawgiver’s pronouncements. This is why jurists turn to analogical reasoning when this is unclear to them.

Furthermore, analogical reasoning may not be available in every case. Even the leading scholars qualified to exercise independent legal judgment among the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness may fail to recognize that a particular case falls under a general pronouncement, or that it can be assessed by comparison with an analogous case. They may thus know of neither a basis for it nor an analogous case. This is despite their extensive study of the Lawgiver’s pronouncements and their knowledge of their meanings and the rulings they indicate. What, then, of someone who is not like them?

---

## Page 5120

Moreover, the seeker’s aim is not to ascertain what is lawful and unlawful. Rather, he seeks to know whether this particular deed is better than that one, and that one better than another, and which is most beloved to Allah for him in those circumstances. This is a vast field that none but Allah fully encompasses. Each seeker has circumstances peculiar to him: he may be commanded to do something that another is forbidden to do, or commanded in one situation to do something he is forbidden to do in another.

They therefore said:
“We do good to the best of our ability, by doing what we know we have been commanded to do. We abandon the root of evil, namely, following our own desires. In everything else, we turn to Allah to guide us to what He loves most and finds most pleasing. Whatever He puts us to doing, we hope falls into this category. Then, if we are right, we receive two rewards; otherwise, we receive one reward, and our error is pardoned.”

Such is their position. Now, if we suppose that someone knows what is prescribed and acts upon it, he is better than this person. Yet many who know what is prescribed neither do it nor seek what is most beloved to Allah. Many others do it with an admixture of personal desire. Thus, one has done what is prescribed while following his desires, whereas the other has refrained from what he did not know to be prescribed, without following his desires. The latter has a deficiency in knowledge, and the former a deficiency in action, for acting out of personal desire is a deficiency in action, even when the deed itself is obligatory.

It may therefore be said: If the one who follows his desires repents of doing so, his knowledge will raise him above the other; but if

---

## Page 5121

he does not repent, he shares something of the character of an evil scholar. For this reason, two men of the early generations quarreled over something similar in the year of the two arbitrators.

One said to the other:
“You are just like a dog: if you drive it away, it pants, and if you leave it alone, it pants.”

The other replied:
“You are like a donkey carrying books.”

This one, then, is better in intention and stronger in knowledge. Thus, you find that people with sincere intentions fault these others precisely for following their desires and loving worldly life and leadership, while people of knowledge fault the former for their deficient knowledge of the revealed Law and their departure from its commands and prohibitions. Such is the situation.

We ask Allah Most High to guide us to the straight path—the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His favor: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

Some (jurists and ascetics) have said: Some people follow “the revealed Law,” while others follow “spiritual reality.” Perhaps they meant these two groups. The former favor one course over another on the basis of what Allah makes easy for them, together with sincere intentions and adherence to the commands and prohibitions known to them, although the evidence from the revealed Law concerning what has been made easy for them remains unclear to them. The latter give preference on the basis of evidence from the revealed Law—the apparent meanings of texts, analogical reasoning, solitary reports, and scholarly opinions—although the course made easy for them remains unclear to them.

(Moreover, these people) may perceive in that divinely decreed act elements of

---

## Page 5122

benefit and goodness, and so favor it on the basis of faith, even if they know of no textual evidence establishing its goodness. The others, however, base their preferences solely on the texts and what is inferred from them. Thus, one group has the Quran, while the other has faith. This is because each group is unaware of the truth possessed by the other, and each group’s path contains both truth and falsehood.

As for those who claim spiritual reality without observing the commands and prohibitions of revealed Law, they are astray, just as those who know the commands and prohibitions but commit whatever major sins they desire are defiantly disobedient.

These are the people of whom it has been said:

“Beware the trial posed by the wicked scholar and the ignorant worshipper, for theirs is a trial for all who are tried.”

“Spiritual reality” may pertain to divine decree, spiritual experience, or revealed Law. The term “law” encompasses revealed law, interpreted law, and altered law.

The purpose here is to discuss those who remain upright within the two groups, and to consider the condition of people devoted to worship and spiritual aspiration who have freed themselves from personal desire—that is, from making distinctions according to natural inclination—and have observed the distinctions prescribed by revealed Law insofar as they know them. There remains a “third category” in which they make no distinction based on natural inclination and know of no distinction prescribed by revealed Law. In this category, they go along with what occurs and with divine decree. As for someone who follows distinctions based on natural inclination, either knowing that he is sinning—in which case he is the scholar

---

## Page 5123

who is wicked—or invoking divine decree or his spiritual experience and ecstasy as justification while turning away from the Quran and Sunnah—in which case he is the ignorant worshipper—such a person is outside the straight path.

This illustrates the perfection of the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—and why they are the best generation of this community. During the prophetic caliphate, they observed the distinctions prescribed by revealed Law in matters great and small, despite the vast scope of their responsibilities. Someone of a later generation may be unable to discern the distinctions prescribed by revealed Law even in his own affairs, just as one of these people may follow his desires in a minor matter. Despite the immense responsibilities they undertook in carrying out commands and observing prohibitions, the Companions possessed the knowledge by which they distinguished good deeds from bad, and the good intent by which they performed good deeds.

Many later scholars and worshippers lack knowledge concerning numerous good and bad deeds, to the point of considering a bad deed good, or vice versa. Or they lack sound intent in many actions, so that they follow their desires even where the commands and prohibitions are clear to them. We therefore ask Allah to guide us to the straight path, the path of those He has blessed among the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous.

All this, by my life, assumes that the scholar truly knows the Lawgiver’s actual commands and prohibitions, and that the worshipper truly possesses good intent free from personal desire.

As for those who mix revealed law with altered and interpreted law, and mix good intent with following personal desire, such people—

---

## Page 5124

are confused in both their knowledge and their practice. Their confusion in knowledge is distinct from their own and others’ confusion in intention; likewise, their confusion in intention is distinct from their own and others’ confusion in knowledge. For whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah grants him knowledge of what he did not know.

“Good intent” is among the greatest aids to acquiring and grasping knowledge. “Knowledge of revealed law” is among the greatest aids to good intent and righteous action. Knowledge leads from the front, while action drives from behind, and the soul is an obstinate mount. If its leader falters, it will not keep to its course at its driver’s urging; and if its driver falters, it will not keep to its course under its leader’s guidance.

When knowledge grows weak, the traveller becomes bewildered and does not know which way to go; all he can do is abandon himself to divine decree. When he abandons action, he loses his way and follows another path, despite knowing that he has left the right one. The former is bewildered, not knowing which way to go despite travelling extensively; the latter has lost his way and deviated from the path despite knowing it.

Allah Most High says:

“When they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”

The former is ignorant, and the latter is a wrongdoer. Allah Most High says:

“And man undertook it; indeed, he was unjust and ignorant.”

Ignorance and wrongdoing are nevertheless closely related. Yet the ignorant person does not know that he is a wrongdoer, while the wrongdoer is ignorant of the reality that bars him from knowledge. Allah Most High says:

“Allah only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterward.”

Abū al-ʿĀliya said: “I asked the Companions of Muhammad, and they said: ‘Everyone who disobeys Allah

---

## Page 5125

is ignorant, and everyone who repents before death has repented soon afterward.’”

Al-Khallāl narrated from Abū Hayyān al-Taymī that he said:

“Scholars are of three kinds: one who knows Allah but does not know Allah’s commands; one who knows Allah’s commands but does not know Allah; and one who knows both Allah and His commands. The one who knows Allah is the one who fears Him, while the one who knows Allah’s commands is the one who knows what He commands and forbids.”

I say: Reverent fear prevents one from following desire. Allah Most High says:

“But as for he who feared standing before his Lord and restrained himself from desire, Paradise will indeed be his refuge.”

Perfection in freedom from desire and in knowledge belongs to the Seal of the Messengers, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning whom Allah said:

“By the star when it descends, your companion has neither gone astray nor erred. Nor does he speak from desire. It is nothing but revelation revealed.”

He thus declared him free of misguidance and error, and described him as one who does not speak from desire: it is nothing but revelation revealed. He thereby negated desire and affirmed perfect knowledge, namely revelation. This is perfection of knowledge, and the former is perfection of intent. May Allah bless him and grant him peace.

He described his enemies as possessing the opposite of these two qualities. Allah Most High says:

“They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, although guidance has already come to them from their Lord.”

Thus, absolute human perfection consists in perfecting one’s servitude to Allah in both knowledge and intent.

Allah Most High says:

“And I did not create

---

## Page 5126

the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him.”

Allah Most High says, recounting the words of Iblīs:

“He said, ‘By Your might, I will surely mislead them all—except Your chosen servants among them.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, you have no authority over My servants.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Thus it was, so that We might turn evil and indecency away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who, through him, associate others with Allah.”

“Worshipping Him” means obeying His command, and His command to us is what the Messenger conveyed from Him. Perfection therefore lies in complete obedience to Allah and His Messenger, inwardly and outwardly.

Those who do not know what Allah has commanded, and therefore abandon their own desires and submit to the divine decree; or strive to obey but err, doing what they believe was commanded instead of what was actually commanded; or find the evidence conflicting and therefore refrain from what is in fact an act of obedience—such people are obedient to Allah. They are rewarded for their sincere intentions toward Allah and for exerting their utmost in obedience to Him. Where they were unable to know what was required and consequently erred by turning to something else, they are forgiven.

This is one of the causes of discord within the Muslim community. Some people say and do things in which they exercise their best judgment, yet err. When word of this reaches others, the latter suppose that they deliberately sinned in these matters, or suppose that their error does not excuse them, while they themselves are also exercising their best judgment and erring. Thus, one exercises his best judgment but errs in his action, while the other exercises his best judgment but errs

---

## Page 5127

in condemning it; all of them are forgiven. Yet one of them may be sinful, just as both may be sinful.

The best speech is Allah’s speech, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The worst matters are newly introduced innovations, and every religious innovation is misguidance.

One of these people may be granted some authority to command and forbid: he appoints and dismisses, gives and withholds. Someone may suppose that this is perfection, but it is perfection only when it accords with Allah’s command and thus constitutes obedience to Him. Otherwise, it belongs to the realm of kingship, and the acts of kings fall into three categories: sin, blameless conduct, or obedience.

The deeds of the Rightly Guided Caliphs are acts of obedience and worship, and they are followers of the servant-Messenger. This is the path of the foremost, those brought near to Allah. As for the path of just kings, it consists of either obedience or blameless conduct. It is the path of the prophet-kings and of the righteous, the people of the right hand.

As for the path of unjust kings, it includes acts of disobedience. It is the path of those who wrong themselves.

Allah Most High says:

“Then We caused those whom We chose from among Our servants to inherit the Book. Among them are those who wrong themselves, among them are those who follow a middle course, and among them are those who are foremost in good deeds, by Allah’s permission. That is the great bounty.”

Thus, every believer must be

---

## Page 5128

in one of these categories: one who wrongs himself, one who follows a middle course, or one who is foremost in good deeds.

“Extraordinary occurrences” take the form either of unveiling, which is a kind of extraordinary knowledge, or of exercising power, which is a kind of extraordinary ability. Those who possess them fall within these same three categories.

---

## Page 5129

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section

My father told me, on the authority of Muhyī al-Dīn ibn al-Nahhās—and I believe I also heard it from him directly—that he saw Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir in a dream, relating these words from the Truth, Most High:

“Whoever comes to Us, We meet him from afar. Whoever acts through Our might, We soften iron for him. Whoever follows Our will, We will what he wishes. Whoever gives something up for Our sake, We give him more than abundance itself.”

I said: These words are spoken from the Lord’s perspective, blessed and exalted is He. The first two statements concern worship and seeking help; the last two concern obedience and disobedience. Going to Allah means worshipping Him alone, as He, Most High, said:

“Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by a forearm’s length. Whoever draws near to Me by a forearm’s length, I draw near to him by an armspan. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him at a run.”

Drawing near through His might means seeking His help and placing one’s trust in Him, for there is no might and no

---

## Page 5130

power except through Allah.

A report states:

“Whoever wishes to be the strongest of people should place his trust in Allah.”

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: “Reliance on Allah encompasses all of faith.” Allah Most High said:

“Whoever puts his trust in Allah, He will suffice him.”

And He said:

“When you sought your Lord’s help, He answered you.”

This accords with the more correct of the two views: reliance on Him—like supplication, likewise according to the more correct of the two views—is a means of securing benefits and warding off harm. It gives the servant strength and the ability to direct events in creation. Hence it predominates among those who experience spiritual states, whether they adhere to the revealed law or not. Through it they exercise influence and bring about effects, “at times” in accordance with Allah’s command, and “at other times” contrary to it.

His words, “Whoever follows Our will,” refer to what Allah wills in His revealed law, as in His words:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And His words:

“Allah wishes to lighten your burden.”

And His words:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you.”

This means obeying His command. A hadith states:

“As for you, O ʿUmar, if you obeyed Allah, He would comply with you.”

An authentic hadith states:

“If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“He answers those who believe and do righteous deeds, and gives them still more out of His bounty.”

His words, “Whoever gives something up for Our sake, We give him more than abundance itself,” mean that whoever gives up what Allah dislikes, whether forbidden or merely disliked, for Allah’s sake—out of hope, love and fear—We give him more than abundance itself. This is because this is the station of patience. Allah Most High said:

“Those who are patient will be given their reward without measure.”

---

## Page 5131

He was asked about *Ihyā’ ʿulūm al-dīn* (The Revival of the Religious Sciences), *Qūt al-qulūb* (Nourishment of Hearts), and so forth.

He replied:

As for *Qūt al-qulūb*, *al-Ihyā’* follows it in its discussion of deeds of the heart, such as patience, gratitude, love, reliance on Allah, affirmation of His oneness, and similar matters. Abū Tālib is more knowledgeable than Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī about hadith, transmitted reports, and the teachings of those versed in the sciences of the heart, whether Sufis or others. His discussions are sounder, more rigorously substantiated, and further removed from religious innovation, although *Qūt al-qulūb* contains weak and fabricated hadiths and much objectionable material.

As for the discussions in *al-Ihyā’* concerning “the causes of spiritual ruin,” such as pride, self-admiration, ostentation, envy, and similar matters, most are drawn from the writings of al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī in *al-Riʿāya*. Some of this is acceptable, some objectionable, and some disputed.

*Al-Ihyā’* contains many beneficial insights, but it also contains blameworthy material. It includes corrupt material drawn from the philosophers’ discussions concerning Allah’s oneness, prophethood, and the Hereafter. Thus, when

---

## Page 5132

he discussed the spiritual knowledge of the Sufis, he was like someone who took an enemy of the Muslims and dressed him in Muslim clothes. The leading scholars of the religion criticized Abū Hāmid for this in his books. They said, “The Cure made him ill,” referring to Ibn Sīnā’s philosophical work, al-Shifā’ (The Cure).

It contains weak hadiths and transmitted reports—indeed, many fabricated ones. It also contains some of the Sufis’ errors and absurdities. Nevertheless, its material from knowledgeable, upright Sufi shaykhs concerning deeds of the heart that accords with the Quran and Sunnah, together with other material on worship and proper conduct that likewise accords with them, outweighs its objectionable content. For this reason, people have differed in their assessments of it and disputed over it.

## Page 5133

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—also said:

Section

The Quran, the Sunnah, and reports from the early generations of the Muslim community have indicated the kinds of remembrance of Allah and supplication to Him that are prescribed and recommended, as they have for other acts of worship. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained the relative merits of different forms of remembrance. For example, in the authentic hadith narrated by Muslim and others from Samurah ibn Jundub, he said:

“The best words after the Quran are four—and they are themselves from the Quran: Glory be to Allah; all praise is due to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest. It does not matter which of them you begin with.”

In his Sahīh, Muslim also narrates that Abū Dharr said:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked, ‘Which words are best?’ He replied, ‘Those Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Him.’”

In Ibn Abī al-Dunyā’s Kitāb al-Dhikr (The Book of Remembrance) and other works, a report traced back to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, states:

“The best remembrance is ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘All praise

---

## Page 5134

is due to Allah.’”

In al-Muwatta and elsewhere, Talhah ibn Abd Allāh ibn Kurayz reports that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The best words that I and the prophets before me have said are: ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs sovereignty, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

The Sunan collections contain the hadith about the man who said, “O Messenger of Allah, I am unable to learn any of the Quran, so teach me something that will suffice for me in my prayer.” He replied:

“Say: ‘Glory be to Allah; all praise is due to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.’”

For this reason, the jurists have said that whoever is unable to recite the Quran in prayer should turn instead to these words, which are enduring good deeds. The virtues of these words and others like them are many, but this is not the place to discuss them. Our concern here, however, is with forms of remembrance and supplication that are not of a prescribed kind, or that are forbidden in themselves or in the manner in which they are performed.

As Allah Most High says:

“Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Indeed, He does not love transgressors.”

And Allah Most High says:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them.”

Thus, He is to be invoked only by His most beautiful names.

Among the forbidden forms is what people used to say in their talbiyah—the pilgrimage response—in the days of ignorance:

“Here I am at Your service. You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You: You own him and all that he owns.”

Another example is what some Bedouins said to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“We seek Allah’s intercession with you.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, replied:

“Allah’s majesty is far greater than that. Allah is not to be invoked as an intercessor with any of His creation.”

Another example is what they used to say in the early days of Islam:

---

## Page 5135

“Peace be upon Allah before His servants.” The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah is al-Salām (the Source of Peace). When one of you sits, let him say: ‘All greetings, prayers, and good things belong to Allah.’”

He thereby indicated that peace is sought only for those who need it. Allah is the Source of Peace, so peace is sought from Him, not for Him. Rather, He is praised, for praise belongs to Him. Thus one says: “All greetings, prayers, and good things belong to Allah.” The True One, glory be to Him, is praised and petitioned, whereas supplications are made on behalf of created beings. Thus one says:

“Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and Allah’s mercy and blessings. Peace be upon us and upon Allah’s righteous servants.”

Allah Most High says:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. I desire no provision from them, nor do I desire that they should feed Me.”

Provision encompasses everything that benefits its recipient. A person is provided with food, drink, clothing, and whatever benefits him through his hearing, sight, and sense of smell. He is also provided with what benefits his inner being: knowledge, faith, joy, happiness, strength, light, support, and other things. Allah, glory be to Him, desires no provision from His creation. They can never harm Him, nor can they ever benefit Him. Rather, He is free of all need, while they are in need. And:

“Allah has certainly heard the words of those who said, ‘Allah is poor, while we are rich.’”

He is the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, and to whom none is equal.

Likewise, there are disliked forms of supplication, such as supplicating for wrongdoing or the severing of family ties, asking for the ranks of the prophets, or the supplication of the Bedouin who said:

“O Allah, whatever punishment You would inflict upon me in

---

## Page 5136

the Hereafter, hasten it for me in this world.”

Another example is what he, peace and blessings be upon him, said to those who cried out upon someone’s death:

“Pray only for good for yourselves, for the angels say ‘Amen’ to what you say.”

Allah Most High says:

“Were Allah to hasten evil for people as they seek to hasten good, their appointed term would already have come to an end.”

And He Most High says:

“Man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man is ever hasty.”

This is a broad subject, and our purpose here is not to cover it exhaustively. We have merely drawn attention to the kinds of supplication that are disliked. Our purpose here is to show that the revealed law recommends only those forms of remembrance that constitute complete, meaningful statements, such as:

“There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah”; “Allah is the Greatest”; “Glory be to Allah, and all praise belongs to Allah”; and “There is no power nor strength except through Allah.”

Other examples include:

“Blessed is the name of your Lord”; “Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion”; “Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah”; and “Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion.”

As for a name uttered on its own, whether explicitly, as in “Allah, Allah,” or as a pronoun, as in “He, He,” this is not prescribed in either the Book or the Sunnah. Nor is it reported from any of the early generations of the Muslim community or from its leading figures who are followed as exemplars. Only some misguided people of later generations have taken to repeating it.

Sometimes, in doing so, they imitate a shaykh overwhelmed by his spiritual state, as is related of al-Shiblī, who used to say:

“Allah, Allah.”

He was asked:

“Why do you not say, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah’?”

---

## Page 5137

He replied:

“I fear that I may die between the negation and the affirmation.”

This is one of al-Shiblī’s lapses, forgiven him because of the sincerity of his faith, the intensity of his spiritual ecstasy, and the overwhelming hold of his spiritual state. He would sometimes lose his reason and be taken to the hospital, and would shave his beard. He did other things of this kind in which it is impermissible to follow his example, even if he himself was excused or rewarded. For if a person intended to say, “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah,” but died before completing it, that would not harm him at all. Actions are judged by intentions; indeed, what he intended would be recorded to his credit.

Some may go to such extremes in this matter that they assign remembrance through an isolated name to the spiritual elite, and remembrance through a complete statement to ordinary people. Some may say:

“‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah’ is for the believers; ‘Allah’ is for those who know Allah; and ‘He’ is for those who have attained spiritual realization.”

One of them may restrict himself, whether in solitary retreat or with his group, to “Allah, Allah, Allah,” or “He,” or “O He,” or “There is no He but He.”

Some writers on the spiritual path may extol this practice, seeking to substantiate it sometimes through spiritual ecstasy, sometimes through personal opinion, and sometimes through a fabricated report. For example, some relate “that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, taught ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib to say: ‘Allah, Allah, Allah.’” The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said it three times, then instructed ʿAlī, who said it three times. This is a fabricated hadith by the consensus of hadith scholars.

---

## Page 5138

Rather, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, taught only the forms of remembrance transmitted from him. Foremost among these is “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.” This is the declaration he urged his uncle Abū Tālib to say as death approached. He said:

“My uncle, say, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah’—a declaration with which I may plead your case before Allah.”

He also said:

“I know a declaration which no servant utters at the time of death without his soul finding relief in it.”

He said:

“Whoever’s last words are ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah’ will enter Paradise.”

He said:

“Whoever dies knowing that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah will enter Paradise.”

He said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. When they do so, they safeguard their lives and property from me, except as its due right requires; and their reckoning rests with Allah.”

There are many hadiths conveying this meaning. In the preceding “Principles,” I have written about some matters relating to these two great, comprehensive declarations that distinguish truth from falsehood: the testimony that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and the testimony that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger—may Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon him and his family.

As for remembrance through an “isolated name,” it has not been prescribed under any circumstances, and there is nothing in the evidence of Islamic law to indicate that it is recommended. As for what some mistaken worshippers suppose concerning the words of the Most High, “Say:

---

## Page 5139

‘Allah,’ then leave them”—and their supposition that what is meant is to utter this name—this is a clear error. Had they reflected on what precedes this, the meaning of the verse would have become clear. For He, glorified be He, says:

“They did not give Allah His due when they said, ‘Allah has not revealed anything to any human being.’ Say, ‘Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for people, which you make into separate sheets, displaying them while concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your forefathers knew.’ Say, ‘Allah.’”

That is: say, “Allah revealed the Book that Moses brought.” This is a complete statement: a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and a predicate, with the predicate omitted because the question indicates the answer.

This is a regular pattern in comparable Arabic expressions, as in His words:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘Have you considered…’”

And so the verse continues. Likewise, His words:

“Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water for you from the sky, by which We brought forth gardens of beauty whose trees you could never have caused to grow? Is there a deity alongside Allah?”

The same applies to the verses that follow it, and to His words:

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?’ They will say, ‘Allah.’”

This is according to the reading of Abū ‘Amr.

In ordinary speech, you ask, “Who came?” and the answer is, “Zayd” (Zaydun). You ask, “Whom did you honour?” and the answer is, “Zayd” (Zaydan). You ask, “Whom did you pass by?” and the answer is, “By Zayd” (bi-Zaydin). Thus, they mention the noun that answers “who” and omit the words connected with it, because these have already been mentioned in the question. They dislike repeating them without any gain in clarity, since that would merely make the expression longer and repetitive.

---

## Page 5140

Stranger still is what one of these mistaken people once said to me concerning His words:

“None knows its interpretation except Allah.”

He said that this meant: “None knows the interpretation of ‘He’”—meaning the name “He” used in the invocation “He, He.” Ibn ‘Arabī wrote a book about this “He.” I replied to him—though I was very young at the time—“If it were as you say, it would have been written in the Quran as two separate words, ta’wīlu huwa (‘the interpretation of “He”’), rather than as one word, ta’wīlahu (‘its interpretation’).”

The falsity of what this man said is self-evident. Many mistaken Sufis offer similar false interpretations of the Quran and Sunnah. The meaning they intend may be sound, but the wording does not indicate it, nor is it what the speaker intended; or the meaning itself may be unsound. Thus, the error sometimes lies in the conclusion and sometimes in the evidence.

For example, some interpret:

“Because he sees himself as self-sufficient”

to mean: “Because he sees his Lord, he becomes self-sufficient.” Yet the meaning is that he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient.

Likewise, some interpret “If you do not see Him” (fa-in lam takun tarāhu) to mean: “If your awareness of yourself is effaced, you will see your Lord.”

This is not the meaning of the hadith. Had that been intended, the wording would have been fa-in lam takun tarahu, whereas it says tarāhu. Moreover, what would he do with the result clause, namely, “He certainly sees you”?

Furthermore, according to their false interpretation, the verb kāna (‘to be’) would express existence in its own right. Thus, “If you are not” would mean: “If you do not occur or exist.” This is an impossible interpretation, for the servant exists; he is not nonexistent. Even if what was intended was his detachment from his desires, or the effacement of his awareness of other things, this would not be expressed by denying his existence, for that is impossible.

Whenever the meaning is sound, but the wording was not intended to convey it, this may be called an “allusion.”

---

## Page 5141

And Shaykh Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī included a selection of such interpretations in his Haqā’iq al-tafsīr. Discussing this, however, is not our present purpose, for it is a separate subject. Our purpose is only to explain the ruling on invoking the name alone, without a complete utterance. The scriptural evidence has shown that this is not recommended, as has rational and experiential evidence.

The name alone conveys neither faith nor unbelief, guidance nor misguidance, knowledge nor ignorance. Someone may mention the name of a prophet, a pharaoh, or an idol, yet no judgment attaches to merely mentioning the name unless he adds something indicating negation or affirmation, love or hatred. He may also name something existent or nonexistent. Thus, scholars of Arabic and all other languages agree that a name alone cannot properly stand on its own: it is neither a complete sentence nor an informative utterance.

For this reason, when an Arab heard a caller to prayer say, “I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,” he asked, “What did he do?” By putting the noun in the accusative, the caller had made it a descriptive qualifier, and a qualifier forms part of the noun phrase it describes. The Arab’s sound linguistic instinct therefore led him to ask for an informative predicate. The caller, however, had intended it as the predicate but made a grammatical error.

---

## Page 5142

Even if a person repeated the name “Allah” a million times, he would not thereby become a believer or merit Allah’s reward or His Paradise. Unbelievers of every nation mention the name alone, whether or not they acknowledge Him and His oneness.

Even when He commanded us to mention His name, as in His words:

“So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it,”

and His words:

“And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned,”

and His words:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,”

and His words:

“So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great,”

and similar passages, mentioning His name was to be done through a complete utterance, such as saying, “In the name of Allah,” or, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High,” and, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great,” and the like. He never prescribed mentioning the name alone. Doing so neither fulfills a command nor establishes [the lawfulness of game] (1) or of a slaughtered animal, or anything else of that kind.

If it is said: A person who utters or hears the name alone may experience a stirring of love and reverence for Allah, and similar feelings.

I reply: Yes, and he is rewarded for that lawful inward experience and state of faith, not because mentioning the name alone is recommended. Hearing it stirs what lies dormant in the heart. Yet what lies dormant may also be stirred by hearing an utterance that is forbidden or disliked. A Muslim may even hear someone associating partners with Allah or reviling Him, and a state of deep feeling and love for Allah surges in his heart because of the intensity of his aversion
