## Page 5143

and hatred of what he has heard. The Companions said to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him):

“One of us finds within himself thoughts that he would rather be burned to a cinder or fall from heaven to earth than utter.”

He asked, “Have you really experienced that?”

They replied, “Yes.”

He said, “That is clear faith.” In another narration, he said, “Praise be to Allah, who has reduced his plotting to mere whispering.”

When Satan cast blameworthy whispers into their hearts, the faith within them stirred in aversion to those thoughts and horror at their enormity. That was clear faith. This does not imply that the cause—those whispers—was something commanded. Likewise, a person may be prompted to disbelief or disobedience, yet seek protection and resist, thereby gaining faith and piety. The cause itself, however, is not something commanded.

Allah Most High said:

“Those to whom people said, ‘Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them.’ But this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

“So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty,” to the end of the verse.

This increase in faith and reliance on Allah arose from their being frightened with the prospect of facing the enemy, yet such intimidation is not prescribed. Indeed, a person may commit a sin that leads him to repent, and Allah loves him for that repentance; this does not mean that the sin was commanded. This is a very broad subject. Thus, a distinction must be drawn between the cause itself producing and entailing good, and

---

## Page 5144

its not doing so, with the good arising instead from the recipient. The good words and righteous deeds that are commanded bring about goodness, mercy, and reward. When accompanied by the strength of the servant’s faith and the sweetness and savor of faith that he experiences, goodness, mercy, and blessing are multiplied.

As for things that are not commanded—whether the servant’s own actions, be they forbidden, disliked, or permissible; the actions of others toward him, whether humans or jinn; or heaven-sent events with which the Lord afflicts him—if they encounter faith and certainty within him, stirring that faith and certainty so that his faith increases, this does not mean that those causes should be loved, praised, or commanded if they are not otherwise deserving of such regard. They do not themselves entail that good; their effect is merely to stir what lies dormant. Often, they have led to evil and harm.

Similar to this is speaking of love, longing, and fear in unqualified terms, together with the poetry and prose expressing them. This too is non-specific: it is shared by believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked. For this reason, Allah and His Messenger have neither prescribed nor commanded such things. Allah commands only goodness, righteous deeds, and piety, and that does not belong to this category. The poetry of lovers, however, is shared by lovers of faith, lovers of idols, lovers of women, lovers of beardless youths, lovers of homelands, and lovers of paramours.

---

## Page 5145

What we have stated thus establishes that invoking the name in isolation is not recommended, let alone being the remembrance of the elect. Still further removed is invoking the “pronominal name,” namely “He.” By itself, this does not designate anyone in particular; its referent depends on something mentioned or known that explains it. Its meaning therefore depends on the speaker’s purpose and intention. Thus, someone who believes that the Real is absolute existence may use it in remembrance.

He may say, “There is no He but He,” while his heart drifts into “the oneness of existence” and the doctrine of Pharaoh, the Ismā‘īlīs, and the heretics among these latter-day Sufis, so that his saying “He” is equivalent to saying “His existence.” By saying, “There is no He but He,” he may mean that He is existence, that there is no creation whatsoever, and that the Lord and the servant, the Real and creation, are one and the same—as I have explained elsewhere when discussing the doctrine of the Ittihādiyya (adherents of union).

Among the causes of these corrupt beliefs and spiritual states is departure from the law and the way with which the Messenger was sent to us, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Religious innovations are the beginnings of disbelief and places where it is likely to arise, just as the prescribed sunnahs are manifestations of faith and strengthen it. Faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience, as Allah has told us of its increase in such verses as His saying:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this increased them in faith.”

And His saying:

“Which of you has this increased in faith?”

---

## Page 5146

and His saying:

“He is the One who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they might increase in faith along with their existing faith,”

and other such verses.

If it is asked, “If this form of remembrance is not prescribed, is it disliked?” I reply: In the case of someone who is overwhelmed, it is not deemed disliked. The heart may experience states in which speech becomes difficult, even while it is filled with states of faith. A person may then be able to invoke the name alone, but not a complete expression. Such people offer what their hearts contain of faith and whatever their tongues are capable of uttering.

For people fall into four categories with regard to remembrance:

(First) Remembrance with both heart and tongue. This is what is commanded.

(Second) Remembrance with the heart alone. If this is because the tongue is unable to speak, it is good; but if the tongue is capable, it means forgoing what is better.

(Third) Remembrance with the tongue alone: keeping one’s tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah. In this connection, there is the account of one in whom the angels found no good except the movement of his tongue in remembrance of Allah. Allah Most High says:

“I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move in remembrance of Me.”

(Fourth) Neither form of remembrance. This is the condition of those who are losers.

---

## Page 5147

But when a complete expression can readily be uttered, restricting oneself to repeating the name alone is an innovation, and the default ruling on innovations is that they are disliked. The reports of Abū Yazīd, al-Nūrī, al-Shiblī and others invoking the name alone are to be understood as cases in which they were overwhelmed, for their states bear this out. Moreover, the shaykhs who were sounder and more accomplished than these men used only complete expressions of remembrance.

When disagreement arises, the matter must be referred back to Allah and the Messenger. The actions of anyone other than the Messenger do not constitute unconditional proof. And Allah knows best.

## Page 5148

The shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Chapter: The Straight Path in Asceticism, Worship, Scrupulousness in Abstaining from Forbidden Things and Desires, and Moderation in Worship

Adherence to the Sunnah protects against the evil of the self and Satan, without recourse to innovated paths. Those who follow such paths inevitably become entangled in burdens and shackles, even if they act on an interpretation; they cannot avoid following their desires. For this reason, the proponents of innovation are called the followers of desires. The way of the Sunnah is knowledge, justice, and guidance, whereas innovation contains ignorance, injustice, and the pursuit of conjecture and whatever the soul desires.

The Messenger has neither gone astray nor erred. Misguidance goes hand in hand with waywardness: everyone who is wayward is misguided. Right conduct is the opposite of waywardness, and guidance is the opposite of misguidance. This entails avoiding the path of the wicked and the proponents of innovation, both of whom the early generations used to warn against.

Allah Most High says:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will therefore meet with ruin.”

---

## Page 5149

And ghayy (waywardness) is originally the verbal noun in the conjugation ghawā–yaghwī–ghayyan (“to be wayward”), just as one says lawā–yalwī–layyan (“to twist”). It is the opposite of right conduct, as Allah Most High says:

“If they see the way of right conduct, they do not take it as their way; but if they see the way of waywardness, they take it as their way.”

Right conduct is action that benefits the person who performs it, while waywardness is action that harms the person who performs it. Thus, doing good is right conduct, and doing evil is waywardness. For this reason, the jinn said:

“We do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends a right course for them.”

They thus contrasted evil with right conduct. And He says at the end of the surah:

“Say: I have no power to bring you harm or guide you to a right course.”

From the same root comes rashīd (a person of sound judgment), to whom his property is handed over: someone who spends his wealth on what is beneficial, not on what is harmful.

Satan said:

“I will surely lead them all astray, except Your chosen servants among them.”

This means that he commands them to do the evil that harms them, and they obey him, as Allah Most High says:

“I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me.”

And He says:

“And Hell will be brought into full view of the wayward,”

until He says:

“Then they and the wayward will be hurled headlong into it, together with all the forces of Iblīs.”

And He says:

“Those against whom the sentence has been passed will say: ‘Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray. We led them astray just as we ourselves went astray.’”

And He says:

“Your companion has neither gone astray nor erred.”

Furthermore, if ghayy denotes an evil action that harms the person who performs it, then the consequence of that action is also called ghayy, just as the consequence of good is called rushd (right conduct), just as

---

## Page 5150

the consequence of evil is called evil, and the consequence of good is called good; the consequences of good deeds are called hasanāt (good things), and the consequences of evil deeds sayyi’āt (bad things).

Thus, in the Book of Allah, “hasanāt and sayyi’āt” refer to good and evil deeds, as well as to blessings and calamities. Recompense corresponds to the deed: whoever does good and performs good deeds encounters good and good things, while whoever does evil and performs evil deeds encounters evil and bad things. Likewise, whoever acts waywardly encounters waywardness. Neglecting prayer and following desires are forms of waywardness whose perpetrator will encounter waywardness.

For this reason, al-Zamakhsharī said:

“To the Arabs, every evil is waywardness, and every good is right conduct.”

As the poet said:

“Whoever encounters good, people praise his conduct;
Whoever goes astray will never lack someone to blame him for his waywardness.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “Its recompense is waywardness,” in accordance with His words:

“He will meet a penalty,”

meaning recompense for sins. And the transmitted hadith states:

“Ghayy is a valley in Hell from which its other valleys seek refuge.”

This expresses the encounter with evil.

He, glorified be He, says:

“They neglected prayer and followed desires.”

Prayer entails seeking the Face of Allah, as Allah Most High says:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

That is, they perform the dawn and afternoon prayers. The one who supplicates directs himself toward his Lord and seeks Him. Thus, in these acts, hearts seek their Lord and love Him.

---

## Page 5151

Following desires means following what the soul craves. The word shahawāt (desires) is the plural of shahwah, which is originally a verbal noun. The object of desire is also called shahwah, thus applying the verbal noun to its object. Allah Most High says:

“Those who follow their desires wish you to stray far away.”

He thus contrasts repentance with following desires, for He wishes to accept our repentance—that is, Allah loves this for us, is pleased with it, and commands it. “Those who follow their desires”—who are the wayward—“wish you to stray far away”: to turn you far away from the straight path toward following desires. The basic meaning of mayl (inclination) is deviation, which is inevitable for those who follow desires. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Remain steadfast, though you will never fully attain it. Know that the best of your deeds is prayer, and none but a believer consistently maintains his ablution.”

Ahmad and Ibn Mājah narrated this from Thawbān. He thus tells us that we cannot fully sustain steadfastness—or encompass its reward if we remain steadfast.

Allah also says:

“You will never be able to treat your wives with complete fairness, however hard you try. But do not incline wholly toward one, leaving another in limbo.”

His words, “incline wholly,” refer to the utmost extent of deviation: straying from the path and turning away from the straight way toward the furthest reaches of evil. Rather, if you are afflicted with this, exercise moderation and return to the path through repentance. As related in the hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“A believer’s straying is like that of a tethered horse: it wanders, then returns to where it is tethered. Likewise, the believer wanders, then returns

---

## Page 5152

to his Lord.” Allah Most High says:

“Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous,”

through to His words:

“How excellent is the reward of those who work!”

He did not say that they never do wrong or commit sins. Rather, He said:

“When they commit an indecency or wrong themselves”—

that is, through another sin besides indecency. He thus joins the general to the specific. Similarly, Moses said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself.”

And Bilqīs said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself.”

Allah Most High also says generally of the inhabitants of the towns that were destroyed:

“We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.”

They wronged themselves by committing what they had been forbidden, disobeying their prophets, and failing to repent to their Lord. And Allah Most High says:

“They remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins.”

Hence He says:

“Allah wishes to accept your repentance.”

Then He says:

“Allah wishes to lighten your burden, for man was created weak.”

Mujāhid and others said that “following desires” refers to fornication. Ibn Zayd said: “They are the followers of falsehood.” Al-Suddī said: “They are the Jews and Christians.” All these interpretations are correct, for following desires may be accompanied by disbelief, or by acknowledgment that it is a sin.

He then mentions that “man was created weak.” The context indicates that man is weak when it comes to abstaining from desires. He therefore needs a lawful outlet for desire that enables him to dispense with what is forbidden. Hence Tāwūs and Muqātil said: “His weakness lies in his limited patience in abstaining from women.” Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Kaysān said: “His resolve is too weak to overcome desire.”

It has also been said: “He is weak in his original constitution, because he was created from a lowly fluid.” This is reported

---

## Page 5153

from al-Hasan. Yet this must also include weakness in exercising patience, to accord with what is mentioned in the verse, for He says:

“Allah wishes to lighten your burden.”

This means easing religious obligations by permitting you what you need and cannot patiently forgo, as He permitted marriage to slave women. Before this, He said:

“This is for those among you who fear hardship. But to be patient is better for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Thus, although He, glorified be He, permitted marriage to slave women when one lacks the means and fears hardship, He said:

“But to be patient is better for you.”

This indicates that patience is possible even when one fears hardship, and that permitting such marriage is not like permitting carrion in cases of severe hunger, when abstaining from it is not possible. Likewise, according to those who permit masturbation in cases of necessity, abstaining from it is better.

It has been reported from Ibn ‘Abbās that marrying slave women is better than masturbation, and masturbation is better than fornication. If refraining from marriage to slave women is better, then refraining from masturbation is all the more preferable. This is especially so since many scholars—or most of them—firmly maintain that it is prohibited in all circumstances. This is one of the positions within Ahmad’s school, adopted by Ibn ‘Aqīl in al-Mufradāt. The well-known position reported from him—meaning Ahmad—is that it is prohibited unless one fears hardship. The third position is that it is disliked unless one fears hardship.

If Allah has said regarding marriage to slave women:

“But to

---

## Page 5154

be patient is better for you,” then refraining from masturbation is all the more preferable. This indicates that refraining from both is possible.

Since He has permitted something from which one can abstain, this is to ease the burden of religious obligations, as the Most High says:

“Allah wishes to lighten your burden, and man was created weak.”

“Masturbation” is not permissible according to most scholars, both earlier and later, whether one fears hardship or not. The statement of Ibn ‘Abbās and what is reported from Ahmad on this matter apply only to someone whose fear of “hardship”—meaning fornication and sodomy—is so intense that he fears falling into such acts. He was therefore permitted this to lessen the intensity of his distress and desire. As for someone who does this for pleasure, to evoke sexual images, or out of habit—picturing someone while masturbating as though he were having intercourse with them—all of this is forbidden. Neither Ahmad nor anyone else holds it to be permissible. Some scholars have even held that it incurs the prescribed punishment. Refraining from this is obligatory, not merely recommended.

Refraining from forbidden things is obligatory, even when the soul desires and craves them. The Most High says:

“Let those who lack the means to marry remain chaste until Allah enriches them out of His bounty.”

“Remaining chaste” means abstaining from what is forbidden, as in the hadith

---

## Page 5155

authentically reported from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Whoever strives for self-restraint, Allah will grant him self-restraint; whoever seeks self-sufficiency, Allah will make him self-sufficient; and whoever strives to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. No one has been given a gift better or more abundant than patience.”

The “one who seeks self-sufficiency” does not inwardly look to what others possess. The “one who exercises self-restraint” does not ask people for anything with his tongue. The “one who practices patience” is the one who does not force himself to be patient. He thus stated that whoever strives to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. This appears to concern patience in poverty: enduring the bitterness of need without becoming distraught over the poverty with which one has been afflicted. This is patience in poverty and hardship. The Most High says:

“And those who are patient in poverty and hardship and during battle.”

“Hardship” here means illness. This is patience in the need, illness, and fear with which one is afflicted.

As for patience in trials one voluntarily undertakes, such as jihad, patience in these is better than patience in an illness with which one is afflicted without choosing it. Thus, if someone experiences hardship during jihad, patience in that hardship is better than patience in it while in his own land, because such patience is part of fully carrying out jihad. Likewise, if he is afflicted during jihad with poverty or illness resulting from it, patience in that is better, as has been explained at length elsewhere. The same applies to the harm a person suffers while performing acts of obedience, such as prayer and enjoining what is right

---

## Page 5156

and forbidding what is wrong, and seeking knowledge—his patience with such afflictions is better than his patience with trials unrelated to these deeds. Likewise, when his soul urges him toward prohibited things—whether leadership, taking wealth, or committing sexual immorality—his patience in resisting them is better than his patience in lesser matters. For the greater the righteous deeds, the greater the patience exercised in them compared with lesser deeds.

For “knowledge,” “governance,” “jihad,” “enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong,” “prayer,” “pilgrimage,” “fasting,” and “zakah” involve temptations of the soul and other trials not found in other pursuits. In these undertakings, the soul may develop an inclination toward leadership, wealth, and physical beauty. When the soul cannot attain these things, it does not covet them as it does when it can. When it has the ability, it seeks those prohibited things, unlike when it lacks that ability. Exercising patience when one has the ability is jihad; indeed, it is among the best forms of jihad.

It is also more complete in three respects:

(First): Patience in refraining from prohibited things is better than patience in afflictions.

(Second): Refraining from prohibited things when one can engage in them and the soul desires them is better than refraining from them without those circumstances.

(Third): When the soul’s desire for them arises because of a religious undertaking—as in the case of someone who

---

## Page 5157

sets out to pray, seek knowledge, or engage in jihad, and is then tested by something of that kind toward which he is inclined—his patience in resisting it entails both doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden. This is unlike the case in which his soul inclines toward it without his being engaged in a righteous deed.

For this reason, Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd would offer three counsels, saying:

“Do not visit a ruler, even if you say, ‘I will enjoin him to obey Allah.’ Do not visit a woman, even if you say, ‘I will teach her the Book of Allah.’ And do not lend your ear to a proponent of religious innovation, even if you say, ‘I will refute him.’”

His advice, then, was to guard against “the causes of temptation,” for when a person exposes himself to them, he may succumb and fail to remain safe. If he happens to be tested in this way without choosing it, or enters into it by choice and is then tested, he must fear Allah, exercise patience, be sincere, and strive. His patience in this and his remaining safe from temptation while fulfilling his duty are among the best deeds. Examples include someone who assumes authority and exercises it justly; someone who refutes proponents of religious innovation with the pure Sunnah without being led astray by them; or someone who teaches women their religion in the prescribed manner, without temptation.

Yet when Allah tests a servant and decrees a trial for him, He helps him; whereas when the servant exposes himself to a trial, Allah leaves him to his own devices. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Samura:

“Do not ask for authority, for if you are given it at your request, you will be left to bear it unaided; but if you are given it without asking, you will be helped in carrying it out.”

Likewise,

---

## Page 5158

he said concerning the plague:

“If it breaks out in a town where you are, do not leave to flee from it; and if you hear of it in a land, do not go there.”

Whoever does what Allah has commanded and then encounters a trial without choosing it will receive Allah’s help in facing it, unlike someone who deliberately exposes himself to it. Yet the door of repentance remains open. A man may ask for authority and be left to bear it unaided, then regret having asked and repent. Allah then accepts his repentance and helps him either to fulfil his duty or to relinquish that authority. The same applies to all other trials.

As He says:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

These matters require a fuller discussion than space permits here. And (the point) is that Allah, glorified is He, wishes to make things clear to us and guide us to the ways of those before us, of whom He said:

“Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance.”

They are those to whose path He has commanded us to ask Him to guide us, in His words:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed.”

He loves us to follow their path and commands us to do so. It is the way of those who turn to Him. Thus, He mentions three matters here: clarification, guidance, and repentance.

It has also been said that the ways intended here are those of both the people of truth and the people of falsehood. That is, He wishes to make clear to us the ways of both groups, guiding His believing servants to the truth

---

## Page 5159

and leading others astray, for guidance and misguidance come only after clarification. As He says:

“We have never sent a messenger except in the language of his people, so that he might make things clear to them. Then Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And He says:

“Allah would never lead a people astray after guiding them until He has made clear to them what they must avoid.”

On this interpretation, “ways”—meaning the ways of the people of falsehood—would be grammatically connected to “make clear,” not to “guide,” while the people of truth would be connected to His words, “and guide you.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “The ‘ways’ are paths. Thus, the meaning is that He directs you to obey Him, just as He directed the prophets and their followers.” This interpretation is preferable, because when two verbs precede a shared object, the first is not made its sole governing verb. Rather, either the second alone governs it, or both do, as in His words:

“Bring me [copper], that I may pour molten copper over it.”

Alternatively, if the intended construction is, “He makes clear to you the ways of those before you and guides you to ways,” this still indicates that He guides us to their ways. What is meant here is the ways of the people of truth, unlike His words:

“There have been precedents before you.”

For He says immediately afterwards:

“So travel through the land and see what was the end of those who denied the truth.”

There, He intended to make the punishment of the wrongdoers known through direct observation. Here, however, He has sent down to us passages of the Quran through which He guides us to the ways of those before us: those whom Allah has blessed.

He mentions three matters: “clarification,” “guidance,” and “repentance.” This is because a person first needs to know good and evil, what he has been commanded to do, and what he has been forbidden to do. Then, after that, he needs

---

## Page 5160

to be guided, so that he pursues the truth and acts upon it rather than falsehood. This is the way of the prophets and the righteous. Thereafter, he will inevitably commit sins and wish to purify himself of them through repentance. Thus, he needs knowledge, action upon it, and repentance alongside both. He will inevitably fall short or become heedless in following those ways to which Allah has guided him, and must therefore repent of whatever negligence he has shown in following each of them.

These “ways” include both obligatory and recommended deeds. Whoever follows them will inevitably fall short and become heedless, so he seeks Allah’s forgiveness and repents to Him. However hard a servant strives, he cannot fully discharge the duty Allah has imposed upon him. He therefore has no recourse but to seek forgiveness and repent after every act of obedience.

It may also be said that “guidance” here means clarification and instruction: that is, He makes known to you the ways of those before you, both the blessed and the wretched, so that you may follow the former and avoid the latter. As the Most High says:

“And shown him the two ways?”

ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd said: “The paths of good and evil.” It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: “The paths of guidance and misguidance.” Mujāhid said: “The paths of bliss and misery”—that is, We gave him an innate awareness of this and made it known to him. All these explanations mean the same thing.

The word najdān means two clear paths, while najd means elevated ground. Thus, the meaning is: Have We not made known to him the paths of good and evil, making them as clear to him as two elevated paths? Yet the guidance, clarification, and instruction in this verse are shared by

---

## Page 5161

all human beings, who recognize it through their reason.

As for the path of the earlier prophets, Allah Most High must inform us of it, as He says:

“Those are accounts of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew them before this.”

The answer to this, however, is that if this meaning were intended, He would have said, “Allah wishes to make clear to you the ways of those before you.” There would have been no need to mention guidance if the meaning were the same. Since He mentions that He wishes both to clarify and to guide, we know that these are distinct. “Clarification” means making known and teaching, while “guidance” means commanding and forbidding: it is calling people to goodness. As the Most High says:

“For every people there is a guide.”

That is, someone who calls them to goodness. Likewise, the Most High says:

“Indeed, you guide to a straight path.”

That is, you call them to it by teaching them.

Here the verb “guide” takes its object directly, without a preposition, for the intended sense is: “And He requires you to adhere to the ways of those before you, so do not turn away from them.” The guidance intended here is not the inward inspiration meant in His words:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

For had He willed that, it would have come to pass, and none of us would have gone astray. Rather, this is His legislative will, expressed through His commands, meaning His love and approval. Hence al-Zajjāj said: “He wishes to direct you to what will bring about your repentance.” He thus understood this will as relating to Allah’s own action. For al-Zajjāj supposed that will in the Quran is only of this kind. Yet it is not as he supposed. Rather, when His will relates to His own action, what He wills does indeed come to pass, for

---

## Page 5162

whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

As for the will expressed in His commands and His law, it is exemplified by His words:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you”—to the end of the verse.

And His words:

“Allah only intends to remove impurity from you, O people of the household.”

And other similar passages. This is His will concerning what He has commanded, meaning that He loves it, approves of it, and rewards the one who does it—not that He wills to create it so that it comes into being, as in His words:

“Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted”—to the end of the verse.

And as Noah said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.”

This is His will concerning what He creates and brings into being. As Muslims say: “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.” This will concerns everything that comes into existence, whereas His legislative will, expressed through His commands, concerns only acts of obedience. Thus people say of someone who does something evil, “He is doing something Allah does not will,” even while saying, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.” For this will is of “two kinds,” as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Guidance may also mean inward inspiration, and the address may be directed to the obedient believers whom

---

## Page 5163

Allah has guided to obey Him. For Allah Most High willed to turn to them in forgiveness and guide them, and so they were guided. Had He not willed this for them, they would not have been guided, as they said:

“Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this! We would never have been guided had Allah not guided us. The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth.”

Yet the address in the verse is directed to all Muslims, just as in the verse on ablution and in His address to the people of the household:

“Allah only intends to remove impurity from you.”

This is why He threatens those who do not obey Him. Likewise, concerning fasting:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

This, then, is His legislative will, expressed through His commands, in the sense of love and approval—not His will to create, which necessarily brings about what is willed. If it were the latter, the verse would address only those who embraced ease and did what they were commanded to do, while those who failed to do so would fall outside the commands and prohibitions contained in the verse. But that is not the case. Rather, the legal ruling is binding upon all Muslims: whoever obeys is rewarded, and whoever disobeys is punished. Those who obeyed Him did so only through His guidance—the guidance of inward inspiration and assistance, by which He made them rightly guided—just as He is the One who makes the person who prays a praying person, and the Muslim a Muslim.

If the human will referred to here necessarily entailed the occurrence of what was willed, it would not have been said:

“Those who follow their desires want you to deviate far from the right path.”

For then the will of these people would have no effect; its existence and nonexistence would be the same. As in Noah’s words:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to

---

## Page 5164

lead you astray.” For whatever Allah wills comes to pass, even if people do not will it; and whatever He does not will does not come to pass, even if people will it. The purpose of the verse is to warn them against following those who follow their desires.

The meaning is: “I desire for you the good that benefits you, whereas these people desire for you the evil that harms you—like Satan, who desires to lead you astray. His followers are those who follow their desires. So do not take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me. Rather, follow the paths of guidance and rectitude, and beware of the paths of error and corruption.”

As the Most High says:

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor fall into misery,”

and the verses that follow.

His words, “follow their desires,” occur in both passages. Following one's appetites is akin to following one's desires, as the Most High says:

“They only follow their own desires. And who is further astray than one who follows his desires without guidance from Allah?”

He also says:

“If the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would fall into ruin.”

The Most High says:

“Do not follow the desires of people who went astray before.”

And the Most High says:

“Is someone who stands upon clear proof from his Lord like those whose evil deeds have been made appealing to them and who follow their own desires?”

And the Most High says:

“Do not follow the desires of those who do not know.”

This occurs frequently in the Quran. The word hawā (desire) is the verbal noun of hawā, yahwī (to desire). The object of desire itself—what one desires—is also called hawā. Following it is thus like following a path, as the Most High says:

“Do not follow

---

## Page 5165

the desires of people who went astray before.” As with the word “appetite,” following desire means following what the verbal noun itself denotes: following one’s will and love, which constitute one’s desire. Following one’s will means doing what the soul desires. This is like His words, the Most High:

“Follow the path of those who turn to Me.”

And His words:

“This is My path, perfectly straight, so follow it. Do not follow other paths, for they will lead you away from His path.”

He also says:

“Do not follow any protectors besides Him.”

The term “following” can thus apply to the one who commands and forbids, to the commands and prohibitions themselves, and to what is commanded and forbidden—the straight path. Likewise, desire has its commands and prohibitions, which are the soul’s commands and prohibitions. As the Most High says:

“I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul persistently commands evil, except where my Lord shows mercy. Indeed, my Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

As for the blameworthy deeds it commands, the one entails the other: following a command means doing what is commanded, and following the soul’s command means doing what it desires. Thus, it becomes clear that following appetites and following desires means following the soul’s appetite and desire by doing what it craves and desires.

Indeed, one may say that this is the only possible meaning of the expression “following appetites and desires.” For what a person craves and desires only comes into existence after he craves and desires it, and a person is censured only when he does what he craves and desires, when it comes into existence

---

## Page 5166

for by then he has already done it; he is not forbidden to do it after it has occurred, nor is he then told, “Do not follow your desire.” Moreover, the intended, craved act that a person desires follows his appetite and desire; appetite and desire do not follow it. Thus, following appetites means following the soul’s appetite.

If you take “appetite” to mean “the object of appetite,” then, besides departing from the primary meaning, this requires positing an external object that is craved and that the person follows, such as a desired woman or desired food—even if a woman, and likewise food, is called an “appetite,” as in the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Every deed of the son of Adam is for him, except fasting. It is for Me, and I shall reward it. He gives up his food, drink, and desire for My sake.”

That is, he leaves his desire: what he actually gives up is what he desires, just as he gives up food. It is not that he gives up his food by abandoning the appetite within his soul, for that appetite is created within him and is part of his innate nature. Rather, he is rewarded when he gives up what that appetite seeks.

“The fact of the matter” is that the two are inseparably linked: whoever follows the appetite present within his soul follows what he craves. Likewise, whoever follows the desire present within his soul follows what he desires. This is among the effects of the will, and following the will means obeying its command and doing what it seeks, like a subordinate who follows his commander’s orders.

A person must conceive within himself what he wants, desires, and craves, and imagine it before acting. That image thus remains like the prayer leader in relation to the worshipper who follows him wherever he is; and his outward action

---

## Page 5167

follows his inward adherence. Thus the image within the soul of what is intended, sought, and desired remains what moves and commands the person.

This is why it is said: “The final cause is an efficient cause.” For it is on account of the final cause—through this conception and volition—that a person becomes the agent of an act. This desired image, conceived within the soul, is what makes the agent act. The person therefore follows it, while Satan drives him further into error, strengthening that image and its influence and making following it attractive to people.

That image encompasses both the image of the object sought—such as a beloved form, food, or drink—and the act itself, namely direct engagement with that sought and beloved object. Satan and the soul love this. Whenever a person conceives that beloved object within himself, he wants it to exist externally. For what comes first in thought comes last in action, and what comes first in seeking comes last in attainment.

For this reason, a person in the grip of his appetite and desire remains their captive, subdued under the authority of desire more completely than by any other overpowering force. This desire-driven force that subdues the servant is a quality inherent in his own soul, which he cannot leave behind at all. The soul seeks the mental image, for it seeks to apprehend the beloved object and represent it within itself. He therefore follows the will, even if it is mental. Adornment derives from beauty, and what is meant is the conception within himself and the object of desire existing externally. He has “two movers”: the conception and the object of desire. One moves him by seeking and commanding, while the other commands him to follow

---

## Page 5168

its demands and commands. Following appetites and desires encompasses all of this.

This is unlike any overpowering force external to a person, from which he can part while his soul remains unchanged. He can escape this inward force only by changing a quality of his own soul. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Three things bring destruction: avarice that is obeyed, desire that is followed, and a person’s admiration of himself. And three things bring salvation: fearing Allah in private and in public, moderation in poverty and wealth, and speaking the truth in anger and contentment.”

His words in the hadith, “desire that is followed,” show that what is followed is something residing within the soul, just as he speaks of avarice being obeyed. He described avarice as being obeyed because it issues commands, and desire as being followed because what is followed may be a leader whose example is emulated without his issuing commands.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Beware of avarice, for avarice destroyed those before you. It commanded them to be stingy, and they were stingy; it commanded them to commit injustice, and they committed injustice; and it commanded them to sever ties of kinship, and they severed them.”

He thus explained that avarice commands stinginess, injustice, and the severing of ties. “Stinginess” means withholding from people the help one could give through one’s own efforts and wealth, while “injustice” means transgressing against them. The former is neglecting what is obligatory; thus a person both neglects his obligations and transgresses against others by doing what is forbidden. He singled out severing ties of kinship for mention to emphasize its gravity, for it falls

---

## Page 5169

under both of the preceding categories. Commenting on the Most High’s words, “Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul,” the Quran commentators explained that this means neither taking anything Allah has forbidden nor withholding anything Allah has commanded one to give. Thus, avarice commands the opposite of what Allah and His Messenger command: Allah forbids injustice and commands kindness, whereas avarice commands injustice and forbids kindness.

(While circumambulating the House and standing at ‘Arafah, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf would frequently say, “O Allah, protect me from the avarice of my own soul.” When asked about this, he replied, “If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I am protected from injustice, stinginess, and severing ties of kinship.” In another report from him, he said, “I fear that I am already ruined.” He asked, “Why is that?” He replied, “I hear Allah say, ‘Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul,’ yet I am an avaricious man: hardly anything leaves my hand.” He replied, “That is not the avarice Allah mentions in the Quran. Avarice is to consume your brother’s wealth unjustly. This is merely stinginess—and what an evil thing stinginess is!”) (*).

The Most High mentions avarice in the context of envy and giving others preference over oneself, saying:

“They harbour no desire in their hearts for what the others have been given, and give them preference over themselves, even though they are in need.”

Then He says:

“And whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul—it is they who will be successful.”

Thus, whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul will not be envious and transgress against the person he envies. Envy is fundamentally hatred of the person envied.
