His report was joined to the preceding report, causing the confusion.
> It appears—and Allah knows best—that the corrected text should read as follows:
> “While circumambulating the House and standing at ‘Arafah, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf would frequently say, ‘O Allah, protect me from the avarice of my own soul.’ When asked about this, he replied, ‘If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I am protected from injustice, stinginess, and severing ties of kinship.’ In another report from him, he said: [‘If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I will neither steal nor commit adultery nor do…’] [A man came to ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, and said to him:] ‘I fear that I may have been ruined.’ He asked, ‘Why is that?’ The man replied, ‘I hear Allah say, “Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul,” yet I am an avaricious man: hardly anything leaves my hand.’ He replied, ‘That is not the avarice Allah mentions in the Quran. Avarice is to consume your brother’s wealth unjustly. This is merely stinginess—and what an evil thing stinginess is!’”

---

## Page 5170

and avarice in a person is accompanied by greed, an intense desire for wealth, hatred of others, and injustice toward them. As the Most High says:

“Allah certainly knows those among you who hold others back and those who say to their brothers, ‘Come over to us,’ yet hardly ever join in battle, withholding their help from you”—through the verses up to His words: “begrudging any good. Those have not believed, so Allah has rendered their deeds worthless.”

Their avarice toward the believers and toward good entails aversion and hatred. Hatred of good urges one toward evil, while hatred of a person urges one to wrong him and sever ties with him, as does envy. For the envier urges the one who envies him to wrong the person envied and sever ties with him, as in the case of Adam’s two sons and Joseph’s brothers.

Envy and avarice thus entail hatred and aversion, prompting one to withhold what is due and to wrong that person. Here the action springs from hatred, unlike desire, where the action springs from love: a person loves something, pursues it, and acts accordingly. The former’s aim is an absence, and absence brings no benefit. Yet that intention commands an actual deed, and its command is obeyed.

Ibn Mas‘ūd regarded stinginess as distinct from avarice, whereas the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described avarice as commanding stinginess.

Some people say that avarice and stinginess are the same. As Ibn Jarīr said: “In Arabic usage, avarice means stinginess and withholding surplus wealth.” But it is not

---

## Page 5171

as he claimed. Rather, what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Ibn Mas‘ūd said is more deserving of being followed. A stingy person may withhold his wealth out of love for the pleasure and comfort it affords him. Or he may derive neither pleasure nor comfort from it, but simply feel reluctant to spend it and dislike doing so, to the point that he dislikes even benefiting himself from it despite his abundant wealth. This may be accompanied by pleasure in amassing wealth and a fondness for looking at it. Or there may be no pleasure at all; rather, he dislikes showing kindness to anyone. Even if someone else wishes to give, he resents it out of hatred for goodness—not for the giver or the recipient, but for goodness itself. Alternatively, this may arise from hatred and envy of the recipient or the giver. This is avarice, and it is certainly what commands stinginess. Yet every instance of stinginess arises from avarice. Thus, every avaricious person is stingy, but not every stingy person is avaricious.

Al-Khattābī said: “Avarice is more extreme in withholding than stinginess. Stinginess concerns individual matters and particular things, whereas avarice is pervasive: it is like an enduring trait rooted in a person’s nature and disposition.”

Al-Khattābī also related that someone said: “Stinginess is for a person to begrudge his wealth, while avarice is for him to begrudge both his wealth and his kindness.” It has also been said: “Avarice is to begrudge the kindness that others show to someone else, whereas stinginess is to withhold one’s own kindness from others.”

Those who follow their desires and their whims love and desire such things, so they followed

---

## Page 5172

what they loved and desired without knowledge, never considering whether it would ultimately benefit or harm them. Hence Allah said:

“Know that they only follow their own desires.”

Then He said:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desires without guidance from Allah?”

Following one’s desires has varying degrees. Among those who do so are the polytheists and those who worship, besides Allah, whatever appeals to them, without knowledge or proof. As Allah said:

“Have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god?”

That is, he takes as the god he worships whichever deity he desires. Allah did not say that his desire itself is his god. Not everyone who desires something worships it, for desire takes different forms. Rather, the meaning is that he makes whatever he desires the object of his worship, so that his worship follows his own desires concerning worship. For he has neither worshipped what Allah loves to be worshipped nor performed the worship he was commanded to perform.

Such is the condition of the people of religious innovation: they have worshipped other than Allah and devised forms of worship through which they claim to worship Allah. They have merely followed their own desires. Each follows his own inclinations, inner experiences, feelings, and desires, without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book. Had he followed knowledge and the illuminating Book, he would have worshipped none but Allah, in the manner He willed, not through newly introduced practices and innovations.

---

## Page 5173

The point is that there are many gods, and the ways in which they are worshipped are varied. In general, whatever a person desires and loves must be conceived in his mind. That mental image moves him towards what he loves and towards all that love entails. Whoever worships it worships other than Allah, and devils appear to him in the form of the one he worships. This is widespread and has always been so. Thus, anyone who worships anything other than Allah is, in fact, worshipping Satan. This is why Satan aligns himself with the sun when it rises, sets, and reaches its zenith, so that those who worship it prostrate to him.

The “devils” would assume the forms of those being worshipped, just as they would speak to people from the idols they worshipped. Likewise, in our own time, many people among those who profess Islam, Christians, and polytheists associate with Allah some of those whom they revere, whether living or dead, including shaykhs and others. Such a person calls upon the one he reveres and seeks his aid during that figure’s lifetime and after his death. He then sees him come to him, speak to him, and fulfil his need. Yet it is only a devil who has assumed his form to lead this polytheist astray.

As for those afflicted with “passionate love,” Satan continually presents the image of the beloved to them or assumes the beloved’s form. The lover thus continues to see the beloved’s image despite his absence, after his death. It is only Satan who has projected that image upon his heart. Hence, when a servant remembers Allah in a way that makes the retreating whisperer withdraw, this satanic apparition withdraws as well. At times, the image of the beloved takes such hold of the lover that he sees nothing else and hears nothing but its words, leaving

---

## Page 5174

his soul preoccupied with it. Those who follow an imperfect path in loving Allah may experience something similar, called “overwhelming absorption” and “annihilation.” Such a person becomes so absorbed in his Beloved that he loses awareness of his own love; in the One he knows, of his own knowledge; and in the One he remembers, of his own remembrance—until he is no longer conscious of any of Allah’s names, attributes, speech, commands or prohibitions. Some may pass from this to “union,” saying: “I am He, and He is I; I am Allah.” Many spiritual seekers imagine that this is their ultimate goal, and that this is the “affirmation of Allah’s oneness” which every seeker ultimately seeks. They are mistaken. Rather, this is akin to what the Christians say. They went astray because, in their inward lives, they did not follow the path prescribed by revelation concerning what Allah has declared and commanded. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point is that those who follow their desires for physical forms, food, drink and clothing find that the object of their desire takes hold of their hearts, overpowering and mastering them until they remain captive, driven by what they crave wherever it leads. Hence, one of the early Muslims said: “For a devout young man, I fear a young boy sitting beside him more than a ravenous beast pouncing on him.”

---

## Page 5175

This is because a pure soul, softened by “spiritual discipline,” yet not drawn wholeheartedly to loving and worshipping Allah, nor possessed of a complete fear of Allah that turns it away from its desires, is overpowered whenever it falls under the sway of a physical form, just as a beast overpowers its prey. The beast seizes its prey by force, and the prey cannot resist it. Likewise, the beloved forms a person pictures in his heart swallow it up and overpower it, leaving it unable to resist. His heart remains absorbed in that form even more completely than prey is engulfed in a lion’s belly, for the beloved object of desire is the soul’s ultimate aim and wields an overwhelming power over it.

The “heart” is engulfed by whatever takes hold of it, whether something loved or something feared, as happens with the love of wealth, status and physical forms. Someone who fears another remains absorbed in him, heart and mind, just as a drowning person is engulfed in water. Just as he is inevitably overcome by the physical matter surrounding him, hearts are overcome by the things they imagine—things feared, loved or disliked. A person seeks what he loves and repels what he dislikes. Hope attaches to what is loved, and fear to what is disliked. None but Allah brings good, and none but Allah removes harm:

“If Allah afflicts you with harm, none can remove it but Him; and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty. He grants it to whomever He wills of His servants. And He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.”

“Whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then, when harm touches you, it is to Him that you cry out.”

---

## Page 5176

When a servant asks his Lord to grant what he seeks and ward off what he fears, Allah grants him faith in Him, love for Him, knowledge of Him, affirmation of His oneness, and hope in Him, while enlivening his heart and illuminating it with the light of faith. These benefits may be greater than what he sought, if it was some worldly possession. But if he asks Allah to help him remember Him, thank Him and worship Him well, and for related matters, then what he seeks may be more beneficial than the act of seeking it—that is, supplication. What he seeks is remembrance, gratitude, worship performed in the best possible manner, and other such things. This is a subject to be discussed at length elsewhere.

And (the point) is that whatever a servant desires and loves, or fears and dreads, may engulf and overpower his heart, whatever it may be. Hence Allah Most High says:

“But their hearts are steeped in heedlessness of this, and they have other deeds besides this that they persist in doing.”

Their hearts are immersed in what distracts them from that of which they have been warned. It engulfs them, keeping them from remembering Allah and the Hereafter, with its bliss and painful punishment.

Allah Most High says:

“So leave them in their heedlessness for a time.”

That is, leave them immersed in the love of wealth and children that engulfs their hearts and prevents them from hastening to good deeds and righteous works.

And He Most High says:

“May the liars be destroyed—
those who are engulfed in confusion and heedless.”

And the following verses. That is, they are heedless of the Hereafter and engulfed in what distracts them from it: love of this world and its enjoyments overwhelms their hearts, while they remain heedless of the Hereafter and of the purpose for which they were created.

This resembles His saying:

“And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows

---

## Page 5177

his own desires and whose affairs are in disarray.” Being engulfed in this way results from following one’s desires, while inattention is a kind of heedlessness. Hence some have said: “Inattention means being heedless of something and having one’s heart turn away from it.” These two—heedlessness and desire—sum up all evil. Heedlessness of Allah and the Hereafter closes the door to goodness, namely remembrance and wakefulness. Desire opens the door to evil, inattention and fear. The heart thus remains engulfed in what it desires and fears, heedless of Allah, seeking something other than Him and inattentive to His remembrance. It becomes preoccupied with something other than Allah; its affairs fall into disorder, and love of this world covers its heart.

As related in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May the slave of the dinar perish! May the slave of the dirham perish! May the slave of the plush covering perish! May the slave of the cloak perish! May he perish and fall headlong, and if a thorn pricks him, may he be unable to remove it! If he is given, he is pleased; if he is denied, he is displeased.”

He described such a person as the slave of whatever pleases him when he possesses it and displeases him when he loses it. Thus he becomes the slave of the dirham and of the other things mentioned in this hadith. The plush covering is something one sits upon, yet he becomes its servant. As one of the early Muslims said: “Wear clothes that serve you; do not wear clothes that you have to serve.” This covering is like a rug upon which one sits, while the cloak is something one wraps around oneself. These are among the least forms of wealth. Rather,

---

## Page 5178

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned these to draw attention to things of greater worth, of which a person likewise becomes a slave. He is subject to disparate lords and quarrelsome partners. Hence the Prophet said:

“If he is given, he is pleased; if he is denied, he is displeased.”

Whatever a person is pleased to obtain and displeased to lose, he is its slave, for a slave is pleased through attachment to such things and displeased when deprived of them. As for the true object of worship, besides whom there is no deity, when the believer worships and loves Him, this brings faith, monotheism, love, remembrance and worship into his heart. He is pleased with this and becomes angry if prevented from it. Likewise, anyone who loves something necessarily forms a conception of it in his heart and desires to be connected to it as far as possible.

Al-Junayd said: “A servant does not truly become a servant until he is free of everything besides Allah Most High.” This accords with the hadith: a person cannot be exclusively Allah’s servant, devoting his religion entirely to Him, until he is no longer a slave to anything besides Him and retains not the slightest trace or fraction of servitude to anything besides Allah. If something other than Allah determines his pleasure and displeasure, he is a slave to that other thing. He therefore has a share of polytheism proportionate to his love for it, and his worship of it adds to that.

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād said: “By Allah, no one has been true to Allah in his servitude who

---

## Page 5179

is subject to the lordship of any created being.”

Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl said:

“Shall I worship one Lord or a thousand lords,
when paths diverge?”

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Tabarānī narrated from Asmā’ bint ‘Umays that she said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wretched is the servant who is conceited and arrogant, forgetting the Most Great, the Most Exalted. Wretched is the servant who acts tyrannically and transgresses, forgetting the Compeller, the Most High. Wretched is the servant who is heedless and distracted, forgetting the graves and decay. Wretched is the servant who oppresses and transgresses, forgetting his beginning and his end. Wretched is the servant who deceitfully seeks worldly gain through religion. Wretched is the servant who undermines religion by exploiting doubtful matters. Wretched is the servant whose craving humiliates him and turns him away from the truth. Wretched is the servant whose greed leads him. Wretched is the servant whose desires lead him astray.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “It is singular.” The authentic hadith quoted earlier contains support for it. Allah knows best. Many other hadiths and reports have likewise been narrated to this effect.

As Allah Most High says:

“Yet among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals to Him, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Someone who seeks leadership—even through falsehood—is pleased by words that exalt him, even if they are false, and angered by words that disparage him, even if they are true.

---

## Page 5180

But the believer is pleased by truthful words, whether they favour him or count against him, and angered by false words, whether they favour him or count against him. For Allah Most High loves truth, honesty, and justice, and hates falsehood and injustice.

Thus, when truth, honesty, and justice—which Allah loves—are expressed, the believer loves them, even when they run counter to his desires, because his desires have become subordinate to what the Messenger brought. When injustice and falsehood are expressed, Allah hates them, and the believer hates them too, even if they accord with his desires.

The same applies to someone who seeks “wealth”—even through falsehood—as Allah Most High says:

“Among them are those who criticize you concerning the distribution of charity. If they are given some of it, they are pleased; but if they are not given any, they become enraged.”

These are the people of whom he said:

“Wretched is the slave of the dinar,”

and the rest of the hadith.

What, then, if the heart is overcome by desires, passions, and objects of love that enslave it more powerfully than dirhams and dinars, drawing it away from complete love and worship of Allah because they compete with Him and involve associating created beings with Him? How they turn the heart aside and divert it from complete love, worship, and fear of its Lord! For every object of love draws the heart of the one who loves it towards itself and diverts it from loving anything else. Likewise, an object of hatred repels the heart, unsettles it, and distracts it from worshipping Allah Most High.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad narrated in his Musnad, as did others, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

---

## Page 5181

said to his Companions:

“Is it poverty that you fear? I do not fear poverty for you. Rather, I fear this world for you, for whenever the heart of any one of you goes astray, it is this world alone that leads it astray.”

The same applies to those who love a person, such as his friends, and those who hate him, such as his enemies. Those who love him draw him towards themselves. If their love for him is not for Allah’s sake, this becomes something that cuts him off from Allah. Those who hate him harm him and show him hostility, distracting him from Allah through the harm they cause. If his friends who love him for reasons other than Allah’s sake treat him kindly, their kindness makes him love them and draws his heart towards them—even if this is not in keeping with upright conduct—and obliges him to repay them. Thus they cut him off from Allah and His worship.

The heart is not freed from temptation unless the servant’s religious devotion is entirely for Allah, Almighty and Majestic. He must love for Allah’s sake and love what Allah loves, hate for Allah’s sake and hate what Allah hates; the same applies to his allegiance and enmity. Otherwise, his love for a created being draws him towards that being, while people’s love for him is a means that draws them towards him. Either of these may be stronger than the other.

If he has mastered his desires, someone overcome by his own desires will not draw him in, nor will the things he loves draw him towards them. This is because he masters his desires and restrains himself from following them, owing to the fear and love of Allah in his heart that prevent him from being drawn towards those things.

As for people’s love for him, it leads them to draw him towards themselves with their own strength. If he does not possess the strength, born of love and fear of Allah, to fend them off

---

## Page 5182

then they will draw him towards themselves and take hold of him, as in the case of the wife of al-ʿAzīz and her love for Joseph. The strength of “Joseph,” his love for Allah, his sincerity and his fear of Him were greater than the beauty and loveliness of the wife of al-ʿAzīz and his love for her. This concerns the case in which someone loves him for his physical appearance, even though the attraction here is strong on both sides. In such circumstances, only those whom Allah protects are safe. Otherwise, when love is mutual, some wrongdoing generally occurs between people. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Let no man be alone with a woman, for Satan will be the third.”

They may also love him for his knowledge, religious devotion, kindness or something else. The temptation in this case is greater, unless he possesses strength of faith, fear of Allah and complete devotion to Allah alone. For knowledge, status and physical beauty are sources of temptation for all who succumb to temptation.

Moreover, they seek to have him fulfil their aims. If he does not, their love diminishes, or some hatred develops. This may grow, or lead them to cease loving him altogether, so that he becomes hated after having been loved. A person’s friends like to enlist his service and employ him for their own purposes until he becomes like a slave to them, while his enemies strive to hurt and harm him. Those friends seek to benefit from him even when this harms him and corrupts his religious commitment; they give no thought to that. Few of them are grateful.

In reality, neither group seeks to benefit him or protect him from harm; rather, they only

---

## Page 5183

seek to use him to achieve their own ends. Unless a person worships Allah, relies upon Him, is loyal to Him, and forms alliances and enmities for His sake, both groups will devour him, bringing about his ruin in this world and the Hereafter.

This is the familiar pattern of human conduct, with the warfare, disputes, disagreements and strife that arise among people. Some support Zayd and oppose Amr, while others do the reverse, all to serve their own ends. Once they have obtained what they want from the one they support—what they seek from Zayd—they turn to Amr. Amr’s supporters do likewise, as happens among all kinds of people.

Likewise, the “leader” on either side inclines towards those who support him. Yet unless their allegiance is for Allah’s sake, they are more harmful to him than his opponents. His opponents seek only to ruin his worldly life, whether by killing him, taking his wealth or removing him from office. All this is worldly harm, of no consequence so long as the servant’s religion remains intact. This is the opposite of the attitude of worldly people and those who love this world: they attach no importance to the corruption of their religion so long as their worldly affairs remain intact. They are unconcerned about it. As for “the servant’s religion,” which is between him and Allah, his opponents have no power over it.

His allies, however, whose allegiance serves their own ends, seek from him only what corrupts his religion, through his helping them achieve their aims and in other ways. If he does not comply, they turn into enemies. Thus harm comes upon him from “two directions”:

---

## Page 5184

from parting ways with them,
and from their hostility.

Their hostility is harder on him than that of his enemies, for they have seen and learned things about him that his enemies do not know. They use this to stir up the hostility of others, multiplying the enmity against him. If he is unwilling to part ways with them, he must appease them and help them achieve what they want, even if this corrupts his religion. If he helps them attain a worldly position, he receives an ample portion and a full share of the injustice and oppression they practise in it. They also demand that he help them achieve their aims, even at the expense of his own worldly aims—let alone his religious aims, if he has any within him or among his concerns. For man is unjust and ignorant, pursuing only his own desires.

Unless he inwardly does good to them, patiently bears their harm, and meets their needs for Allah’s sake, while seeking Allah’s help against them fully and placing his complete trust in Him, they will corrupt both his religion and his worldly life. This is what is plainly witnessed among people seeking worldly leadership: one demands of another acts of injustice and disobedience through which to attain that leadership, makes this course seem attractive to him, and turns against him if he does not stand by him, as has indeed

---

## Page 5185

happened with more than one person. The same occurs when someone loves a person for his appearance: he serves and honours him, gives him whatever he can, and asks him for forbidden acts that corrupt his religion. It also occurs when someone loves an adherent of a “religious innovation” because he advocates that innovation on his behalf: the latter compels him to support falsehood that he knows to be false, or else turns against him. Thus, scholars among the disbelievers and the people of innovation defend falsehood, despite knowing that they are following it, for the sake of their followers and admirers. They oppose the people of truth and disparage their way.

Whoever loves someone other than Allah and gives his allegiance to another hates those who love Allah and are His allies. Whoever loves someone for other than Allah’s sake suffers greater harm from his friends than from his enemies. His enemies can, at most, come between him and this worldly object of his love; yet separating him from it is a mercy to him. His friends help deprive him of that mercy and drive it away from him. What kind of friendship is this? They want that object of his love to remain so that they can use him for their own purposes and desires. Both are harmful to him.

Allah Most High says:

“When those who were followed disown their followers, and they see the punishment, and all ties between them are severed.”

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād reported from Layth

---

## Page 5186

from Mujāhid:

“They are the bonds of affection that were not for Allah’s sake, and the ties that existed between them in this world.”

“Those who followed will say, ‘If only we could return, we would disown them as they have disowned us.’ Thus will Allah show them their deeds as a source of bitter regret, and they will never emerge from the Fire.”

The deeds that Allah shows them as a source of regret are those they performed for one another in this world that were not for Allah’s sake. These include allegiance, companionship and love for other than Allah’s sake. All goodness lies in worshipping Allah alone, associating nothing with Him. There is neither power nor strength except through Allah.

Section

What further establishes these matters is that the lover draws, while the beloved is drawn. Whoever loves something draws it towards himself according to his strength. Whoever loves a form is drawn by that form towards the beloved existing in the external world, according to his strength. For the lover functions as an efficient cause, and the beloved as a final cause; each contributes to bringing about the effect.

The lover draws the beloved only through the image of the beloved that he holds in his heart. That image draws him in the sense that he is drawn towards it, not that the image itself has intention or acts. For the beloved possesses a quality suited to the lover that draws him towards it, just as a person is drawn to food to eat it, to a woman to be intimate with her, and to

---

## Page 5187

his friend to enjoy his company, and just as the hearts of those who love Allah and His Messenger are drawn to Allah, His Messenger, and His righteous servants because of the attributes of Allah—glory be to Him—for which He deserves to be loved and worshipped.

Indeed, nothing in existence may be loved for its own sake except Him—glory and praise be to Him. Everything else that is loved in this world may be loved only for the sake of something else, not for its own sake. The Lord Most High alone must be loved for His own sake. This is one of the meanings of His divinity and of His words:

“Had there been in the heavens and the earth gods besides Allah, both would have fallen into ruin.”

For loving anything else for its own sake is to associate partners with Allah. None, then, is to be loved for His own sake except Allah, for this is a prerogative of His divinity, which none but Allah alone deserves. Anything loved besides Him, unless it is loved for His sake or for the sake of something loved for His sake, is loved with a corrupt love.

Allah Most High has instilled in human souls a love of food and a love of women, because these preserve their bodies and perpetuate humankind. Were it not for the love of food, people would not eat, and their bodies would perish. Were it not for the love of women, they would not marry, and procreation would cease. The purpose of these inclinations is to preserve the life of each of them so that they may worship Allah alone, and He may be the One loved and worshipped for His own sake—a distinction none but He deserves.

The prophets and the righteous are loved only as a consequence of loving Him, for loving what He loves is part of the completeness of love for Him. He loves the prophets and the righteous, and He loves righteous deeds, so loving them

---

## Page 5188

for Allah’s sake is part of the completeness of love for Him. Loving others alongside Him, however, is the love of the polytheists, who love their rivals to Allah as they love Allah. When a created being loves for Allah’s sake, that love draws him toward loving Allah. When two men love one another for Allah’s sake, meeting and parting on that basis, each draws the other toward loving Allah, as the Most High said:

“My love is assured for those who love one another for My sake; My love is assured for those who sit together for My sake; and My love is assured for those who give generously to one another for My sake. Indeed, Allah has servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whose closeness to Allah will be the envy of prophets and martyrs. They are people who love one another through Allah’s mercy, without wealth they exchange or ties of kinship they maintain. Their faces will surely shine with light, and they will be seated upon seats of light. They will not fear when people fear, nor grieve when people grieve.”

When you love someone for Allah’s sake, Allah is the One loved for His own sake. Whenever you picture that person in your heart, you picture someone beloved to the True One, and so you love him, and your love for Allah increases. Likewise, when you remember the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the prophets and messengers before him, and their righteous companions, and picture them in your heart, this draws your heart toward loving Allah, who bestowed His blessings upon them and through them—provided that you love them for Allah’s sake.

Thus, the person loved for Allah’s sake is drawn toward loving Allah. When someone who loves for Allah’s sake loves another person for His sake, Allah is the One he loves, so he wishes to draw that person toward Allah Most High. Both the one who loves for Allah’s sake and the one loved for His sake are drawn toward Allah. The same applies when love is for something other than Allah, as when each of two people loves

---

## Page 5189

the other for their appearance—as in the case of a woman and a man. The lover seeks the beloved, and the beloved seeks the lover by being drawn toward him. If they love one another, each both attracts and is attracted in both respects, so union necessarily follows. Even if love were confined to one side, the lover would draw the beloved, and the beloved would draw the lover. Yet the beloved does not intend to draw the lover, whereas the lover intends to draw the beloved and is himself drawn.

This is “the cause of the effect on the beloved”: either an image takes shape in the beloved’s heart, producing attraction, or the beloved is drawn without feeling love—as when a man eats food, wears clothing, inhabits a house, or uses other beloved things that have no will of their own.

As for “living beings,” some love others because they bring them kindness. Souls are naturally disposed to love those who treat them kindly. In reality, however, this is merely love of the kindness, not of the benefactor himself. Were that kindness to cease, the love would fade away and might even give way to hatred, for it is not love for Allah’s sake, Mighty and Majestic is He.

Whoever loves someone because he gives to him loves nothing but the giving. Whoever claims that he loves the one who gives to him for Allah’s sake makes a false, untenable, and deceitful claim. Likewise, whoever loves someone because he supports him loves only the support, not the supporter. All of this amounts to following what the soul desires, for in reality he loves only what comes to him by way of securing a benefit or averting harm. Thus, he loves only that benefit and the averting of harm. He only

---

## Page 5190

loved that because it was a means to what he loved. This is neither love for Allah’s sake nor love for the beloved’s own sake. Most people’s love for one another is of this kind. They receive no reward for it in the Hereafter, nor does it benefit them. Indeed, it may lead to hypocrisy and insincere flattery, so that in the Hereafter they become close friends who are enemies to one another—except for the Allah-fearing.

What benefits them in the Hereafter is love rooted in devotion to Allah and offered solely for His sake. As for someone who hopes to receive benefit and support from a person, then claims to love him for Allah’s sake, this is among the soul’s hidden deceptions and the hypocrisy of speech. What benefits a servant is loving, for Allah’s sake, those of His creation whom Allah loves, such as the prophets and the righteous, because loving them draws one closer to Allah and to loving Him. These are the ones who deserve Allah’s love.

Our Prophet would give to those whose hearts were to be won over, while leaving others without gifts who were dearer to him than those he gave to, relying on the faith in their hearts. He gave to those whose hearts were to be won over because of the anxiety and impatience in their hearts, so that his gifts would draw their hearts toward loving Islam and thus loving Allah. His purpose was to call their hearts to love Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and turn them away from the opposite. Thus, he would give to some people for fear that Allah would cast them into the Fire on their faces, and through those gifts he restrained them from what

---

## Page 5191

he disliked in them. Thus, he gave for Allah’s sake and withheld for Allah’s sake. He said:

“Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

Sahīh al-Bukhārī records that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Allah, I am only a distributor. I neither give to anyone nor withhold from anyone; rather, I allocate as I am commanded.”

The image of the beloved represented within the soul stirs the lover to action. For its sake he desires, loves and hates, and he feels delight and gladness whenever it is mentioned, whatever kind of image it may be. It thus becomes like someone who commands and forbids him. Hence, he feels inwardly as though it addresses him with commands, prohibitions and other speech, just as many people see someone they love and revere in their dreams, commanding them, forbidding them and telling them things. Devils appear to the polytheists in the forms of those they worship, commanding and forbidding them.

Those who espouse the notion of the shāhid (the contemplated figure) and profess to follow the spiritual path may claim that they are addressed inwardly through the shāhid’s tongue. Some pray at night with that person opposite them so that they can contemplate him in the light. Others contemplate him in another person during devotional listening. They imagine that they are being addressed and thereby experience an increase within their hearts. This happens because they represent him within themselves. The devil may also appear in his form, so that they experience inward speech coming from that image and say, “We have been addressed by him.” Although this does occur within

---

## Page 5192

the person being addressed, who is addressing him? Here lies the crucial distinction. What he is addressed with comes only from the whisperings of Satan and the self. They may be addressed with good things as a bribe from Satan. They are not addressed with what they recognize as false, lest they be repelled by him. Rather, Satan addresses each of them with what that person considers true.

When a monk disciplines himself, he sometimes sees within himself an image of the Trinity and may even be addressed by it. This is because he had previously pictured it to himself; once his soul was polished through spiritual discipline, it appeared to him. The believer who loves Allah and His Messenger sees the Messenger in his dreams in accordance with his faith. Likewise, he sees Allah Most High in his dreams in accordance with his faith, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

For this reason, many who practise asceticism and devotion become helpers of the disbelievers. They claim that they have been commanded to do this and are addressed with such instructions, imagining that Allah is the One who commanded them. Allah is far exalted above that. Rather, what commands them to do this is the self, Satan, and the polytheism within their souls. Had they been sincere in their devotion to Allah, none of this would have befallen them. This happens only to someone whose worship contains some association of partners with Allah, or who follows a religious innovation. It never happens to someone who is sincere and adheres to the Sunnah.

And since “dreams” are of “three kinds”:
a dream from Allah;

## Page 5193

and a dream arising from one’s own thoughts; and a dream from Satan—what is cast into a person’s mind while awake likewise falls into “three kinds.” Thus spiritual states are also “three”: those from the Most Merciful, those from the self, and those from Satan. Experiences of unveiling and the exercise of powers fall into “three categories”: angelic, arising from the self, and satanic. For an angel has power, the self has power, Satan has power, and the believer’s heart has power.

Whatever comes from an angel or from the believer’s heart is true, while whatever comes from Satan or the whisperings of the self is false. Many groups have confused the two and failed to distinguish between Allah’s allies and His enemies. Consequently, some of these people consider it permissible to fight the prophets, while others believe themselves superior to the prophets, along with other notions of this kind. that they were among Allah’s allies, when in fact the opposite was true. The root of this is that they worshipped through what their own selves loved. ## Page 5195

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

I have written a section in the notebook on events concerning “The Essence of Renunciation and Scrupulousness,” explaining that “renunciation” means abstaining from what brings no benefit: either because it has no benefit at all, or because its benefit is outweighed, since it causes one to forgo something more beneficial or brings about something whose harm exceeds its benefit.

As for things whose benefit is unalloyed or outweighs their harm, renouncing them is foolish. “Scrupulousness,” by contrast, means refraining from what may cause harm. This includes prohibited and doubtful matters, since they may cause harm. Whoever guards against doubtful matters safeguards his honour and religion, while whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd grazing around a protected pasture who is liable to stray into it.

As for “scrupulousness” concerning what involves no harm, or harm that is outweighed—owing to what

---

## Page 5196

accompanies it in the form of a greater benefit or the prevention of another, greater harm—is ignorance and injustice. This encompasses “three categories” from which one should not abstain out of scrupulousness: benefits that equal their attendant harms, outweigh them, or are unalloyed—such as what is simply permissible, recommended, or obligatory. Abstaining from these out of scrupulousness is misguidance.

I shall explain this in detail here:

“Renunciation” is the opposite of desire. One says, “So-and-so renounces such-and-such,” and “So-and-so desires it.” “Desire” is a form of volition. Renouncing something therefore means having no desire for it, whether accompanied by aversion to it or by the absence of both desire and aversion, so that one neither desires nor dislikes it. Anyone who does not desire or want something renounces it.

Just as, on Allah’s path, it is praiseworthy to renounce those worldly excesses that Allah has encouraged people to renounce, so too is it praiseworthy to desire and seek what Allah has praised people for wanting and desiring. This is why volition is the foundation of the path. As Allah Most High says:

“And do not turn away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is those whose striving will be appreciated.”

There are numerous similar passages.

---

## Page 5197

He has likewise encouraged “renunciation” and condemned its opposite in His words:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornments—We will repay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Competition for more distracts you”—and the rest of the surah.

Allah Most High says:

“And you devour inheritance altogether, and love wealth with immense love.”

He also says:

“Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord, and he himself bears witness to that. And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth.”

Allah Most High says:

“Know that the life of this world is but play, amusement, adornment, and boasting among yourselves”—and the rest of the verse.

This is a vast subject. The purpose here is simply to distinguish “renunciation prescribed by the revealed law”—which is praiseworthy—from other forms of renunciation, and “desire prescribed by the revealed law”—which is praiseworthy—from other forms of desire. Renunciation is often confused with laziness, incapacity, and idleness in fulfilling the commands of the revealed law. Likewise, prescribed desire is often confused with greed, covetousness, and activity whose undertaking amounts to misguided striving.

As for “scrupulousness,” it means avoiding an action, guarding against it, refraining and holding back from it, and being wary of it. It comes down to disliking something, feeling averse to it, and hating it. This, too, is a positive reality—although there is disagreement over what a prohibition requires: is it the nonoccurrence of the prohibited act, or the performance of its opposite? Most proponents of affirmation hold the latter view. There is thus no doubt that a person cannot be described as scrupulous, as exercising scrupulous restraint, or as guarding against sin unless he actually refrains and holds back, which constitutes doing the opposite of what is prohibited.

---

## Page 5198

And the “correct analysis” is that when the prohibited act does not occur, a person is spared its harmful consequences—censure, punishment, and the like. When he actively refrains, guards against it, and avoids it, he has performed a righteous deed, an act of obedience and piety, and so receives the benefits of that deed—praise, reward, and so forth. Thus, the absence of harm results from the absence of evil deeds, while the attainment of benefit results from the performance of good deeds.

In sum, “renunciation” consists in not wishing for or desiring what one renounces, whereas “scrupulousness” consists in feeling aversion and dislike toward what one scrupulously avoids. The absence of desire is appropriate only toward something that offers no unmixed or predominant benefit. By contrast, aversion is appropriate only toward something that entails unmixed or predominant harm.

If we suppose that something has neither benefit nor harm, or that its benefit and harm are equal in every respect, then it is appropriate neither to desire it nor to dislike it. Renunciation is therefore appropriate toward it, but scrupulousness is not. It thus becomes clear that everything toward which scrupulousness is appropriate is also something toward which renunciation is appropriate, but not vice versa. This is plain: whatever it is appropriate to dislike and feel averse to, it is also appropriate not to desire or wish for. For where aversion is appropriate, the absence of desire is all the more so; and the presence of aversion entails the absence of desire, but not vice versa.

Not everything that it is appropriate not to desire is something that it is appropriate to dislike. Indeed, matters may arise that it is appropriate neither to desire nor to dislike, neither to love nor to hate, and neither to command nor to forbid.

---

## Page 5199

This makes it clear that neither renunciation nor scrupulousness is appropriate toward obligatory or recommended acts, whereas both are appropriate toward forbidden or disliked acts. As for permissible acts, renunciation is appropriate, but scrupulousness is not. This much is clear and can be understood with the slightest reflection.

The real issue arises when conflicting considerations bear on an act: is it commanded, forbidden, or permissible? It also arises when something ordinarily permissible is accompanied by a factor that makes it commanded or forbidden, or when something commanded is accompanied by a factor that makes it forbidden, and vice versa. Thus, when good and ill effects, benefits and harms, coexist and conflict, discernment is needed.

Examples include excessive hunger or thirst that harms the mind and body and prevents the performance of obligatory or recommended acts more beneficial than it. The same applies to going barefoot, going unclothed, and walking in ways that harm a person without any benefit. An example is the report of Abū Isrā’īl, who vowed to fast and to remain standing without sitting down, seeking shade, or speaking. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Tell him to sit down, seek shade, speak, and complete

## Page 5201

his fast.” Reported by al-Bukhārī. This is a broad subject.

As for reward being proportionate to obedience, obedience to Allah and His Messenger may consist in an easy deed, just as Allah has made the “two phrases” easy for Muslims, although they are the best of deeds. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy in the balance, and beloved to the Most Merciful: ‘Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him; glory be to Allah, the Magnificent.’”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both related it in their Sahīh collections.

If it were said, “Reward is proportionate to the benefit and usefulness of the deed,” that would be correct. The “former” characterization concerns its relation to the command, and the “latter” its inherent quality. A deed’s benefit and usefulness may derive solely from its being commanded, from its inherent quality, or from both. From the first perspective, deeds are classified as obedience or disobedience; from the second, as good or evil. Obedience and disobedience describe a deed in relation to the command, whereas good and evil describe it in itself. ... (1)

Yet many people affirm only the “first,” as do the Ash'arīs and a group of jurists from our school and others. Some affirm only the “second,” as do the Mu'tazilah and a group

## Page 5202

of jurists from our school and others. The correct position is to affirm both considerations, as indicated by the explicit statements of the imams, the words of the early generations, and the majority of scholars from our school and others.

As for a deed’s being arduous, this is not what gives it merit or makes it superior. A meritorious deed may, however, be arduous; its merit then derives from something other than its hardship. Persevering in it despite the hardship increases its reward and recompense. Thus, reward increases with hardship, just as someone who travels farther to the Sacred House for Hajj or ‘umrah receives a greater reward than someone nearby. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ‘Ā’ishah concerning ‘umrah:

“Your reward is proportionate to your exertion.”

This is because the reward is proportionate to the effort involved in covering the distance: the greater the distance, the greater the exertion, and thus the greater the reward. The same applies to jihad, and to his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The one proficient in the Quran is with the noble, righteous scribes, while the one who recites it, stumbling over it and finding it difficult, has two rewards.”

Reward therefore often increases in proportion to hardship and fatigue—not because fatigue and hardship are themselves the purpose of the deed, but because the deed necessarily entails them. This applies to our revealed law, in which burdens and shackles have been lifted from us, no hardship has been imposed upon us, and no difficulty is intended for us. Under the revealed laws of those before us, however, hardship may have been required of them.

Many worshippers regard hardship, pain, and fatigue in themselves as things sought for their own sake and as means of drawing closer to Allah, because they cause the soul to turn away from pleasures and from attachment

## Page 5203

to this world, and sever the heart’s attachment to the body. This is the kind of asceticism practised by the Sabians, the Indians, and others. Thus, you find these people, together with monks who resemble them, undertaking arduous, severe, exhausting forms of worship and asceticism, although these bring no benefit, bear no fruit, and serve no useful purpose—except for whatever slight benefit there may be, which cannot offset the painful torment they experience.

A parallel to this corrupt principle is the praise offered by some ignorant people when they say, “So-and-so has neither married nor slaughtered an animal.” This is praise of monks who neither marry nor slaughter animals. As for those of pure monotheistic faith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

These practices are part of corrupt religion, which is blameworthy, just as being content with the life of this world is blameworthy. been prescribed by Allah in the form of worship and ascetic practices.

## Page 5205

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section: Purifying the Soul, and How It Is Purified by Refraining from Prohibited Acts While Performing Commanded Acts

Allah Most High says:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it,”

and:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself.”

Qatādah, Ibn ʿUyaynah, and others said: “Successful indeed is the one who purifies his soul through obedience to Allah and righteous deeds.”

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: “Successful indeed is a soul that Allah has purified, and failed indeed is a soul that Allah has debased.” Al-Wālibī likewise related this from Ibn ʿAbbās, but its chain of transmission is disconnected. This, however, is not what the verse means (1). Rather, the first interpretation is unquestionably what is intended, both in wording and meaning.

As for the wording, in His statement, “whoever purifies it,” “whoever” is a relative pronoun, and there must be a pronoun referring back

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) The printed edition reads: “And this is not what is intended by the verse.”
> Usāmah ibn al-Zahrā’

---

## Page 5206

to “whoever.” Thus, if one says, “Successful indeed is the person who purifies it,” the subject pronoun in “purifies it” refers back to “whoever.” This is the unquestionably sound construction, just as one says, “Successful indeed is whoever fears Allah,” or, “Successful indeed is whoever obeys his Lord.”

If, however, the meaning were “Successful indeed is whoever Allah has purified,” there would no longer be any pronoun in the clause referring back to “whoever.” On this interpretation, the subject pronoun refers to Allah, who is not the referent of “whoever,” while the object pronoun refers to the soul previously mentioned. Thus neither the subject pronoun nor the object pronoun refers back to “whoever.” The relative clause would therefore lack a pronoun referring back to its antecedent, which is impermissible.

Admittedly, had it said, “Successful indeed is whoever Allah has purified his soul,” or, “whoever Allah has purified it for,” or something similar, the construction would have been sound. It is astonishing that this escaped those grammarians who advocated that interpretation.

He did not say, “Successful indeed is a soul He has purified.” In that case, “He has purified” would be an adjectival clause describing “a soul,” rather than a relative clause. Instead, He said:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it.”

The clause is therefore a relative clause attached to “whoever,” not an adjective describing it.

Nor did He say, “Successful indeed is the soul which He has purified.” Had that been said, with the subject pronoun in “has purified it” referring back to Allah’s name, the construction would have been sound.

If, then, they force the interpretation and say that the implied meaning of “Successful indeed is the one who purifies it” is “the soul which He has purified,” and argue that the object pronoun in “purifies” refers back to “whoever,” which can refer to both masculine and feminine

---

## Page 5207

and to singular and plural, with the pronoun thus referring to its feminine sense, its femininity being grammatical rather than natural—hence “Successful indeed is” uses the masculine form qad aflaha rather than the feminine qad aflahat—the answer to them is: Besides departing from eloquent Arabic, this construction is valid only when the wording indicates that meaning, as in “And whoever …” (1), on the understanding that what is intended is “for us”; likewise in His words:

“Among them are those who listen to you,”

and similar expressions.

Here, however, neither the word “whoever” nor what follows it indicates that it refers to the grammatically feminine noun “soul.” Words cannot be assigned an intended meaning for which they provide no indication. The speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is above such a thing.

Even supposing that the pronoun in “purifies it” could refer either to “a soul” or to “whoever”—although nothing in the word “whoever” requires the pronoun to refer back to it—referring it to the feminine noun would be more appropriate than referring it to a word that admits both masculine and feminine reference. Indeed, the latter is more evidently masculine, since it gives no indication of femininity.

When a statement admits two meanings, it must be understood according to the more apparent of the two. Whoever forces another interpretation departs from established Arabic usage, and the Quran is above that. Departing without evidence from what the wording plainly indicates to something it does not indicate is absolutely impermissible. How much more so when its meaning is unequivocal! Allah has stated that He inspires both piety and wickedness. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

## Page 5208

The point here is to command people to purify their souls and warn them against corrupting them, as in His words:

“Successful indeed is he who purifies himself.”

If the meaning were assumed to be, “Successful indeed is he whose soul Allah has purified,” this would contain neither a command nor a prohibition addressed to them, neither encouragement nor warning. When the Quran commands or prohibits, it does not speak merely of “divine decree.” It does not say, “Whomever Allah has made a believer.” Rather, it says:

“Successful indeed are the believers.”

“Successful indeed is he who purifies himself.”

Mentioning divine decree alone in this context would defeat the intended purpose. Such speech would be unworthy even of someone with the weakest intellect—how, then, could it befit the speech of Allah? Do you not see that, when commanding, prohibiting, encouraging, and warning, He mentions the corresponding promises and threats, praise and blame? He mentions divine decree only when explaining His blessings upon them, whether blessings unrelated to their own actions or His blessing of faith and righteous deeds. He also mentions it when speaking of His power and will. In the context of commands, however, He mentions it only in connection with His blessings, as in His words:

“Were it not for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, there would have been no purification…”

—and the rest of the verse. This is appropriate to that context.

His words, “Successful indeed is he who purifies himself,” and the verse under discussion belong to the second category, not the first.

The point is to discuss purification. Allah Most High says:

“Tell the believers to lower…”

—and the rest of the verse. He also says:

“Then go back; that is purer for you.”

And:

“Those who do not give zakah.”

And:

“You are not responsible if he does not purify himself.”

The basic meaning of “zakah” is an increase in goodness. Hence one speaks of the growth of crops and of the growth of

---

## Page 5209

wealth when it increases. Goodness will never grow except by abandoning evil. Crops do not flourish until the tangled growth among them is removed. Likewise, the soul and its deeds do not flourish until whatever opposes their goodness is removed. A person cannot purify himself without abandoning evil, for evil sullies and debases the soul.

Al-Zajjāj explained dassāhā (he debased it) as making the soul lowly, contemptible, and base. Al-Farrā explained the expression by noting that the miser conceals himself, his home, and his wealth. Ibn Qutayba explained it as concealing the soul through wickedness and disobedience. The wicked man buries his soul—that is, he suppresses and hides it—whereas the doer of good makes himself known and elevates his soul. Generous Arabs would settle on hilltops to make themselves known, while the mean-spirited would settle in outlying places and valleys.

Righteousness and piety expand the soul and bring ease to the heart, so that a person finds within himself a spaciousness and openness beyond what he experienced before. As he opens himself through righteousness, piety, and goodness, Allah expands his soul and brings ease to his heart. Wickedness and miserliness, by contrast, suppress, abase, and humiliate the soul, leaving the miser feeling constricted within himself.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, illustrated this in an authentic hadith, saying:

“The miser and the giver of charity are like two men wearing coats of iron, with their hands pressed up against their collarbones. Whenever the giver intends to give charity, his coat expands and loosens around him until it covers his fingertips and wipes away his footprints. But whenever the miser intends to give charity, his coat contracts, and each ring grips its place.”

“I saw Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gesturing with his finger inside the neck opening of his garment. If only you could have seen it as he tried to widen it, yet it would not widen!”

Reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

## Page 5210

Concealing or displaying one’s home follows from this. Allah Most High says:

Likewise, the owner of a miserly, wicked soul has buried it within his body, folded in upon itself. Thus, at death, it is pulled from his body as a skewer is pulled from wet wool. By contrast, the righteous, God-fearing, pure soul, which its owner has purified so that it has risen, expanded, and grown in dignity and nobility, flows out of the body at death like a drop from the mouth of a waterskin, or slips out like a hair from dough.

Ibn ʿAbbās said:

Allah Most High says:

“And the good land,” to the end of the verse.

---

## Page 5211

his Lord and has faith in what has come from his Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This affirmation, faith, aversion, and struggle against the soul involve deeds performed by the purified soul, through which it becomes purer still. By contrast, when it commits evil deeds, it becomes defiled, buried, and stunted, like crops among which tangled growth has sprung up. Reward is granted only for an actual deed, and the same applies to punishment.

As for the mere absence of action, it entails neither reward nor punishment, but rather the absence of both. Allah, glorified be He, has commanded good and forbidden evil. There is agreement that a command requires an actual deed, but disagreement over whether a prohibition requires something positive or merely an absence. One view holds that it requires something positive—namely, refraining. This is the majority view. Another holds that what is required is the absence of evil: that one simply does not commit it.

“The correct analysis” is that when a believer forbids wrongdoing, he must not approach it, must resolve to refrain from it, and must find its commission abhorrent. This is undoubtedly something positive. It is therefore inconceivable that a believer who knows that it is . . . (1) positive in nature. Yet he may have no desire for it, just as one has a natural aversion to eating carrion. Even so, he must believe that it is forbidden and resolve to refrain from it in obedience to the Lawgiver. This goes beyond natural aversion: it is something positive for which he is rewarded. His reward, however, is not like that of someone who restrains his soul and struggles against it to keep it from pursuing

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank space in the original.

---

## Page 5212

what is forbidden. As for someone whose aversion to forbidden things springs from faith, and whose faith has overcome the influence of his natural disposition, his is the highest of these three states. He possesses the tranquil soul and ranks above the possessor of the self-reproaching soul, which commits a sin and reproaches its possessor for it, wavering and hesitating over whether to commit it. As for someone to whom it has not occurred that Allah has forbidden a thing, and who has no desire for it but simply does not do it, he is neither punished nor rewarded, since he has performed no actual deed for which he might be rewarded or punished.

Thus, if someone says, “What is required is that he does not do it,” and means that this suffices to escape punishment, he is correct. But if he means that one is rewarded for this mere absence of action, that is not so. When a disbeliever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, he inevitably occupies himself with deeds that distract him from faith; abandoning deeds is disbelief for which punishment is incurred. Hence, when Allah mentions the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire, He mentions actual deeds, which defile and bury the soul. Thus, affirming Allah’s oneness and having faith are the greatest means of purifying the soul, while associating partners with Him is the greatest cause of its defilement. The soul is also purified through righteous deeds and charity. All of this was mentioned by the early generations.

Concerning the words,

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself,”

they said: he purifies himself of associating partners with Allah and of disobedience through repentance. Abū Sa‘īd, ‘Atā’, and Qatādah explained it as the alms given at Eid al-Fitr.

They did not mean that the verse referred exclusively to these alms. Rather, they meant that whoever gives these alms and performs the Eid prayer falls within the scope of this verse and the one that follows it. Thus,

---

## Page 5213

whenever Yazīd ibn Habīb went out to pray, he took something to give in charity before the prayer, even if he could find nothing but onions.

Al-Hasan explained the words,

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself,”

as referring to one whose deeds are pure. Abū al-Ahwas said: “Purification in all matters.” Al-Zajjāj said: “He purifies himself by obeying Allah, Mighty and Majestic.” The word zākī denotes growth and abundance.

They offered similar explanations of His words:

“And woe to those who associate partners with Allah, who do not give zakat.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “They do not testify that there is no god but Allah.” Mujāhid said: “They do not purify their deeds,” meaning that their deeds are not pure. It was also said: “They do not purify them through sincere devotion.” It seems that he meant—and Allah knows best—those who act to be seen by others, for this is a form of associating partners with Allah.

Al-Hasan explained it as: “They neither believe in zakat nor acknowledge it.” Al-Dahhāk said: “They neither give charity nor spend in obedience to Allah.” Ibn al-Sā’ib said: “They do not pay zakat on their wealth.” He said: “They used to perform Hajj and ‘umrah, but did not pay zakat.”

The correct understanding is that the verse encompasses everything through which a person purifies himself, including affirming Allah’s oneness and performing righteous deeds. It is like His words:

“Would you be willing to purify yourself?”

and His words:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself.”

The obligatory alms had not yet been prescribed when this verse was revealed.

If it is objected that “give” is a transitive verb, the answer is that this resembles His words:

“Then, if they were asked to lapse into disbelief, they would readily do so.”

It was stated before this that

---

## Page 5214

the Messenger called them, which was a request on his part. This wording therefore implies that proof had been established against them through the messengers, who call them only to that which purifies their souls.

Relevant to the fact that purification entails cleansing—for their meanings coincide—are His words:

“Take from their wealth charity by which you cleanse them”

of evil,

“and purify them”

with good.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O Allah, cleanse me with water, hail, and snow.”

He would offer this supplication at the opening of prayer, when standing upright after bowing, and when bathing. These things cool whatever is washed with them, and hail imparts strength and firmness. Things that bring joy are described in terms of coolness and as a delight to the eyes. Thus, tears of joy are cold, whereas tears of sorrow are hot: what distresses the soul brings it sorrow and grief, while what pleases it brings it joy and gladness, which cool the inner self. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, therefore asked Allah to wash away sins in a manner that would cool hearts to the utmost, through the joy and gladness of having the sins that distress the soul removed.

His words, “with snow, hail, and cold water,” express this through a likeness drawn from things possessing this quality; sins themselves are not washed away with these substances. Similarly, one might say: “Let us taste the coolness of Your pardon and the sweetness of Your forgiveness.” When Abū Qatādah paid off the debtor’s debt, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Now

---

## Page 5215

you have cooled his skin.” People also speak of “the coolness of certainty and the heat of doubt.” They say, “This brings cool relief to the heart,” when something is true and the heart recognizes it and rejoices in it, until it becomes as cool as snow. The soul’s illness consists of doubt, desire, or anger, and all three generate heat. Of someone who attains what he seeks, people say, “His heart has cooled,” for the seeker experiences the heat of seeking.

His words:

“Take from their wealth”

show that doing good deeds cleanses the soul and purifies it of past sins, for He said this after His words, “And others have acknowledged,” to the end of the verse. Repentance and righteous deeds thus bring about cleansing and purification. This is why, in the passage beginning, “Tell the believing men to lower their gaze,” and the subsequent verses, He said, “And turn to Allah in repentance,” to the end of the verse. He commanded them all to repent in connection with what He had mentioned, because no one is free of shortcomings of this kind. As recorded in the Sahīh:

“Allah has decreed for the son of Adam his share of unlawful sexual conduct,”

and the rest of the hadith.

It is likewise recorded in the Sahīh that His words:

“Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds”

were revealed on account of a man who had engaged in every form of intimacy with a woman except intercourse. He then felt remorse, whereupon the verse was revealed.

In this regard, a Muslim needs to fear Allah and restrain his soul from its desires. Mere inclination and desire are not punishable; rather, punishment is for following them and acting upon them. If his soul desires something and he restrains it, his restraint is an act of worship devoted to Allah and a righteous deed.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet said:

“The fighter in Allah’s cause is the one who struggles against his own soul for Allah’s sake.”

He is therefore commanded to struggle against his soul

---

## Page 5216

just as he is commanded to struggle against those who command sinful acts and call others to them. Yet his need to struggle against his own soul is greater, for this is an individual obligation, whereas the other is a collective obligation. Perseverance in this is among the finest deeds, for this struggle is the very essence of that other struggle: whoever perseveres in it will persevere in the other.

As he said:

“The emigrant is the one who abandons evil deeds.”

In this struggle, however, a person is praiseworthy only if he prevails, unlike in the former, for:

“Whoever is killed or prevails, We shall grant him a great reward.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The strong man is not the one who overpowers others in wrestling,”

and so on.

This is because Allah has commanded a person to restrain his soul from its desires and to fear standing before his Lord. He thus acquires faith that helps him in this struggle. If he is overcome, it is because his faith is weak, and he is therefore remiss in neglecting what he was commanded to do. This is unlike facing a disbelieving enemy, whose body may be stronger. Sins occur only when the soul fails to comply with what it has been commanded to do. When it complies with the command, it does not commit what is forbidden, for the two are opposites.

Allah Most High said:

“Thus We would turn evil away from him,”

and the rest of the verse.

And he said—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them.”

Thus Satan does not lead Allah’s sincere servants astray. Going astray is the opposite of following right guidance; it consists in following one’s desires. Whoever finds his soul inclining toward something forbidden should worship Allah as Allah has commanded, devoting his religion sincerely to Him. This will turn evil and indecency away from him. … (1) out of fear and love; and worship is for Him

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Blank in the original.

---

## Page 5217

alone, and this prevents sins. If he is repentant, then, should [his faith] be deficient and he commit sins, it effaces them after they occur. It is like an antidote that wards off the effects of poison and removes them once they occur; like nourishment from food and drink; and like lawful enjoyment, which prevents the soul from seeking what is forbidden. If such a desire arises, he seeks to remove it. It is also like knowledge, which prevents doubt and dispels it once it arises, and like medicine, which preserves health and wards off illness. Likewise, the faith within the heart is preserved by kindred qualities present within it. If an illness involving doubts and desires develops within it, these remove it. Illness arises only when the means of maintaining health are deficient; likewise, the heart becomes ill only because its faith is deficient.

Faith and disbelief are likewise opposites. With any pair of opposites, one sometimes prevents the other and at other times removes it, as with blackness and whiteness … (1) takes its place and removes it if it is already present. The same applies to good deeds, evil deeds, and nullification … (2) and the Mu‘tazilah [hold] that a major sin nullifies good deeds, even faith itself, and that whoever dies persisting in it would not be … (3) al-Jubbā’ī and his son, regarding the weighing of deeds against one another.

However, they said:

“Whoever’s evil deeds outweigh his good deeds will remain in the Fire forever.”

Weighing deeds against one another without eternal punishment is a view. As for nullification, what is unanimously agreed upon is that all good deeds are nullified by disbelief, as He said:

“Whoever among you turns back from his religion,”

and the rest of the verse. And His saying:

“And whoever rejects faith
