objected to the state that had prompted al-Shiblī to utter these words, since it was incompatible with contentment. Had he uttered them in the prescribed manner, he would not have objected. Among the reports he mentions are weak ones, such as the following, which he cites without a chain of transmission:

He said: “It is related that Moses said, ‘My God, guide me to a deed which, if I perform it, will earn Your pleasure.’

“He replied, ‘You are unable to do that.’ Moses then fell prostrate, humbly supplicating, and Allah revealed to him: ‘O son of ʿImrān, My pleasure lies in your contentment with Me.’”

This Israelite account is questionable, for it may be said that it is not fitting to relate such a thing about Moses son of ʿImrān. It is well known that these Israelite accounts have no chains of transmission and cannot establish proof in any religious matter unless they have been authentically transmitted to us, as with accounts about the Children of Israel authentically related by our Prophet. Some of them, however, are known to be false, such as this one. Moses is among the greatest of the messengers of firm resolve and among the foremost Muslims. How, then, can it be said that he is unable to perform deeds that earn Allah’s pleasure, when Allah Most High is pleased with the first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers and those who followed them in righteousness? Would He then not be pleased with Moses son of ʿImrān, to whom the Most Merciful spoke? The Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation.”

“Their reward with their Lord is Gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.”

It is well known that Moses son of ʿImrān, peace be upon him, is among the best of those who believe and do righteous deeds.

---

## Page 5268

Moreover, Allah singled Moses out for an honor beyond His pleasure, saying:

“And I bestowed upon you love from Me that you would be brought up under My eye.”

Furthermore, addressing him as “O son of ‘Imrān” differs from the manner of address Allah records in the Quran, where He says, “O Moses.” That other manner of address evidently carries a measure of disparagement.

Another example is the report that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī:

“To proceed: All goodness lies in contentment. If you can be content, then do so; otherwise, be patient.”

These are fine words, even though their chain of transmission is unknown. Since the reports he cites—with chains of transmission, with disconnected chains, or with the opening links omitted—include both authentic material and otherwise, this particular saying must be considered accordingly: he attributes it to Abū Sulaymān only through a disconnected report. By common agreement, such a report cannot establish its attribution to Abū Sulaymān.

Although some maintain that a disconnected report constitutes proof, here it is not known how such a report stands in relation to weak and non-weak reports. Once that is known, however, it no longer constitutes proof, by scholarly consensus—as with someone known sometimes to remember the chain correctly and sometimes to err in it.

The books that provide chains of transmission for accounts and sayings of these shaykhs—such as Abū Nu‘aym’s Hilyat al-Awliyā’ (The Adornment of the Saints), Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān’s Tabaqāt al-Sūfiyya (The Generations of the Sufis), Ibn al-Jawzī’s Safwat al-Safwa (The Choicest of the Chosen), and similar works—do not mention this saying as something attributed to Shaykh Abū Sulaymān.

Consider what he did transmit from him with a chain of transmission, saying: “He said to Ahmad ibn Abī al-Hawārī: ‘O Ahmad, I have indeed been granted, of contentment,

---

## Page 5269

a share such that, were He to cast me into the Fire, I would be content with that.’” This saying is transmitted from Abū Sulaymān with a chain of transmission. Accordingly, al-Qushayrī related it from him through his teacher Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān, unlike that other saying, which was not related from him through a chain of transmission. There is therefore no basis for attributing it to Shaykh Abū Sulaymān.

Al-Qushayrī then paired this second saying of Abū Sulaymān with a better one, for before relating it he said:

“Abū ‘Uthmān al-Hīrī al-Naysābūrī was asked about the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘I ask You for contentment after the decree.’ He replied, ‘Because contentment after the decree is true contentment.’”

These words of Shaykh Abū ‘Uthmān are fine and sound.

After this, it was related through a chain of transmission that Shaykh Abū Sulaymān said:

“I hope that I have come to know some measure of contentment. Were He to admit me into the Fire, I would be content with that.”

This makes clear that what Abū Sulaymān spoke of is not contentment, but only a resolve to be content. Contentment is only that which follows the decree. If this is a resolve, then resolve may endure or come undone. How often resolutions come undone—especially those of the Sufis!

Thus, one of them was asked, “How did you come to know your Lord?”

He replied, “Through the undoing of resolutions and the thwarting of aspirations.”

Allah Most High said to those superior to these shaykhs:

“And you had certainly wished for death before you encountered it, and you have now seen it while you were looking on.”

And He Most High said: “O you who believe, why do you say what you do not

## Page 5270

do?”

“Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do.”

“Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks as though they were a solidly joined structure.”

Al-Tirmidhī reports: “Some of the Companions said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘If we knew which deed was most beloved to Allah, we would do it.’ Then Allah Most High revealed this verse.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Have you not seen those who were told, ‘Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakah’? But when fighting was prescribed for them, a group of them feared people as they feared Allah, or even more. They said, ‘Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had granted us a little more time!’” To the end of the verse.

These people had resolved to fight and had desired it, yet when they were tested with it, they disliked it and fled from it. How can the pain of fighting compare with the pain of the Fire and Allah’s punishment, which no one can bear?

Similar to this is what they relate about Sumnūn al-Muhibb, who used to say:

“I desire nothing but You;
So test me however You will.”

He was immediately afflicted with distress—that is, he was unable to pass urine. He would go around the schools, handing out walnuts to the children and saying, “Pray for your lying uncle.”

Abū Nuʿaym al-Asbahānī related from Abū Bakr al-Wāsitī that Sumnūn said, “My Lord, I am content with whatever You decree for me.” He was then unable to pass urine for fourteen days, writhing like a snake, twisting to the right and left. Then, when

---

## Page 5271

he was able to pass urine again, he said, “My Lord, I have repented to You.”

Abū Nuʿaym said: The slightest trial exposed the error in Sumnūn’s claim to contentment. Yet Sumnūn was held up as an example, and his station in love was renowned. It is even related that Ibrāhīm ibn Fātik said, “I saw Sumnūn addressing the people in the Sacred Mosque. A small bird approached, drawing ever nearer until it perched on his hands. Then it kept striking the ground with its beak until it bled, and the bird died.” He also said, “One day I saw him speaking about love, and the mosque’s lamps began swaying and smashed against one another.”

In his chapter on contentment, al-Qushayrī relates a similar account concerning Ruwaym the Quran reciter, Sumnūn’s companion. He says: Ruwaym said, “If Hell were placed to the right of a person who is content, he would not ask Allah to move it to his left.”

This resembles Sumnūn’s words:
“So test me however You will.”

If he could not patiently endure difficulty passing urine, could he bear having the Fire on his right?

Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyād was of a higher spiritual rank than these men. He was afflicted with difficulty passing urine, and the pain overwhelmed him until he said, “By my love for You, I implore You to relieve me!” And he was relieved.

Although Ruwaym was one of al-Junayd’s companions, they did not regard him as belonging to this rank. Rather, the Sufis say that he returned to worldly pursuits and abandoned Sufism. It is even related that Jaʿfar al-Khuldī, al-Junayd’s companion, said, “Whoever wishes a secret to be kept

---

## Page 5272

should do as Ruwaym did. He concealed his love of this world for forty years.”

He was asked, “How could that be?”

He replied, “Ismā'īl ibn Ishāq the judge was appointed to the judgeship of Baghdad. A firm friendship existed between them, so he drew Ruwaym close to him and appointed him as his agent at his door. Ruwaym abandoned Sufi dress and began wearing khazz cloth, fine linen, and dībaqī cloth, eating fine foods, and building houses. As it turned out, he had concealed his love of this world only while it remained beyond his reach. When he obtained it, he revealed the love for it that he had concealed.”

Nevertheless, he—may Allah have mercy on him—was known for his acts of worship, and he followed the school of Dāwūd.

Such utterances, voiced by someone in a spiritual state who has not considered the implications and consequences of his words, must not be made into a method or adopted as a path. They may, however, indicate the contentment, love, and similar qualities he possesses, along with his limited understanding of the demands of the path and of the piety and patience he can and cannot sustain.

The Messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—have greater knowledge of the path to Allah, are better guided, and offer more sincere counsel. Whoever departs from their Sunnah and their way is deficient, mistaken, and deprived, even if he is not a sinner, a defiantly disobedient person, or an unbeliever.

A similar case is that of “the Bedouin whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, visited when he was ill and as frail as a fledgling. He asked, ‘Had you been supplicating to Allah for anything?’

“He replied, ‘I used to say: O Allah, whatever punishment You would inflict upon me in the Hereafter, inflict it upon me in this world.’

“He said, ‘Glory be to Allah! You cannot withstand it or bear it. Why did you not say: “Our Lord, grant us in

---

## Page 5273

this world good, and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire”?’”

This man, too, was driven by his fear of the punishment of the Fire and his desire for a safe outcome to ask that his punishment be hastened in this world. Yet he was mistaken and wrong to do so. Errors and mistakes are exceedingly common even when a person’s intentions are good and sound, and despite his righteousness, virtue, religious devotion, asceticism, scrupulousness, and miraculous gifts. Being a friend of Allah does not require being protected from errors and mistakes, or even from sins. The greatest friend of Allah after the Messengers is Abū Bakr al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him. Yet it is authentically reported that, when he interpreted a dream, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him:

“You were right about some of it and wrong about some of it.”

It seems—and Allah knows best—that when Abū Sulaymān said, “If He cast me into the Fire, I would be content with that,” someone may have conveyed what he understood these words to mean by reporting that he said, “Contentment means neither asking Allah for Paradise nor seeking His protection from the Fire.”

Abū Sulaymān’s actual statement does not indicate that he is content with that; rather, it indicates his resolve to be content with it. Yet we know that this resolve will not endure but will collapse. We also know that it would have been better to leave those words unsaid, and that they call for correction, just as the claims of Sumnūn and Ruwaym, and other such claims, called for correction. Nevertheless, there is an enormous difference between this statement and the other one.

The other statement implies that whoever asks Allah for Paradise and seeks His protection from the Fire is not content. There is a difference between someone who says, “If He did such-and-such, I would be content,” and

---

## Page 5274

someone who says, “Only a person who neither seeks good nor flees evil is content.”

This and other considerations show that Shaykh Abū Sulaymān was far above making such a statement. He was among the most eminent and distinguished spiritual masters, and among the most faithful in following the Sharia. Indeed, he said:

“An insight of the kind known among the Sufis may occur to my heart, but I do not accept it without two witnesses: the Book and the Sunnah.”

How could someone who refuses to accept the insights of his own heart without two witnesses say such words?

Shaykh Abū Sulaymān also said:

“A person inspired to do something good must not act upon it until he hears a transmitted report supporting it. Once he hears such a report, it is light upon light.”

Indeed, even his companion Ahmad ibn Abī al-Hawārī was among the spiritual masters most faithful in following the Sunnah—how much more so Abū Sulaymān himself! The full vindication of Abū Sulaymān against the attribution of these words will become clear in the discussion of

“The Second Issue”

This concerns the statement, whoever its speaker may be: “Contentment means neither asking Allah for Paradise nor seeking His protection from the Fire.”

Before addressing this, we shall offer an introduction that explains the root of the confusion and inconsistency found in such statements. Many people among those versed in jurisprudence, Sufis, speculative theologians, and others have imagined that Paradise consists of enjoying created things: eating, drinking, sexual relations, clothing, hearing pleasant sounds, and smelling pleasant fragrances. They have not included any other kind of bliss within the meaning of Paradise.

They then divided into two groups:

---

## Page 5275

One group denied that the believers would see their Lord, as was the position of the Jahmiyyah among the Mu‘tazilah and others.

Others affirmed the vision: either the vision described by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as affirmed by Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah; or a vision they interpreted as an increase in unveiling or knowledge, or as occurring through a sixth sense. Such views were held by Dirār ibn ‘Amr and groups of speculative theologians who claimed to defend Ahl al-Sunnah on the question of the vision, even though what they affirm is of the kind denied by the Mu‘tazilah and the Dirāriyyah. Their disagreement with one another is verbal, whereas their disagreement with Ahl al-Sunnah is substantive. Thus Bishr and others like him interpreted the vision in much the same way as these people.

The point here is that some who affirm the vision denied that the believer would find bliss in the very act of seeing his Lord. They argued that there is no affinity between the temporally originated and the eternal. This was stated by the scholar Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī in al-Risālah al-Nizāmiyyah (The Nizāmiyyah Epistle), and by Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl in some of his books. It is related that Ibn ‘Aqīl heard a man say:

“I ask You for the delight of looking upon Your Face.”

He replied:

“You there! Suppose that He has a Face: does He have a Face that one can delight in looking upon?”

Abū al-Ma‘ālī stated that Allah creates bliss for them through certain created things, coinciding with the vision. As for finding bliss in the vision itself, he denied it, and counted this among the secrets of divine oneness.

---

## Page 5276

Most of those who affirm the vision also affirm that the believers will find bliss in seeing their Lord. This is the position of the early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and the masters of the spiritual path, as expressed in the hadith recorded by al-Nasā’ī and others from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, keep me alive if life is better for me, and cause me to die if death is better for me. O Allah, I ask You for fear of You in private and in public. I ask You to enable me to speak the truth in anger and contentment. I ask You for moderation in poverty and wealth. I ask You for bliss that never ends and joy that never ceases. I ask You for contentment after Your decree and a life of comfort after death. I ask You for the delight of looking upon Your Face, and I ask You for longing to meet You, without affliction that harms or a trial that leads astray. O Allah, adorn us with the adornment of faith, and make us rightly guided guides.”

In Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, Suhayb reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will proclaim, ‘O people of Paradise, Allah has a promise for you that He wishes to fulfil.’ They will say, ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and protected us from the Fire?’”

He said:

“Then He will lift the veil, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than looking upon Him.”

The dearer something is, the greater the delight in attaining it. This is agreed upon by the early generations, the leading scholars, and the masters of the spiritual path. Thus, al-Hasan al-Basrī is reported to have said:

“If the worshippers knew that they would not see their Lord in the Hereafter, their souls would melt away in

---

## Page 5277

this world out of longing for Him.” Their statements on this subject are numerous.

Those who agreed with the early generations, the leading scholars, and the spiritual masters that bliss is found in looking upon Allah Most High nevertheless disagreed over “the question of love,” which underlies that bliss. Various groups of … (1) and jurists held that Allah Himself is not the object of love; rather, love means loving obedience to Him and worship of Him. They also said that He does not love His believing servants; rather, His love means His will to bestow kindness upon them and take them under His protection.

This view was adopted by speculative theologians who professed to defend the Sunnah. Indeed, groups among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad fell into it, including Judge Abū Bakr, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī, and others like them. In reality, this is an offshoot of Jahmism and Mu‘tazilism. The first person in Islam to deny “love” was al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham, the teacher of al-Jahm ibn Safwān. Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī slaughtered him as a sacrifice, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices; may Allah accept them. I am sacrificing al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as an intimate friend and did not truly speak to Moses.”

Then he descended and slaughtered him.

What the Quran and Sunnah establish, and what the early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and the masters of the spiritual path agreed upon, is that Allah loves and is loved. Hence, they were joined in this view by those who embraced Sufism among

the speculative theologians, such as Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, and others like them. Abū Hāmid defended this position in al-Ihyā’ and elsewhere. they agreed with these people that Paradise consists only of these things in which created beings take pleasure. Yet they agreed with the early generations and the imams in affirming the vision of Allah and the delight of looking upon Him, and in this they were correct. They began seeking this bliss, their aspirations rising towards it, and fearing that they might miss it. One of them would say:

“I have not worshipped You out of longing for Your Paradise or fear of Your Fire, but to look upon You and out of reverence for You.”

They used other similar expressions. What they intend by this is something higher than eating, drinking, and enjoying created things. But they erred in excluding it from Paradise. They may also err in supposing that they worship Allah without any personal benefit or desire, and that anything sought from Him is a gratification of the self. They imagined that a human being could act without any desire, any object sought, or anything loved. This reflects a poor understanding of the true nature of faith, religion, and the Hereafter.

The reason for this is that a person’s aspiration, attached to the One he seeks, loves, and worships, makes him oblivious to himself, until he is no longer conscious of himself or his own desire. He then supposes that he acts for something other than what he desires, whereas what is sought and holds his aspiration is the ultimate object of his desire, pursuit, and love.

This resembles the condition of many righteous and sincere people and those who experience spiritual states and attain spiritual stations. One of them may have a genuine spiritual experience and sound inward perception, yet lack the words to express himself clearly. Consequently, his speech contains error and a lack of due reverence, despite the soundness of his intent—although, for some people, the error also affects their intent and belief.

Thus, if those who spoke in this way meant by it to seek the vision of Allah

Most High, they were correct in this. But they erred by placing this outside Paradise, thereby failing to accord the name Paradise its due reverence; and objectionable consequences followed from this.

This resembles what is related about al-Shiblī, may Allah have mercy on him: he heard someone reciting:

“Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter.”

He cried out, “Where is the one who desires Allah?” His desire for Allah is praiseworthy, but he was mistaken in supposing that those who desired the Hereafter did not desire Allah. This verse concerns the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who were with him at Uhud, and they are the best of creation. If they did not desire Allah, would those beneath them, such as al-Shiblī and others like him, desire Allah?

Something similar is an incident I know involving one of the shaykhs, who once asked about the words of Allah Most High:

“Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, killing and being killed.”

He said, “If lives and wealth are the price of Paradise, then by what is the vision of Allah attained?” Someone gave him an answer of the same kind as his question. What must be understood is that all the bliss Allah has prepared for His allies—looking upon Him and everything else—is within Paradise, just as everything with which He has threatened His enemies is within the Fire.

Allah Most High has said:

“No soul knows what joy is kept hidden for them as a reward for what they used to do.”

And in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, relates:

“Allah says: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived; rather, he has what I have disclosed to them.’”

Once it is understood that

all of this is included in Paradise, its inhabitants occupy differing ranks, as He says:

“See how We have favored some over others; but the Hereafter is greater in rank and greater in distinction.”

Everything a servant seeks of the Hereafter, whether through worship, supplication, or otherwise, is in Paradise. Seeking Paradise and refuge from the Fire is the way of Allah’s prophets and messengers and all His allies: the foremost who are brought near, and those of the right. Thus, it is related in the Sunan collections:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked one of his Companions, ‘What do you say in your supplication?’

“He replied, ‘I say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and seek refuge in You from the Fire. But I do not know how to make murmured supplications like yours or those of Mu‘ādh.’

“He said, ‘Our murmured supplications revolve around these two.’”

He thus stated that his own murmured supplications, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those of Mu‘ādh—the finest of the regular prayer leaders in Medina during the Prophet’s lifetime—revolved only around Paradise. Could anyone’s words, then, surpass those of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Mu‘ādh, and the Emigrants and Helpers who prayed behind them? Whatever this servant were to seek, it would be within Paradise.

The people of Paradise are of two kinds: the foremost who are brought near, and the righteous, who are those of the right. Allah Most High says:

“No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ‘Illiyyūn.”

“And what will make you know what ‘Illiyyūn is?”

“A written record,”

“witnessed by those brought near.”

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss,”

“on couches, gazing.”

“You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.”

“They will be given a sealed, pure wine to drink.”

“Its seal is musk—so for this let those who compete compete.”

“And its blend is from Tasnīm,”

“a spring from which those brought near drink.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “It is served mixed to those of the right, while those brought near drink it pure.”

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When you hear the caller to prayer, repeat what he says, then invoke blessings upon me. Whoever invokes blessings upon me once, Allah will bless him ten times. He thus stated that al-Wasīlah—which befits only one of Allah’s servants, and which he hoped would be his—is a rank in Paradise. Can there then be anything higher than al-Wasīlah, outside Paradise, that created beings could attain?

It is also established in the Sahīh, in the hadith about the angels who seek out people in gatherings of remembrance, that he said:

“Then He says:

‘What if they had seen it?’ They reply: ‘Had they seen it, they would seek refuge from it even more earnestly.’ Then He says: ‘I call you to witness that I have given them what they seek and granted them refuge from what they seek refuge from’—or words to that effect. Then they say: ‘Among them is so-and-so, a habitual sinner who came for something he needed and sat with them.’ Then He says: ‘They are people in whose company no one will be wretched.’”

These people, who are among the best of Allah’s close friends, sought Paradise and sought to escape the Fire.

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, accepted the pledge of the Ansār on the night of al-ʿAqabah, those who pledged allegiance to him were among the foremost early believers, who were better than all these shaykhs. They said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Stipulate your conditions on behalf of your Lord, yourself, and your Companions.” He said:

“For myself, I stipulate that you protect me from whatever you protect yourselves and your families from. For my Companions, I stipulate that you share your means with them.”

They asked: “If we do that, what will we receive?”

He said: “Paradise will be yours.”

They said: “Extend your hand! By Allah, we will neither release you from this pledge nor ask you to release us.”

During the pledge, they had also said to him: “There are bonds and covenants between us and those people, and we are going to break them.”

Those who pledged allegiance to him were among the greatest of Allah’s creation in their love for Allah and His Messenger and in sacrificing their lives and wealth to please Allah and His Messenger—so much so that none of these later people can match them. Yet the ultimate thing they sought through this was Paradise. Had there been any higher goal, they would have sought it. But they knew that Paradise contains everything beloved and sought after. Indeed, Paradise contains things unknown to souls, which they therefore do not seek. For

---

## Page 5284

seeking, love, and desire depend on awareness, sensation, and conception. A person cannot seek, love, or desire anything of which he has no conception, sensation, or awareness. Paradise contains both kinds.

As Allah Most High says:

“They will have whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more.”

And He says:

“And therein is whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in.”

Thus, Paradise contains what they desire, and it contains still more: things beyond their knowledge, which they therefore could not desire. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined.”

This is a vast subject. Once you understand this “premise,” consider the statement: “Contentment means not asking Allah for Paradise or seeking His protection from the Fire.” If the speaker means that you should not ask Allah for anything included within the meaning of Paradise in revelation—that you should not ask Him to gaze upon Him, or for anything else sought by all the prophets and Allah’s close friends, and that you should not seek His protection from His veiling Himself from you or from His punishing you in the Fire—then this statement, besides contradicting all the prophets and messengers and the rest of the believers, is internally contradictory and unsound according to plain reason.

For someone who refrains from asking out of contentment does so only because he is content with Allah; and his contentment with Him comes only after knowing Him and loving Him. If neither contentment with Allah nor love for Him remains, it is as though the speaker were saying: “He is content not to be content.” This combines two contradictory states. Undoubtedly, these are the words of someone who has neither conceived nor understood what he is saying. This becomes clear when we consider that a contented person is only moved to endure hardships and pain by

---

## Page 5285

the pleasure and sweetness he finds in contentment. If he loses that sweetness and pleasure, he can no longer endure pain and bitterness. How, then, can he conceivably be content without possessing enough of the sweetness of contentment to bear the bitterness of hardships?

Such words are of the kind uttered by someone in a state of spiritual intoxication and self-effacement, who has experienced the sweetness of contentment within himself and imagines that it will remain with him whatever his condition. This is a grave error on his part, like the error of Sumnūn discussed earlier.

If, however, he means that he should not ask for enjoyment of created things, but should instead ask for something higher, then he has erred in two respects. First, he has failed to include what he seeks within Paradise, although it is Paradise’s highest bliss. Second, he has acknowledged that he seeks something while remaining content. If contentment does not conflict with this request, neither does it conflict with another request when he needs what he is seeking.

It is well known that his enjoyment of gazing upon Allah can only be complete if he is safe from the Fire and enjoys the lesser delights of Paradise. Whatever is indispensable to attaining what is sought is itself sought. Thus, his request to gaze upon Allah is also a request for everything that this necessarily entails, including deliverance from the Fire. His contentment therefore does not conflict with seeking benefit and protection from harm, nor with seeking Paradise and protection from the Fire, nor with seeking anything else necessarily entailed by that vision. The contradiction in his statement is thus clear.

---

## Page 5286

Furthermore, if he does not ask Allah for Paradise or seek refuge in Him from the Fire, then either he asks Allah for lesser things that he needs—benefits to obtain and harms to avert—or he does not. If he asks for lesser things and seeks refuge from lesser harms, then he has all the more reason to ask for Paradise and seek refuge from the Fire.

If contentment means never asking for anything, even when one desperately needs it, and never seeking refuge from anything, even when it is harmful, then one of two things must be true: either his heart turns to Allah for Him to do these things for him, or he turns away from this. If his heart turns to Allah, then he is asking and seeking refuge through his inward state. There is no difference between asking through one’s state and asking in words. Asking is more complete and perfect when both are combined, so he should not turn away from that.

If, however, he turns away from all of this, it is well known that he can remain alive only through what sustains his life and wards off harm. As for the benefits and protection from harm by which he lives, either he loves them, seeks them, and desires them from someone, or he neither loves nor seeks nor desires them. If he loves them, seeks them, and desires them from someone other than Allah, he would be a blameworthy person who associates partners with Allah, far from being praiseworthy. If he says, “I neither love nor seek nor desire them, whether from Allah or from His creation,” the reply is:

This is impossible for a living being, for a living being cannot fail to love what ensures its survival. This is known through sensory experience. Someone in such a condition could not be described as content, for a content person possesses a particular kind of love and will, which contentment necessarily entails. How, then, can he be said to lack all of this?

---

## Page 5287

This and similar considerations demonstrate the unsoundness of this statement.

Its unsoundness in relation to Allah’s way, His path, and His religion can be shown in several respects.

First: One who is content must do what pleases Allah. Otherwise, how can someone who does not do what pleases Allah be content with Allah? How can it be permissible to approve of what Allah hates, is displeased with, condemns, and forbids?

To explain: praiseworthy contentment must either be something Allah loves and approves of, or not. If He does not love and approve of it, then such contentment is neither obligatory nor recommended. Indeed, some forms of approval constitute disbelief, such as the disbelievers’ approval of associating partners with Allah, killing the prophets and rejecting them, and their approval of what displeases Allah and what He hates.

Allah Most High says:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and hated what pleased Him, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

Whoever follows what angers Allah, by approving of it and acting upon it, has indeed angered Allah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a sin is committed on earth, whoever was absent but approved of it is like someone who was present; and whoever witnessed it but was displeased with it is like someone who was absent and rejected it.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“After me there will be rulers whose conduct you will approve of in some respects and reject in others. Whoever rejects their wrongdoing is free of blame, and whoever hates it is safe; but whoever approves and follows them will perish.”

Allah Most High says:

“They swear to you so that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, then indeed Allah

---

## Page 5288

is not pleased with defiantly disobedient people.” Our approval of defiantly disobedient people is therefore not something Allah loves and approves of, for He is not pleased with them.

Allah Most High says:

“Are you content with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? Yet the enjoyment of this worldly life is but little compared with the Hereafter.”

This is a form of contentment that Allah has condemned. Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, who are content with the life of this world and feel secure in it…”

This, too, is blameworthy contentment, and there are many other examples besides these two. Whoever approves of his own disbelief and that of others, his own wickedness and that of others, and his own sins and those of others is neither pursuing Allah’s pleasure nor a believer in Allah. Rather, he is displeasing his Lord, and his Lord is angry with him, curses him, condemns him, and threatens him with punishment.

The path to Allah that rightly guided spiritual teachers enjoin consists precisely in enjoining obedience to Allah and forbidding disobedience to Him. Whoever commands, recommends, or praises a form of contentment that Allah hates, condemns, forbids, and punishes those who embrace it is an enemy of Allah, not a friend of Allah. He turns people away from Allah’s way and path rather than following His path and way.

If, then, the contentment found among human beings includes forms that Allah loves, forms that He hates and is displeased with, and forms that are permissible, belonging to neither category—like all other deeds of the heart, such as love, hatred, and the like, which are likewise divided into what Allah loves, what Allah hates, and what is permissible—

---

## Page 5289

then, that being the case, the person who is content yet neither asks Allah for Paradise nor seeks His protection from the Fire should be told:

Asking Allah for Paradise and seeking His protection from the Fire must be either obligatory, recommended, permissible, or disliked. No Muslim would say that it is forbidden or disliked. Nor is it merely permissible, with doing it and refraining from it being equally acceptable.

Even if it were said to be so, performing a permissible act of this kind does not contradict contentment. Contentment does not require a person to abstain from eating, drinking, dressing, or doing similar things. If doing these things does not contradict his contentment, would a permissible supplication or request contradict it? If such requests and supplications are obligatory or recommended, then it is well known that Allah is pleased with the performance of obligatory and recommended acts. How, then, could a contented person who is one of Allah’s friends fail to do what Allah loves and is pleased with, and instead do what angers Him and what He hates? This is the characteristic of Allah’s enemies, not His friends.

Al-Qushayrī mentioned this near the beginning of the “Chapter on Contentment,” saying:

“Know that the servant is obliged to be content with those decrees of Allah with which He has commanded contentment. For not everything that occurs by His decree is something with which the servant may, or must, be content, such as sins and the various ordeals suffered by Muslims.”

More than one scholar before him, after him, and in his own time said the same, including Qādī Abū Bakr, Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, and others like them. This was when the Qadariyyah argued against them that contentment with Allah’s decree is commanded, so if sins were

---

## Page 5290

decreed by Allah, we would be commanded to be content with them, whereas being content with what Allah has forbidden is impermissible. Ahl al-Sunnah offered three answers to this argument:

The first—which is the answer given by these scholars and the great majority of the leading scholars—is that this generalization is invalid. We are not commanded to be content with everything Allah has decreed and ordained. No such command appears in the Quran or the Sunnah. Rather, we must be content with whatever He has commanded us to be content with, such as obedience to Allah and His Messenger. This is what Abū al-Qāsim mentioned.

The second answer was: We are content with the decree, which is Allah’s attribute or act, not with what is decreed, which is the result of His act. There is a weakness in this answer, which we have explained elsewhere.

The third answer was: These sins have two aspects: one relating to the servant, insofar as they are his action, his doing, and his acquisition; and another relating to the Lord, insofar as He created, decreed, and ordained them. One is therefore content with them insofar as they are attributed to Allah, but not insofar as they are attributed to the servant. For their being evil, reprehensible, forbidden, a cause of punishment and blame, and the like, pertains only to their attribution to the servant.

This subject involves the disclosure of truths and mysteries, some of which we have discussed elsewhere; there is no room for them here. For

---

## Page 5291

this concerns questions of “the divine attributes and decree,” which are among the greatest subjects of religion, the noblest branches of knowledge among earlier and later generations, and the most difficult for most people’s minds to grasp. The point here is that the Sufi shaykhs, scholars, and others have explained that some forms of contentment are permissible, while others are not even permissible, let alone recommended or characteristic of those brought near to Allah. Abū al-Qāsim also mentioned this in the Epistle.

If it is asked: “What you have mentioned is clear and evident. How, then, did those who say that contentment means neither asking Allah for Paradise nor seeking His protection from the Fire fall into error? And how did those who approve of such words, whoever they may be, fall into error?”

The answer is: They erred because they thought that someone content with something does not seek anything else. Thus, when a servant is in a particular state, they considered it part of his contentment not to seek any other state. They then saw that Paradise is the ultimate object of desire, and the Fire the ultimate object of aversion.

They therefore said: “He should seek nothing, even Paradise, nor dislike whatever befalls him, even the Fire.” This is where they went wrong.

They were led astray in two ways:

The first was their assumption that being content with everything that happens is something Allah loves and is pleased with

---

## Page 5292

and that this is among the greatest paths followed by Allah’s allies. They therefore made contentment with every event and occurrence, or with every state in which a servant finds himself, a path to Allah, and thus went clearly astray. The path to Allah is only to please Him by doing what He loves and is pleased with—not to be content with everything that happens and occurs. He has neither commanded you to do this, nor approved it for you, nor loved it. Rather, He—glorified be He—dislikes, is angered by, and hates specific acts that occur, which none but He can enumerate.

Being an ally of Allah means being in accord with Him: loving what He loves, hating what He hates, disliking what He dislikes, being angered by what angers Him, befriending those He befriends, and opposing those He opposes. If you love and are pleased with what He dislikes and is angered by, you are His enemy, not His ally, and every condemnation directed at those who are pleased with what angers Allah applies to you. Reflect on this, for it draws attention to a fundamental principle concerning which countless people among the ascetics, Sufis, worshippers, and common people have gone astray—so many that none but Allah can number them.

The second way:

They do not distinguish between supplications they have been commanded to offer, whether as an obligation or as a recommendation, and supplications they have been forbidden to offer, or those they have neither been commanded nor forbidden to offer. A servant’s supplication to his Lord and his requests of Him are of three kinds:

“One kind” is that which the servant is commanded to offer, either as an obligation or as a recommendation, such as

---

## Page 5293

the words “Guide us to the straight path,” and the supplications he offers at the end of the prayer, such as the supplication the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) instructed his Companions to offer, saying:

“When one of you sits during the prayer, let him seek refuge in Allah from four things: the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trials of life and death, and the trial of the False Messiah.”

This is a supplication the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded them to offer at the end of their prayers. The Muslim community has unanimously agreed that it is prescribed and that Allah and His Messenger love and approve of it, though they have differed over whether it is obligatory. Tāwūs and a group of scholars held it to be obligatory, and this is also one position within the school of Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him. Most scholars, however, held it to be recommended.

The supplications the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) used to offer are either obligatory or recommended. Allah loves and approves of both what is obligatory and what is recommended. Whoever does either, Allah is pleased with him and grants him contentment. Can abandoning what He loves and approves of, then, be a form of contentment?

“Another kind of supplication” is forbidden, such as transgressing the bounds in supplication. An example is a man asking for something inappropriate for him that is exclusive to the prophets, although he is not a prophet; it may even be something exclusive to the Lord, glorified and exalted is He. For example, he might ask for al-Wasīlah (a rank in Paradise) for himself, although it befits only one of Allah’s servants; or ask Allah Most High to make him all-knowing or all-powerful, or to remove every veil that prevents him from beholding unseen matters, and similar requests.

Another example is someone who supplicates to Him under the impression that He needs His servants and that they can harm or benefit Him. He therefore asks Him to perform a particular act, and states that if He does not do so

---

## Page 5294

harm will come to Him from His creatures. This and similar notions reflect ignorance of Allah and transgression in supplication, even if some shaykhs have fallen into them.

Another example is saying, “O Allah, forgive me if You wish,” imagining that Allah, like kings, may sometimes act under compulsion and sometimes by choice. Thus, one says, “Forgive me if You wish.” Yet the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade this, saying:

“Let none of you say, ‘O Allah, forgive me if You wish; O Allah, have mercy on me if You wish.’ Rather, let him ask with resolve, for no one can compel Allah.”

Other examples include deliberately seeking rhymed prose in supplication, gasping, speaking with affected eloquence, and similar practices. Such supplications and others like them are forbidden. Some supplications are permissible, such as asking for nonessential things that involve no sin.

And (the point is that contentment which belongs to the path to Allah does not entail abandoning anything obligatory or recommended. Abandoning an obligatory or recommended supplication cannot therefore be an expression of contentment, just as abandoning other obligations cannot be an expression of prescribed contentment, nor is committing forbidden acts prescribed.

Their error has thus become clear on two counts: they assume that contentment is prescribed with regard to everything that is decreed, and they fail to distinguish between supplication that is prescribed, whether obligatory or recommended, and supplication that is not prescribed. It is a self-evident teaching of Islam that asking Allah for Paradise and seeking refuge in Him from the Fire are among the greatest supplications prescribed for all the messengers

---

## Page 5295

and prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, and that doing so is either obligatory or recommended. The path followed by Allah’s friends consists entirely of fulfilling obligations and performing recommended deeds, for anything else is forbidden, disliked, or merely permissible and of no religious benefit.

What led these people into this error was that they found many people asking Allah to bring them benefit and ward off harm—even asking for Paradise and seeking refuge from the Fire—not because doing so is worship, obedience, and goodness, but because their souls desire these things. They therefore thought that the path required abandoning whatever the soul chooses and desires, and that none of them should have any will whatsoever; rather, his aim—whoever he may be—should be to let himself be carried along by the divine decree.

This is what led many of them into monasticism and departure from the Sharia, to the point that they gave up food, drink, clothing, and marriage that they needed and without which their religious well-being could not be secured. For they saw that ordinary people treated these matters as dictated by natural inclination, desire, and habit. It is well known that actions performed in this manner do not constitute worship, obedience, or a means of drawing near to Allah. Those people therefore regarded the path to Allah as abandoning these acts of worship and natural activities. They persisted in hunger, sleeplessness, seclusion, silence, and other practices involving the renunciation of pleasures and the endurance of hardships, to such an extent that they fell into abandoning obligatory and recommended deeds and committing disliked and forbidden acts.

---

## Page 5296

Neither course is commendable, commanded, or a path to Allah: the course of the negligent, who perform these necessary activities without treating them as worship or a means of drawing near to Allah, and the course of those who overstep the bounds by abandoning them. Rather, what is prescribed is to perform them with the intention of drawing near to Allah and to thank Him.

Allah Most High says:

“Eat of the good things and do righteous deeds.”

He also says:

“Eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah.”

Thus, He commands eating and drinking. Whoever eats without giving thanks is blameworthy, and whoever neither eats nor gives thanks is blameworthy. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is indeed pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, and drinks a drink and praises Him for it.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Saʿd:

“You will never spend anything seeking thereby the Face of Allah without being raised in rank and standing—even the morsel you place in your wife’s mouth.”

It is also authentically reported that he said:

“A believer’s spending on his family, when he seeks Allah’s reward for it, is charity.”

The same applies to supplications here. Some people ask Allah to bring them benefit and ward off harm out of natural inclination and habit, rather than in obedience to His law and as an act of worship. It is not prescribed for me to abandon supplication altogether because of such a person’s shortcomings and negligence. Rather, I should supplicate in obedience to Allah’s law and as an act of worship.

Know, moreover, that someone who does this in obedience to Allah’s law and as an act of worship is only pursuing his own welfare and seeking his own praiseworthy benefits. He seeks his welfare in both this world and the Hereafter, unlike

---

## Page 5297

one who does so out of natural inclination, for he seeks only his welfare in this world. As Allah Most High says:

“Among people are those who say, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world,’ but they will have no share in the Hereafter.”

“And among them are those who say, ‘Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’”

“Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.”

Thus, whoever seeks Paradise and seeks refuge from the Fire is seeking the good of the Hereafter and is therefore praiseworthy.

Another way to clarify this matter is to refute these people’s position by pointing out its implication: the servant would neither carry out any command nor refrain from anything forbidden. He would neither pray, fast, give charity, perform pilgrimage, undertake jihad, nor perform any act that brings him nearer to Allah, since the benefit of these acts lies in attaining reward and averting punishment. If he seeks neither to attain the reward, which is Paradise, nor to avert the punishment, which is the Fire, then he would neither carry out any command nor refrain from anything forbidden. He would say, “I am content with whatever He does to me, even if I fall into disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience.”

Indeed, he would go so far as to say, “I will disbelieve, act wickedly, and disobey so that He punishes me, and I will be content with His punishment, thereby attaining the station of contentment with His decree.”

Such words come from someone who is among the most ignorant, foolish, misguided, and unbelieving of all creatures. As for his ignorance and foolishness, this is because such contentment is impossible and unattainable, since it entails combining two contradictories.

---

## Page 5298

As for his disbelief, this is because his position entails setting aside Allah’s religion, with which He sent His messengers and revealed His scriptures. Undoubtedly, preoccupation with divine decree and predestination has led many Sufi spiritual aspirants to neglect commands and commit forbidden acts, thereby becoming either deficient and deprived, disobedient and sinful, or disbelievers. I have witnessed many forms of this.

“Anyone to whom Allah gives no light has no light.”

These people and the Muʿtazilah, along with others like them among the Qadariyyah, stand at opposite extremes: the former attend to divine decree while disregarding Allah’s commands, whereas the latter attend to His commands while disregarding divine decree. Both groups think it impossible to give due consideration to both command and decree, while another group considers this contrary to wisdom and justice.

These three categories are the Magian Qadariyyah, the polytheistic Qadariyyah, and the Satanic Qadariyyah. We have discussed them at length elsewhere. The principal affliction besetting spiritual seekers and the general public in our time is “polytheistic Qadariyyah”: they contemplate divine decree while disregarding Allah’s commands. As one scholar said of them: “When it comes to obedience, you are a Qadarī; when it comes to disobedience, you are a Jabrī. Whichever doctrine suits your desires, you adopt it.”

What is prescribed, however, is the reverse: when it comes to obedience, one should seek Allah’s help before acting and thank Him afterwards.

---

## Page 5299

and strive not to disobey Him. If one sins and disobeys, one should hasten to repent and seek forgiveness, as in the hadith concerning the foremost supplication for forgiveness:

“I acknowledge before You Your blessing upon me, and I acknowledge my sin.”

Likewise, in the authentic divine hadith:

“O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you, then recompense you for them in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.”

Through this same approach, some spiritual aspirants came to abandon supplication, while others classified reliance upon Allah and love for Him as spiritual stations belonging to ordinary people. These and similar errors are matters we have discussed elsewhere, explaining what is right and what is wrong in them.

For this reason, these shaykhs’ teachings contain exhortations to follow knowledge and the revealed law. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī even said:

“Every spiritual experience unsupported by the Quran and Sunnah is false.”

Al-Junayd ibn Muhammad said:

“Our knowledge is bound by the Quran and Sunnah. Whoever has not read the Quran and written down hadith is not qualified to speak about this knowledge of ours.”

And Allah knows best.

## Page 5300

What do the esteemed scholars say concerning someone who firmly resolves to commit a “forbidden act,” such as unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, or drinking wine, but is unable to carry it out because of death or some other cause? Does he incur sin merely for his resolve, or not?

If you say that he incurs sin, how do you answer someone who argues that no sin is incurred, citing the saying:

“When My servant intends an evil deed but does not carry it out, it is not recorded against him,”

and the saying:

“Allah has pardoned my community for their inner thoughts, so long as they neither act upon them nor speak of them”?

He bases his argument on the latter in two ways. First, it declares that inner thoughts are pardoned, and resolve falls within this general wording. Resolve and intention are one and the same, as Ibn Sīdah stated. Second, it makes this pardon extend until speech or action occurs; whatever precedes that falls within the scope of the pardon.

He further contends that the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire,”

does not prove that resolve alone incurs sin, because what warrants the slain man’s entry into the Fire is his confronting his brother: this is an action, not merely an intention.

Nor, he argues, is there evidence for this in the Prophet’s statement—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning the man who said, “If I had wealth, I would do such and such,” that “the two are equal in sin and equal in reward,” because that man had spoken,

---

## Page 5301

and the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“so long as they neither act upon them nor speak of them.”

This man had indeed spoken. Much has been said concerning this question, and a lengthy, clear, and comprehensive explanation is needed.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave—replied:

Praise be to Allah. This question and others like it require a sound understanding before their ruling can be discussed. Most of the confusion people have experienced concerning these matters has arisen from two causes:

First, failing to understand precisely the states and qualities of the heart that are under discussion.

Second, failing to give the scriptural evidence its due. Consequently, many people have become so confused in this area that anyone examining their statements finds them claiming scholarly consensuses that appear to contradict one another.

It should therefore be understood that each attribute of a living being—knowledge, power, will, and the like—has degrees, from its lowest to its highest, that human beings cannot fully encompass: doubt, then conjecture, then knowledge, then certainty with its various degrees. The same applies to intention, will, firm resolve, and so forth. Thus, the correct view according to the great majority of Ahl al-Sunnah—which is also

---

## Page 5302

the apparent position of Ahmad, the more authentic of the two views reported from him, and the view of most of his followers—is that knowledge, reason, and similar qualities admit of increase and decrease. Indeed, the same applies to qualities found in nonliving things, such as colours, tastes, and scents.

We begin, then, by saying that a decisive will is one that necessarily results in action when the ability to act is present. Whenever decisive will and full ability are both present, the action must occur, since the cause is fully present without any countervailing impediment. Whenever will and full ability are present but the action does not occur, the will is not decisive. This describes the will of created beings to perform actions that they are capable of performing but do not perform, although such willing varies greatly in strength and weakness. Yet wherever the intended action does not occur despite full ability, the will is not completely decisive.

Disagreement over this “question” has become widespread only because people have supposed that there can be a decisive will to act without any accompanying action whatsoever. This cannot occur. It can occur only with a resolve to act: someone may resolve to perform an action in the future without doing any part of it in the present. Resolving to act in the future is not sufficient to bring the action about. Rather, when the action occurs, the will must become complete in a way that necessarily entails the action. This is decisive will.

When a person has “decisive will” and does whatever lies within his ability, he is regarded under Islamic law as equivalent to someone who performs the action in full: he receives the reward, and incurs the punishment, of the person who performs it in full

---

## Page 5303

who has performed the entire intended action, so that he is rewarded and punished even for what lies beyond the scope of his ability. This applies, for example, to those who act jointly and cooperate in righteous deeds. It also includes the consequences arising from a person’s actions, as with someone who calls to guidance or misguidance, or establishes a good or bad practice. As authentically reported in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever calls to guidance will have a reward equal to the rewards of those who follow him, without their rewards being diminished in the least. Whoever calls to misguidance will bear a burden of sin equal to the burdens of those who follow him, without their burdens being diminished in the least.”

It is also authentically reported from him in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“Whoever establishes a good practice will have its reward and the reward of everyone who acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without their rewards being diminished in the least.”

The person who calls to guidance or misguidance seeks and wills what he calls to, with complete intent and will. His ability, however, is exercised through calling and instructing, while the ability of the person who acts is exercised through following and accepting.

For this reason, Allah Most High mentions actions performed directly alongside their resulting effects in His Book, saying:

“That is because no thirst, fatigue, or hunger afflicts them in the cause of Allah, nor do they tread any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they inflict any loss upon an enemy, without a righteous deed being recorded for them on account of it. Indeed, Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

“Nor do they spend any amount, small or large, or cross any valley, without it being recorded for them, so that Allah may reward them according to the best of what they used to do.”

In the first verse, He mentions what results from their actions without being brought about by their ability alone:

---

## Page 5304

namely, the thirst, hunger, and fatigue that afflict them, the rage they cause the disbelievers, and the losses they inflict upon the enemy. He says:

“A righteous deed is recorded for them on account of it.”

He thus explains that these things, which arise and result from their own actions together with other actions independent of them, earn them a recorded righteous deed. In the second verse, He mentions the actions they themselves perform directly: spending and covering distances. Hence, He says there:

“Without it being recorded for them.”

These actions are themselves righteous deeds. In both cases, their will is firmly directed toward their objective: that all worship should be devoted to Allah alone and that Allah’s word should be supreme. Whatever results alongside this resolute will, with their ability contributing to it in some measure, counts as a righteous deed for them.

Likewise, “the one who calls to guidance or misguidance,” whose will is resolutely and fully directed toward his followers’ guidance or misguidance, and who does whatever he can to help bring that about, is like someone who has performed the entire action. His recompense is therefore equal to that of everyone who follows him: the one who guides receives rewards equal to those of the rightly guided, and the one who misleads bears burdens of sin equal to those of the misguided.

The same applies to someone who establishes a good or bad practice, for a practice is a pattern laid down for deliberate observance. The person establishing it fully intends every instance of its being followed, while his own action is limited by his ability.

Another example is the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith reported by Ibn Masʿūd and recorded in both Sahīh collections:

“No soul is killed unjustly without the first son of Adam bearing a share of the guilt for its bloodshed, for he was the first to establish killing.”

Thus, the share

---

## Page 5305

means a portion equal to that of the killer, as the other hadith explains. Since he regarded the killing of those whose lives are inviolable as permissible in principle, nothing restrained him from killing any such person. He thus became a partner in the killing of every soul. Related to this is the saying of Allah Most High:

“For that reason, We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul—unless in retribution for murder or for corruption in the land—it is as though he has killed all mankind; and whoever saves a life, it is as though he has saved all mankind.”

Similarly, rejecting any particular messenger is tantamount to rejecting the messengers as a whole, as Allah says:

“The people of Noah rejected the messengers.”

“ʿĀd rejected the messengers.”

There are other similar passages. Also belonging to this category is the saying of Allah Most High:

“Those who disbelieve say to those who believe, ‘Follow our way, and we will bear your sins.’ Yet they will bear none of their sins. They are certainly liars. They will surely bear their own burdens, and other burdens along with their own, and on the Day of Resurrection they will surely be questioned about what they used to fabricate.”

He thus states that the leaders of misguidance bear none of their followers’ sins, while also stating that they bear their burdens—that is, the sins of their followers—without diminishing their followers’ burdens of sin in the least. This is because their will was firmly resolved upon that outcome, and they did all that lay within their power. They therefore incur the recompense of everyone who acts accordingly, for recompense for an action is deserved when there is a resolute will to perform it together with doing whatever lies within one’s power to accomplish it.

This accords with what is established in both Sahīh collections in the hadith narrated by Ibn ʿAbbās from Abū Sufyān:

## Page 5306

that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) wrote to Heraclius: “But if you turn away, you will bear the sin of the arīsiyyīn.”

He thus explained that, since Heraclius was the leader whom they followed in their religion, he would bear the sin of the arīsiyyīn—that is, his followers. Although it has been said that this word originally denoted farmers and tillers, like the term tā’ in Turkish, its meaning is extended beyond that. It is well known that if he turned away from following the Messenger, he would bear sins equivalent to theirs, without their sins being diminished in the least, as the other texts of the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Another example is the saying of Allah Most High:

“Your God is One God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are in denial, and they are arrogant. Without doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. He certainly does not love the arrogant. When they are asked, ‘What has your Lord sent down?’ they say, ‘Tales of the ancients.’ Thus they will bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge.”

His words, “and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead,” refer to the burdens arising from the followers’ misguidance. These arise both from the one giving the command and from the one who obeys it: the powers of both contribute to bringing about that misguidance. Thus each bears a share of it. Yet each of these two shares is equivalent to the full burden of sin borne by one who commits the deed, as the other texts indicate, such as his saying:

## Page 5307

“Whoever calls others to misguidance will bear its burden of sin and the burden of everyone who acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection.”

He, glorified be He, thus tells us that the followers will call for the punishment of the leaders of misguidance to be doubled, just as He relates elsewhere:

He, glorified be He, also tells us that both those who are followed and their followers will have their punishment doubled. The followers, however, do not know of this doubling. This is why the leaders of guidance receive such great praise and commendation, while the leaders of misguidance receive such great condemnation and cursing. Indeed, it is related in a report—whose chain of transmission I do not presently recall—that no torment in the Fire is inflicted without its beginning with Iblīs and then rising to others, and no delight in Paradise is bestowed without its beginning with the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and then passing to others. For he is the supreme leader in guidance for all the children of Adam, from the first to the last.

As he said:

“I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting. Adam and all those below him will be under my banner on the Day of Resurrection

—and I say this without boasting.” He is the intercessor for the first and last generations when judgment is passed among them, and he is the first to ask for the gate of Paradise to be opened. Allah Most High says:

He thus began the statement with the lām that introduces an oath, which is used when a statement contains both an oath and a condition. He placed this lām before the conditional particle mā to indicate its comprehensive scope. The meaning is: Whatever Scripture and wisdom I give you, when that confirming prophet comes to you, you must believe in him and support him.

As Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Allah never sent a prophet without taking a covenant from him that, if Muhammad were sent while he was still alive, he would certainly believe in him and support him.”

Allah Most High exalted his mention and proclaimed it in the highest assembly between the creation of Adam’s body and the breathing of the spirit into him. This is related in the hadith of Maysara al-Fajr, who said:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, when were you a prophet?’—or, according to another narration, ‘When were you recorded as a prophet?’ He replied, ‘When Adam was between spirit and body.’”

Narrated by Ahmad. Likewise, in the hadith of al-‘Irbād ibn Sāriya, narrated by Ahmad—a hadith with a sound (hasan) grading—the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Indeed, with Allah I am the Seal of the Prophets, while Adam was still lying in his clay”—and the rest of the hadith.

## Page 5309

Allah thus recorded and decreed the affairs of the leader of Adam’s descendants at that time and in that state, just as He records and decrees the circumstances of each child descended from Adam between the formation of its body and the breathing of the spirit into it, as established in the two Sahīh collections in the hadith of Ibn Mas‘ūd. Whoever among the earlier and later generations believes in him is rewarded for doing so, although the reward of those who believe in him and obey him in the detailed laws is greater than that of those whose faith is only general. He is, moreover, the universal leader of all Adam’s descendants and has a share in the faith of every believer, from the earliest generations to the last, just as Iblīs has a share in every instance of error and deviation among jinn and human beings. This substantiates the transmitted report and supports what appears in Shu‘ayb ibn Abī Hamza’s collection of narrations from al-Zuhrī, attributed directly to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) by a Successor—either al-Zuhrī himself or one of the Successors before him:

“I was sent to call people, but guidance is not in my power at all. Iblīs was sent to make evil alluring and lead people astray, but misguidance is not in his power at all.”

Also related to this subject, in certain respects, is his statement in the hadith found in the Sunan collections:

“I was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then Abū Bakr was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then ‘Umar was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then the scales were lifted away.”

That the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) outweighs the community is clear, for he receives a reward equal to that of the entire community in addition to his own reward. As for Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, this is because they have

## Page 5310

a role in fostering the faith of the entire community, coupled with a firm resolve to do so. Abū Bakr preceded ‘Umar in this and was stronger in resolve. “On the day of Uhud, Abū Sufyān asked, ‘Is Muhammad among the people? Is Ibn Abī Quhāfa among the people? Those you named are alive, and what will distress you still awaits you.’”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated this from al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib. Abū Sufyān—the leader of disbelief at that time—asked only about these three because they were the leaders of the believers. Likewise, it is established in the two Sahīh collections that:

“When ‘Umar’s bier was set down, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib said, ‘By Allah, there is no one on the face of the earth whose deeds I would rather meet Allah with than those of this shrouded man. By Allah, I hope that Allah will gather you with your two companions, for I often heard the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) say, “Abū Bakr, ‘Umar and I entered; Abū Bakr, ‘Umar and I went out; Abū Bakr, ‘Umar and I went.”’”

Many similar texts explain why they would deserve the equivalent of the deeds of the entire community, if that is indeed what they receive: because they possessed firm resolve together with the means and ability
