## Page 5311

to do all of this, unlike someone who assisted in some of these matters but not others, and intended some of them but not others.

Furthermore, someone who has a firm resolve and does all that is within his power is equivalent to someone who performs the deed in full, even if he is not a leader or someone who calls others to it. As Allah, Glorified is He, says:

“Those believers who remain behind—except those with disabilities—are not equal to those who strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives. Allah has raised those who strive with their wealth and their lives one degree above those who remain behind. To both Allah has promised the best reward, but Allah has favoured those who strive over those who remain behind with a tremendous reward: ranks from Him, forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.”

Allah Most High thus denies equality between the one who fights and the one who remains behind despite being able to fight. He does not deny equality between the one who fights and the one who remains behind because he is unable. Indeed, one may say that the implied contrast entails their equality. The wording of the verse is explicit: those with disabilities are excepted from the denial of equality. The exception here is thus to a negation, which entails that those with disabilities may equal those who remain behind, even if they do not equal them in every respect. This is supported by the established report that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said during the expedition to Tabūk:

“There are men in Medina who have been with you whenever you travelled any distance or crossed any valley.”

They asked, “Even while they are in Medina?”

He replied, “Even while they are in Medina. A valid excuse held them back.”

He thus stated that someone who remained in Medina, held back only by a valid excuse, was like those accompanying them on this expedition. It is well known that each person accompanying him on the expedition receives the reward of a fighter according to his intention

---

## Page 5312

and so too do those who remain behind solely because a valid excuse holds them back.

Another example is the report established in the two Sahīhs from Abū Mūsā, who narrated that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“When a servant falls ill or travels, he is credited with the deeds he used to perform when healthy and at home.”

If someone regularly performed a deed when healthy and at home, then ceased doing it only because of illness or travel, this establishes that he stopped because of inability and hardship, not because his intention had weakened or faltered. He therefore possesses the same firm resolve as the person who performs the deed; only diminished ability prevents him from acting. Although a traveller may be able to perform the deed with hardship—as is also the case with certain illnesses—the ability recognized by Islamic law is that which allows the deed to be performed without harm outweighing its benefit. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by those who are able to make their way there.”

And He says:

“Whoever cannot do so must feed sixty needy people.”

The same applies to similar passages. What Islamic law takes into account is not merely the ability to perform an act by whatever means possible. Rather, that ability must involve no harm outweighing its benefit, or even equalling it.

Another example is the established saying of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Whoever equips a fighter has himself fought, and whoever takes good care of his family in his absence has himself fought.”

And his saying:

“Whoever provides a fasting person with food to break his fast will have a reward equal to his, without diminishing the fasting person’s reward in the least.”

For a military campaign requires striving both in person and with wealth. When one commits his person and another his wealth, and both possess firm resolve, each is a fighter

---

## Page 5313

by virtue of his firm resolve and to the extent of his ability. Likewise, a fighter needs someone to look after his family in his absence. Whoever takes good care of his family is therefore also a fighter. Similarly, fasting requires abstention, but it also requires the evening meal with which the fast is completed; otherwise, someone unable to have an evening meal would be unable to fast.

Another example is his saying in the authentic hadith:

“When a woman spends from her husband’s wealth without being wasteful, she receives a reward for what she spends, and her husband receives an equal reward, without either diminishing the other’s reward in the least.”

Likewise, he said in the hadith narrated by Abū Mūsā:

“The trustworthy treasurer who willingly gives what he has been instructed to give, fully and undiminished, is one of those giving charity.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it. This is because the trustworthy treasurer’s willing delivery of what he has been instructed to give, without diminishing it, necessarily involves a firm resolve that accords with the intention of the person giving the instruction. He has done what lies within his ability—namely, carrying out the instruction—and thus becomes one of those giving charity.

Also belonging to this category is the hadith of Abū Kabshah al-Anmārī, narrated by Ahmad and Ibn Mājah from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who said:

“This world is for four kinds of people: a man whom Allah has granted knowledge and wealth, who uses it in obedience to Allah. Another man said, ‘If I had what so-and-so has, I would do as he does.’ The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said, ‘They are equal in reward.’”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated a longer version and graded it good and authentic. This equality with regard to “reward and burden of sin” describes the case of someone who said this

---

## Page 5314

and was sincere in it, and Allah knew that his resolve was firm, such that only a lack of ability prevented him from acting. This is why the two were equal in reward or punishment.

This does not apply to everyone who says:

“If I had what so-and-so has, I would do as he does.”

It applies only if his resolve is firm and would necessarily lead to action if he had the ability. Otherwise, many people say this with a resolve that would dissolve if they actually gained the ability, just as people commonly make pledges and then break them. Not everyone who firmly resolves to do something before being able to do it, and in the absence of anything dissuading him, retains that resolve when he gains the ability but encounters things that dissuade him. As Allah Most High says:

“You certainly wished for death before you encountered it. Now you have seen it with your own eyes.”

And as Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?”

And as He says:

“Among them are those who pledged to Allah, ‘If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous.’”

“But when He gave them of His bounty, they withheld it and turned away in aversion.”

The hadith of Abū Kabshah concerning intentions is like the hadith of the card concerning words. This is the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“For a man from the nation of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), Allah will spread out ninety-nine records on the Day of Resurrection, each extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked, ‘Do you deny any of this? Have I wronged you?’ He will say:

---

## Page 5315

‘No, my Lord.’

He will be told, ‘You will suffer no injustice today.’ Then a card bearing the affirmation of Allah’s oneness will be brought. It will be placed in one pan of the balance and the records in the other. The records will rise, and the card will weigh heavily.”

This is because of the truthfulness, sincerity, purity, and sound intention accompanying this declaration. For although words and acts of worship may be identical in outward form, they differ enormously according to the state of the heart.

A similar example is the account of the prostitute who gave a dog water to drink, for which Allah forgave her. This was because of the sound intention and mercy present in her heart at that moment. Likewise, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“A servant may utter words pleasing to Allah, never imagining how far-reaching they will be, and Allah records His pleasure with him on their account until the Day of Resurrection. And a servant may utter words displeasing to Allah, never imagining how far-reaching they will be, and Allah records His displeasure with him on their account until the Day of Resurrection.”

Section

This makes it clear that the hadiths distinguishing between someone who intends an action and someone who performs it, and similar reports, concern only intentions falling short of firm resolve, which must necessarily be accompanied by action.

Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUtāridī narrates from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who related from his Lord, Blessed and Exalted, that He said:

---

## Page 5316

“Allah has recorded good deeds and bad deeds, then explained this: Whoever intends a good deed but does not perform it, Allah records it with Him as one complete good deed. If he intends it and performs it, Allah records it with Him as ten good deeds. Whoever intends a bad deed but does not perform it, Allah records it for him as one complete good deed. If he intends it and performs it, Allah records it for him with Him as one bad deed.”

A similar report is narrated from Abū Hurayrah in the two Sahīh collections. This distinction concerns someone who is able to act. Hence the expressions “then performs it” and “does not perform it.” Someone who is able to act but does not do so has not formed a firm will to act. For a firm will, coupled with the ability, necessarily entails action. As explained earlier, this combination is sufficient to bring about the act and necessarily produces it. If the act depended on anything further, a firm will coupled with ability would not constitute a complete and sufficient basis for its occurrence. Yet direct experience plainly shows otherwise.

Undoubtedly, “intending,” “resolving,” “willing,” and similar terms may denote a determination so firm that action fails to follow only because of inability; or they may fall short of this degree of firmness. It is in this “second category” that a distinction is made between someone who intends an act and someone who performs it. Indeed, a distinction is made between one intention and another, for willing is an act of the heart, which is the king of the body.

As Abū Hurayrah said: “The heart is a king, and the limbs are its soldiers. When the king is good, its soldiers are good; when the king is corrupt, its soldiers are corrupt.”

This is borne out by the hadith in the two Sahīh collections narrated by al-Nu‘mān ibn Bashīr from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

---

## Page 5317

“Indeed, within the body is a morsel of flesh: when it is sound, the whole body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”

When someone intends a good deed but does not perform it, he has nevertheless done something good: intending that good deed. It is therefore recorded for him as one complete good deed, for this is itself an act of obedience and goodness. People likewise recognize this, as the poet said:

I shall surely thank you for the kindness you intended;
Your intention to do good is itself a kindness.
I shall not blame you should destiny not bring it to pass;
For all things are governed by destiny’s irrevocable decree.

If he performs it, Allah records ten good deeds for him, in accordance with what He has already ordained in His mercy: whoever brings a good deed receives ten times its like, up to seven hundredfold. As Allah Most High says:

“The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, each containing a hundred grains.”

Likewise, in an authentic hadith, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said to someone who brought a she-camel:

“For it, you will have on the Day of Resurrection seven hundred she-camels, haltered and bridled, multiplied many times over.”

It has also been narrated from Abū Hurayrah, in a report traced back to the Prophet:

“He is granted a million good deeds for it.”

As for someone who intends a bad deed but does not perform it, despite being able to do so, Allah does not record it against him, as he stated in the authentic hadith. Whether his intention is called willing or resolve, or is given neither name, whenever someone is able to act, intends and resolves to do so, yet does not act despite having the ability, his will is not firm. This accords with the Prophet’s words in the authentic hadith

---

## Page 5318

the hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah has pardoned my community for what they say within themselves, so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it.”

For when a servant intends something that he is capable of saying or doing, but neither says nor does it, his will to do it is not firm. Such things are among those that Allah does not record against him, as attested by his words:

“Whoever intends a bad deed but does not perform it.”

The consensus reported by Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr and others on this issue, on the basis of this hadith, is correct when understood in this sense.

Someone who intends a bad deed either abandons it out of fear and awe of Allah or abandons it for some other reason. If he abandons it out of fear of Allah, Allah records it with Him as one complete good deed, as explicitly stated in the hadith. Another hadith likewise states:

“Record it for him as a good deed, for he only abandoned it for My sake”—or he said, “on My account.”

If, however, he abandons it for some other reason, it is not recorded against him as a bad deed, as stated in another hadith:

“If he does not perform it, it is not recorded against him.”

In this way, the meanings of the hadiths are reconciled.

If he does perform it, only one bad deed is recorded against him. For Allah Most High does not multiply bad deeds apart from the doer’s own actions, nor does He recompense a person in the Hereafter except for what that person himself has done. Hell will be filled only with the followers of Iblīs among the jinn and humankind, as Allah Most High says:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.”

Thus, it is established in the two Sahīh collections, in the hadiths of Abū Hurayrah and Anas:

“There will be space left over in Paradise, so Allah will create people for it in the Hereafter. As for the Fire, parts of it will draw in toward

---

## Page 5319

one another until He places His foot upon it, and it becomes filled with those followers of Iblīs who have entered it.”

For this reason, the correct position explicitly stated by upright imams such as Ahmad and others is to withhold judgment concerning the children of polytheists. No particular child among them is categorically assigned to Paradise or Hell. Rather, we say concerning them what the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said in the two authentic hadiths narrated by Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ‘Abbās:

“Allah knows best what they would have done.”

Abū Hurayrah’s hadith is in the two Sahīh collections, while Ibn ‘Abbās’s hadith is in al-Bukhārī. The hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub, narrated by al-Bukhārī, states that “some of them will enter Paradise.” It is also established that “some of them will enter the Fire,” as related in Sahīh Muslim in the account of the boy whom al-Khadir killed. This confirms what has been narrated through several channels: they will be tested on the Day of Resurrection, so that what Allah knows concerning them becomes manifest. He will then recompense them for their obedience and disobedience. This is the position that al-Ash‘arī reported from the people of the Sunnah and hadith and himself adopted.

As for the leaders of misguidance—who bear the burdens of sin of those whom they have led astray—and others like them, we have explained that they are punished only because they possess a firm resolve together with the ability to act. This is indicated by the Prophet’s words in the hadith of Abū Kabshah:

“They are equal in their burden of sin.”

And by his words:

“Whoever calls others to misguidance will bear a burden of sin equal to the burdens of those who follow him.”

When firm resolve and the ability to act are both present, they have the same status as someone who has fully performed the deed. Someone who contemplates a bad deed but does not commit it despite being able to do so has not formed a firm resolve; and the one who commits

---

## Page 5320

a bad deed and carries it through is recompensed for it with only a single bad deed, as the scriptural text attests. This clarifies the statement of the imams, as Imam Ahmad said:

“Contemplation” is of two kinds: passing thoughts and persistent resolve.

Passing thoughts occur in someone capable of acting, for if his contemplation amounted to firm, persistent resolve while he was able to act, the deed would have taken place. Joseph’s contemplation belongs to this category, as Allah Most High says:

“She certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord.”

As for the intention of the woman who sought to seduce him, it has been said that it was persistent resolve, because she did what lay within her power. Likewise, Allah Most High says of the hypocrites:

“They intended what they could not attain.”

The intention mentioned here is blameworthy, just as Allah condemned them for it. An intention of this kind is blameworthy even if it is not firm, as we shall explain at the end of this answer when distinguishing between what is incompatible with faith and what is not.

Likewise, someone who is eager to commit sins and firmly resolved to do so, prevented only by his inability, receives the same punishment as the person who commits them. This is indicated by the hadith of Abū Kabshah and by the authentic hadith:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.” It was asked, “That applies to the killer, but what about the one killed?” He replied, “He was eager to kill his companion.”

Another wording states:

“He intended to kill his companion.”

This “intention” is that eagerness: it is firm resolve, accompanied by the action within his power—namely, fighting—although he was unable to kill. This is not the kind of contemplation that goes unrecorded. Nor should it be said that he deserved this merely for saying, “If I had what so-and-so has

---

## Page 5321

, I would do just as he did.” For merely expressing a wish to commit major sins does not incur the same punishment as committing them; something more is required. He did not say that the man would be punished for his words, but only that the two would bear an equal burden of sin.

Accordingly, his statement:

“Allah has pardoned my community for what crosses their minds, so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it”

does not preclude punishment for a firm intention, which must necessarily be accompanied by action. A “firm intention” is one accompanied by whatever action lies within a person’s power. If it is not accompanied by such action, it is not firm. Thus, when someone intends and resolves to commit unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, or drink wine, if his intention is truly firm and resolute, it must be accompanied by whatever action he can take, even if this only brings him closer to the sin. Examples include a thief approaching the place where the property to be stolen is kept; someone intending unlawful intercourse looking at, listening to, and speaking with the intended partner; or someone seeking and trying to obtain wine, and similar acts.

A firm intention must therefore be accompanied by some preliminary action within the person’s power. Indeed, preliminary actions may occur even without a firm intention to carry out the deed, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“The eyes commit unlawful intercourse, and their unlawful intercourse is looking; the tongue commits unlawful intercourse, and its unlawful intercourse is speaking; the hand commits unlawful intercourse, and its unlawful intercourse is grasping; the foot commits unlawful intercourse, and its unlawful intercourse is walking. The heart wishes and desires, and the private parts either confirm this or deny it.”

Likewise, in the hadith of Abū Bakrah recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire. It was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, that applies to the killer, but what about the one killed?’

---

## Page 5322

He replied, ‘He intended to kill his companion.’” In another version recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim: “He was intent on killing his companion.”

His intention was firm, and he did whatever lay within his power; only his inability prevented him from killing his companion. This was neither a mere passing thought nor merely a resolve to perform some future act. He therefore deserved the Fire, as we explained earlier: someone who has a firm intention and does whatever is possible is treated like someone who fully carries out the deed.

As we have explained, a “complete intention” must be accompanied by whatever action lies within one’s power, or some of it. If a person refrains from an action he is capable of performing, his intention is not firm. Rather, it may be firm regarding what he does, but not what he refrains from doing despite being able to do it. An example is someone who engages in acts preliminary to unlawful sexual intercourse—touching, looking, and kissing—but refrains from the greater indecency itself.

Hence, in the authentic hadith of Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet said:

“The eye commits unlawful intercourse, the ear commits unlawful intercourse, and the tongue commits unlawful intercourse”—until he said—“and the heart wishes and desires.”

That is, it wishes for and desires intercourse. He did not say “intends.” Mere desire and wishing are not a firm intention, nor do they necessarily lead to action, so a person is not punished for them. Rather, he is punished when he has a firm intention together with the ability to act—a firm intention that the private parts confirm.

Another example is the hadith narrated from Ibn Masʿūd in both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“A man kissed a woman, then came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and mentioned this

---

## Page 5323

to him, whereupon Allah Most High revealed the verse:

‘Establish prayer at both ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds.’

The man asked, ‘Is this for me?’ He replied, ‘It is for whoever among my community acts upon it.’”

A man such as this, and others like him, will generally entertain thoughts of something more serious than that, as the Prophet said:

“The heart wishes and desires, and the private parts either confirm this or belie it.”

Yet his inward intention to kiss was firm, so, having the ability, he acted upon it and kissed her. His intention to have intercourse, however, may not have been firm; alternatively, it may have been firm, but he lacked the ability. What seems more likely concerning the man about whom the verse was revealed is that he was able to do so but did not.

Thus, the distinction drawn by Ahmad and others between an inclination arising from passing thoughts and one involving persistent resolve provides the basis for the answer. If nothing prevents a person from acting except inability, he will necessarily undertake whatever preliminary acts lie within his power. If he commits the act while determined to return to it whenever he can, he is persisting in sin. Hence Ibn al-Mubārak said: “The persistent sinner is someone who drinks wine today, then does not drink it for a month—or, in another narration, for thirty years—yet intends to drink it whenever he is able.”

A person may also be persisting in sin when he resolves to commit an act at one time but not another, such as someone who resolves to refrain from sins during Ramadan but not at other times. Such a person has not repented in an unqualified sense. He does, however, refrain from the act during Ramadan, and he is rewarded if he refrains for Allah’s sake, out of reverence for Allah’s sacred ordinances and to avoid what He has forbidden during that time. Nevertheless, he is not among those who repent and thereby receive complete forgiveness, nor is his persistence in sin absolute. As for the one whom

---

## Page 5324

Ibn al-Mubārak described, he is persisting in sin if he intends to return to drinking it.

I say:

Someone who refrains from sins during Ramadan while intending to return to them outside Ramadan is also persisting in sin. However, intending to drink it if one becomes able is different from intending to do so when one already has the ability. Once he becomes able, his intention may or may not remain. Yet whenever his resolve is firm and nothing prevents him except inability, he is liable to punishment for that, as explained earlier. It has also been explained that such a person’s intention must necessarily be accompanied by whatever action lies within his power.

This clarifies what is reported from al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī: that he related a consensus that someone who intends an act is not on the same footing as someone who performs it. This consensus is valid when the person has the ability, for someone who intends an act and is able to perform it is not on the same footing as someone who actually performs it. But someone whose intention is firm and who does whatever he can is on the same footing as someone who performs the act in full, as explained earlier.

Further clarification comes from the fact that Allah, Glorified is He, has made reward and punishment in the Quran contingent upon intention alone, as in His words, Most High:

“Whoever desires this fleeting life, We hasten for him therein whatever We will, for whomever We wish. Then We assign Hell to him, where he will burn, condemned and banished.”

He also says:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornments, We repay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be shortchanged therein. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire.”

And He says:

“Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of

---

## Page 5325

this world, We give him some of it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter.”

Thus He made reward and punishment contingent upon a person’s desiring this fleeting life, the life of this world, and the harvest of this world. In the verse from Surah Hūd, He says:

“We repay them in full for their deeds therein”—until He says—“and worthless is what they used to do.”

This indicates that they had deeds that came to nothing, that they were punished for other deeds they had committed, and that the desire mentioned here necessarily entails action. When He mentioned desiring the Hereafter, He said:

“But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he ought to, while being a believer…”

That is because, although desiring the Hereafter entails working for it, reward is only for deeds that have been commanded, not for every kind of striving. Faith is also indispensable.

Another example is His saying:

“O Prophet, say to your wives: ‘If you desire the life of this world and its adornments’”—to the end of the verse—and: “But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter…”

This parallels the verse in Surah Hūd. It also accords with his words, “When two Muslims confront each other with their swords,” except that he said, “For he intended to kill his companion,” or, “He was eager to kill his companion.” Thus he mentioned eagerness and intent to kill, which must necessarily be accompanied by action. This is not covered by the hadith concerning pardon:

“Allah has pardoned my community for their inward thoughts.”

Another matter arising from this is a well-known issue of disagreement—between Ahl al-Sunnah and most scholars

---

## Page 5326

and some of the Qadariyyah—namely, “the repentance of one unable to perform the act,” such as an emasculated man’s repentance from fornication, or the repentance of a man with an amputated hand who is unable to steal, and similar cases of incapacity. Such repentance is valid according to the great majority of scholars, both Ahl al-Sunnah and others. Some of the Qadariyyah disagreed, on the grounds that someone unable to perform an act cannot be rewarded for refraining from it, but is instead punished for refraining from it. This is not so. Rather, the intention of someone who is incapable is subject to reward and punishment, as we have explained. We have also explained that firm resolve accompanied by ability places a person on the same footing as someone who fully performs the act.

Thus, if someone who is incapable does what he can, through his words and actions, to distance himself from the causes of sin, and forsakes and abandons it in his heart, he is exactly like a repentant person who is capable of committing it. The repentance of someone unable to complete the act is thus analogous to the persistence in sin of someone unable to complete it.

Another issue arising from this is “the well-known question concerning divorce”: if a man divorces his wife inwardly and firmly resolves upon it, but does not utter it, the divorce does not take effect according to the majority of scholars. According to one of the two reports from Mālik, however, it does take effect. Ahmad and other imams cited as evidence that it does not take effect the Prophet’s words:

“Allah has pardoned my community for their inward thoughts.”

An opponent objected: “What is pardoned here is only inward thought; a firm inward resolve is not inward thought.”

Their opponent replied: He said:

“so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it.”

He thus stated that pardon for inward thoughts extends up to this limit, namely speaking of them

---

## Page 5327

and acting upon them, as mentioned at the beginning of the question when presenting the argument advanced by some people. This is a sound argument: if someone were held accountable for inward thought once it became firm resolve, despite neither speaking of it nor acting upon it, that would contradict the text. However, the reply is as follows:

This applies to a person subject to the divine commands who has the ability to speak and act, yet does neither. As for a firm intention accompanied by doing all that is within one’s power, it is treated like an intention accompanied by full performance of the act. This is illustrated by someone unable to speak, who may also be unable to act with his hands or other limbs. If he nevertheless gestures to the utmost of his ability, his gestures are treated like another person’s speech with respect to legal rulings, reward, punishment, and other matters.

As for the other argument he advanced—namely, that resolve and an inclination to act fall without qualification within the inward thoughts that are pardoned—this is not so. Rather, it is correct to say that a firm intention necessarily entails the occurrence of some action to which blame, punishment, and other consequences attach. For if the intended act is within one’s power, then, given a firm intention, it must occur. If it is impossible, a firm intention must nevertheless be accompanied by some of the actions leading up to it. Where no action whatsoever occurs, there is only an inclination. Inward thought is not a firm intention.

For this reason, the scriptural texts do not grant pardon for everything described as intention, love, hatred, envy, arrogance, self-admiration, or other acts of the heart. Whenever these acts bring blame and punishment upon people, it is because they have reached completion, becoming speech and action.

---

## Page 5328

Accordingly, the hadith in which the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) says, “Allah has pardoned my community,” is true, as is accountability for intentions that necessarily entail bodily actions.

Some people, however, held that a firm intention may exist without any action or speech. They then disagreed over whether it incurs punishment. Al-Qādī Abū Bakr and those who followed him, such as Abū Hāmid and Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī, held that it does incur punishment. Yet they have no evidence that a person is held accountable when no speech or action occurs.

Al-Qādī based this position on his principle concerning “faith,” in which he followed Jahm and al-Sālihī. This is also the position commonly attributed to Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī: faith consists solely of the heart’s assent, even if a person denies it with his tongue and verbally reviles Allah and His Messenger; reviling Allah and His Messenger constitutes disbelief only outwardly; and whatever constitutes disbelief in reality cannot coexist with any assent in the heart.

This principle is unsound according to both revelation and reason. Indeed, leading scholars such as Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū ‘Ubayd, and others declared those who held this view of “faith” to be disbelievers. This is unlike the Murji’ah among the jurists, who say that faith is affirmation by the heart and tongue: none of the leading scholars declared them disbelievers, though they did declare them innovators.

“Faith” and related matters have been discussed at length elsewhere, where it has been explained that some people believe things can exist without what they necessarily entail. They thus posit what has no existence.

---

## Page 5329

And Jahm’s principle concerning “faith” contained errors in several respects:

One was his assumption that it consists solely of the heart’s assent and knowledge, without any deeds of the heart, such as love of Allah, fear of Him, and the like. Another was his assumption that faith can exist in the heart without any words or deeds.

Another was his assumption that anyone whom revelation judges to be a disbeliever condemned to remain eternally in the Fire cannot possibly have any assent in his heart. They categorically asserted that Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, and others like them had none of this in their hearts.

Such is also their discourse concerning will, aversion, love, hatred, and the like. When these things are passing impulses and inner thoughts, they are pardoned. But when they become firm resolve, love, and hatred, action necessarily follows and occurs. No one may then suppose that they exist in isolation and say, “There is no sin in them.”

This makes clear the answer to the questioner’s argument. The Muslim community unanimously agrees that Allah rewards love of Him and His Messenger, and love and hatred for His sake; and that He punishes hatred of Him, His Messenger, and His allies, as well as love of rivals besides Him and the intentions encompassed by this love

---

## Page 5330

and firm resolutions. For whether love is a form of will or something distinct that necessarily entails will, it must be accompanied by intention and resolve. It therefore cannot be said, “This is among the inner thoughts that are pardoned.” Rather, as stated in the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī:

“The firmest bonds of faith are love for Allah’s sake and hatred for Allah’s sake.”

In the two Sahih collections, Anas reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his father, and all people.”

In Sahih al-Bukhārī, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hishām reported:

“We were with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while he was holding ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb’s hand. ‘Umar said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than everything except myself.’

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘No, by Him in whose hand is my soul—not until I am dearer to you than your own self.’

“‘Umar said, ‘Then you are now dearer to me than my own self.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Now, O ‘Umar.’”

Indeed, Allah Most High has said:

“Say, ‘If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your clan, wealth you have acquired, trade whose decline you fear, and homes you delight in are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.’”

Consider this stern warning with which Allah has threatened those whose families and wealth are dearer to them than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause. It is therefore clear that it is obligatory

---

## Page 5331

for Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause to be dearer to the believer than family, wealth, homes, businesses, companions, and brothers. Otherwise, he is not truly a believer. A similar teaching appears in the two Sahih collections, where Anas reports that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No one tastes the sweetness of faith until he loves another person solely for Allah’s sake, until being cast into the Fire is dearer to him than returning to unbelief, and until Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than everything else.”

This is al-Bukhārī’s wording. He thus stated that no one tastes the sweetness of faith except through these three forms of love.

First, Allah and His Messenger must be dearer to him than everything else. This is among the obligatory foundations of faith without which a person cannot be a believer.

Second, he must love another person solely for Allah’s sake. This necessarily follows from the first.

Third, being cast into the Fire must be dearer to him than returning to unbelief. Likewise, for someone who repents of sins, these qualities are among the strongest signs of sincerity in repentance.

Love for Allah and His Messenger, and love for the believers for His sake, although directed toward those loved rather than toward our own actions—as the will is—necessarily entails such willing. For whoever holds Allah and His Messenger dearer than his own self, his family, and his wealth must necessarily

---

## Page 5332

intend to do what this love entails, such as supporting Allah, His Messenger, and His religion, seeking nearness to Allah and His Messenger, and hating those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.

This also includes the widely transmitted reports in the authentic hadith collections, narrated by Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Mūsā, and Anas, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A person will be with those whom he loves.”

In another version:

“A man loves some people but has not yet joined them”—that is, he has not yet performed deeds like theirs. He replied:

“A person will be with those whom he loves.”

Anas said: “After embracing Islam, nothing brought the Muslims as much joy as this hadith. I love the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar, and I hope that Allah will place me with them, even though I have not performed deeds like theirs.”

This hadith is true. Being with the one whom one loves is a matter of innate nature; it cannot be otherwise. The extent to which one is with the beloved corresponds to the extent of one’s love. If that love is moderate, or nearly so, one will be with him accordingly; if it is complete, one will be with him accordingly. Complete love necessarily entails acting in accordance with what the beloved loves, provided the lover is able to do so. Whenever such conformity is lacking despite the ability, love is diminished to that extent, even though it remains present. Loving and desiring something entails hating and disliking its opposite, when one knows that they are opposites.

For this reason, Allah Most High said:

“You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Day

---

## Page 5333

of Judgment showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.”

Affection is an act of the heart. Faith in Allah necessarily entails affection for Him and His Messenger, which is incompatible with affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. Whatever contradicts faith necessarily entails resolve and punishment because of the absence of faith. For whatever contradicts faith—such as doubt, turning away, apostasy of the heart, and hatred of Allah and His Messenger—necessarily entails blame and punishment, since it involves abandoning an obligation that Allah has commanded His Messenger to fulfil. Whoever abandons it therefore deserves blame and punishment. The greatest obligation is faith in the heart; whatever contradicts it necessarily entails blame and punishment for abandoning this obligation.

This differs from what deserves blame because it is prohibited, such as indecency and wrongdoing. It is concerning such things that the discussion of contemplating and intending an act arises, provided that this does not contradict the foundation of faith, even though it contradicts its perfection.

Indeed, performing acts of obedience itself involves refraining from sins, and refraining from sins itself involves performing acts of obedience. This is why prayer restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing. Prayer thus comprises two things:

First, it restrains one from sins. Second, it includes remembrance of Allah, which is the greater of the two. The remembrance of Allah within prayer is greater than its restraining one from indecency and wrongdoing. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

---

## Page 5334

The point here is that perfect love for Allah and His Messenger necessarily entails doing what He loves. Thus, the hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhī states:

“Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

When a person’s love and hatred—which are acts of the heart—and his giving and withholding—which are bodily acts—are all for Allah’s sake, this indicates the perfection of his love for Allah and, consequently, the perfection of his faith. Perfect faith means that all devotion is for Allah: worshipping Allah alone, without any partner. Worship encompasses perfect love and complete humility. Love is the source of all voluntary actions, and every living being necessarily has love and hatred. Thus, when someone loves those whom Allah loves and hates those whom Allah hates, this indicates the soundness of faith in his heart. Yet this may grow stronger or be weakened by the soul’s opposing appetites and desires. This becomes evident when giving away wealth, which provides the means of sustaining oneself. When his love, giving, and withholding are all for Allah’s sake, this indicates the perfection of faith both inwardly and outwardly.

The root of polytheism among the polytheists—those who divided their religion and became sects—is their taking rivals whom they love as they love Allah. As the Most High says:

“Among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah.”

As for someone whose love and hatred are for Allah’s sake—who loves only for Allah’s sake, hates only for Allah’s sake, gives only for Allah’s sake, and withholds only for Allah’s sake—this is the state of the foremost among Allah’s close servants, as al-Bukhārī narrated

---

## Page 5335

in his Sahīh, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards a close servant of Mine, I have declared war against him. Nothing by which My servant draws near to Me compares to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues drawing near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I hesitate over nothing I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet he must inevitably undergo it.’”

These people loved Allah with perfect love and drew near to Him through the voluntary acts He loves, after drawing near to Him through the obligatory acts He loves. Allah loved them with perfect love until they attained their station. Each of them came to perceive through Allah and move through Allah, such that Allah answers his requests and protects him from whatever he seeks refuge against.

In His Book, Allah has condemned those who love rivals besides Him. The Most High says:

“Their hearts were imbued with love of the calf because of their disbelief.”

He has also condemned whoever takes his own desire as his god—that is, worships whatever he desires and loves. This may be an act of the heart alone.

In numerous places in His Book, the Most High has praised and condemned people on account of love, desire, hatred, displeasure, joy, grief, and other such acts of the heart. For example, He says:

“But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

And He says:

“No! Rather, you love the fleeting life
and neglect the Hereafter.”

There are many such examples in Allah’s Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the believers are agreed that praise and blame attach to such strivings and deeds of the heart as Allah wills. For example, he says in the authentic hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Do not hate one another or envy one another.”

And he says:

“None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother the good that he loves for himself.”

And:

There are many similar examples.

Indeed, the heart’s speech and action are the foundation, such as its affirmation and denial, its love and hatred. Some of these entail praise or blame, reward or punishment, without any action by the outward limbs; others entail these only when accompanied by action of the outward limbs

---

## Page 5339

when one is able to perform them. As for outward actions left undone because of inability, the person concerned is judged like one who performs them. The heart’s speech and actions thus fall into three categories:

First, that which is itself a good deed or a sin.

Second, that which is not sinful in itself until acted upon—namely, a sin one is able to commit, as explained above.

Third, that which, in the case of inability, is equivalent to a good deed or sin actually committed, but is not equivalent to it when one has the ability, as explained above.

The first category concerns the foundations of faith: affirmation and denial, love and hatred, and what follows from these. Reward and punishment, elevated ranks and the lowest depths, result from the presence of these matters in people’s hearts, even when they find no outward expression.

Indeed, the hypocrites outwardly utter righteous words and perform righteous deeds, yet their punishment and their being in the lowest depth of the Fire are due to the diseases in their hearts. Although this may sometimes be accompanied by hatred of speech and action, their punishment is not confined to that slight hatred; rather, that hatred is an indication, as the Most High says:

“And if

---

## Page 5340

We willed, We would show them to you, and you would recognize them by their marks; but you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech.” He thus states that they will inevitably be recognized by the tone of their speech.

As for the “second category” and the “third,” these concern actions that do not contradict the foundations of faith, such as sins arising from natural desires: unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, and drinking wine. As established in the authentic hadith collections, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever dies testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah will enter Paradise, even if he committed unlawful sexual intercourse, stole, or drank wine.”

Likewise, in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, testified in favor of a man who frequently drank wine and whom he would flog whenever he was brought before him. When a man cursed him, he said:

“Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.”

In another narration:

“One of them said, ‘May Allah disgrace him! How often he is brought in for drinking wine!’ The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘Do not help Satan against your brother.’”

This is reported in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, in a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah.

For this reason, he said:

“Allah has pardoned my community for the thoughts that pass through their minds, so long as they neither speak of them nor act upon them.”

This pardon for inward thoughts was granted only to Muhammad’s community who believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day. It is therefore clear that this pardon concerns matters that do not undermine faith. Whatever contradicts faith, however, is not covered by the wording of the hadith, because if it contradicts faith, the person harboring it is not among

---

## Page 5341

Muhammad’s community in reality; rather, he is in the same position as the hypocrites. It does not therefore follow that he is pardoned for the words or deeds he contemplates inwardly. This is a clear distinction indicated by the hadith, and through it the scriptural evidence is reconciled.

This is like Allah’s pardoning this community for mistakes and forgetfulness, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah. Those whose faith is sound are pardoned for mistakes, forgetfulness, and thoughts that pass through their minds, just as they will be brought out of the Fire. This is unlike someone who has no faith: the texts do not indicate that he will not be held accountable for what is within himself, his mistakes, or his forgetfulness. [Hence the report:

“A believer’s intention is better than his deed.”

Abū al-Shaykh al-Asbahānī narrated this report in Kitāb al-Amthāl (The Book of Proverbs) among the disconnected reports of Thābit al-Bunānī. Ibn al-Qayyim also mentioned it in his discussion of intention, through several chains traced back to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, then judged those chains weak. Allah knows best. For a believer is rewarded for his intention alone] (*) and it counts as a deed when nothing but inability prevents him from acting upon it. This is possible for him with regard to good deeds in general, whereas bodily action is restricted by his ability and can be undertaken only to a limited extent.

For this reason, some of the early Muslims said:

“The believer’s strength is in his heart and his weakness in his body, while the hypocrite’s strength is in his body and his weakness in his heart.”

This principle is also indicated by the words of the Most High: “Whether you reveal what is within yourselves

> It seems to me that the discussion of this hadith is not by the shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him. Rather, I suspect that it was originally a marginal note that some copyists interpolated into the text. Several points support this:
> 
> First, the passage following the documentation of the hadith’s sources is closely connected to the hadith itself. The wording appears to be as follows: “Hence it is reported: ‘A believer’s intention is better than his deed,’ for a believer is rewarded for his intention alone…” The material between these two statements is an interpolation.
> 
> Another point is that, upon examining the discussion of the hadith, you will find it self-contained: it begins with “This report…” and ends with “Allah knows best.” This strengthens the possibility that it was a marginal note in the manuscript that someone incorporated into the main text.
> 
> Another is its mention of Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, by name.
> 
> This is what seems apparent to me, and Allah knows best.

## Page 5342

or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills”—to the end of the verse.

Although some of the early Muslims said that this verse was abrogated—as al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Marwān al-Asfar, from one of the Prophet’s Companions, namely Ibn ‘Umar—the term “abrogation” had a broader meaning in the usage of the early Muslims than it does among later scholars. They used it for any setting aside of a text’s implications, including restricting a general statement, qualifying an unrestricted one, and other such cases, as is well known from their usage. Others denied that the verse was abrogated, for lack of evidence. Some maintained that it was a statement of fact, and that statements of fact cannot be abrogated. Others replied that it was a statement concerning a religious ruling, like a statement conveying a command or prohibition.

Those who hold that it was abrogated identify the abrogating text as the subsequent verse, namely His words:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

This is as Muslim narrated in his Sahīh in a hadith from Anas concerning this verse. What they were exempted from would thus be what the hadiths explain: things within their power which they contemplate or discuss inwardly, so long as they neither speak of them nor act upon them. They were also exempted from liability for mistakes, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do. As Ibn Mājah and others narrated with a sound chain of transmission:

“Allah has pardoned my community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do.”

The truth of the matter is that His words, glorified be He:

“Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it”

do not indicate that they will be punished for it; rather, they indicate that they will be called to account for it, and it does not

---

## Page 5343

follow that being called to account means being punished. Hence He said:

“Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.”

This does not imply that He forgives and punishes without cause or order, nor that He forgives everything or punishes for everything, given what is known—that He does not punish the believers, that He does not forgive the association of partners with Him except upon repentance, and other such matters.

The fundamental principle is to distinguish between what is compatible with the foundation of faith and what contradicts it, and also between an act that a person was capable of doing but did not do, and one left undone only because of inability. These two distinctions are decisive in resolving these confusing issues.

This detailed explanation makes clear that the dispute over this “question” arose only because they envisaged a firm resolve never accompanied by any action. This can occur only when the action accompanies the resolve. If inability accompanies the will, the intended outcome cannot occur; yet such a will is not resolute, for a resolute will to do what one is incapable of doing is itself impossible. Thus, a resolute will is accompanied by whatever preliminary steps and attendant actions the person is capable of, even if the act itself does not occur.

A person finds within himself that, when he is capable of an action, his pursuit of it, his hope of attaining it, and his will to do it grow stronger; when he is incapable of it, that hope weakens. Yet he is not equally incapable of what he says and what he does, nor of what appears on his face

---

## Page 5344

or slips from his tongue—such as a cheerful expression or a frown, turning toward something or turning away from it. These and similar bodily actions entail blame and punishment, just as they entail praise and reward.

Some people conceive of a firm resolve that is never accompanied by any action. This can occur only because of an incapacity that arises afterward, through death or otherwise. They therefore call the determination to act in the future a firm resolve; there is no dispute over the use of words. Some people distinguish between resolve and intention, saying: “What accompanies the act is intention, while what precedes it is resolve.” Others regard them as the same. They have also disputed whether Allah’s will concerning what He will do in the future may be called resolve. This is a verbal dispute.

However, when a person performs something he previously resolved to do in the future, there must be a renewed will distinct from his earlier resolve. This is the will that necessarily entails the occurrence of the act when the ability is present. They have also disputed whether an act must occur when both the ability and the motive are present, expressing two views on this as well. The more evident view is that ability, together with a complete motive, necessarily entails the occurrence of the act within one’s power, and that will, together with ability, necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed.

Of those disputing this issue, one sought to affirm punishment without qualification for every resolve to perform a future act, even if no action accompanied it, while the other sought to rule out punishment

---

## Page 5345

without qualification for any firm intentions or the like within the soul, both disputants assuming that the particular intention in question had not manifested itself in word or deed. Both positions depart from the middle course. Once it is understood that, given the ability, firm will cannot fail to produce action except because of an incapacity, the person possessing such a will is treated, in terms of reward and punishment, as one who has fully performed the act. If, however, an act within his power does not follow from that will, then the act left undone was not firmly willed. Rather, it was merely a passing intention of the kind that has been pardoned. In this way, the scriptural texts and foundational principles are reconciled.

There are, moreover, “many questions” concerning conflicting intentions that coexist in the heart, just as conflicting beliefs may coexist: willing something and its opposite, for example, when the soul desires a sin while the heart hates it. Another example is inward thoughts containing disbelief when accompanied by some such aversion and by seeking refuge from them. Thus, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, complained to him, saying:

“One of us finds within himself thoughts that he would rather be burned to a cinder, or fall from heaven to earth, than utter.”

He asked, “Have you indeed experienced this?” They replied, “Yes.” He said, “That is pure faith.”

Muslim narrated this from Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Hurayrah. It also contains the words:

“Praise be to Allah, who has reduced his scheming to mere whisperings.”

When I wrote this response, I did not have at hand any books that could be of assistance

---

## Page 5346

in preparing this response, for there is a wealth of material relevant to it. Here, when the whisperings were accompanied by this hatred and aversion, that was pure faith—faith unmixed and unalloyed. Neither the hypocrite nor the disbeliever experiences such hatred and aversion alongside these whisperings. Rather, if a person is in a state of simple disbelief—turning away from what the Messenger brought and failing to believe in it, even without believing that he spoke falsely—Satan may not trouble him with such whisperings. Whispering suggestions that oppose and contradict faith is needed only when something conducive to faith is present. If there is nothing within him conducive to faith, there is no need for an opposing force to repel it. If, however, he is in a state of compound disbelief, namely, denial, then his disbelief goes beyond mere whisperings, and he has no faith through which to abhor them.

Such whisperings, then, are something that believers generally experience. As Allah Most High says:

“He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity, and the torrent carries swelling foam. And from what they heat in the fire, seeking ornaments or utensils, there is similar foam.”

And the verses that follow.

Allah thus likened the faith and Quran He sends down to water descending into the valleys of the earth, and likened hearts to valleys: some large and some small. As related in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me are like rain falling upon a land. One part absorbed the water and brought forth abundant grass and vegetation. Another part retained the water, and people used it for watering and drinking. And another part consisted only of

---

## Page 5347

flat expanses that retain no water and therefore grow no grass. Such is the likeness of one who gains understanding of Allah’s religion and whom Allah benefits through the guidance and knowledge with which He has sent me, and of one who pays no heed to it and does not accept Allah’s guidance with which I have been sent.”

This is one of the two parables. The “other parable” concerns metals—gold, silver, iron and the like—which are heated to make ornaments and utensils. Allah tells us that the torrent carries swelling foam, and that what people heat in the fire produces similar foam. Then He says:

“Thus Allah illustrates truth and falsehood. As for the foam”—

that which rises upon the water and the metal being heated—it corresponds to the doubts and misgivings concerning matters of belief, and the corrupt desires, that arise in believers’ hearts, as the Companions complained to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah Most High says:

“It is cast away.”

The heart rejects it and casts it out, just as water casts off and rejects foam.

“But that which benefits people remains in the earth.”

This is like the certainty and faith that remain firmly established in people’s hearts. As Allah Most High says:

“A parable: a good word is like a good tree,”

and the rest of the passage, up to His words:

“Allah keeps those who believe firm with the firm word, in worldly life and in the Hereafter. And Allah lets the wrongdoers go astray, and Allah does what He wills.”

Whenever thoughts of disbelief or hypocrisy arise in a believer’s heart and he hates them and casts them away, he grows in faith and certainty. Likewise, whenever someone feels prompted to commit a sin, but hates it, banishes it from himself and abandons it for Allah’s sake, he grows in righteousness, goodness and piety.

---

## Page 5348

As for the hypocrite, if desires and opinions associated with hypocrisy arise in him and he neither hates nor rejects them, then the evil of disbelief has arisen in him without any good arising from faith to counteract or dispel it. Both faith and hypocrisy may arise in hearts: sometimes one predominates, and sometimes the other.

The words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Allah has pardoned my community for the whisperings or thoughts that arise within them,”

as found in some wordings in the Sahīh, are restricted to pardoning believers, not those who are outwardly Muslim but inwardly hypocrites. Such people have been numerous among those professing Islam, both in earlier times and more recently. In these later times, in some places, they are more numerous than they were when faith first prevailed. Whoever professes faith sincerely, avoiding whatever contradicts or weakens it, is pardoned for thoughts that he could express in speech or put into action, but not for what is otherwise, as the wording of the hadith indicates.

Thus, the two categories in which we have explained that a person is rewarded or punished for actions of the heart fall outside the scope of this hadith. Likewise, his words,

“Whoever intends a good deed,”

and

“Whoever intends an evil deed,”

refer only to a believer who intends an evil or good deed that he is capable of doing, and who may either do it or leave it undone. For he stated that a good deed is multiplied seven hundredfold, and many times beyond that.

---

## Page 5349

And this applies only to those who do good deeds for Allah’s sake. As the Most High says:

“The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah,”

and

“seeking Allah’s pleasure,”

and

“seeking the Face of his Lord.”

This applies to believers. Although Allah rewards a disbeliever for his good deeds with provision in this world and may lessen his punishment in the Hereafter—as He lessened Abū Tālib’s punishment because of his kindness to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and through the Prophet’s intercession—no disbeliever has been promised this multiplication of reward for his good deeds. Another hadith explicitly qualifies this as applying to a Muslim whose Islam is sound.

And Allah, glorified is He, knows best. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.
